There is one more thing to know about Anathoth. Three centuries later a boy is born in that village to a priestly family, and his book opens: the words of Jeremiah, the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin (Jer. 1:1). The line that was put out of the priesthood here produced the prophet of the exile.

Verse 28 explains Joab's flight: Joab had supported Adonijah although he had not supported Absalom. Forty years of unbroken loyalty to David through a civil war, a rebellion, and every crisis of the reign, and at the very end, with nothing left to gain, he picked the losing son.

His answer in verse 30 is five words, and they are entirely in character. He is not pleading and he is not repenting. He has worked out that he is a dead man either way, and he has decided where.

Whether he thought the altar would protect him is doubtful; he knew the law as well as anybody. More likely he is doing the last calculation of a long career: make them kill me at the sanctuary, in front of the priests, so that the blood is on the new king's reign.

Benaiah, to his credit, will not simply do it. He goes back and asks, and Solomon's answer (v. 31) stands on the law, and the law is explicit about this exact case.

The altar was sanctuary for a man who killed without intending it, but Exodus says: but if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die (Ex. 21:14).

By cunning. Joab took Abner aside at the gate as though to speak privately with him. Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him. Both times the weapon was in the other hand.

The altar does not cover that, and the law says so in as many words, and the writer expects his reader to know it, because Adonijah held these same horns one chapter ago and was sent home alive.

In verse 32 Solomon names Abner and Amasa, and says two things that repay attention. The first is without the knowledge of my father David. Solomon is careful about this, because a king is responsible for what his officers do in his name. He is establishing that these were not royal acts.

The second is more righteous and better than himself. Abner ran a rebellion against David for years and killed Asahel; Amasa commanded the army that lost twenty thousand men in the forest of Ephraim. Neither was a saint, and both are called better than Joab, and the comparison is not about their careers. It is that they were killed by cunning, in peacetime, by a man they trusted enough to stand still for.

In verse 35 both posts change hands, Benaiah over the army and Zadok as priest, and both were held by men who went to Adonijah's feast.
verseByVerse.note: Anathoth lay about three miles north-east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–46 — You Shall Know for Certain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon confines Shimei to Jerusalem: build a house and live there, and do not go out from there to any place whatever. For on the day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall die (vv. 36-37). Shimei agrees and swears to it (vv. 38, 42-43). Three years later two of his slaves run to Gath and he saddles a donkey and goes after them and brings them back (vv. 39-40). Solomon summons him: did I not make you swear by the LORD and solemnly warn you...? Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the commandment with which I commanded you? (vv. 42-43). Benaiah strikes him down. So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon (v. 46).
verseByVerse.theology: The terms are exact and public and generous: a house in the capital and a boundary he chose to swear to. He kept it for three years and then crossed it for two runaway slaves.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends on the sentence it began with: verse 12 said the kingdom was firmly established in his hand, and verse 46 says it again, after three deaths and a banishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Build yourself a house in Jerusalem and dwell there, and do not go out from there to any place whatever. For on the day you go out and cross the brook Kidron, know for certain that you shall die. Your blood shall be on your own head." And Shimei said to the king, "What you say is good; as my lord the king has said, so will your servant do." So Shimei lived in Jerusalem many days. But it happened at the end of three years that two of Shimei's servants ran away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. And when it was told Shimei, "Behold, your servants are in Gath," Shimei arose and saddled a donkey and went to Gath to Achish to seek his servants. Shimei went and brought his servants from Gath. And when Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and returned, the king sent and summoned Shimei and said to him, "Did I not make you swear by the LORD and solemnly warn you, saying, 'Know for certain that on the day you go out and go to any place whatever, you shall die'? And you said to me, 'What you say is good; I will obey.' Why then have you not kept your oath to the LORD and the commandment with which I commanded you?" The king also said to Shimei, "You know in your own heart all the harm that you did to David my father. So the LORD will bring back your harm on your own head. But King Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established before the LORD forever." Then the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, and he went out and struck him down, and he died. So the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The terms of verse 36 are generous, and it should be said so. David's instruction was to bring the man's grey head down with blood. Solomon does not do that. He lets him build a house in the capital, and gives him one restriction: do not leave the city.

That is house arrest in a comfortable form, and for a man who publicly cursed the LORD's anointed and threw stones at him it is a good deal less than he could have expected.

Know for certain and your blood shall be on your own head (v. 37) leave no ambiguity anywhere, and no discretion to anybody. The line is a named brook on the east side of the city, and it is the one David crossed barefoot and weeping on the day Shimei came out to curse him.

Note also that this is the second time in two chapters that Solomon has done this. Adonijah was given terms on the first day. Shimei is given terms here. Both are told exactly what will end their lives, in public, before anything happens.

His father, faced with a dangerous man, said nothing at all for two years and let a rebellion grow.

Shimei accepts (v. 38), and verse 42 will tell us he did more than accept: Solomon made him swear by the LORD, so there is now an oath of Shimei's own on the arrangement.

Three years later two slaves run (v. 39). (Servitude in Israel was often a form of debt service, hedged by protections the surrounding nations lacked, as in Exodus 21:2, 26-27 and Deuteronomy 15:12-15; it was still servitude, and the gospel would later work against it from within, Philemon 16.)

He goes and gets them (v. 40). Look at how small the thing is. Not a conspiracy, not a message to Benjamin, not a plot with the house of Saul, but two runaway slaves and a piece of property he wanted back. He saddles a donkey and rides out of the city and fetches them and rides home, and it probably took a few days.

He kept a sworn boundary for three years and crossed it for a debt he could have written off.

It is the ordinary shape of ruin. Nobody talks themselves into the large disobedience. They keep the line for years and then step over it for something that seemed too minor to count, and the boundary was never about the size of what was on the other side.

Note Gath as well. It is Philistine territory, the town Goliath came from and David hid in twice, and Achish is the name of the king David dealt with there. Shimei has gone out of Israel altogether.

The charge in verses 42-43 is not the cursing. It is the oath. Solomon quotes the terms, quotes the warning, and quotes Shimei's own answer back at him. Every element of the case is something Shimei said or agreed to himself three years ago.

Your oath to the LORD. That is the head of the charge, and it puts this chapter in line with everything the two books of Samuel have been arguing about promises with God's name on them. Saul broke one to the Gibeonites and there was a famine. David kept one to a dead friend and fed a crippled man at his own table. Shimei swore one and rode to Gath for two slaves.

Then the old matter is added (vv. 44-45), and it is not the ground of the sentence but it is not pretended away either.

Four men are dealt with in forty-six verses. Two of them, Joab and Shimei, were on a list David gave from his deathbed, and one of those was under an oath David himself had sworn. That much is genuinely troubling and the previous chapter said so.

And what Solomon actually does is not simply to execute the list.

Abiathar is on nobody's list and is spared, with reasons given. Adonijah dies for breaking terms he was given in public. Joab dies under a written law that covers his case exactly, and Solomon names the two men and the manner. Shimei dies for breaking an oath he swore himself, three years later, over two slaves, not for the cursing, which is mentioned second and is not the charge.

None of that makes the chapter comfortable. Three men are dead and a fourth banished at the start of a reign, and the writer does not soften it. What it does mean is that the new king is not merely settling his father's scores; he is doing something his father could not do, which is to state a rule, apply it, and be seen to apply it the same way twice.

The chapter ends in verse 46 where verse 12 began. The same clause stands at both ends, and everything in between is what the space was filled with. A throne, a charge, a deathbed list, a request for a young woman, an old priest sent to a village, a soldier holding the horns of an altar and refusing to come out, and a man who rode to Gath for two slaves.

That is what establishing a kingdom looked like, and the writer states it twice without a word of approval or regret, and turns the page to Gibeon.

2.theology:
What he tells him to do (v. 3). Not statecraft, not alliances, not the army, but to walk as it is written in the Law of Moses: written, available, and the same for a king as for anybody, which is what Deuteronomy 17:18-19 had required of Israel's kings in the first place. And the charge rests on what God has already done: it is the charge of the LORD your God, and the next verse quotes a promise already sworn. Solomon is not told to earn a throne he has been given, but to live as the son of a covenant God has made.

Which half of the covenant he quotes (v. 4). The promise had two sides: a throne established forever, and discipline with the rod of men for iniquity. David gives Solomon the conduct half, which is what a father says to a son about to inherit. The covenant holds whatever the house does, and a great deal depends on what the house does. Chapter 11 records how Solomon handled it. No son of David kept this charge whole but one, who obeyed in the place of those who do not; for a believer, failure here is met by his obedience counted as ours and by the way back God promised (1 John 1:9), and what the written law could not produce in a king, the Spirit now works in God's people (Romans 8:4).

The seam that is not there (vv. 5-9). One breath: walk in the ways of the LORD as it is written. Next breath: you know what Joab did. The verse notes set out both charges. Joab's guilt is real, and the discomfort is that David never acted on it himself. The Shimei instruction keeps the letter of David's oath while arranging for someone who did not swear it to break its substance. The book records the mercy at the Jordan and this, and reconciles neither. Both are David.

A word from Shiloh, completed (v. 27). Abiathar's banishment ends the line of Eli, as a man of God had foretold at Shiloh (1 Sam. 2:31-35), and Zadok stands in his place. The faithful priest promised there is answered first in Zadok's line, yet no priest of that line served for ever; Christians have long seen the promise's final answer in Jesus, whom Hebrews calls a merciful and faithful high priest whose priesthood never passes to another (Hebrews 2:17; 7:23-25).

The honest reckoning. Three men are dead and a fourth banished at the start of a reign, and the chapter does not soften it. Yet Solomon does not simply execute his father's list: each man is dealt with on stated grounds, and the new king has stated a rule, applied it, and been seen to apply it the same way twice, which his father, faced with a dangerous son, could not do.

The same clause at both ends (vv. 12, 46). The kingdom is said to be established at the start and again at the end, and everything between is what filled the space. Set beside the Son of David who is greater than Solomon, the contrast is plain. Solomon's kingdom was secured by removing his enemies; Christ's is secured by dying for his, who are reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). And Christ too states his terms in advance and in public: God now commands all people everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day of judgment by the man he has appointed (Acts 17:30-31).
2.examples:
Then: A man was given a house in the capital and one condition — do not cross the brook — and he swore to it in the name of the LORD and kept it for three years. Then two of his slaves ran off to a Philistine town, and he saddled a donkey and went and fetched them back, and it cost him his life.

Now: Three things. Shimei is the study in how boundaries actually get broken: not by defiance, and not over anything large. He held the line for three years and stepped over it for a piece of property, because the thing on the other side looked too small to count — and the line had never been about the size of it. The help is not more grit but staying near the God who drew the line in kindness, whose Spirit is given to keep us, and who, unlike Solomon's court, receives back those who confess they have crossed it (Psalm 32:5). Second, David's speech, which should be read whole rather than in the half that flatters him: the finest charge in the book about walking in God's written word, an accurate account of a murderer he had never been willing to touch, an oath he named while arranging for someone else to break it, and in the middle of all of it a years-old debt of kindness he had not forgotten. And third, Solomon's method, which is the contrast the chapter is built on: terms stated out loud, in advance, in public, and then applied. His father managed dangerous men by leaving everything unsaid, and it cost him a kingdom and a son.

3.title: Wisdom at Gibeon and the Two Mothers
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>The people were sacrificing at the high places, however, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places.<sup>4</sup>And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon used to offer a thousand burnt offerings on that altar.<sup>5</sup>At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, "Ask what I shall give you."<sup>6</sup>And Solomon said, "You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward you. And you have kept for him this great and steadfast love and have given him a son to sit on his throne this day.<sup>7</sup>And now, O LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father, although I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in.<sup>8</sup>And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted for multitude.<sup>9</sup>Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?"<sup>10</sup>It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this.<sup>11</sup>And God said to him, "Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern what is right,<sup>12</sup>behold, I now do according to your word. Behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you.<sup>13</sup>I give you also what you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that no other king shall compare with you, all your days.<sup>14</sup>And if you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days."<sup>15</sup>And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.<sup>16</sup>Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.<sup>17</sup>The one woman said, "Oh, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was in the house.<sup>18</sup>Then on the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. And we were alone. There was no one else with us in the house; only we two were in the house.<sup>19</sup>And this woman's son died in the night, because she lay on him.<sup>20</sup>And she arose at midnight and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast.<sup>21</sup>When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, behold, he was not the child that I had borne."<sup>22</sup>But the other woman said, "No, the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours." The first said, "No, the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine." Thus they spoke before the king.<sup>23</sup>Then the king said, "The one says, 'This is my son that is alive, and your son is dead'; and the other says, 'No; but your son is dead, and my son is the living one.'"<sup>24</sup>And the king said, "Bring me a sword." So a sword was brought before the king.<sup>25</sup>And the king said, "Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other."<sup>26</sup>Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death." But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him."<sup>27</sup>Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother."<sup>28</sup>And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.
3.overview:
The chapter opens with three verses that anybody reading quickly would take as favourable, and each has something in it the rest of the history comes back for: a marriage alliance with Egypt, a plausible excuse for scattered worship, and the finest compliment in the book, Solomon loved the LORD, followed at once by the writer's needle, only.

At Gibeon God asks him what he wants, with no terms and no hint of a right answer. He asks for an understanding mind, a heart that listens and discerns before it rules, so that he can govern people who are not his but God's. God names the three things he did not ask for, gives him wisdom and riches and honour outright, and attaches an if to long life.

Then, straight after a thousand burnt offerings and an appearance of God, two prostitutes are standing in a room: the least important case in the kingdom and the hardest to decide, and it goes to the king in person. He cannot detect the liar, so he makes a situation in which love has to reveal itself. The nations came to hear that wisdom (4:34), and Jesus pointed to it and said that something greater than Solomon was standing in front of them (Matthew 12:42).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Only at the High Places
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem (v. 1). The people were sacrificing at the high places, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD (v. 2). Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The first fact recorded about the reign after the executions is a foreign marriage, and to Egypt of all places. The writer states it and adds nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 has the needle in it: Solomon loved the LORD, only he sacrificed at the high places. The high places are the thing that will still be standing at the end of both books.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon made a marriage alliance with Pharaoh king of Egypt. He took Pharaoh's daughter and brought her into the city of David until he had finished building his own house and the house of the LORD and the wall around Jerusalem. The people were sacrificing at the high places, however, because no house had yet been built for the name of the LORD. Solomon loved the LORD, walking in the statutes of David his father, only he sacrificed and made offerings at the high places.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first thing recorded about the reign, once the executions are over, is a wedding to Egypt. Politically it is a triumph and everybody at the time would have read it that way. Egypt had long refused to give its daughters to foreign kings; the Amarna letters (Egyptian royal correspondence of the fourteenth century BC) have a pharaoh saying flatly that a daughter of Egypt is given to nobody. That Solomon got one is a measure of how large Israel had suddenly become.

Two things stand against it. The first is the law about Israel's kings, which this history keeps quietly measuring people by. Only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses... And he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:16-17). Egypt and wives, in consecutive clauses, and this verse has both.

And there is the older command about marrying into the nations of the land: you shall not intermarry with them... for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut. 7:3-4). The reason given in the law is never about race. It is about what happens to worship in a household.

The second is what chapter 11 says happened. Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh... For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods (11:1-4).

The daughter of Pharaoh is named first in that list, and she arrives here, in verse 1, before the temple is built and before Gibeon. This writer does not editorialise. He plants and waits, and this is a plant.

The high places of verse 2 are open-air sanctuaries on hilltops, and they are going to be the running problem of both books. The writer gives the excuse himself, which is unusually generous of him: because no house had yet been built. There is no temple yet. The tabernacle is at Gibeon and the ark is in a tent in Jerusalem, and worship is scattered.

Solomon loved the LORD (v. 3) is a remarkable thing to say, and the writer of Kings says it of nobody else. Not of Asa, not of Jehoshaphat, not of Hezekiah or Josiah, who get his highest marks. Solomon alone is said to have loved God.

Then comes only. That little word is this writer's needle and he uses it for the rest of both books. King after king will be told he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, only the high places were not taken away, only the people still sacrificed there. It is the standing qualification on almost every good reign in the history.

Here it appears for the first time, and it is attached to Solomon on the page before he asks for wisdom.

So the chapter opens with three verses that anybody reading quickly would take as a favourable introduction: a magnificent alliance, a plausible explanation for irregular worship, and the finest compliment in the book. And each of the three has something in it that the rest of the history will come back for.

Why is Gibeon a fault when the tabernacle was there (2 Chr 1:3)? The fault is the many high places (v. 2), not Gibeon itself; Gibeon was the great high place, where the tabernacle and altar stood until the temple was built.
verseByVerse.note: “High places” were local hilltop shrines; they were later condemned because the law required sacrifice at the one place the LORD chose (Deut 12), and because they easily drew in pagan worship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Gibeon Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings, and God appears to him in a dream by night: ask what I shall give you (vv. 4-5). He answers with what God did for David, and then: I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in... Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people? (vv. 7-9). It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this (v. 10), and God names what he did not ask for — long life, riches, the life of his enemies — and gives him a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you, and riches and honour as well (vv. 11-13). And one condition: and if you will walk in my ways... then I will lengthen your days (v. 14). He wakes, and it was a dream (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: What he asks for in verse 9 is an understanding mind, to discern between good and evil — a mind that listens, which is what a judge needs before anything else, and what his father stopped having.
verseByVerse.examples: And the gifts are not given on the same terms. Wisdom and riches are given outright; length of days has an if attached to it. Chapter 11 is where that matters.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, for that was the great high place. Solomon used to offer a thousand burnt offerings on that altar. At Gibeon the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream by night, and God said, "Ask what I shall give you." And Solomon said, "You have shown great and steadfast love to your servant David my father, because he walked before you in faithfulness, in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart toward you. And you have kept for him this great and steadfast love and have given him a son to sit on his throne this day. And now, O LORD my God, you have made your servant king in place of David my father, although I am but a little child. I do not know how to go out or come in. And your servant is in the midst of your people whom you have chosen, a great people, too many to be numbered or counted for multitude. Give your servant therefore an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil, for who is able to govern this your great people?" It pleased the Lord that Solomon had asked this. And God said to him, "Because you have asked this, and have not asked for yourself long life or riches or the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern what is right, behold, I now do according to your word. Behold, I give you a wise and discerning mind, so that none like you has been before you and none like you shall arise after you. I give you also what you have not asked, both riches and honor, so that no other king shall compare with you, all your days. And if you will walk in my ways, keeping my statutes and my commandments, as your father David walked, then I will lengthen your days." And Solomon awoke, and behold, it was a dream. Then he came to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings and peace offerings, and made a feast for all his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gibeon (v. 4) is where the tabernacle was: the tent Moses made, with the bronze altar, still standing there (2 Chron. 1:3-5). So this is not one of the irregular hilltop shrines; it is the national sanctuary, at the town whose people tricked Joshua into a treaty and were spared for the sake of an oath.

A thousand burnt offerings is an enormous act. A burnt offering is the sacrifice that is entirely consumed, with nothing kept back for the worshipper to eat.

In verse 5 God asks him what he wants: ask what I shall give you. It is a startling question, put to one person, open, with no terms attached and no hint of what would be a good answer. Any reader knows immediately that this is a test, and the reason is plain. Nothing reveals a person like what they ask for when they can have anything. The request is a photograph of the heart taken from the inside.

Solomon does not begin with a request (v. 6). He begins with what God has already done, and the word he uses twice is hesed, the covenant love that keeps its promises after the reasons for keeping them are gone.

His picture of his father as walking in faithfulness and uprightness may be hard to take for a reader who has just finished 2 Samuel, and it needs saying plainly that it is a son's account and not a full one. It is also not false. David never served another god, and repented when he was confronted, and the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 was grounded in God's character rather than his. Solomon is describing the shape of a life, not auditing it.

I am but a little child (v. 7): he is not literally a child; he is a grown man who has just had three men executed and married a princess of Egypt. Josephus's figures would make him fourteen, and many estimates put him around twenty. Whatever the figure, the phrase is a confession of competence, not of age.

I do not know how to go out or come in is a soldier's idiom for leading an army out and bringing it home, and it is what the elders said about David when they made him king: it was you who led out and brought in Israel (2 Sam. 5:2). Solomon is saying: I cannot do what my father did.

Note whose people they are in verse 8: your people whom you have chosen. He is new on the throne and he already knows that the nation is not his.

And there is a small barb in too many to be numbered, since the last thing his father did before the plague was count them.

Take the words of verse 9 exactly. What he asks for is an understanding mind, in Hebrew lev shomea, a hearing heart, and he says what it is for: that I may discern between good and evil.

Not a large memory or a quick answer or the ability to out-argue people, but a heart that listens. In Hebrew the heart is not the seat of the feelings as it is in English; it is where a person thinks and decides. So this is a deciding faculty that listens before it rules, and it is precisely what a judge needs and precisely what his father had stopped having. Two men came to David with stories in 2 Samuel: he heard one side from Ziba and handed over an estate in a sentence, and then heard the other side and split the land rather than admit he had judged carelessly.

And note the purpose he attaches to it: to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil. The request is not for his own benefit. It is a tool for a job, and the job is other people.

The last clause is the honest one. Who is able to govern this your great people? That is not modesty; it is a real question with an implied answer, which is nobody. He has looked at what is in front of him and concluded that it cannot be done, and asked for the one thing that would let him try.

In verse 11 God names what Solomon did not ask for, which is the most revealing verse in the chapter. There are three things, and they are the three things every king in the ancient world wanted: long life, to enjoy what he had; riches, the measure of a reign then as now; and the life of your enemies, to have the men who threaten you dead. Solomon had reason to want the third. He had spent his first years dealing with a brother, a general, a priest and a Benjaminite, and there were more where they came from.

He asked for none of the three. Here is what makes this passage useful rather than merely admirable. God did not tell him the right answer beforehand. There was no hint, no list of approved requests, no indication that asking for wealth would disappoint. The question was genuinely open, and what came out of him was an understanding mind to do a job for somebody else's people.

That is why it pleased God: not the eloquence of it, but the fact that when a man could have had anything at all, this is what was in him.

He gets exactly what he asked for, and more of it than anyone before or since (v. 12). Then one of the three things he did not ask for is given anyway, with honour besides (v. 13).

There is a principle here that the Lord Jesus states directly, a few sentences after naming Solomon in all his glory (Matt. 6:29): seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you (Matt. 6:33). The order is the whole of it. Solomon did not get riches because he declined to want them as a technique; he got them because the man who asks for an understanding mind is the man it is safe to give them to.

Whether it stayed safe is chapter 10's question.

Now read the difference between verse 14 and the two before it, because it is deliberate and it is the hinge of Solomon's whole life.

Wisdom: behold, I give you. Riches and honour: I give you also. Given, with no condition, no requirement, no test.

The one thing he did not receive outright is the one thing hedged with an if, and the condition is conduct, and the standard named is his father.

Keep it, because the writer will come back for it. In chapter 11 God says to Solomon: since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you (11:11). The gifts were never withdrawn, for he died the wisest and richest man in the world; it was the conditional side that came due.

He wakes up, and the writer says plainly what it was (v. 15): behold, it was a dream. That is not scepticism; the writer has just told us God appeared to him. It is precision. Solomon did not have a vision he could point to or a stone he could show anybody. He woke up in the dark at Gibeon with a conversation in his head.

He goes to Jerusalem, stands in front of the ark, offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, and throws a feast for his whole household. Burnt offerings are wholly consumed; peace offerings are eaten. So there is a sacrifice that keeps nothing back, and then a meal, and everybody who works for him is at it.

A man is given the greatest promise of his life in his sleep, and the first thing he does when he wakes is go and worship where the ark is, and then feed his servants.

Can I ask God for anything and get it? This was a unique offer to a king at the start of his reign. But God does promise wisdom to all who ask: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God (Jas 1:5). The riches and honour were God’s added gift to Solomon, not a promise to every believer.
verseByVerse.note: Gibeon lay about 6 miles north-west of Jerusalem; the tabernacle stood there at the time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–28 — Give Her the Living Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two prostitutes come to the king. They live in one house; both bore sons three days apart; one child died in the night, and each says the living one is hers (vv. 16-22). The king states the deadlock — the one says, "This is my son that is alive"... and the other says, "No; but your son is dead" — and calls for a sword: divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other (vv. 23-25). Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death." But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him." (v. 26). The king gives the child to the first — she is his mother (v. 27). And all Israel hears, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Note who gets a hearing: two prostitutes with no husbands, no witnesses, no standing and nothing to offer, and the case goes to the king in person.
verseByVerse.examples: He does not detect a liar. He makes a situation in which love has to show itself, because love will act against its own interest and a false claim will not.

verseByVerse.quote: Then two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him. The one woman said, "Oh, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house, and I gave birth to a child while she was in the house. Then on the third day after I gave birth, this woman also gave birth. And we were alone. There was no one else with us in the house; only we two were in the house. And this woman's son died in the night, because she lay on him. And she arose at midnight and took my son from beside me, while your servant slept, and laid him at her breast, and laid her dead son at my breast. When I rose in the morning to nurse my child, behold, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely in the morning, behold, he was not the child that I had borne." But the other woman said, "No, the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours." The first said, "No, the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine." Thus they spoke before the king. Then the king said, "The one says, 'This is my son that is alive, and your son is dead'; and the other says, 'No; but your son is dead, and my son is the living one.'" And the king said, "Bring me a sword." So a sword was brought before the king. And the king said, "Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one and half to the other." Then the woman whose son was alive said to the king, because her heart yearned for her son, "Oh, my lord, give her the living child, and by no means put him to death." But the other said, "He shall be neither mine nor yours; divide him." Then the king answered and said, "Give the living child to the first woman, and by no means put him to death; she is his mother." And all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered, and they stood in awe of the king, because they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The placement of this story is the argument. The previous paragraph had a thousand burnt offerings, an appearance of God, and a promise that no king would compare with him. The very next sentence is two prostitutes standing in a room.

Consider what these women are and are not. They have no husbands and no male relative to speak for them. They have no standing in any court. They have nothing to give and nobody to bribe, and their profession puts them at the bottom of the society. The whole case rests on one woman's word against another's, in a house with no other adults in it, and there are no witnesses of any kind.

It is the least important case in the kingdom and the hardest to decide, and it goes to the king in person. That is the point. The wisdom that was promised in a dream at Gibeon shows up first in a hearing that nobody powerful cared about, and the writer put the two paragraphs next to each other so that the reader would see it.

And it is the sentence that summarised David's reign at its best, operating: David administered justice and equity to all his people (2 Sam. 8:15). All was always the test, because the courts of that world were judged by how they treated the people nobody had to be fair to.

The first woman states the evidential problem herself (v. 18): there was no one else with us in the house. There are no witnesses. She knows it, and says it, and comes anyway.

Verse 21 has the detail that makes the story real: when I looked at him closely in the morning. She woke to feed a baby and the baby was dead, and in the half-light she did not know at first. It took looking properly.

In verse 23 the king states the deadlock back to them, exactly, and that is the first thing an understanding mind does. He has listened closely enough to reproduce both positions without favouring either, and he has established out loud that there is nothing to choose between them on the evidence. No amount of further questioning will settle it.

Then he calls for a sword (vv. 24-25). It has to be said that this is a terrible thing to say in front of a woman holding a baby, and the writer does not soften it. A sword is fetched. The order is given in plain words. Neither woman knows it is a test, and one of them is about to watch her child be cut in half.

The text does not raise the question whether Solomon would have gone through with it, and the answer is surely not. But she does not know that.

Now see what he has actually done, because it is not a trick and it is not cleverness for its own sake.

He could not tell which woman was lying. Nobody could; there was no evidence and no witness. So he stopped trying to detect a liar and made a situation in which love would have to show itself.

The insight underneath it is this: love acts against its own interest, and a false claim never does. A woman who wants a baby will not give it up. A woman who loves a baby will give up anything, including the baby, to keep him alive.

So the sword does not test their honesty. It tests what each of them wants more: the child, or winning.

In verse 26 take the narrator's clause first, because he tells us the reason before he gives us her words: because her heart yearned for her son.

The Hebrew is physical: her compassion grew warm. It is the word for the deep, tender love of a parent, felt in the body, the churn a person feels when someone they love is in danger. Joseph felt it when he saw his brother Benjamin and had to leave the room because his compassion grew warm for his brother, and he sought a place to weep (Gen. 43:30).

Now what she says: give her the living child. She loses. That is the whole point and it should not be hurried past. In order to keep her son alive she has to hand him to the woman who stole him, and go home without him, and live the rest of her life knowing where he is and unable to say a word about it.

She does it in one sentence, and the second half of the sentence is the only thing she cares about: and by no means put him to death.

The other woman says the coldest sentence in the chapter: he shall be neither mine nor yours. Notice what she is actually choosing. She is not choosing the child; she has already lost that option, because the king has ruled that neither gets him whole. She is choosing that the other woman shall not have him either.

That is what a grief with nothing underneath it turns into when it is refused. She lost her own son in the night and lay there and swapped the bodies, and what she wants now is not a baby. It is that the woman across the room should not be happy.

Anybody who has watched a bitter dispute go past the point where either party can gain anything has seen this exact sentence. Neither mine nor yours. If I cannot have it, destroy it.

Her sin was the theft and the cruelty, not the grief. A mother who loses a baby, as she did, has lost something real, and Scripture never treats that sorrow lightly: the LORD is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18), and Jesus wept at a grave. What she shows is what grief can become when it is nursed into envy, and that is a warning held out gently, not a judgment on anyone who mourns.

In verse 27 he gives the verdict in her own words. By no means put him to death is what she said, and he says it back, and then four words: she is his mother.

The last verse is careful about what it is praising. The wisdom is God's, given at Gibeon a page ago, and it is identified by what it produced: a right verdict in a case nobody could have decided, for a woman with no standing whatever.

That is what Solomon asked for. He wanted an understanding mind to discern between good and evil so that he could govern God's people, and the first thing it did was find a baby's mother.

And the scene points beyond this courtroom. Isaiah promised a shoot from the stump of Jesse on whom the Spirit of wisdom and understanding would rest, who would not judge by what his eyes see or decide by what his ears hear, but would judge the poor with righteousness (Isaiah 11:1-4). Solomon needed a sword to bring the truth out. The Son of David needed no one to tell him what was in a person, for he knew (John 2:25), and Paul calls him the wisdom of God, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (1 Corinthians 1:24; Colossians 2:3). When Jesus said that something greater than Solomon was here (Matthew 12:42), this was part of what he meant.

3.theology:
The plant in verse 1. The first fact recorded after the executions is a wedding to Egypt, stated flatly and left there. The law had warned Israel's king against both Egypt and many wives, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:16-17), and chapter 11 names the daughter of Pharaoh first among the women who turned Solomon's heart. This writer does not editorialise; he plants and waits.

The word only (v. 3). Solomon loved the LORD is said of no other king in Kings. Yet the qualification attached to him on the page before he asks for wisdom is the one this writer will attach to almost every good reign that follows: the high places were not taken away.

An understanding mind (v. 9). What he asks for is a hearing heart. In Hebrew the heart is where a person thinks and decides, so this is a mind that listens and discerns before it rules, which is what a judge needs before anything else. And it is a tool for a job, and the job is other people.

Given outright, and given with an if (vv. 12-14). Wisdom, riches and honour are given with no condition; long life alone is hedged with if you will walk in my ways. The riches come on the principle Jesus states in the Sermon on the Mount: the one who seeks God's kingdom first is the one to whom other things can safely be added. The gifts were never withdrawn, for Solomon died the wisest and richest man alive; it was the conditional side that came due in chapter 11.

Who gets a hearing (v. 16). The wisdom promised at Gibeon shows up first in a case nobody powerful cared about, for two women with no standing at all. That is justice and equity to all his people operating, and all was always the test.

What the last verse praises (v. 28). Not that the king was clever: they perceived that the wisdom of God was in him to do justice. The wisdom is God's, given a page earlier, and it is identified by what it produced. Many Christians have also heard an echo here, and it is no more than an echo: a mother gave up her claim so that her son might live, and God did not spare his own Son so that people with no standing might live (Romans 8:32).
3.examples:
Then: God appeared to a young king in his sleep and told him to ask for anything at all, with no hint of what a good answer would be — and he asked for a heart that could listen, so that he could do the job properly for people who were not his. The first case it was used on was two prostitutes and a baby, with no witnesses and nothing to decide it by.

Now: Three things. Verse 5 is the test that never stops being a test: what you would ask for if you could have anything is a photograph of you, and nobody is going to tell you the right answer beforehand. Yet the God who asks is the one who gives: he promises wisdom generously to any who ask him (James 1:5), and it is his Spirit who changes what we want. Second, what he asked for was a tool for a job, and the job was other people — which is the difference between wanting wisdom and wanting to be thought wise. And third, the sword. He could not tell who was lying, so he stopped trying and made a situation in which love had to declare itself, because love will act against its own interest and nothing else will. Know that about other people, and know it about yourself: the question is never what you claim to care about but what you will give up to keep it.

4.title: Solomon's Officials and His Wisdom

Each man had to make provision for one month in the year.<sup>8</sup>These were their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim;<sup>9</sup>Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elonbeth-hanan;<sup>10</sup>Ben-hesed, in Arubboth (to him belonged Socoh and all the land of Hepher);<sup>11</sup>Ben-abinadab, in all Naphath-dor (he had Taphath the daughter of Solomon as his wife);<sup>12</sup>Baana the son of Ahilud, in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean that is beside Zarethan below Jezreel, and from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the other side of Jokmeam;<sup>13</sup>Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead (he had the villages of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, and he had the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars);<sup>14</sup>Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim;<sup>15</sup>Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he had taken Basemath the daughter of Solomon as his wife);<sup>16</sup>Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth;<sup>17</sup>Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar;<sup>18</sup>Shimei the son of Ela, in Benjamin;<sup>19</sup>Geber the son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life.<sup>22</sup>Solomon's provision for one day was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal,<sup>23</sup>ten fat oxen, and twenty pasture-fed cattle, a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl.<sup>24</sup>For he had dominion over all the region west of the Euphrates from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the Euphrates. And he had peace on all sides around him.<sup>25</sup>And Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon.<sup>26</sup>Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen.<sup>27</sup>And those officers supplied provisions for King Solomon, and for all who came to King Solomon's table, each one in his month. They let nothing be lacking.<sup>28</sup>Barley also and straw for the horses and swift steeds they brought to the place where it was required, each according to his duty.<sup>29</sup>And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore,<sup>30</sup>so that Solomon's wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt.<sup>31</sup>For he was wiser than all other men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, and his fame was in all the surrounding nations.<sup>32</sup>He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005.<sup>33</sup>He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of birds, and of reptiles, and of fish.<sup>34</sup>And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and from all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.
4.overview:
A cabinet list, like those at the end of 2 Samuel 8 and 20, but longer, and the difference is the point: Solomon governs a state rather than a court. Twelve districts, drawn across the old tribal inheritances, feed his table a month at a time.

Then the high-water mark of the Old Testament, told in the words of God's promise to Abraham: a people like the sand by the sea, borders from the Euphrates to Egypt, every man under his vine and fig tree. Woven through it are two quiet warnings: the minister of forced labour, and forty thousand stalls of horses. The chapter ends with the wisdom God gave Solomon, and the nations who came to hear it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Officials and the Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cabinet (vv. 1-6), ending with the minister of forced labour; then twelve officers who each feed the court for one month (v. 7), and their districts (vv. 8-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The new offices make this a state rather than a court, and the last name on the list matters most.
verseByVerse.examples: The twelve districts are not the twelve tribes. Several are named by town or region rather than by tribe, and the old boundaries are cut across to make a revenue map: efficient, and chapter 12 shows what it cost.

verseByVerse.quote: King Solomon was king over all Israel, and these were his high officials: Azariah the son of Zadok was the priest; Elihoreph and Ahijah the sons of Shisha were secretaries; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder; Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was in command of the army; Zadok and Abiathar were priests; Azariah the son of Nathan was over the officers; Zabud the son of Nathan was priest and king's friend; Ahishar was in charge of the palace; and Adoniram the son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor. Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, who provided food for the king and his household. Each man had to make provision for one month in the year. These were their names: Ben-hur, in the hill country of Ephraim; Ben-deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elonbeth-hanan; Ben-hesed, in Arubboth (to him belonged Socoh and all the land of Hepher); Ben-abinadab, in all Naphath-dor (he had Taphath the daughter of Solomon as his wife); Baana the son of Ahilud, in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean that is beside Zarethan below Jezreel, and from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah, as far as the other side of Jokmeam; Ben-geber, in Ramoth-gilead (he had the villages of Jair the son of Manasseh, which are in Gilead, and he had the region of Argob, which is in Bashan, sixty great cities with walls and bronze bars); Ahinadab the son of Iddo, in Mahanaim; Ahimaaz, in Naphtali (he had taken Basemath the daughter of Solomon as his wife); Baana the son of Hushai, in Asher and Bealoth; Jehoshaphat the son of Paruah, in Issachar; Shimei the son of Ela, in Benjamin; Geber the son of Uri, in the land of Gilead, the country of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan. And there was one governor who was over the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reader has seen two cabinet lists before, at the end of 2 Samuel 8 and 20, both times to say the kingdom was in working order. This one is longer, and the difference is the point of the chapter.

Two secretaries where David had one. Jehoshaphat the recorder is the same man who held the post under David, which means somebody in that administration has now served two kings.

Abiathar is still listed, although he was expelled to Anathoth in chapter 2, which suggests the writer is giving the offices of the reign rather than a snapshot of one afternoon.

There is now an officer set over the officers, a layer of administration that did not exist under David.

And two sons of Nathan in one verse. If this is the prophet who confronted David and then arranged the succession at Gihon, his family is now inside the government, and one of them holds the title Hushai held: king's friend.

Adoniram is the name to keep, though he stands at the bottom of the list where nobody looks. His office appeared once before, in the last cabinet list in 2 Samuel, and it was new even then: Adoram was in charge of the forced labor (2 Sam. 20:24). Same post, and probably the same man under a fuller form of his name.

Now follow him forward. Under Solomon the forced labour becomes enormous: chapter 5 has thirty thousand men conscripted in shifts, and seventy thousand burden-bearers, and eighty thousand quarrymen. And when Solomon dies, the northern tribes come to his son with exactly one request: your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you (12:4).

Rehoboam refuses, with the line about scorpions. And then: then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones (12:18).

The man in this verse is stoned to death eight chapters from now, and the kingdom splits over his department. The writer puts him last on the list and says nothing.

Each of the twelve officers supplies the court for one month of the year. It is an elegant arrangement: the burden is spread, so no region is ruined; the supply is continuous, so the court never runs short; and the whole country is now organised around the maintenance of the capital.

Read the district list as a whole, because the shape of it is the information: these are not the twelve tribes.

Some districts carry a tribal name: Naphtali, Asher, Issachar, Benjamin, Gilead. Others are defined by towns and regions that cut straight across the old inheritances: the hill country of Ephraim, Makaz and Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh, Arubboth, Naphath-dor, Taanach and Megiddo and Beth-shean.

The tribal boundaries were not administrative conveniences. They were allotments, given by lot under Joshua, each family's portion of the land God promised Abraham, and the law made them almost impossible to alienate permanently. A man's field was his tribe's and his tribe's was God's gift.

The new map is drawn over the top of them to collect food. It is more efficient, and it is also the beginning of the dissolution of the thing that made Israel a covenant people rather than a country, and when the north finally walks out in chapter 12 the slogan they use is about inheritance: what portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse (12:16).

Mahanaim, one of the district seats, is where David fled across the Jordan when Absalom drove him out, and where three men brought him beds and cheese.

Two of Solomon's daughters are married to district officers, and a son of Hushai holds a district. Hushai is the friend in the torn coat who walked into a captured Jerusalem and lied to Absalom's face to save David's life.

The families that stood by the father are being provided for by the son.

A reader who counts will notice something the writer does not mention: Judah is not on the list.

The last verse is difficult and translations differ over whether a twelfth district in Judah is being referred to. What is not in doubt is that the districts named lie outside Judah, and that the tribe the king belongs to does not appear among them.

Whether Judah was exempt from the monthly provision, the text does not say outright. But the ten tribes will say something in chapter 12 that sounds very much as though they thought so.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — Every Man Under His Vine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abraham's promise in numbers and borders (vv. 20-21), the daily provision of the king's table (vv. 22-23), peace on every side and every man under his fig tree (vv. 24-25), and forty thousand stalls of horses (v. 26), all kept supplied by the officers (vv. 27-28).
verseByVerse.theology: The writer tells the high-water mark of the Old Testament in the words of the promise to Abraham.
verseByVerse.examples: In the middle of the plenty stand forty thousand stalls of horses, which the law told Israel's king not to gather (Deut. 17:16). His father had hamstrung captured chariot horses in obedience to that command; the son builds stables.

verseByVerse.quote: Judah and Israel were as many as the sand by the sea. They ate and drank and were happy. Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. They brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life. Solomon's provision for one day was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal, ten fat oxen, and twenty pasture-fed cattle, a hundred sheep, besides deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened fowl. For he had dominion over all the region west of the Euphrates from Tiphsah to Gaza, over all the kings west of the Euphrates. And he had peace on all sides around him. And Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan even to Beersheba, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, all the days of Solomon. Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots, and 12,000 horsemen. And those officers supplied provisions for King Solomon, and for all who came to King Solomon's table, each one in his month. They let nothing be lacking. Barley also and straw for the horses and swift steeds they brought to the place where it was required, each according to his duty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the high-water mark of the Old Testament. As many as the sand by the sea is not a general expression for a crowd; it is the promise God swore to Abraham on the mountain in the land of Moriah, after the ram was found in the thicket: I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore (Gen. 22:17).

Here it is, in a sentence about ordinary people eating dinner: not conquering, not building, not fighting, but eating, drinking, and content.

The borders are Abraham's too. To your offspring I give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates (Gen. 15:18).

Nothing before this and nothing after it comes as close. Joshua took the land; David subdued the neighbours; and here, for one generation, the map matches the promise.

The figures are for a single day. A cor is something like six bushels, so this is several tons of flour and meal daily, thirty head of cattle, a hundred sheep, and game and poultry on top. Estimates of how many people that fed run into the thousands.

It is splendour, and it is also an invoice.

Somebody grew that grain and raised those animals, and the twelve districts of the previous section exist precisely to deliver it, one month each. What reads as a description of the king's glory is, from the other end, a description of the country's tax burden, and the writer has put the two paragraphs in that order.

Hold both. The prosperity is real and the people are happy, and the machinery underneath it is what the north will complain about the day Solomon dies.

His name is tied to peace in the promise itself, his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quiet to Israel in his days (1 Chron. 22:9) — and there is a reason for it. God told David he would not build the temple because you have shed much blood and have waged great wars (1 Chron. 22:8), and promised instead a son who would be a man of rest.

This verse is that promise in operation. The wars were fought by the father so that the son could build.

The man under his own vine and fig tree is the picture the prophets will use for the age to come, and its power is that it is domestic. Not an empire, not a temple, not an army, but a man sitting outside his own house in the shade of things he planted himself. A vine takes years to bear and a fig tree longer, so nobody sits under either unless he has been in one place long enough to plant them and safe enough to wait.

Micah takes it up for the day when the nations beat their swords into ploughshares: they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid (Mic. 4:4). Zechariah uses it of the day God removes the iniquity of the land in a single day (Zech. 3:10).

So the settled prosperity of Solomon's reign becomes the standing Old Testament shorthand for what God intends to give the world. Peace, in Scripture, does not look like a throne. It looks like an ordinary person, unafraid, sitting in the shade of his own fig tree.

Then, in the middle of it, comes forty thousand stalls of horses, stated as one more item of glory.

The law about Israel's kings has three prohibitions, and the first is: only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, "You shall never return that way again" (Deut. 17:16).

And the reader has watched somebody obey this command, recently and at cost. When David captured Hadadezer's cavalry he had almost all of the chariot horses hamstrung on the field, keeping enough for a hundred chariots and destroying the rest: the finest military asset in the region, deliberately ruined, because of one clause in a book (2 Sam. 8:4).

The father cut the tendons. The son built the stables.

And chapter 10 will complete it: Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt (10:28), which is the other half of the same prohibition, the half about sending people back where they came from.

The reason the law gives is never economic. It is that a chariot corps is the thing a nation leans on instead of God, and a psalm of David says so directly: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7).

The writer records the forty thousand stalls between a verse about men sitting under their fig trees and a verse about the officers never letting the supply fail, and he does not say one word about it.

The officers let nothing be lacking. The system works perfectly, and the last verse of the section is about feeding the horses.

Solomon’s rule reached the borders promised to Abraham (v. 21; Gen 15:18), so the land promise was fulfilled in its Old Testament sense; the New Testament looks for its fuller fulfilment in the whole earth inherited by Christ’s people (Rom 4:13). Christians differ over whether a further fulfilment in the land itself still awaits the Jewish people: some read the promises that way, and others read them as widened in Christ to the renewed earth (Hebrews 11:10-16), since the New Testament speaks of Abraham's heirs inheriting the world. Faithful believers hold both views, and both rejoice that God keeps his word to Abraham.

Why do the numbers differ from the parallel account? Numbers in Hebrew manuscripts were easily miscopied, since they were often written with letters or abbreviations; and the two accounts sometimes count different things, such as chariots and charioteers, or a total and a part. Neither touches what the passage teaches, and those who hold Scripture to be without error have always meant what was first written, not every later copy.

Here Kings has 40,000 stalls and Chronicles 4,000 (2 Chr 9:25); most likely the larger figure was miscopied.
verseByVerse.note: “The Euphrates” is “the River” in Hebrew (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — Wisdom Like the Sand on the Seashore
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's gift of wisdom beyond the east, Egypt and the famous sages (vv. 29-31); the proverbs and songs (v. 32), the study of trees and creatures (v. 33), and the nations who come to hear (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Solomon's wisdom is God's gift, and verse 33 shows what it was: sustained attention to what God has made.
verseByVerse.examples: Heman and Ethan, two of the men Solomon is measured against, have psalms in the psalter with their names in the headings. And the nations who come to hear him prepare for the Queen of Sheba in chapter 10, whom the Lord Jesus will set beside himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding beyond measure, and breadth of mind like the sand on the seashore, so that Solomon's wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the people of the east and all the wisdom of Egypt. For he was wiser than all other men, wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol, and his fame was in all the surrounding nations. He also spoke 3,000 proverbs, and his songs were 1,005. He spoke of trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He spoke also of beasts, and of birds, and of reptiles, and of fish. And people of all nations came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and from all the kings of the earth, who had heard of his wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The promise God made at Gibeon is reported as fact, in the same figure the writer has just used of the population: sand on the seashore.

Breadth of mind is literally largeness of heart. It is not a moral phrase here; it means range, the capacity to hold a great many things and see how they fit.

The east and Egypt were the two great wisdom traditions of the ancient world, and the writer names them because his readers would have known the comparison was a real one. Egypt had centuries of instruction literature; the east had its own. Solomon is being placed above both.

The four men named were famous enough to need no explanation, and two of them turn up in the psalter. Psalm 88 is a maskil of Heman the Ezrahite, and it is the darkest psalm in the book, the one that ends my companions have become darkness. Psalm 89 is a maskil of Ethan the Ezrahite, and it is the long meditation on the covenant with David that asks, when the crown has been thrown to the ground, Lord, where is your steadfast love of old, which by your faithfulness you swore to David?

The men Solomon is measured against wrote about unanswered grief and a broken covenant. That is what wisdom was understood to be in Israel: not a stock of good advice, but the ability to look steadily at things that do not resolve.

Of three thousand proverbs, the book of Proverbs contains a few hundred. Of a thousand and five songs, the Song of Songs is one, and two psalms carry his name (Pss. 72, 127). Almost all of it is lost.

This verse tells us what kind of thing his wisdom was. Trees, beasts, birds, reptiles, fish: that is Genesis 1. It is the order of the created world as the first chapter of the Bible sets it out, and Solomon went through it and paid attention.

The range within the first category is the whole point: from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. The cedar is the largest and most valuable tree in the region, the timber kings imported for palaces and temples. Hyssop is a small bushy plant that grows in cracks in masonry, and it is what the Israelites used to daub blood on the doorposts in Egypt, and what was lifted to the cross with a sponge of sour wine.

He looked at both, the biggest tree and the weed in the wall.

So the wisdom God gave was not a mystical faculty or a stock of clever rulings. It was attention: sustained, curious, unembarrassed attention to what God had made, from the cedars down to whatever is growing out of the brickwork.

That is what the book of Proverbs does on every page. Go to the ant. Look at the badger and the locust and the lizard. Watch how a lazy man's field looks in the spring. Israel's wisdom tradition believed the world was made by a God who is consistent, and that a person who watches it carefully will learn how to live.

One of those who came, the Queen of Sheba, gets chapter 10 to herself, and says the half was not told her.

The Lord Jesus said one more thing about this verse. Speaking to a generation that wanted a sign from him, he said: the queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here (Luke 11:31; cf. Matt. 12:42).

A foreign queen crossed a desert on a rumour. And the people standing in front of the wisdom of God in person asked him to do a trick.
verseByVerse.note: In the Hebrew Bible, 4:21-34 is numbered 5:1-14.

4.theology:
A state, not a court (vv. 2-6). Two secretaries, an officer set over the officers, a palace manager, and a department of forced labour: layers David never had. The forced labour is the office to watch. It was new when it first appeared at 2 Samuel 20:24, under Solomon it becomes enormous (5:13-15), and when he dies the north asks his son for one thing only, to lighten the yoke (12:4). Samuel had warned that a king would take Israel's sons for his chariots and his fields (1 Samuel 8:11-17), and this list is that warning beginning to come true.

A revenue map over an inheritance (vv. 7-19). The tribal boundaries were each family's portion of what was promised to Abraham. Drawing a food-collection map over them is efficient, and it begins to dissolve what made Israel a covenant people rather than a country. When the north finally walks out, its slogan is about inheritance (12:16).

The promise kept, and the bill (vv. 20-23). For one generation the people are as many as the sand and the borders reach the Euphrates, as God swore to Abraham (Gen. 22:17; 15:18), and the sentence that says so is about ordinary people eating dinner. The writer then sets the king's daily table beside it, so that what reads from one end as glory reads from the other as the country's tax burden. Both are true, and the reader is meant to hold both.

Peace, and the King who gives it (vv. 24-25). The son of peace, a man of rest, builds what the warrior father could not (1 Chron. 22:8-9). The man under his own vine and fig tree becomes the prophets' picture of what God intends to give the world (Mic. 4:4; Zech. 3:10). But Solomon's peace lasted all the days of Solomon and no longer. Isaiah promised a son on David's throne of whose government and peace there would be no end (Isaiah 9:6-7), and Paul says of Christ that he himself is our peace, having broken down the wall of hostility (Ephesians 2:14). The fig tree Micah saw is his to give.

What the horses mean (v. 26). The law forbade the king many horses not for economic reasons but because a chariot corps is what a nation leans on instead of God. The writer records the stables without comment, between the fig trees and the full storehouses, and chapter 10 will show where the horses came from.

Wisdom as a gift and as attention (vv. 29-34). God gave Solomon wisdom: it begins as a gift. Its range is the order of Genesis 1, from the cedar to the hyssop, and it is measured against men who wrote about unanswered grief and a broken covenant (Pss. 88, 89). Wisdom in Israel was never a stock of clever answers; it was the capacity to look steadily at the world God made, including what does not resolve. And the one who gives it is greater than Solomon (Matt. 12:42).
4.examples:
Then: a king whose court ate thirty head of cattle and a hundred sheep a day reorganised the whole country into twelve supply districts drawn straight across the tribal inheritances, and the minister he put in charge of the conscripted labour that built it all was stoned to death by ten of the tribes on the day the kingdom broke in half.

Now: two things. First, verse 33 is what wisdom looks like when the Bible describes it, and it is more ordinary and more demanding than most people expect: sustained attention to what God has actually made. And it is a gift before it is a discipline: God gave Solomon wisdom (v. 29), and he still gives it generously to those who ask (James 1:5). Solomon was the wisest man alive and he spent it looking at fish and lizards. Second, notice the shape of the chapter. Everything in it is a genuine good (peace, plenty, safety, a man under his own fig tree, a promise to Abraham arriving), and the writer lays the machinery that pays for it right alongside. Prosperity is not neutral. It has a bill attached and somebody is carrying it, and it quietly acquires the things it was told not to.

5.title: Preparations for the Temple
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon when he heard that they had anointed him king in place of his father, for Hiram always loved David.<sup>2</sup>And Solomon sent word to Hiram,<sup>3</sup>"You know that David my father could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the warfare with which his enemies surrounded him, until the LORD put them under the soles of his feet.<sup>4</sup>But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is neither adversary nor misfortune.<sup>5</sup>And so I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD said to David my father, 'Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place, shall build the house for my name.'<sup>6</sup>Now therefore command that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me. And my servants will join your servants, and I will pay you for your servants such wages as you set, for you know that there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians."<sup>7</sup>As soon as Hiram heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly and said, "Blessed be the LORD this day, who has given to David a wise son to be over this great people."<sup>8</sup>And Hiram sent to Solomon, saying, "I have heard the message that you have sent to me. I am ready to do all you desire in the matter of cedar and cypress timber.<sup>9</sup>My servants shall bring it down to the sea from Lebanon, and I will make it into rafts to go by sea to the place you direct. And I will have them broken up there, and you shall receive it. And you shall meet my wishes by providing food for my household."<sup>10</sup>So Hiram supplied Solomon with all the timber of cedar and cypress that he desired,<sup>11</sup>while Solomon gave Hiram 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household, and 20,000 cors of beaten oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram year by year.<sup>12</sup>And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. And there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.<sup>13</sup>King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men.<sup>14</sup>And he sent them to Lebanon, 10,000 a month in shifts. They would be a month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the draft.<sup>15</sup>Solomon also had 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hill country,<sup>16</sup>besides Solomon's 3,300 chief officers who were over the work, who had charge of the people who carried on the work.<sup>17</sup>At the king's command they quarried out great, costly stones in order to lay the foundation of the house with dressed stones.<sup>18</sup>So Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders and the men of Gebal did the cutting and prepared the timber and the stone to build the house.
5.overview:
The first foreign embassy of the reign arrives unasked, because Hiram always loved David; the king whose cedar once prompted David's wish to house the ark now supplies the timber for the temple. Solomon builds on a promise, as the LORD said to David my father, and a Phoenician king blesses the LORD by name.

Then the levy: thirty thousand Israelites conscripted in monthly shifts under Adoniram. The terms are humane for the age and the work is glorious, and this is the department the kingdom will eventually break over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Now the LORD My God Has Given Me Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hiram's embassy (v. 1) and Solomon's reply: the wars that kept David from building, the rest now given, the intention to build as the LORD said to David my father, and a request for cedar and Sidonian woodcutters (vv. 2-6).
