verseByVerse.theology: Solomon gives the wars as the reason his father could not build; God gave the blood (1 Chron. 22:8). The verse note explains why both are true, and why a son would give the first in a letter to a foreign king.
verseByVerse.examples: Rest on every side is the condition that makes building possible, and the word that opened the covenant chapter (2 Sam. 7:1). The father fought so that the son could build.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Hiram king of Tyre sent his servants to Solomon when he heard that they had anointed him king in place of his father, for Hiram always loved David. And Solomon sent word to Hiram, "You know that David my father could not build a house for the name of the LORD his God because of the warfare with which his enemies surrounded him, until the LORD put them under the soles of his feet. But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is neither adversary nor misfortune. And so I intend to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD said to David my father, 'Your son, whom I will set on your throne in your place, shall build the house for my name.' Now therefore command that cedars of Lebanon be cut for me. And my servants will join your servants, and I will pay you for your servants such wages as you set, for you know that there is no one among us who knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first embassy of the reign arrives unasked, and the reason given is personal. Loved is the ordinary word, which in treaty language also meant loyal alliance, and the writer has used it of Jonathan, of Michal, and of Solomon toward the LORD.

Hiram had sent cedar and craftsmen to build David a house at Jerusalem, unasked, years earlier (2 Sam. 5:11). That cedar is what made David uncomfortable enough to say I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells in a tent , which produced the greatest promise in the Old Testament.

So the man who supplied the timber that started the whole conversation is now going to supply the timber for the building.

What Solomon says next is true but not the whole truth, and the difference matters. His account is that his father was prevented by the wars. That is accurate as far as it goes, and it is not the reason God gave.

The reason is recorded twice, in David's own mouth, in Chronicles. Speaking to Solomon: the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "You have shed much blood and have waged great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed so much blood before me on the earth" (1 Chron. 22:8). And again to the assembled leaders: God said to me, "You may not build a house for my name, for you are a man of war and have shed blood" (1 Chron. 28:3).

It was not that David was too busy. It was that his hands were too bloody.

Solomon is not lying: the same wars are the reason for the disqualification, so the two accounts touch. But they are not the same, and the one he gives reflects better on his father.

It is also, in fairness, a letter to a foreign king with whom he wants a timber contract. A man does not open a trade negotiation by telling a Phoenician that his father was refused a building permit by God on account of bloodshed.

The writer records what was said and lets a reader who knows Chronicles hold the other half.

Rest on every side is the condition, and the word the whole thing turns on. When God made the covenant with David, the chapter opened: when the king lived in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his surrounding enemies (2 Sam. 7:1). Rest was what prompted David to think about the tent in the first place.

Rest is what Solomon has been given rather than won. He has fought nobody. His father broke the Philistines from Geba to Gezer, destroyed a Syrian army twice, subdued Moab and Edom and Ammon, and hamstrung the horses; and the son inherits a country with neither adversary nor misfortune and builds in the quiet.

Twice in two verses he says the LORD my God, where in verse 3 he spoke of the LORD his God when speaking of David. He has taken possession of the relationship.

The whole warrant for the project is a quotation. He is not building because a king ought to have a temple, but because God said so to his father in a night vision before he was born: he shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever (2 Sam. 7:13).

David wanted to build and was told no, and told instead that God would build him a house, and that a son would build the other kind. Every stone that goes up in the next three chapters goes up on the strength of that sentence.

He asks for the timber and the men, and concedes the point that makes the request necessary: Israel had no forests of that kind and no tradition of felling and hauling and rafting great timber. The Phoenicians did it for the whole eastern Mediterranean, and Egypt bought from them, and so did Assyria later.

So the temple of the LORD is going to be built out of foreign wood, cut by foreign hands, by an arrangement in which Israel admits it cannot do this part.

Solomon offers to pay the going rate: such wages as you set. He does not ask for a gift and he does not name his own price.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was the great Phoenician port on the coast north of Israel. Lebanon’s cedars were prized timber.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Blessed Be the LORD This Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hiram blesses the LORD for David's wise son (v. 7), agrees to raft cedar and cypress down the coast in return for food year by year (vv. 8-11), and the two make a treaty, with the wisdom credited to the LORD (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: A Phoenician king blesses the LORD by name and credits him with Solomon's wisdom. It should not be overclaimed, since Hiram's own gods were Baal and Astarte, and Jezebel comes from next door in Sidon a century later; but it should not be skipped either. The writer records a foreigner getting the credit right.
verseByVerse.examples: Read the terms as terms. Tyre had the finest timber and craftsmen in the region and almost no farmland; Israel had grain and oil and no cedar. This is not charity in either direction but two kings each supplying what the other could not grow.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Hiram heard the words of Solomon, he rejoiced greatly and said, "Blessed be the LORD this day, who has given to David a wise son to be over this great people." And Hiram sent to Solomon, saying, "I have heard the message that you have sent to me. I am ready to do all you desire in the matter of cedar and cypress timber. My servants shall bring it down to the sea from Lebanon, and I will make it into rafts to go by sea to the place you direct. And I will have them broken up there, and you shall receive it. And you shall meet my wishes by providing food for my household." So Hiram supplied Solomon with all the timber of cedar and cypress that he desired, while Solomon gave Hiram 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household, and 20,000 cors of beaten oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram year by year. And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him. And there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Phoenician king blesses the LORD by name, and it needs to be taken carefully in both directions. What he says is right in every particular: the covenant name, not a generic word for god; the credit given to God rather than Solomon; and the thing that has actually happened, a wise son given to David.

That is better theology than a great many Israelites managed, and the writer records it without comment. But it should not be turned into a conversion. Hiram is the king of Tyre, and Tyre's gods are Baal and Astarte; his people's worship is not in doubt. A century later a king of Israel marries a princess of Sidon called Jezebel, and what she brings with her burns through the northern kingdom for three generations.

Kings of that world habitually acknowledged the god of a neighbouring country as a courtesy, and some of that is certainly in this sentence.

What can be said is that the writer of Kings, who is merciless about Israelite kings, gives a foreigner an unqualified good line and lets it stand. It is a pattern the reader has met before (Uriah the Hittite, Ittai the Gittite, Obed-edom, the Ammonite who brought bedding to Mahanaim), and it will recur in this book with a widow at Zarephath and a Syrian general.

Cedar was felled in the mountains, dragged to the coast, lashed into rafts, and floated down the Mediterranean by sea to a landing point (Chronicles names Joppa, 2 Chron. 2:16), and then hauled some thirty-five miles up to Jerusalem overland. Every beam in the house of God came that way.

Hiram's price is food. Tyre was a trading city on a rocky coast with almost no agricultural land behind it, and it fed itself by importing. What Israel had that Tyre needed was grain and oil.

The payment comes year by year: not a single purchase but a standing annual obligation for as long as the work goes on, and the wheat and oil have to come from somewhere, which is what the twelve districts of the previous chapter are for.

Beaten oil is the best grade, from olives crushed by hand rather than pressed, and it is the quality specified for the lamps of the sanctuary (Ex. 27:20).

Notice where the writer puts verse 12. He has just described a shrewd and favourable trade agreement, negotiated at market rates, with the one supplier in the world who had what Israel needed, and his comment on it is the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as he promised him.

He does not say that Solomon negotiated well. The wisdom in a timber contract is the wisdom given in a dream at Gibeon, and as he promised him is the receipt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The levy: thirty thousand Israelites in monthly shifts under Adoniram (vv. 13-14), the burden-bearers, stonecutters and officers (vv. 15-16), and the costly foundation stones prepared by three workforces (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the department the kingdom eventually breaks over. The one thing the northern tribes ask of Solomon's son is to lighten his father's yoke (12:4), and when he refuses they stone the man named in verse 14 (12:18). The work it served was glorious, and the cost was real.
verseByVerse.examples: A tension should be stated rather than smoothed: 9:22 says Solomon made no slaves of the people of Israel, and this section says he drafted forced labour out of all Israel. The usual answer, set out in the note below, is plausible; the men of chapter 12 evidently did not feel the distinction as a large one.

verseByVerse.quote: King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men. And he sent them to Lebanon, 10,000 a month in shifts. They would be a month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the draft. Solomon also had 70,000 burden-bearers and 80,000 stonecutters in the hill country, besides Solomon's 3,300 chief officers who were over the work, who had charge of the people who carried on the work. At the king's command they quarried out great, costly stones in order to lay the foundation of the house with dressed stones. So Solomon's builders and Hiram's builders and the men of Gebal did the cutting and prepared the timber and the stone to build the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 13 is the sentence the kingdom eventually dies of.

The word is mas, a corvée: compulsory unpaid labour owed to the crown. Israel had been here before, under the same word: in Egypt taskmasters were set over them to afflict them with heavy burdens (Ex. 1:11).

The terms are humane by the standards of the age, and that should be said. One month away and two at home is a third of a man's time, not all of it; a farmer could still get a crop in. It is rotational conscription, not slavery.

The man in charge is Adoniram from the cabinet list. When Solomon dies the northern tribes bring Rehoboam a single request, and when he refuses they stone Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor (12:18). The kingdom split over this department and never came back together.

Here is a tension in the text that ought to be named rather than smoothed over.

Four chapters from now the writer says this: but of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. They were the soldiers, they were his officials, his commanders, his captains, his chariot commanders and his horsemen (9:22). And the verses before it say the permanent labour gangs were drawn from the surviving Canaanite peoples of the land.

And this chapter says King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel.

The usual reconciliation is a real one and it is probably right: two different arrangements are being described. The Canaanite population was in permanent bondage; the Israelite levy was rotational, temporary, and for the temple project specifically.

That distinction is genuine and it is legal, and it is also the sort of distinction that looks much smaller from underneath.

Because the men who came to Rehoboam did not say "your father enslaved us". They said your father made our yoke heavy, and they said it about a system that had been described in its own records as fair.

The work is glorious. This is the house of God going up, and the men quarrying stone in the hill country are building the place where the ark will rest and where Israel will meet God for nearly four centuries. Every one of them could tell his grandchildren what he had a hand in.

And it is being paid for by conscripted labour on a scale the country had never seen, administered by a department that did not exist under David, and the bill arrives at the end of Solomon's life and is presented to his son.

The writer states the numbers and does not comment. He has done this from the beginning of the book (the wedding to Egypt in 3:1, the forty thousand stalls in 4:26, the levy here), laying things down in sequence and trusting the reader to still be holding them in chapter 11.

The foundation, which no one would ever see, gets great, costly stones, the best material, and that says something about how this building was made.

The last verse lists three workforces, and two of them are foreign: Solomon's men, Hiram's men, and the men of Gebal, which is Byblos, another Phoenician port up the coast, famous for stonework.

So the house of the LORD is quarried, dressed, felled and rafted by Israelites and Phoenicians working side by side, on a foreign king's timber, to a plan given to David by God, on ground bought from a Jebusite for fifty shekels of silver.

Kings has 3,300 chief officers, Chronicles 3,600 (2 Chr 2:18). The two books seem to divide the ranks differently, for the totals agree: the 3,300 here plus the 550 senior officers of 9:23 make 3,850, and so do Chronicles' 3,600 plus 250 (2 Chronicles 8:10).

5.theology:
Two true reasons that are not the same (v. 3). Solomon says the wars prevented his father; God said the blood disqualified him (1 Chron. 22:8; 28:3). The accounts touch, because the same wars produced the bloodshed, but they are not interchangeable. A son writing to a Phoenician about a timber contract is not going to say that his father was refused a building permit by God, and the writer trusts the reader to hold the other half.

Rest is given, not won (v. 4). The word that opened the covenant chapter (2 Sam. 7:1), the rest that first set David thinking about the tent, is now Solomon's inheritance. He has fought nobody. His father broke the Philistines and subdued the neighbours, and the son inherits neither adversary nor misfortune and builds in the quiet. Much of what any of us enjoy was won by people before us.

The warrant is a quotation (v. 5). Solomon builds because of 2 Samuel 7:13, spoken in a night vision before he existed. David wanted to build and was told no, and told instead that God would build him a house. The temple is not a good idea being executed; it is a promise being kept. And the promise looked past Solomon. The prophets spoke of a man called the Branch who would build the temple of the LORD and rule as priest and king (Zechariah 6:12-13); Jesus, David's greater Son, spoke of the temple of his body raised in three days, and of the church he would build (John 2:19-21; Matthew 16:18). Solomon's house was burned. The house the Son builds is still going up.

Help from outside (vv. 6-12). Israel admits it cannot cut timber like the Sidonians, and Solomon offers the going rate rather than asking for a gift or naming his own price. Then a Phoenician king blesses the LORD by the covenant name. It is not a conversion: Tyre's gods were Baal and Astarte, and a courtesy to a neighbour's god was common form. But this writer, who is merciless about Israelite kings, lets a foreigner's good line stand, as he does elsewhere with Uriah, Ittai, a widow at Zarephath and a Syrian general. And he credits the shrewd trade agreement to the wisdom God promised at Gibeon, not to Solomon's bargaining: as he promised him is the historian checking the account against the promise.

The levy, held both ways (vv. 13-18). Israel remembered taskmasters from Egypt (Ex. 1:11), and this levy, though rotational and humane by the standards of the age, is felt as a yoke by the men who carry it (12:4). The reconciliation with 9:22 is real, and it is also the kind of distinction that looks smaller from underneath. Yet the work is glorious. The men quarrying in the hill country are building the place where Israel will meet God for nearly four centuries, on a foundation of costly stones nobody would ever see. The writer states the numbers and comments on none of it, trusting the reader to still be holding them in chapter 11.

Built by Israel and the nations together (v. 18). Solomon's men, Hiram's men and the men of Byblos work side by side, on a foreign king's timber, to a promise given to David, on ground bought from a Jebusite. Isaiah saw the picture enlarged: foreigners building up Zion's walls, and the glory of Lebanon brought to beautify God's sanctuary (Isaiah 60:10, 13). Paul sees it fulfilled when Gentiles once far off are built together with Israel into a holy temple, with Christ Jesus himself the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:19-22), the chosen and precious stone of 1 Peter 2:4-6.
5.examples:
Then: every cedar beam was cut by Phoenician woodcutters, rafted down the coast and hauled thirty-five miles inland, and paid for with wheat and the finest hand-crushed oil, every year, for as long as the building took.

Now: two things. First, Solomon's version of why his father was excluded is the honest one to sit with: it was true, it was kinder than the truth God had given, and it was told to somebody who was never going to check. Most of the half-accounts people give of their families are exactly that shape: not lies, just the version that reflects better, offered where the fuller one would cost something. Second, the levy. Everything about that project was good; the thing being built was the house of God, and the arrangement was legal and by the standards of the age humane. And the people carrying it experienced it as a yoke, and said so the moment the man who imposed it was dead. Those who lead anything, a church building project included, do well to ask the people carrying the load how it feels while there is still time to change it. It is possible to build something genuinely magnificent on terms the builders would not have chosen, and to find out what they thought only when it is too late to ask. The king the prophets promised lays a different yoke on those who come to him: my yoke is easy, and my burden is light (Matt. 11:30).

6.title: Solomon Builds the House
6.text: <sup>1</sup>In the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.<sup>3</sup>The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and ten cubits deep in front of the house.<sup>4</sup>And he made for the house windows with recessed frames.<sup>5</sup>He also built a structure against the wall of the house, running around the walls of the house, both the nave and the inner sanctuary. And he made side chambers all around.<sup>6</sup>The lowest story was five cubits broad, the middle one was six cubits broad, and the third was seven cubits broad. For around the outside of the house he made offsets on the wall in order that the supporting beams should not be inserted into the walls of the house.<sup>7</sup>When the house was built, it was with stone prepared at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built.<sup>8</sup>The entrance for the lowest story was on the south side of the house, and one went up by stairs to the middle story, and from the middle story to the third.<sup>9</sup>So he built the house and finished it, and he made the ceiling of the house of beams and planks of cedar.<sup>10</sup>He built the structure against the whole house, five cubits high, and it was joined to the house with timbers of cedar.<sup>11</sup>Now the word of the LORD came to Solomon,<sup>12</sup>"Concerning this house that you are building, if you will walk in my statutes and obey my rules and keep all my commandments and walk in them, then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father.<sup>13</sup>And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel."<sup>14</sup>So Solomon built the house and finished it.<sup>15</sup>He lined the walls of the house on the inside with boards of cedar. From the floor of the house to the walls of the ceiling, he covered them on the inside with wood, and he covered the floor of the house with boards of cypress.<sup>16</sup>He built twenty cubits of the rear of the house with boards of cedar from the floor to the walls, and he built this within as an inner sanctuary, as the Most Holy Place.<sup>17</sup>The house, that is, the nave in front of the inner sanctuary, was forty cubits long.<sup>18</sup>The cedar within the house was carved in the form of gourds and open flowers. All was cedar; no stone was seen.<sup>19</sup>The inner sanctuary he prepared in the innermost part of the house, to set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD.<sup>20</sup>The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high, and he overlaid it with pure gold. He also overlaid an altar of cedar.<sup>21</sup>And Solomon overlaid the inside of the house with pure gold, and he drew chains of gold across, in front of the inner sanctuary, and overlaid it with gold.<sup>22</sup>And he overlaid the whole house with gold, until all the house was finished. Also the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary he overlaid with gold.<sup>23</sup>In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olivewood, each ten cubits high.<sup>24</sup>Five cubits was the length of one wing of the cherub, and five cubits the length of the other wing of the cherub; it was ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other.<sup>25</sup>The other cherub also measured ten cubits; both cherubim had the same measure and the same form.<sup>26</sup>The height of one cherub was ten cubits, and so was that of the other cherub.<sup>27</sup>He put the cherubim in the innermost part of the house. And the wings of the cherubim were spread out so that a wing of one touched the one wall, and a wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; their other wings touched each other in the middle of the house.<sup>28</sup>And he overlaid the cherubim with gold.<sup>29</sup>Around all the walls of the house he carved engraved figures of cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, in the inner and outer rooms.<sup>30</sup>The floor of the house he overlaid with gold in the inner and outer rooms.<sup>31</sup>For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olivewood; the lintel and the doorposts were five-sided.<sup>32</sup>He covered the two doors of olivewood with carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers. He overlaid them with gold and spread gold on the cherubim and on the palm trees.<sup>33</sup>So also he made for the entrance to the nave doorposts of olivewood, in the form of a square,<sup>34</sup>and two doors of cypress wood. The two leaves of the one door were folding, and the two leaves of the other door were folding.<sup>35</sup>On them he carved cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, and he overlaid them with gold evenly applied on the carved work.<sup>36</sup>He built the inner court with three courses of cut stone and one course of cedar beams.<sup>37</sup>In the fourth year the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid, in the month of Ziv.<sup>38</sup>And in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished in all its parts, and according to all its specifications. He was seven years in building it.
6.overview:
The writer dates the temple from the exodus, not from a dynasty or a foreign king's reign: Israel's calendar runs from the night God brought them out of slavery, and the temple is a chapter in that story. The floor plan is the tabernacle doubled, the wilderness tent built in stone and cedar and gold and no longer portable, and every stone was finished at the quarry so that no iron tool was heard on the site.

Then, in the middle of the building specification, God speaks, and every clause is about conduct, not one about the house. A magnificent building secures nothing; the promise rests on God's word to David. Three centuries later Jeremiah had to stand in the gate of this house and rebuke people chanting the temple of the LORD like a charm.

Inside, no stone is seen: cherubim, palm trees and open flowers on every surface, Eden remembered in cedar and gold. Seven years to build it, and the very next verse gives the figure for his own house.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — No Hammer or Axe Was Heard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The date (v. 1), the dimensions, vestibule, windows and side chambers (vv. 2-6, 8-10), and the stone finished at the quarry so that no iron tool was heard on the site (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The date is given from the exodus, not from a dynasty or a foreign king's reign, which says what the building is for before a single dimension is given.
verseByVerse.examples: Every stone was finished at the quarry so that no iron tool would be heard on the site: not efficiency but reverence, as the verse note explains.

verseByVerse.quote: In the four hundred and eightieth year after the people of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, which is the second month, he began to build the house of the LORD. The house that King Solomon built for the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. The vestibule in front of the nave of the house was twenty cubits long, equal to the width of the house, and ten cubits deep in front of the house. And he made for the house windows with recessed frames. He also built a structure against the wall of the house, running around the walls of the house, both the nave and the inner sanctuary. And he made side chambers all around. The lowest story was five cubits broad, the middle one was six cubits broad, and the third was seven cubits broad. For around the outside of the house he made offsets on the wall in order that the supporting beams should not be inserted into the walls of the house. When the house was built, it was with stone prepared at the quarry, so that neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built. The entrance for the lowest story was on the south side of the house, and one went up by stairs to the middle story, and from the middle story to the third. So he built the house and finished it, and he made the ceiling of the house of beams and planks of cedar. He built the structure against the whole house, five cubits high, and it was joined to the house with timbers of cedar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer could have dated this by the monarchy, or by a foreign king's reign, as the ancient world usually did. He dates it from the exodus. No other date in the historical books is reckoned this way, and it is one of the main fixed points for Old Testament chronology.

And it says what the building is for before a single dimension is given. Israel's calendar runs from the night God brought them out of a country where they were slaves. The temple is a chapter in that story, not the start of a new one; the house being built is for the God who did that.

There is a second thing in the same verse. The month is named twice, Ziv and the second month, because Ziv is an old Canaanite month-name that had gone out of use, and the writer glosses it for readers who no longer knew it. That small editorial habit suggests this account was written down a long time after the event and from records.

The house is roughly ninety feet by thirty by forty-five. By the standards of the great temples of Egypt and Mesopotamia that is not large. Anyone who came from Thebes or Babylon would have found it modest. It was never meant to hold a congregation; Israel worshipped in the courts, and the building itself was the dwelling.

And the proportions are not invented. Set them against the tabernacle: the tent Moses made was thirty cubits by ten, with walls ten cubits high. This is exactly double on the ground, and three times as high.

So what is going up is not a new idea. It is the tent Israel carried through the wilderness for forty years and set up at Shiloh and lost the ark from at Aphek, rebuilt at twice the size, in stone and cedar and gold, and no longer portable.

That last change is the significant one, and God has something to say about it in chapter 7 of 2 Samuel and again in the middle of this chapter.

The windows were narrow, probably wider on the inside than the outside, letting light in and keeping weather and eyes out.

Three storeys of chambers, storerooms and service rooms, are built all round the outside of the temple. And the builders went to deliberate trouble to make sure that not one beam of those chambers was set into the wall of the house itself. Instead the temple wall was stepped, narrowing as it rose, so that each floor of the side structure could rest on a ledge.

It would have been far easier to socket the beams straight in. They designed round it, and the house of God carries no holes.

Every stone was cut, squared and finished at the quarry in the hill country, then carried to the site and set in place. The whole enormous structure went up in something close to silence, with no ring of iron on stone anywhere on the mountain.

Every block had to be measured before it left the quarry, and a mistake could not be corrected on site. Eighty thousand stonecutters were working in the hills to make that possible.

Why go to that trouble? The law gives the instinct. When God gave Israel the rule for altars at Sinai he said: if you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it (Ex. 20:25). Iron on the stone of an altar profanes it.

Whatever the full reason, the effect is that the noise and violence of manufacture are kept away from the place where God will be met. The work is done somewhere else. What arrives at the site is finished.

Peter takes the picture further. He tells scattered Christians: as you come to him, a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious, you yourselves like living stones are being built up as a spiritual house (1 Pet. 2:4-5).

Each stone shaped somewhere else, out of sight, and brought to the place already fitted for where it goes. That is what is happening to people, and the cutting is not done on the site.

Does the 480 years fix the date of the exodus? Faithful readers who hold Scripture’s full authority take it two ways. Read as a plain count, it puts the exodus about 1446 BC, since Solomon’s fourth year was about 966 BC; those who hold this early date point to the plain sense of the figure and to Jephthah’s 300 years in the land (Judges 11:26). Others hold a later date, about 1260 BC: Exodus 1:11 names a store city Raamses, which fits the reign of Ramesses II, and much of the archaeology of Canaan seems to fit the thirteenth century better; they read 480 as twelve generations of forty years, a round figure, with real generations nearer twenty-five. Early-daters reply that the name Raamses may have been updated for later readers, as in Genesis 47:11. Both views take the verse as true; they differ over what kind of number it is, and the question is still debated. The Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) reads 440 years here. Paul’s “about 450 years” (Acts 13:20) covers a different span.
verseByVerse.note: The 480th year after the exodus: about 966 BC. The temple was about 90 feet long, 30 wide and 45 high (60 × 20 × 30 cubits).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — Concerning This House That You Are Building
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the specification the narrative stops, and the word of the LORD comes to Solomon about the house he is building (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The placement is the message. God interrupts a building account to say that the house secures nothing; the if is about walking in his statutes, not the quality of the stonework.
verseByVerse.examples: The promise at the end is what the whole building exists for: God will dwell among his people and not forsake them. The temple was always the sign of that and never the cause of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the word of the LORD came to Solomon, "Concerning this house that you are building, if you will walk in my statutes and obey my rules and keep all my commandments and walk in them, then I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father. And I will dwell among the children of Israel and will not forsake my people Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer is in the middle of a building specification, and he breaks off to record that God spoke.

Nothing in the surrounding verses prepares for it and nothing follows from it structurally; the narrative goes straight back to cedar boards in verse 15. The three verses sit in the middle of the masonry like a hand laid on somebody's arm.

That placement is the message. God begins by naming the very thing Solomon is standing in the middle of, the project that has consumed a hundred and fifty thousand men, the finest timber in the world and the wealth of a kingdom, and then says something about it that has nothing to do with building.

There are four clauses, and every one of them is about conduct; not one is about the house. There is no "if you build it well". The condition attached to the greatest building project in Israel's history is entirely about whether the man building it keeps the commandments.

And what is promised is not a good building but I will establish my word with you, which I spoke to David your father: the covenant of 2 Samuel 7, already given by grace, the throne, the house that means a dynasty and not a temple. The commands are not the price of God's favour; they are the way of life inside a promise God made first.

Think about the temptation this guards against. A man in the fourth year of a seven-year project, watching a magnificent thing rise out of the ground that God himself asked for, is in real danger of a particular confusion: that the building is the relationship, that God will be secured by it, that a house this good must guarantee something.

God says it in the middle of the scaffolding, before the roof is on. The house does not secure anything; walking with the God who made the promise is what matters. Solomon himself did not keep these four clauses (11:4-6), and no son of David did until the one who could say I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29). His obedience is counted to those who trust him, and his Spirit now writes these statutes on their hearts (Ezek. 36:27).

Israel forgot this comprehensively, and Jeremiah had to stand in the gate of this very building three centuries later and shout at people who were chanting the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD as though the words were a charm, and tell them to go and look at Shiloh, where God had made his name dwell at first, and see what he did to it (Jer. 7:4, 12).

And the promise at the end is the sentence the whole building exists to serve: God will dwell among the children of Israel. Not in this house; among the people.

That is what God has been saying since Sinai: let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst (Ex. 25:8). The tabernacle was never a residence; it was a sign that God had come to live in the middle of a camp. The temple is the same sign in stone.

And will not forsake my people Israel is the other half, and it is the promise that outlasts the building. The house that Solomon is standing in will be looted by Shishak within a generation, stripped by later kings to pay tribute, defiled, and finally burned to the ground by Nebuchadnezzar's men.

And God does not forsake his people. He goes into exile with them, and Ezekiel sees him there by a canal in Babylon.

And Jesus, standing in the courts of the temple that later replaced this one, said destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up, and John adds that he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19, 21). The place where God dwells with people is finally a person.

The whole line runs out to a sentence in John's Gospel that uses the tabernacle word: and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (literally, pitched his tent among us) and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). And out further still to a voice at the end of the Bible: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people (Rev. 21:3).

God dwelling with people is the thing. Every building in between is a sign of it, and the signs get destroyed, and the thing does not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–30 — The Inner Sanctuary He Overlaid with Pure Gold
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cedar lining, and the Most Holy Place partitioned at the rear, prepared for the ark and overlaid with gold (vv. 14-22); the two olivewood cherubim (vv. 23-28); and the carvings of cherubim, palm trees and open flowers (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The house is the tabernacle at double scale, built in stone and cedar and gold, and standing still; and its heart is the room for the ark.
verseByVerse.examples: The cherubim over the ark recall the guardians of Eden, and the carvings of palm trees and flowers on every wall make the whole house a remembered garden.

verseByVerse.quote: So Solomon built the house and finished it. He lined the walls of the house on the inside with boards of cedar. From the floor of the house to the walls of the ceiling, he covered them on the inside with wood, and he covered the floor of the house with boards of cypress. He built twenty cubits of the rear of the house with boards of cedar from the floor to the walls, and he built this within as an inner sanctuary, as the Most Holy Place. The house, that is, the nave in front of the inner sanctuary, was forty cubits long. The cedar within the house was carved in the form of gourds and open flowers. All was cedar; no stone was seen. The inner sanctuary he prepared in the innermost part of the house, to set there the ark of the covenant of the LORD. The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high, and he overlaid it with pure gold. He also overlaid an altar of cedar. And Solomon overlaid the inside of the house with pure gold, and he drew chains of gold across, in front of the inner sanctuary, and overlaid it with gold. And he overlaid the whole house with gold, until all the house was finished. Also the whole altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary he overlaid with gold. In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olivewood, each ten cubits high. Five cubits was the length of one wing of the cherub, and five cubits the length of the other wing of the cherub; it was ten cubits from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other. The other cherub also measured ten cubits; both cherubim had the same measure and the same form. The height of one cherub was ten cubits, and so was that of the other cherub. He put the cherubim in the innermost part of the house. And the wings of the cherubim were spread out so that a wing of one touched the one wall, and a wing of the other cherub touched the other wall; their other wings touched each other in the middle of the house. And he overlaid the cherubim with gold. Around all the walls of the house he carved engraved figures of cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, in the inner and outer rooms. The floor of the house he overlaid with gold in the inner and outer rooms.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rear third of the building is partitioned off, and this is the room the whole structure exists for.

Nothing about it is designed to be seen. It has no windows. Nobody goes in except the high priest, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, with blood.

Hebrews reads this room as a copy of the true one. Christ entered once for all into the holy places, not with the blood of animals but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12, 24). The room one man entered once a year with borrowed blood was waiting for the one who would enter with his own.

The whole interior is lined so that not one inch of the masonry is visible. Every surface a person could look at is worked wood, carved with gourds and flowers.

The eighty thousand men in the hill country cut and squared and finished those stones to a tolerance that allowed the building to go up without a hammer being heard, and then the stones were covered over and nobody ever saw them again.

The care was not for the audience. It was for the God who would be in the room.

And here is what all of this is for: a box. The gold and the cedar and the seven years and the hundred and fifty thousand men are to make a room to put the ark in: the chest Moses had made in the wilderness, with the tablets of the covenant inside it and the mercy seat on top, and the two cherubim of hammered gold where God said there I will meet with you (Ex. 25:22).

It is the same chest the Philistines captured at Aphek, the same one that came home on a cart pulled by two cows. The one that stood in a private house at Kiriath-jearim for decades while nobody thought about it, and killed a man at a threshing floor, and blessed a Gittite's household for three months, and came into Jerusalem with a king dancing in front of it in a linen ephod.

It has been in a tent since David pitched one for it. Now it gets a room.

The inner room is twenty cubits each way, a perfect cube. That looks deliberate, and the only other place where Scripture says length, width and height are equal is at the far end of the Bible. When John is shown the holy city coming down out of heaven, the angel measures it: the city lies foursquare, its length the same as its width... its length and width and height are equal (Rev. 21:16).

The New Jerusalem is shaped like the Most Holy Place. And the thing John notices about that city is what is missing from it: and I saw no temple in the city, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev. 21:22).

The room where one man went once a year becomes the shape of a city where everybody lives.

The writer repeats the word gold until the repetition is the effect: gold over everything.

The two cherubim stand fifteen feet high, each with a fifteen-foot wingspan, and the four wings span the entire thirty feet of the room wall to wall, meeting in the centre, over the place where the ark will stand.

The reader first met cherubim at the end of Genesis 3. A man and a woman are driven out of a garden, and God placed at the east of the garden of Eden the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life (Gen. 3:24). Cherubim are what stand between people and the presence of God, with a sword, to keep them out.

And here are two of them, fifteen feet high, standing over the exact place where God has promised to meet his people.

The guards are still there. The sword is not mentioned.

And the cherubim were also woven into the curtain that hung before this room (2 Chronicles 3:14). When Jesus died, that curtain, in the temple of his day, was torn in two from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), and Hebrews says believers now enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Hebrews 10:19–20). The way to the tree of life that the cherubim guarded is opened by him.

And the same three things are carved on every surface of the building: cherubim, palm trees and open flowers, guardians and growing things. Whoever designed this room wanted a person standing in it to be reminded of a garden with something watching over it. Palm trees and flowers in a stone box, and winged figures among them.

It is Eden, remembered in cedar and gold, in a building whose innermost room nobody may enter.

Did the carved cherubim break the second commandment? God himself commanded them (Exodus 25:18); they represented the angels around his throne, not God, and they were never worshipped. The commandment forbids images of God and images made for worship, not all art.
verseByVerse.note: A cubit was about 18 inches (45 cm), the length of a forearm.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The carved doors of the inner sanctuary and the nave (vv. 31-35), the inner court (v. 36), and the dates: begun in the fourth year, finished in the eleventh, seven years in building it (vv. 37-38).
verseByVerse.theology: The doors carry the same garden carvings as the walls, and the chapter closes with a date and a number worth holding: seven years.
verseByVerse.examples: Hold the seven years for one verse, because the next chapter opens with the time he spent on his own house.

verseByVerse.quote: For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olivewood; the lintel and the doorposts were five-sided. He covered the two doors of olivewood with carvings of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers. He overlaid them with gold and spread gold on the cherubim and on the palm trees. So also he made for the entrance to the nave doorposts of olivewood, in the form of a square, and two doors of cypress wood. The two leaves of the one door were folding, and the two leaves of the other door were folding. On them he carved cherubim and palm trees and open flowers, and he overlaid them with gold evenly applied on the carved work. He built the inner court with three courses of cut stone and one course of cedar beams. In the fourth year the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid, in the month of Ziv. And in the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was finished in all its parts, and according to all its specifications. He was seven years in building it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same three motifs appear again, this time on the doors of the Most Holy Place. Olivewood is used for the doors and the cherubim inside, cedar for the walls, cypress for the floor and the outer doors. Every material in the building is a living thing that grew and was cut down.

The last verse gives the figure: seven years. Some see in the seven a hint of completeness; the writer does not say so, and the figure is simply the time it took.

The house was finished according to all its specifications, and Chronicles tells us where they came from: David gave Solomon the pattern for all of it (the porch, the houses, the treasuries, the courts, the chambers) and said, all this he made clear to me in writing from the hand of the LORD (1 Chron. 28:11-19). Which is what Moses was told about the tabernacle: see that you make them after the pattern for them, which is being shown you on the mountain (Ex. 25:40).

Solomon did not design this building. He built to a drawing.

And the next sentence in the book is this: Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house (7:1).

Seven years for the house of God, and thirteen for his own. The writer sets them in consecutive verses, does not remark on the difference, and goes straight on to describe the palace. That is not by itself a rebuke: the palace was a complex of several buildings, and David had gathered much of the temple’s material in advance. But the reader is allowed to notice.
verseByVerse.note: Ziv (v. 1) falls around April and May; Bul (v. 38) around October and November.

6.theology:
Dated from the exodus (v. 1). The house is for the God who brought slaves out of Egypt, and the date says so before a single dimension is given. (What the 480 years means for the date of the exodus, about 1446 BC or about 1260 BC, is debated among faithful scholars; the commentary on verses 1–10 sets out both views.)

The tent made still (vv. 2-10). The tabernacle Israel carried through the wilderness is built again at double scale, not large by the standards of Thebes or Babylon, and never meant to hold a congregation: the building was the dwelling, and Israel worshipped in the courts. Even the side chambers are designed so that no beam is set into the wall of the house.

Silence on the mountain (v. 7). Iron is kept away from the place where God will be met, as the law kept it from altars. Peter takes the picture further than any reader of this chapter could have predicted: Christians are living stones being built into a spiritual house (1 Pet. 2:4-5), shaped somewhere else, out of sight, and brought to the site already fitted for their place.

The house secures nothing (vv. 11-13). In the middle of the scaffolding God speaks, and no clause is about the building. What is promised is his word to David, already given by grace. The temptation guarded against is permanent: to mistake the thing we build for God for our standing with God. Solomon did not keep these clauses, and no son of David did until Christ, whose obedience is counted to those who trust him. Israel forgot the lesson, and Jeremiah stood in this gate rebuking those who chanted the temple of the LORD as a charm (Jer. 7:4).

Among, not in (v. 13). God promised to dwell among his people, not in a house, and that promise outlasts the building. This house is looted, stripped and finally burned, and God goes into exile with his people. The line runs out to John, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14), to Jesus speaking of the temple of his body (John 2:21), to a church that is itself God’s temple by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16), and to the city where the dwelling place of God is with man (Rev. 21:3). Every building in between is a sign; the signs are destroyed, and the thing they signify is not.

The room for the ark (vv. 16-20). All the gold and cedar and labour is for a windowless cube that held the ark, where God said there I will meet with you (Ex. 25:22), and which one man entered once a year with blood. Its shape returns at the end of the Bible in a city with no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple (Rev. 21:22). The covered stones and hidden gold say that the care was not for an audience but for the God who would be in the room.

The guards are still there (vv. 23-29). Cherubim first appear guarding the way back to Eden with a sword (Gen. 3:24). Here they stand over the place where God meets his people, and the sword is not mentioned; and the walls all round are carved with palm trees and open flowers. Eden is remembered in cedar and gold, but the innermost room is still closed. When Jesus died, the curtain before it was torn from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), and the way in is now through him (Hebrews 10:19–20).

Built to God's pattern, in seven years (vv. 37-38). Solomon did not design this house; he built to the drawing God gave David (1 Chron. 28:11-19), as Moses built the tabernacle to the pattern shown on the mountain (Ex. 25:40). The next verse gives thirteen years for his own house. As the note on verses 31-38 says, that is not by itself a rebuke, since the palace was several buildings and the temple's materials were gathered in advance, but the writer lets the reader notice.
6.examples:
Then: A building the size of a large barn went up on a hilltop over seven years without one blow of an iron tool being heard on the site: every stone measured, cut and finished miles away in the hill country and carried up already fitted, and when it was done, every one of those stones was panelled over in cedar so that nobody ever saw them again.

Now: three things. God's interruption in verses 11-13 is the one to carry, because the confusion it guards against is permanent: the condition attached to the greatest building project in Israel's history had nothing whatever to do with the building. It is very easy to mistake the thing you are doing for God for your standing with God, and the more magnificent the thing, the easier it gets. Our standing rests on the obedience of Christ, and what God asks of us is a walk with him that his Spirit makes possible. Second, the covered stones. Work done to a standard nobody will ever inspect, for an audience of one, is not wasted: it is most of what the Christian life actually consists of. And third, Peter's use of the quarry: the shaping happens off-site, out of sight, before the stone is set in place. If your life feels like being worked on in a noisy place a long way from anything that looks finished, that is where the cutting is supposed to happen, and the one doing it knows the place he is fitting you for.

7.title: The Palace and the Temple Furnishings
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house.<sup>2</sup>He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Its length was a hundred cubits and its breadth fifty cubits and its height thirty cubits, and it was built on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars.<sup>3</sup>And it was covered with cedar above the chambers that were on the forty-five pillars, fifteen in each row.<sup>4</sup>There were window frames in three rows, and window opposite window in three tiers.<sup>5</sup>All the doorways and windows had square frames, and window was opposite window in three tiers.<sup>6</sup>And he made the Hall of Pillars; its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth thirty cubits. There was a porch in front with pillars, and a canopy in front of them.<sup>7</sup>And he made the Hall of the Throne where he was to pronounce judgment, even the Hall of Judgment. It was finished with cedar from floor to rafters.<sup>8</sup>His own house where he was to dwell, in the other court at the back of the hall, was of like workmanship. Solomon also made a house like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had taken in marriage.<sup>9</sup>All these were made of costly stones, cut according to measure, sawed with saws, back and front, even from the foundation to the coping, and from the outside to the great court.<sup>10</sup>The foundation was of costly stones, huge stones, stones of eight and ten cubits.<sup>11</sup>And above were costly stones, cut according to measurement, and cedar.<sup>12</sup>The great court had three courses of cut stone all around, and a course of cedar beams; so had the inner court of the house of the LORD and the vestibule of the house.<sup>13</sup>And King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre.<sup>14</sup>He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in bronze. And he was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for making any work in bronze. He came to King Solomon and did all his work.<sup>15</sup>He cast two pillars of bronze. Eighteen cubits was the height of one pillar, and a line of twelve cubits measured its circumference. It was hollow, and its thickness was four fingers. The second pillar was the same.<sup>16</sup>He also made two capitals of cast bronze to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital was five cubits, and the height of the other capital was five cubits.<sup>17</sup>There were lattices of checker work with wreaths of chain work for the capitals on the tops of the pillars, a lattice for the one capital and a lattice for the other capital.<sup>18</sup>Likewise he made pomegranates in two rows around the one latticework to cover the capital that was on the top of the pillar, and he did the same with the other capital.<sup>19</sup>Now the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars in the vestibule were of lily-work, four cubits.<sup>20</sup>The capitals were on the two pillars and also above the rounded projection which was beside the latticework. There were two hundred pomegranates in two rows all around, and so with the other capital.<sup>21</sup>He set up the pillars at the vestibule of the temple. He set up the pillar on the south and called its name Jachin, and he set up the pillar on the north and called its name Boaz.<sup>22</sup>And on the tops of the pillars was lily-work. Thus the work of the pillars was finished.<sup>23</sup>Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference.<sup>24</sup>Under its brim were gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast.<sup>25</sup>It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward.<sup>26</sup>Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held two thousand baths.<sup>27</sup>He also made the ten stands of bronze. Each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.<sup>28</sup>This was the construction of the stands: they had panels, and the panels were set in the frames,<sup>29</sup>and on the panels that were set in the frames were lions, oxen, and cherubim. On the frames, both above and below the lions and oxen, there were wreaths of beveled work.<sup>30</sup>Moreover, each stand had four bronze wheels and axles of bronze, and at the four corners were supports for a basin. The supports were cast with wreaths at the side of each.<sup>31</sup>Its opening was within a crown that projected upward one cubit. Its opening was round, as a pedestal is made, a cubit and a half deep. At its opening there were carvings, and its panels were square, not round.<sup>32</sup>And the four wheels were underneath the panels. The axles of the wheels were of one piece with the stands, and the height of a wheel was a cubit and a half.<sup>33</sup>The wheels were made like a chariot wheel; their axles, their rims, their spokes, and their hubs were all cast.<sup>34</sup>There were four supports at the four corners of each stand. The supports were of one piece with the stands.<sup>35</sup>And on the top of the stand there was a round band half a cubit high; and on the top of the stand its stays and its panels were of one piece with it.<sup>36</sup>And on the surfaces of its stays and on its panels, he carved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, according to the space of each, with wreaths all around.<sup>37</sup>After this manner he made the ten stands. All of them were cast alike, of the same measure and the same form.<sup>38</sup>And he made ten basins of bronze. Each basin held forty baths, each basin measured four cubits, and there was a basin for each of the ten stands.<sup>39</sup>And he set the stands, five on the south side of the house, and five on the north side of the house. And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.<sup>40</sup>Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished all the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of the LORD:<sup>41</sup>the two pillars, the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars, and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars;<sup>42</sup>and the four hundred pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars;<sup>43</sup>the ten stands, and the ten basins on the stands;<sup>44</sup>and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath the sea.<sup>45</sup>Now the pots, the shovels, and the basins, all these vessels in the house of the LORD, which Hiram made for King Solomon, were of burnished bronze.<sup>46</sup>In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan.<sup>47</sup>And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because there were so many of them; the weight of the bronze was not ascertained.<sup>48</sup>So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of the LORD: the golden altar, the golden table for the bread of the Presence,<sup>49</sup>the lampstands of pure gold, five on the south side and five on the north, before the inner sanctuary; the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold;<sup>50</sup>the cups, snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold; and the sockets of gold, for the doors of the innermost part of the house, the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the nave of the temple.<sup>51</sup>Thus all the work that King Solomon did on the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, the silver, the gold, and the vessels, and stored them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD.
7.overview:
The previous sentence in the book was he was seven years in building it, about the house of the LORD. This one gives thirteen years for his own, and the palace is then described at greater length than the temple. Among its rooms is a courtroom panelled in cedar, built by the man who asked for an understanding mind.

Then the bronze, cast by a widow's son from Naphtali who is described in the words used of Bezalel, the tabernacle's Spirit-filled craftsman: two named pillars at the door that hold nothing up, a vast basin for washing on twelve oxen, wheeled stands, and at the end the gifts David dedicated to a house he was not allowed to build.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thirteen years for his own house (v. 1): the House of the Forest of Lebanon (vv. 2-5), the Hall of Pillars and the Hall of Judgment (vv. 6-7), his dwelling and a house for Pharaoh's daughter (v. 8), all of costly stone (vv. 9-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Seven years for the house of the LORD; thirteen for his own. The writer puts the two figures in consecutive sentences, describes the palace at greater length than the temple, and lets the reader weigh it.
verseByVerse.examples: The daughter of Pharaoh gets a house of her own, named as such. She entered the story in 3:1, before Gibeon and before the temple, and she is named first among the women who turn his heart in 11:1. The writer keeps mentioning her and never comments.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon was building his own house thirteen years, and he finished his entire house. He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. Its length was a hundred cubits and its breadth fifty cubits and its height thirty cubits, and it was built on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams on the pillars. And it was covered with cedar above the chambers that were on the forty-five pillars, fifteen in each row. There were window frames in three rows, and window opposite window in three tiers. All the doorways and windows had square frames, and window was opposite window in three tiers. And he made the Hall of Pillars; its length was fifty cubits, and its breadth thirty cubits. There was a porch in front with pillars, and a canopy in front of them. And he made the Hall of the Throne where he was to pronounce judgment, even the Hall of Judgment. It was finished with cedar from floor to rafters. His own house where he was to dwell, in the other court at the back of the hall, was of like workmanship. Solomon also made a house like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter whom he had taken in marriage. All these were made of costly stones, cut according to measure, sawed with saws, back and front, even from the foundation to the coping, and from the outside to the great court. The foundation was of costly stones, huge stones, stones of eight and ten cubits. And above were costly stones, cut according to measurement, and cedar. The great court had three courses of cut stone all around, and a course of cedar beams; so had the inner court of the house of the LORD and the vestibule of the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The previous sentence in the book gave seven years for the house of the LORD. This one gives thirteen for the king's own house. The writer sets the two figures in consecutive verses with no comment of any kind. He does not say it was too long. He does not say Solomon loved his own comfort. He gives a seven and then a thirteen and moves on to the specifications.

Then he does something else, which is harder to miss the more carefully you read. He describes the palace complex at greater length and in more admiring detail than he described the temple.

Some things can fairly be said in mitigation. The palace complex is much bigger (several buildings, including an armoury, a colonnade, a courtroom, a residence and a second residence), where the temple is one modest structure. And the two projects overlap; the twenty years of 9:10 covers both. Probably nobody in Israel thought thirteen years unreasonable for a royal quarter.

The figures are still seven and thirteen, and the writer still put them next to each other.

The House of the Forest of Lebanon is a hundred and fifty feet by seventy-five by forty-five, which makes it more than four times the floor area of the temple.

It is called the House of the Forest of Lebanon because of the forty-five cedar pillars standing in rows inside it: a man walking through it was walking through trees. Chapter 10 tells us what it was for: three hundred shields of beaten gold were kept there (10:17). It is an armoury and a treasury and a very large statement.

One room deserves a moment: the Hall of Judgment, a purpose-built courtroom. The man who asked at Gibeon for an understanding mind to govern your people, that I may discern between good and evil has built a room for doing it in, panelled in cedar from floor to rafters.

Two things should be held together here. It is right that a king who takes justice seriously should have somewhere proper to hear cases; that is 2 Samuel 8:15 given an address.

And a hall is not a hearing. Two prostitutes with no standing walked in front of this man in chapter 3 and got a verdict. What Absalom found at the gate a generation earlier was not a shortage of buildings; it was that there is no man designated by the king to hear you (2 Sam. 15:3).

The room is not the thing. It is the same point God made in the middle of the temple site one chapter ago.

Pharaoh's daughter is here again. She arrived in 3:1, in the first sentence of the reign after the executions, before Gibeon and before the temple. She gets a house of her own here, built to the same standard as the Hall of Judgment. Chapter 9 records that she went up from the city of David to her own house (9:24); Chronicles gives the reason, that the places where the ark of the LORD has come are holy (2 Chron. 8:11).

And chapter 11 opens: now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh (11:1).

Five mentions in nine chapters (3:1; 7:8; 9:16, 24; 11:1), each one flat and factual, and no comment attached to any of them. The writer is doing what he has done since the first chapter: putting things down in order and trusting the reader to be holding them when the account comes due.

The last verse of the section quietly joins the two building projects together. The great court of the palace is built to the same specification as the inner court of the temple: three courses of cut stone and a course of cedar beams.

The house of God and the house of the king are going up on the same hill, out of the same quarry, by the same workforce, to the same standard.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hiram, a widow's son from Naphtali, skilled in bronze (vv. 13-14), casts the two pillars and their capitals (vv. 15-20) and sets them at the vestibule as Jachin and Boaz (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The craftsman is half-Israelite, a widow's son from Naphtali by a Tyrian father, and he is described in the words used of Bezalel, whom God filled with his Spirit to build the tabernacle (Ex. 31:1-5).
verseByVerse.examples: The two pillars stand at the door, twenty-seven feet high, free of the building. They hold nothing up; their whole function is to say something as a person walks in.

verseByVerse.quote: And King Solomon sent and brought Hiram from Tyre. He was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man of Tyre, a worker in bronze. And he was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill for making any work in bronze. He came to King Solomon and did all his work. He cast two pillars of bronze. Eighteen cubits was the height of one pillar, and a line of twelve cubits measured its circumference. It was hollow, and its thickness was four fingers. The second pillar was the same. He also made two capitals of cast bronze to set on the tops of the pillars. The height of the one capital was five cubits, and the height of the other capital was five cubits. There were lattices of checker work with wreaths of chain work for the capitals on the tops of the pillars, a lattice for the one capital and a lattice for the other capital. Likewise he made pomegranates in two rows around the one latticework to cover the capital that was on the top of the pillar, and he did the same with the other capital. Now the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars in the vestibule were of lily-work, four cubits. The capitals were on the two pillars and also above the rounded projection which was beside the latticework. There were two hundred pomegranates in two rows all around, and so with the other capital. He set up the pillars at the vestibule of the temple. He set up the pillar on the south and called its name Jachin, and he set up the pillar on the north and called its name Boaz. And on the tops of the pillars was lily-work. Thus the work of the pillars was finished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This Hiram is a different man from the king. He is the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali. His mother was an Israelite from a northern tribe, and she is a widow, and her son is the finest bronze-worker in the region. His father was a Tyrian.

(Chronicles calls his mother a woman of the daughters of Dan (2 Chronicles 2:14). Probably she was a Danite by birth who lived in, or married into, Naphtali; the two notes need not conflict.)

So the man who casts every piece of bronze in the house of the LORD is half a foreigner, brought in from a Phoenician port, and the son of a woman with no husband.

The book keeps doing this: the timber is foreign, the stonemasons of Gebal are foreign, and now the metalwork. Then comes a description a reader of the Pentateuch will recognise, full of wisdom, understanding, and skill. In Exodus God names the man who will make the tabernacle: see, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri... and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze (Ex. 31:2-4).

That correspondence is deliberate, and it says something Scripture says in very few places and means every time. Skill in a craft is a gift of God. It is not a natural talent that God happens to tolerate, nor a lesser thing than teaching or prophesying: the ability to make a beautiful object out of metal is listed in Exodus as a filling of the Spirit of God, and both of the men described this way work in metal.

A widow's son from Naphtali, who learned his trade in a Phoenician foundry, is filled with wisdom and understanding and skill, and he casts the pillars of the house of God.

The pillars are twenty-seven feet high and about six feet across, hollow, with walls three inches thick.

Casting an object that size in bronze in the tenth century before Christ is a serious technical achievement, and verse 46 tells us where it was done: out in the Jordan valley, in the clay ground, where there was earth suitable for the moulds.

The capitals carry lilies and pomegranates, seven and a half feet of them on each pillar.

The temple interior was carved with palm trees and open flowers, and the great bronze basin has lilies at the brim, and here are pomegranates and lily-work in cast metal. Everything decorative in this building is a growing thing.

The two pillars have names. Jachin probably means "he will establish"; the meaning of Boaz is uncertain, and it is wiser not to build on guesses. But a king does not name two columns unless they are there to say something, and the pillars are free-standing. They are not part of the structure. They hold up no roof and support no beam; they stand in front of the vestibule, one either side of the door, carrying nothing at all.

Which means their entire function is to say something. Every priest going in to serve, and every Israelite coming up to the courts, walked between two enormous bronze columns whose only purpose was to stand at the door of the house of the God who had promised David, I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever (2 Sam. 7:13).

Two and a half centuries later a king of Judah will strip the gold off the doors of this house to pay tribute to Assyria. A century after that, when Nebuchadnezzar's men come, the writer of Kings records what they did with these pillars: and the pillars of bronze that were in the house of the LORD... the Chaldeans broke in pieces and carried the bronze to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13).

The promise to David was still true, which is what the rest of the Old Testament is about. An angel would one day say of Mary’s son that the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David... and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:32–33). The bronze went to Babylon; the throne it stood beside went to Christ.

Kings gives the pillars 18 cubits; Chronicles 35 (2 Chronicles 3:15), most likely the two pillars’ combined length, or a copying difference.
verseByVerse.note: Jachin probably means “he will establish”; the meaning of Boaz is uncertain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–39 — The Sea of Cast Metal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sea of cast metal on twelve oxen (vv. 23-26), the ten bronze stands on wheels (vv. 27-37), and their ten basins (vv. 38-39).
verseByVerse.theology: The sea is the laver of the tabernacle at enormous scale, and Chronicles says plainly what it was for: the sea was for the priests to wash in (2 Chron. 4:6).
verseByVerse.examples: Twelve oxen carry it, three to each point of the compass: probably the tribes, facing the whole earth, holding up water for washing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he made the sea of cast metal. It was round, ten cubits from brim to brim, and five cubits high, and a line of thirty cubits measured its circumference. Under its brim were gourds, for ten cubits, compassing the sea all around. The gourds were in two rows, cast with it when it was cast. It stood on twelve oxen, three facing north, three facing west, three facing south, and three facing east. The sea was set on them, and all their rear parts were inward. Its thickness was a handbreadth, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily. It held two thousand baths. He also made the ten stands of bronze. Each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high. This was the construction of the stands: they had panels, and the panels were set in the frames, and on the panels that were set in the frames were lions, oxen, and cherubim. On the frames, both above and below the lions and oxen, there were wreaths of beveled work. Moreover, each stand had four bronze wheels and axles of bronze, and at the four corners were supports for a basin. The supports were cast with wreaths at the side of each. Its opening was within a crown that projected upward one cubit. Its opening was round, as a pedestal is made, a cubit and a half deep. At its opening there were carvings, and its panels were square, not round. And the four wheels were underneath the panels. The axles of the wheels were of one piece with the stands, and the height of a wheel was a cubit and a half. The wheels were made like a chariot wheel; their axles, their rims, their spokes, and their hubs were all cast. There were four supports at the four corners of each stand. The supports were of one piece with the stands. And on the top of the stand there was a round band half a cubit high; and on the top of the stand its stays and its panels were of one piece with it. And on the surfaces of its stays and on its panels, he carved cherubim, lions, and palm trees, according to the space of each, with wreaths all around. After this manner he made the ten stands. All of them were cast alike, of the same measure and the same form. And he made ten basins of bronze. Each basin held forty baths, each basin measured four cubits, and there was a basin for each of the ten stands. And he set the stands, five on the south side of the house, and five on the north side of the house. And he set the sea at the southeast corner of the house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sea is a bronze basin fifteen feet across and seven and a half feet deep, cast in one piece.

It is called the sea, which is not a technical term but a description of the impression it made. Nobody had seen that much standing water in a vessel.

(The measurements have generated a good deal of unnecessary argument about the ratio of circumference to diameter. The figures are round numbers to the nearest cubit in an account describing a physical object; the brim was like the flower of a lily, so it flared, and the walls were a handbreadth thick, so a diameter across the outer brim and a circumference taken lower down or inside would not give the ratio of a perfect circle. There is no error here to explain away.)

Twelve bronze oxen carry it, facing outward to the four points of the compass. The twelve probably recall the tribes, and the four directions the whole earth. And what they are holding up, facing outward, is a great mass of water for washing.

It held something in the order of ten thousand gallons, and it was for the priests to wash in. That sends the reader back to Exodus, and to a small basin and a hard sentence. God told Moses to make a bronze laver and set it between the tent of meeting and the altar and put water in it, with which Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet. When they go into the tent of meeting, or when they come near the altar to minister... they shall wash with water, so that they may not die (Ex. 30:18-21).
