A man who is going to handle holy things does not simply walk up. He washes first, and the law attaches the penalty in as many words. And when Israel builds the permanent house, the little laver becomes ten thousand gallons standing on twelve oxen.

There is a great deal of blood in this building and there is also a great deal of water, and both of them are there because people cannot come near God as they are.

The New Testament takes up both. Because Jesus has opened a way through his own blood, believers may draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water (Hebrews 10:19–22). What ten thousand gallons could only picture, he does: he makes unclean people fit to come in.

The stands are ten wheeled trolleys, six feet square, with panels showing lions, oxen and cherubim.

The writer spends eleven verses on the engineering of these things (the frames, the axles, the wheels, the hubs and spokes and rims, the wreaths on the supports), in more mechanical detail than he gave for anything in the temple itself.

Each carried a basin of about two hundred gallons, so that water could be moved about the court. Chronicles supplies the use, and the division of labour is exact: in these they were to rinse off what was used for the burnt offering (2 Chron. 4:6). The great sea is for the men; the ten wheeled basins are for the equipment.

Two thousand baths here, three thousand in 2 Chronicles 4:5: either Chronicles gives the full capacity and Kings the usual filling, or a numeral was miscopied.
verseByVerse.note: A bath was a liquid measure of roughly 22 litres (about 5 gallons), though estimates vary.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–51 — The Weight of the Bronze Was Not Ascertained
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of Hiram's bronze, cast in the Jordan plain and never weighed (vv. 40-47); the gold furnishings (vv. 48-50); and David's dedicated things brought into the finished house (v. 51).
verseByVerse.theology: One measurement was never taken: the bronze was simply too much to weigh.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends by bringing in what David dedicated: the tribute of Edom and Moab and Ammon and Amalek and Hadadezer, set apart for the LORD by a man who was told he could not build (2 Sam. 8:11-12). He funded it for years and never saw a stone laid.

verseByVerse.quote: Hiram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Hiram finished all the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of the LORD: the two pillars, the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars, and the two latticeworks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars; and the four hundred pomegranates for the two latticeworks, two rows of pomegranates for each latticework, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars; the ten stands, and the ten basins on the stands; and the one sea, and the twelve oxen underneath the sea. Now the pots, the shovels, and the basins, all these vessels in the house of the LORD, which Hiram made for King Solomon, were of burnished bronze. In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zarethan. And Solomon left all the vessels unweighed, because there were so many of them; the weight of the bronze was not ascertained. So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of the LORD: the golden altar, the golden table for the bread of the Presence, the lampstands of pure gold, five on the south side and five on the north, before the inner sanctuary; the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold; the cups, snuffers, basins, dishes for incense, and fire pans, of pure gold; and the sockets of gold, for the doors of the innermost part of the house, the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the nave of the temple. Thus all the work that King Solomon did on the house of the LORD was finished. And Solomon brought in the things that David his father had dedicated, the silver, the gold, and the vessels, and stored them in the treasuries of the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The inventory begins with pots and shovels. The same craftsman who cast a twenty-seven-foot column and a ten-thousand-gallon basin also made the pots for carrying ash and the shovels for clearing the altar, and the writer lists them in the same sentence as the pillars.

There was a great deal of ordinary work in that building. Somebody had to shovel out a fire that never went out.

Verse 46 gives the one glimpse of how it was done. The casting happened forty miles away, down in the Jordan valley, because that is where the right clay was. Everything in these chapters was made somewhere else and brought: the stone finished in the hill country, the cedar rafted down the coast from Lebanon, the bronze cast in the mud of the Jordan plain.

Nothing was manufactured on the mountain. Everything in these two chapters has been measured, down to four hundred pomegranates counted; the bronze alone was not weighed, because there was too much of it.

Read plainly, it is a note about scale, and that is probably all the writer intends by it.

It is also the first thing in this reign that was too big to count, and it is not the last. Within four chapters the gold coming in yearly will be six hundred and sixty-six talents; the silver will be as common in Jerusalem as stone (10:27); there will be seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines. A reign that begins by measuring everything to the cubit ends with quantities nobody bothers to total.

The gold furniture is the tabernacle's at scale: Moses had one lampstand, and Solomon has ten. Even the door sockets, the hinge-pivots in the floor that nobody would ever see, are gold.

The last verse of the building account belongs to a man who has been dead for more than a decade.

The dedicated things are listed in 2 Samuel 8: the tribute of Toi of Hamath, and the plunder of Edom and Moab and Ammon and the Philistines and Amalek and the whole treasury of Hadadezer of Zobah: these also King David dedicated to the LORD, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued (2 Sam. 8:11-12).

He could not build. He was told plainly why: you have shed much blood and have waged great wars (1 Chron. 22:8). And what he did about it, for the rest of his working life, was win wars and hand every penny of the proceeds to a project he was forbidden to work on, and lay up gold and silver and bronze and iron beyond weighing, and give his own personal fortune to it at the end, and die before the foundations went in (1 Chron. 22:14; 29:2-5).

The house is finished, and the last thing carried into it is his.

7.theology:
Seven and thirteen (vv. 1-12). The writer accuses no one. He sets the two figures side by side, gives the palace a longer and warmer description than the temple, and lets the reader weigh it, mitigations and all. The great court of the palace is even built to the pattern of the temple's inner court: the house of God and the house of the king go up on the same hill, from the same quarry, to the same standard.

A hall is not a hearing (v. 7). The man who asked at Gibeon for an understanding mind builds a courtroom, cedar from floor to rafters. It is right that justice should have a proper address, and the Hall of Judgment is 2 Samuel 8:15 given a building. But what makes justice is a king who listens, as Solomon did to two prostitutes in chapter 3; what Absalom exploited at the gate a generation earlier was not a shortage of rooms but the lack of anyone to hear. The room is not the thing, which is what God said in the middle of the temple site one chapter ago.

Pharaoh's daughter (v. 8). Five flat, factual mentions in nine chapters (3:1; 7:8; 9:16, 24; 11:1), with no comment attached to any of them, until 11:1 names her among the women who turned his heart. The writer puts things down in order and trusts the reader to be holding them when the account comes due.

Skill as a gift of the Spirit (vv. 13-14). Hiram is described as Bezalel was, the man God filled with his Spirit to work in gold, silver and bronze for the tabernacle (Ex. 31:2-4). Scripture says this in very few places and means it every time: skill in a craft is a gift of God, not a natural talent he tolerates and not a lesser thing than teaching or prophesying. And the man who had it most here was half a foreigner and a widow's son.

Pillars that hold nothing up (vv. 15-22). Their whole function is to stand at the door of the house of the God who had promised to establish David's throne forever (2 Sam. 7:13). Nearly four centuries later the Chaldeans broke them in pieces and carried the bronze to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13). The promise was still true: it is kept in Mary’s son, to whom God gives the throne of his father David (Luke 1:32).

So that they may not die (vv. 23-39). The law told the priests to wash before they came near the altar, and attached the penalty in as many words (Ex. 30:18-21); here the little laver of the wilderness becomes a sea. There is a great deal of blood in this building and a great deal of water, and both are there because people cannot come near God as they are. The washing the sea pictured is given in Christ: through his blood we draw near with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water (Hebrews 10:22).

Too much to count (vv. 40-50). Everything is measured to the cubit except the bronze. Read plainly it is a note about scale, and that is probably all the writer intends; but it is the first thing in this reign too big to count, and by chapter 11 the gold, the silver and the wives are past counting too. Alongside the splendour stand the pots and shovels: somebody had to shovel out a fire that never went out.

The last thing carried in (v. 51). David could not build, because he had shed much blood (1 Chron. 22:8). He spent the rest of his life handing the spoils of his wars to a project he was forbidden to work on, and died before the foundations went in (1 Chron. 22:14; 29:2-5). Some of the best work God gives his people is finished by someone else. The house is complete, and the last thing carried into it is his.
7.examples:
Then: Two hollow bronze columns twenty-seven feet high were cast in the mud of the Jordan valley, hauled forty miles up to Jerusalem, and stood one on either side of the temple door holding up absolutely nothing, because their entire purpose was to stand at the door of the house of the God who had promised to establish David's throne forever.

Now: three things. Verse 1 is the writer's method at its purest: he does not accuse Solomon of anything, he puts a seven and a thirteen in consecutive sentences, and anybody honest can do the arithmetic on their own life with the same two columns. It is safe to do, before a God who forgives misplaced loves and whose Spirit reorders them. Second, Hiram the craftsman, because Scripture says something here it says almost nowhere else: the ability to make something beautiful out of metal is described in the language of the filling of the Spirit of God. Skill in a trade is a gift, and the man who had it most was half a foreigner and a widow's son. And third, the pillars. They carried no weight and were broken up and carted to Babylon in the end, and the promise they stood beside was true the whole time and stayed true after they were gone.

8.title: The Glory Fills the House: Solomon's Prayer
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel, before King Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion.<sup>2</sup>And all the men of Israel assembled to King Solomon at the feast in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month.<sup>3</sup>And all the elders of Israel came, and the priests took up the ark.<sup>4</sup>And they brought up the ark of the LORD, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the priests and the Levites brought them up.<sup>5</sup>And King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, were with him before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered.<sup>6</sup>Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the Most Holy Place, underneath the wings of the cherubim.<sup>7</sup>For the cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim overshadowed the ark and its poles.<sup>8</sup>And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary; but they could not be seen from outside. And they are there to this day.<sup>9</sup>There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>And when the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD,<sup>11</sup>so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness.<sup>13</sup>I have indeed built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever."<sup>14</sup>Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood.<sup>15</sup>And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father, saying,<sup>16</sup>'Since the day that I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there. But I chose David to be over my people Israel.'<sup>17</sup>Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>18</sup>But the LORD said to David my father, 'Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart.<sup>19</sup>Nevertheless, you shall not build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name.'<sup>20</sup>Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made. For I have risen in the place of David my father, and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>21</sup>And there I have provided a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with our fathers, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt."<sup>22</sup>Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven,<sup>23</sup>and said, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above or on earth beneath, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart;<sup>24</sup>you have kept with your servant David my father what you declared to him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day.<sup>25</sup>Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you have promised him, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me as you have walked before me.'<sup>26</sup>Now therefore, O God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken to your servant David my father.<sup>27</sup>"But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!<sup>28</sup>Yet have regard to the prayer of your servant and to his plea, O LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that your servant prays before you this day,<sup>29</sup>that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which you have said, 'My name shall be there,' that you may listen to the prayer that your servant offers toward this place.<sup>30</sup>And listen to the plea of your servant and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. And listen in heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive.<sup>31</sup>"If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath and comes and swears his oath before your altar in this house,<sup>32</sup>then hear in heaven and act and judge your servants, condemning the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.<sup>33</sup>"When your people Israel are defeated before the enemy because they have sinned against you, and if they turn again to you and acknowledge your name and pray and plead with you in this house,<sup>34</sup>then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel and bring them again to the land that you gave to their fathers.<sup>35</sup>"When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and acknowledge your name and turn from their sin, when you afflict them,<sup>36</sup>then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and grant rain upon your land, which you have given to your people as an inheritance.<sup>37</sup>"If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew or locust or caterpillar, if their enemy besieges them in the land at their gates, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is,<sup>38</sup>whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all your people Israel, each knowing the affliction of his own heart and stretching out his hands toward this house,<sup>39</sup>then hear in heaven your dwelling place and forgive and act and render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways (for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind),<sup>40</sup>that they may fear you all the days that they live in the land that you gave to our fathers.<sup>41</sup>"Likewise, when a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, comes from a far country for your name's sake<sup>42</sup>(for they shall hear of your great name and your mighty hand, and of your outstretched arm), when he comes and prays toward this house,<sup>43</sup>hear in heaven your dwelling place and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you, in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel, and that they may know that this house that I have built is called by your name.<sup>44</sup>"If your people go out to battle against their enemy, by whatever way you shall send them, and they pray to the LORD toward the city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name,<sup>45</sup>then hear in heaven their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause.<sup>46</sup>"If they sin against you— for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to the land of the enemy, far off or near,<sup>47</sup>yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive, and repent and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly,'<sup>48</sup>if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies, who carried them captive, and pray to you toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name,<sup>49</sup>then hear in heaven your dwelling place their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause<sup>50</sup>and forgive your people who have sinned against you, and all their transgressions that they have committed against you, and grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive, that they may have compassion on them<sup>51</sup>(for they are your people, and your heritage, which you brought out of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace).<sup>52</sup>Let your eyes be open to the plea of your servant and to the plea of your people Israel, giving ear to them whenever they call to you.<sup>53</sup>For you separated them from among all the peoples of the earth to be your heritage, as you declared through Moses your servant, when you brought our fathers out of Egypt, O Lord GOD."<sup>54</sup>Now as Solomon finished offering all this prayer and plea to the LORD, he arose from before the altar of the LORD, where he had knelt with hands outstretched toward heaven.<sup>55</sup>And he stood and blessed all the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying,<sup>56</sup>"Blessed be the LORD who has given rest to his people Israel, according to all that he promised. Not one word has failed of all his good promise, which he spoke by Moses his servant.<sup>57</sup>The LORD our God be with us, as he was with our fathers. May he not leave us or forsake us,<sup>58</sup>that he may incline our hearts to him, to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his rules, which he commanded our fathers.<sup>59</sup>Let these words of mine, with which I have pleaded before the LORD, be near to the LORD our God day and night, and may he maintain the cause of his servant and the cause of his people Israel, as each day requires,<sup>60</sup>that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God; there is no other.<sup>61</sup>Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments, as at this day."<sup>62</sup>Then the king, and all Israel with him, offered sacrifice before the LORD.<sup>63</sup>Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people of Israel dedicated the house of the LORD.<sup>64</sup>The same day the king consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the LORD was too small to receive the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings.<sup>65</sup>So Solomon held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt, before the LORD our God, seven days.<sup>66</sup>On the eighth day he sent the people away, and they blessed the king and went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people.
8.overview:
Everything in the last three chapters has been building toward moving one object half a mile uphill, in the week of Booths. The ark, holding nothing but the two tablets of the covenant, is set in its room; the cloud fills the house, as at the tabernacle, and the priests cannot stand to minister.

Then the sentence the book turns on, spoken by the builder on the day of dedication: will God indeed dwell on the earth, when heaven itself cannot contain him? He corrects himself in public, and then kneels and prays one of the longest prayers in the Old Testament, most of whose petitions are about sin, with the refrain hear in heaven... and forgive. The answer to his question came a thousand years later in a way he could not have guessed: God did dwell on the earth, in the flesh of his Son (John 1:14), and the forgiveness this prayer kept asking for was secured by that Son’s one sacrifice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Glory of the LORD Filled the House
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ark brought up from Zion at the feast of the seventh month, with the tent of meeting and the holy vessels (vv. 1-5); set beneath the cherubim with the poles left in (vv. 6-8); nothing in it but the two tablets (v. 9); the cloud filling the house (vv. 10-11); and Solomon's first words (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The cloud fills the house as it filled the tabernacle when Moses finished it (Ex. 40:35). The priests have to walk out of the building because God has come into it.
verseByVerse.examples: Inside the ark are two stone tablets and nothing else: a copy of the covenant God made with slaves he had brought out of Egypt. That is what the whole house was built to hold.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers' houses of the people of Israel, before King Solomon in Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD out of the city of David, which is Zion. And all the men of Israel assembled to King Solomon at the feast in the month Ethanim, which is the seventh month. And all the elders of Israel came, and the priests took up the ark. And they brought up the ark of the LORD, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the priests and the Levites brought them up. And King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel, who had assembled before him, were with him before the ark, sacrificing so many sheep and oxen that they could not be counted or numbered. Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, in the Most Holy Place, underneath the wings of the cherubim. For the cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, so that the cherubim overshadowed the ark and its poles. And the poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the Holy Place before the inner sanctuary; but they could not be seen from outside. And they are there to this day. There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone that Moses put there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the people of Israel, when they came out of the land of Egypt. And when the priests came out of the Holy Place, a cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD. Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that he would dwell in thick darkness. I have indeed built you an exalted house, a place for you to dwell in forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in the last three chapters has been building toward moving one object about half a mile uphill.

The ark has been in the tent David pitched for it since 2 Samuel 6, since the second attempt, after Uzzah, when it was carried properly on poles on Levites' shoulders and a king danced in front of it in a linen ephod.

The seventh month is Tishri, and the feast is Booths, the week when Israel lived in shelters made of branches to remember that their fathers had no houses at all, and God travelled with them.

That is the week Solomon chooses to move God into a permanent building.

The tent comes too, and this is the end of something. The tent of meeting is the tabernacle, the structure Moses made at Sinai to a pattern God showed him, carried through forty years of wilderness, set up at Shiloh, and standing at Gibeon in Solomon's own day. It is brought up and stored, and nearly five centuries of portable worship end in this verse.

The two olivewood cherubim from chapter 6, their wings meeting in the middle of the room, now stand over the ark.

So there are now two sets of cherubim in that room: The great olivewood ones Solomon made, and the small hammered-gold ones on the mercy seat that Moses made, where God said there I will meet with you (Ex. 25:22).

The poles stay in, as the law required: the poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it (Ex. 25:15). They were never removed, ever, so that the ark could always be lifted and never handled. That is the law a cart made it impossible to keep, and a man died at a threshing floor because of it.

Now the ark has arrived at the place it will stay for nearly four hundred years, and still the poles stay in.

(A reader may ask how the poles can be there to this day when the temple was burned before the book was finished. The phrase most likely comes from the earlier record the writer used, written while the temple stood, and he kept its wording.)

God is settling into a stone house and the carrying poles are left where they are, and their ends can be seen sticking out from inside the Holy Place, which is presumably why the writer mentions it at all. A priest standing in the outer room could see them: a reminder that God is not tied to the building.

Here is what all of it was for. Seven years of building. A hundred and fifty thousand labourers. Cedar from Lebanon rafted down a coast, stone finished at the quarry so no iron would be heard on the mountain, gold over every surface until no stone was seen, two bronze pillars twenty-seven feet high, a basin holding ten thousand gallons on twelve oxen. All of it to make a room, for a box, containing two pieces of stone. And the writer says what the stones are and when they were cut: the tablets Moses put there at Horeb, from the covenant made as Israel came out of Egypt.

The centre of the most expensive building in Israel's history is a copy of the terms on which God bound himself to a company of runaway slaves.

One note on the contents, since readers ask. Hebrews describes the tabernacle as having in the ark a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron's staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant (Heb. 9:4). Exodus and Numbers record the jar and the rod being placed before the testimony (Ex. 16:34; Num. 17:10), which may mean in front of the ark rather than inside it, and in any case this verse describes the situation four centuries later. What is certain is what Kings says: by Solomon's day there were two stone tablets in that box and nothing else.

And it works. The priests set the ark in place, walk out of the inner room, and the building fills with cloud until they cannot do their jobs. They have to leave.

Four hundred and eighty years earlier, Moses finished the tabernacle in the wilderness and set up everything exactly as he had been told, and then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle (Ex. 40:34-35).

The same thing, in the same words, at the completion of the same design at twice the scale.

God has done what he did before. He has come into the building.

And the effect on the professionals is that they cannot work, which is not how anybody plans a dedication. The priests have spent their lives learning a liturgy and the moment the glory arrives the liturgy stops, and a room full of trained men walk out into the courtyard because there is nothing they can do in there.

The room has no windows, and the cloud is in it, and the king says the darkness is the point.

God said at Sinai that he would come in a thick cloud (Ex. 19:9), and Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was (Ex. 20:21). The dark is not the absence of God in that room. It is where he is.

Solomon's first sentence about his own work is a proud one, and he is about to correct it himself fourteen verses later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–27 — Will God Indeed Dwell on the Earth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon blesses the assembly and rehearses the promise to David, now fulfilled (vv. 14-21); then, before the altar with hands spread to heaven, he praises the covenant-keeping God, holds him to his word (vv. 22-26), and asks whether God will indeed dwell on the earth (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: He has just spent seven years and the wealth of a kingdom on this building, and on the day he dedicates it he says out loud that it cannot possibly do what it was built for. Nobody made him say that.
verseByVerse.examples: He prays before the altar in the courtyard with his hands open toward heaven, and verse 54 reveals that he had been kneeling.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king turned around and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood. And he said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who with his hand has fulfilled what he promised with his mouth to David my father, saying, 'Since the day that I brought my people Israel out of Egypt, I chose no city out of all the tribes of Israel in which to build a house, that my name might be there. But I chose David to be over my people Israel.' Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. But the LORD said to David my father, 'Whereas it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart. Nevertheless, you shall not build the house, but your son who shall be born to you shall build the house for my name.' Now the LORD has fulfilled his promise that he made. For I have risen in the place of David my father, and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised, and I have built the house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. And there I have provided a place for the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that he made with our fathers, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt." Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven, and said, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like you, in heaven above or on earth beneath, keeping covenant and showing steadfast love to your servants who walk before you with all their heart; you have kept with your servant David my father what you declared to him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand have fulfilled it this day. Now therefore, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you have promised him, saying, 'You shall not lack a man to sit before me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons pay close attention to their way, to walk before me as you have walked before me.' Now therefore, O God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you have spoken to your servant David my father. "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain you; how much less this house that I have built!
verseByVerse.commentary:
He begins with a promise being kept, and the phrasing is exact: what he promised with his mouth, done with his hand.

Look at what God says he chose. For four hundred and eighty years, from the exodus to this morning, God picked no city and no site for a house. What he chose was a man.

That is the answer to the whole question of chapter 6 stated from the other direction. God's interest was never in real estate. He selected a shepherd out of a field in Bethlehem and made promises to him, and the building is downstream of that. The promise ran on past Solomon to another son of David from Bethlehem, who is faithful over God's house as a son, and whose house is his people (Hebrews 3:6).

You did well that it was in your heart is one of the kindest sentences in the Old Testament, and it is easy to read past.

David wanted to build the temple and was refused. He never laid a stone of it; he was told no, and told why, and died more than a decade before this morning. And God says it was good that he wanted to. The desire is commended even though the project was denied. That is not a consolation prize and it is not politeness. God is saying that the wanting itself was right and that he saw it and valued it.

Anybody who has had a genuine desire to do something for God and been prevented (by health, by circumstance, by other people's decisions, by simply being the wrong person for it) is looking at the verse that speaks to it. The thing was refused. The wanting was not wasted.

Twice in four verses he grounds all of this in the exodus. The covenant in the box was made with people coming out of Egypt, and the building exists to house it.

Notice where he is standing: not on a throne, not in the building, but before the altar in the courtyard, in front of everybody, with his hands open and lifted. Verse 54 will add something this verse does not: he was on his knees.

The prayer opens where every good prayer in Scripture opens: with who God is.

And the thing he singles out is not power or majesty but keeping covenant and showing steadfast love. God's distinguishing characteristic, in the mouth of a man dedicating a temple, is that he keeps his promises.

He prays the promise back, which is exactly what his father did in the same situation.

When Nathan brought the covenant to David, David went in and sat before the LORD and said do as you have spoken, and gave his reason: you... have made this revelation to your servant... therefore your servant has found courage to pray this prayer to you (2 Sam. 7:25-27).

Solomon does the same thing. Let your word be confirmed. He is not informing God of anything. He is taking him at his word in his hearing.

Verse 27 is one of the theological centres of the book, and what matters is who says it and when: the man who has just finished seven years of work, with conscripted labour, the finest timber in the world, and gold over every surface.

He is standing in front of it, on the day of its dedication, with the glory of God visibly inside it and the entire nation watching, and he says that it cannot possibly hold God.

Will God indeed dwell on the earth? The question is genuine, and it is not "will God dwell in this building" but whether God will dwell on the earth at all. Is such a thing even a category?

Neither the sky nor the sky beyond the sky will hold him; there is no volume of anything anywhere that is large enough.

And then he adds the four words that make the sentence what it is: that I have built. He does not distance himself from it. He names it as his own work and says his own work is not adequate to the purpose, on the day the work was finished.

Nobody made him say this, and no prophet stood there to correct him. The assembly would have been perfectly satisfied with verse 13, and he corrects it himself fourteen verses later, out loud, in public.

That is what an understanding mind looks like when it has been used for seven years. He has thought about what he is doing, and the more magnificent it got the clearer it became that it could not do the one thing it was for.

The sentence has a long life ahead of it. Isaiah picks it up and gives it as God's own words: heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool; what is the house that you would build for me?... All these things my hand has made... But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word (Isa. 66:1-2).

And Stephen echoes Solomon, standing in front of the council that was about to stone him for speaking against the temple: yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands (Acts 7:48). And Paul, standing on the Areopagus in a city full of temples: the God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man (Acts 17:24).

It was said by the man who built the finest religious building of his age, on the day he opened it.

Where does God dwell now? The temple pointed to Christ, who spoke of the temple of his body (John 2:21), and to the church, God’s temple by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 3:16). Solomon’s question has its astonishing answer in him: God did dwell on the earth, and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). Worship is no longer bound to a place but offered in spirit and truth (John 4:23), and people no longer pray toward a building but come to the Father through the Son.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — Hear in Heaven, and Forgive
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prayer proper: that God's eyes be open toward this house (vv. 28-30); then the petitions, each turning on hear in heaven: the oath at the altar (vv. 31-32), defeat (vv. 33-34), drought (vv. 35-36), and famine and plague (vv. 37-40).
verseByVerse.theology: Most of the petitions are about sin and its consequences, and none asks for prosperity, victory or a secure throne. The refrain is hear in heaven... and forgive.
verseByVerse.examples: In a national dedication, the prayer stops for the one man who knows the affliction of his own heart (v. 38).

verseByVerse.quote: Yet have regard to the prayer of your servant and to his plea, O LORD my God, listening to the cry and to the prayer that your servant prays before you this day, that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which you have said, 'My name shall be there,' that you may listen to the prayer that your servant offers toward this place. And listen to the plea of your servant and of your people Israel, when they pray toward this place. And listen in heaven your dwelling place, and when you hear, forgive. "If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath and comes and swears his oath before your altar in this house, then hear in heaven and act and judge your servants, condemning the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness. "When your people Israel are defeated before the enemy because they have sinned against you, and if they turn again to you and acknowledge your name and pray and plead with you in this house, then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel and bring them again to the land that you gave to their fathers. "When heaven is shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and acknowledge your name and turn from their sin, when you afflict them, then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and grant rain upon your land, which you have given to your people as an inheritance. "If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence or blight or mildew or locust or caterpillar, if their enemy besieges them in the land at their gates, whatever plague, whatever sickness there is, whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all your people Israel, each knowing the affliction of his own heart and stretching out his hands toward this house, then hear in heaven your dwelling place and forgive and act and render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways (for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind), that they may fear you all the days that they live in the land that you gave to our fathers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The single word yet is the turn. He has just said the building cannot contain God, and now he asks God to pay attention to it anyway.

He is not being inconsistent. He is holding two things that both need holding: God is not contained by any building, and God has chosen to make himself available at a particular place to people who cannot come to heaven.

Here is what the temple actually is, in the phrase Solomon keeps returning to: my name shall be there.

He does not say "I shall be there", as though God were resident in a room like a householder, but his name: his reputation, his self-disclosure, the way he has made himself known and findable. The house is where God has put his name so that people know where to turn.

Which is why every petition that follows is about praying toward this place, not in it. Almost nobody in Israel could get to Jerusalem often, and the exiles of verse 46 will not be able to get there at all.

He has just built God a dwelling place and he does not call it that. Heaven is God's dwelling place; the house on the hill is where you face when you speak.

And then the word the whole prayer runs on, arriving for the first time: forgive.

The first petition is about a lawsuit with no evidence: the case that cannot be settled in court: one man's word against another's, so the accused is put on oath at the altar. Solomon asks God to be the court of last resort where human justice runs out.

He knows about such cases: two women stood in front of him with a baby and no witnesses.

The procedure behind this petition is in the law. Where property was in dispute and there was no proof either way, an oath by the LORD shall be between them both to see whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property. The owner shall accept the oath, and he shall not make restitution (Ex. 22:11). The oath ends the case, because there is nothing else to end it with.

Which means the whole thing rests on the man swearing believing that God is listening. Take that away and the oath is a formula, and the guilty man simply says the words and walks out with his neighbour's ox.

And notice what Solomon asks for. Not mercy, for this petition has no forgive in it; he asks God to act, condemning the guilty by bringing his conduct on his own head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.

Both halves matter. There is a man in that scenario who has been wronged and has no way to prove it, and the prayer is that he should be publicly cleared. Every court in the world produces people who were right and could not show it, and the first thing Solomon asks of the new temple is that God be the place where that is finally sorted out.

With the second petition the pattern of all seven is established. Watch the shape: a disaster, and the disaster is because they have sinned, and then turning and praying, and then hear in heaven and forgive.

Solomon is not asking God to keep trouble away from Israel. He is assuming trouble, assuming that much of it will be deserved, and asking that there be a way back from it.

That is a striking thing to build into a dedication. The obvious prayer for a new national sanctuary is that the nation should prosper. What he asks for is a road back from disasters that have not happened yet and will be their own fault.

And the specific request at the end of it is territorial: bring them again to the land that you gave to their fathers. Defeat in the ancient world meant deportation: populations moved, land lost, families broken up across an empire. He is asking that the losing of the land not be final.

Which is exactly the ground the seventh petition will stand on, thirteen verses later, when the loss is total.

The third petition is about drought, and a clause is slipped into the middle of it: when you teach them the good way in which they should walk. The affliction is teaching, and he is asking that a shut sky do its work.

Elijah is going to stand in front of a king in chapter 17 and shut the sky for three and a half years, and this petition is what he is standing on.

The theology of it comes straight out of Deuteronomy, and every Israelite farmer knew it. Rain in that country is not a weather event; it is the covenant made visible. If you will indeed obey my commandments... he will give the rain for your land in its season, and the warning attached: then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain (Deut. 11:13-17).

So a dry sky was a sermon. A nation that had gone after other gods for the very reason that they were thought to control the weather would find the weather stopped.

That clause lifts the petition above a bargain: the drought is not simply a penalty but instruction, and Solomon asks that it actually teach what it was sent to teach.

Anybody who has been in a long dry season of their own can pray verse 36 as it stands: not "take this away" first, but teach me the good way, and then the rain. Not every dry season is a punishment, but every one can be a school, and the God who teaches in it is the same God who sends the rain.

In the fourth petition he simply lists everything that can go wrong (famine, plague, blight, mildew, locusts, caterpillar, siege) and then, because no list is complete, adds whatever plague, whatever sickness there is.

Each knowing the affliction of his own heart is the most personal clause in the whole prayer.

Solomon is standing in front of the entire nation on the greatest public occasion of his reign, with twenty-two thousand oxen about to be sacrificed, and he stops and asks God to hear the individual man who knows what is wrong with him.

After the plagues and blight and locusts, the prayer turns inward: the word behind affliction is the same word he has just used for the plagues.

Most of the other petitions in this prayer are corporate: when the people are defeated, when the land has no rain, when they go out to battle. This one is any man, alone, who knows something about himself that nobody else in that crowd knows, and stretches out his hands.

Whatever else the temple was for, it was for him.

The parenthesis, you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind, is the reason it works.

The man knows the affliction of his own heart. God knows it too, and God is the only one who does.

That is why the prayer can be made without words that anybody else hears, and why the judgment asked for is exact: render to each whose heart you know. Nobody is being processed in a group.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — The Foreigner, and the Far Country
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The foreigner who comes for the sake of the name (vv. 41-43), Israel at war (vv. 44-45), and the last petition, for captives in the land of the enemy who turn and repent (vv. 46-53).
verseByVerse.theology: The foreigner's petition carries no condition, unlike Israel's, and the reason given is missionary: that all the peoples of the earth may know God's name.
verseByVerse.examples: The seventh petition foresees the exile centuries before it happened, and the book's first readers were captives reading a prayer that had already asked God to hear them there.

verseByVerse.quote: "Likewise, when a foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, comes from a far country for your name's sake (for they shall hear of your great name and your mighty hand, and of your outstretched arm), when he comes and prays toward this house, hear in heaven your dwelling place and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you, in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel, and that they may know that this house that I have built is called by your name. "If your people go out to battle against their enemy, by whatever way you shall send them, and they pray to the LORD toward the city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name, then hear in heaven their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause. "If they sin against you— for there is no one who does not sin—and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to the land of the enemy, far off or near, yet if they turn their heart in the land to which they have been carried captive, and repent and plead with you in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly,' if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their enemies, who carried them captive, and pray to you toward their land, which you gave to their fathers, the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name, then hear in heaven your dwelling place their prayer and their plea, and maintain their cause and forgive your people who have sinned against you, and all their transgressions that they have committed against you, and grant them compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive, that they may have compassion on them (for they are your people, and your heritage, which you brought out of Egypt, from the midst of the iron furnace). Let your eyes be open to the plea of your servant and to the plea of your people Israel, giving ear to them whenever they call to you. For you separated them from among all the peoples of the earth to be your heritage, as you declared through Moses your servant, when you brought our fathers out of Egypt, O Lord GOD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth petition is about somebody who has no covenant, no claim, no inheritance in the land, and no business being there at all.

What draws him is a reputation. The great name, the mighty hand and the outstretched arm are exodus words, the phrases Deuteronomy uses over and over for what God did in Egypt. What reaches a foreigner in a far country is the story of God rescuing slaves.

Now read that against every other petition in this prayer, because the difference is startling.

For Israel, the asking has conditions. If they turn again to you and acknowledge your name. If they pray toward this place and acknowledge your name and turn from their sin. If they repent with all their heart and with all their soul. The petitions for defeat, drought, plague and exile all run through repentance.

For the foreigner it is do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you, with no conditions attached, no repentance specified, and no requirement that he become an Israelite first. A man arrives from a far country having heard something about the God of Israel, faces a building, and asks, and Solomon asks God to give him everything he asks for.

The reason given is missionary: that all the peoples of the earth may know his name.

This is not a footnote about hospitality. In the middle of the dedication of Israel's national sanctuary, on the day it became the one place on earth where Israel's God had put his name, the king asks God to answer foreigners generously specifically so that the whole world will hear about him.

The temple was never meant to be a wall. Isaiah says it in as many words, quoting God about foreigners who join themselves to the LORD: these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer... for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples (Isa. 56:6-7).

And a thousand years later a man walked into the outer court of the rebuilt temple (the court of the Gentiles, the one place a foreigner could stand) and found it full of money changers and cattle, and threw them out, and said: is it not written, "My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations"? But you have made it a den of robbers (Mark 11:17).

They had filled the only room a foreigner could pray in with livestock.

Solomon asked God to hear that man on the day the building opened.

The sixth petition is the shortest, and like the foreigner's it does not mention sin. Israel goes out to fight, and there is no suggestion that the war is a judgment or that anybody has done anything wrong. Sometimes trouble is simply trouble.

And notice the qualification he attaches, about the way God sends them: he is not asking God to bless whatever war Israel decides to fight. The petition covers armies God has sent, and it quietly excludes the rest, which is a good deal more restraint than most national prayers manage, and it is being prayed by a king with twelve thousand horsemen and forty thousand stalls.

The request itself is two words in effect: maintain their cause. He does not say "give them victory" but take up their case and see that right is done. It is the same phrase he uses for the exiles in verse 49, and it is what a man asks for when he trusts the judge more than he trusts the verdict he wants.

The seventh petition looks a long way ahead. First comes a parenthesis that should not be hurried: for there is no one who does not sin.

He puts it in as a matter of course, in the middle of a sentence, as a fact so obvious it needs no argument. Nobody is excepted. Paul will build a chapter of Romans on that proposition and quote the Old Testament repeatedly to establish it, and here it is, stated in passing at a temple dedication. And Paul goes on to the answer this prayer could only ask for: all have sinned, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood (Romans 3:23–25). Hear in heaven and forgive is answered at the cross.

Then the scenario: defeat, captivity, deportation to the land of the enemy. Think about who first read this. The books of Kings were completed in their final form during the exile. The last thing recorded in them is a Judean king eating at a Babylonian table (2 Kings 25:27-30). The people who first read this account of the temple were people who had watched that temple burn.

And what they found, in the record of the day it opened, was a prayer that had already asked God to hear them where they were.

Solomon names the land of their captors three times, nearly four centuries before it happened.

A man in Babylon reading this could put his finger on the sentence and know that on the greatest day in Israel's history somebody had prayed for him: not for the nation in the abstract, but for the specific situation of an Israelite far from a ruined city, facing the wrong direction, with nothing left to bring.

Notice what the prayer asks for on his behalf: not, in the first instance, a return, but compassion in the sight of those who carried them captive. Make their captors kind to them.

That is the smaller, humbler request underneath the large one, and it is the one that got answered first. Daniel in a Babylonian court. Nehemiah as cupbearer to a Persian king. Esther. Every one of them a case of God granting his people compassion in the sight of those who held them.

The prayer ends where the whole day has kept returning, in Egypt. The iron furnace is Deuteronomy's phrase for the slavery (Deut. 4:20). Standing in the most beautiful building in the world, in the richest reign in Israel's history, the king's final argument for why God should hear his people is that he brought them out of a smelting furnace.

The claim is never merit. It is always the exodus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 54–66 — Not One Word Has Failed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon rises from his knees and blesses the assembly: not one word of God's promise has failed (vv. 54-56). He asks God to incline their hearts (vv. 57-60) and calls them to hearts wholly true (v. 61). Then the great peace offerings, the feast, and the people sent home joyful (vv. 62-66).
verseByVerse.theology: Not one word has failed of all his good promise is Joshua's claim (Josh. 21:45; 23:14) restated at the high-water mark of the whole story, by a man standing in a finished temple with the glory of God inside it.
verseByVerse.examples: The benediction ends with a call to hearts wholly true, and chapter 11 will measure Solomon by that very word.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Solomon finished offering all this prayer and plea to the LORD, he arose from before the altar of the LORD, where he had knelt with hands outstretched toward heaven. And he stood and blessed all the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying, "Blessed be the LORD who has given rest to his people Israel, according to all that he promised. Not one word has failed of all his good promise, which he spoke by Moses his servant. The LORD our God be with us, as he was with our fathers. May he not leave us or forsake us, that he may incline our hearts to him, to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments, his statutes, and his rules, which he commanded our fathers. Let these words of mine, with which I have pleaded before the LORD, be near to the LORD our God day and night, and may he maintain the cause of his servant and the cause of his people Israel, as each day requires, that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God; there is no other. Let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments, as at this day." Then the king, and all Israel with him, offered sacrifice before the LORD. Solomon offered as peace offerings to the LORD 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. So the king and all the people of Israel dedicated the house of the LORD. The same day the king consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the LORD was too small to receive the burnt offering and the grain offering and the fat pieces of the peace offerings. So Solomon held the feast at that time, and all Israel with him, a great assembly, from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt, before the LORD our God, seven days. On the eighth day he sent the people away, and they blessed the king and went to their homes joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we are told what he had been doing for the last twenty-six verses: he was on his knees. Verse 22 said he stood before the altar and spread out his hands. It did not say this. The writer holds it back until the prayer is over, and then mentions it in passing as the king gets up.

The wealthiest monarch in the world, on the day of the greatest achievement of his reign, prayed one of the longest prayers in the Old Testament from his knees in a courtyard, in front of the whole nation, with his hands open and empty.

Not one word has failed is the verdict on the whole story so far.

Joshua said this twice at the end of the conquest: not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass (Josh. 21:45), and again in his farewell: not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you (Josh. 23:14).

Now Solomon says it again, from a finished temple, at the widest borders Israel ever held, with the glory of God in the building behind him.

Count what is behind that sentence. A promise to a childless man about offspring like the stars and the sand. A promise about a land, made to a man who owned one field in it, and that a grave. Four hundred years of slavery, and a bush that would not burn up, and a night with blood on the doorposts. Forty years of wandering with a tent. Judges, and a period when everyone did what was right in his own eyes. A boy with a sling. A man in a cave. A promise in a night vision about a son who would build a house.

All of it, and God kept every word.

That he may incline our hearts to him is the most theologically acute request in the chapter.

He does not ask God to help them keep the commandments. He asks God to bend their hearts toward himself in the first place.

Solomon has understood something about people that a man could easily miss on a day like this. The problem is not information; they have the law, and it has just been read and the covenant is in a box inside the house. The problem is that the heart does not lean the right way on its own, and if God does not tilt it, nothing else will help.

It is the prayer of Jeremiah's new covenant, three hundred years early: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer. 31:33). And of Ezekiel's: I will give you a new heart... and I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes (Ezek. 36:26-27).

A reader who knows chapter 11 will feel the weight of it. Solomon prays that God would incline the hearts of Israel, and the sentence recorded about him at the end is his wives turned away his heart after other gods (11:4).

He asked for the one thing he needed most, and in the end did not keep it.

The foreigner appears again in verse 60, the second time in this prayer that the horizon opens to the whole world, and the phrase is Deuteronomy's great confession: the LORD is God; there is no other (Deut. 4:35, 39).

The last word of the benediction is the word he will be measured by.

Wholly true is shalem: whole, complete, undivided, at peace. It shares a root with his own name.

He calls the nation to hearts wholly true toward God: not partly, not mostly, but undivided, and he calls them to it on the ground of the promise he has just praised as kept (v. 56).

And here is what the writer records about him at the end of his life: for when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father (11:4).

These are the exact words of his own blessing, negated and applied to him.

The writer does not point it out. He has never pointed anything out. He puts the word in Solomon's mouth in chapter 8 and takes it away from him in chapter 11, and leaves the reader to lay the two verses side by side.

That is why the command of verse 61 rests on the prayer of verse 58: God must incline the heart he commands. No son of David kept it undivided until the one who did, and his obedience is counted to those who fail, while the way back for them is the confession and forgiveness this whole prayer has asked for.

The numbers are enormous, and the kind of offering matters. These are peace offerings, which are the sacrifices that get eaten. A burnt offering is entirely consumed; a peace offering is shared, with a portion burned and the rest given back to the worshipper as a meal.

So a hundred and forty-two thousand animals means a national feast on a scale no one there had ever seen. This is not slaughter for its own sake. It is dinner for everybody in the country who came, for two weeks.

Can the numbers be real? A hundred and forty-two thousand animals over the days of the feast is roughly ten thousand a day. With thousands of priests and Levites, many altars in a consecrated court, and the whole nation present, it is enormous but not impossible, and the next verse says the bronze altar could not cope. Some think large numbers in Hebrew were sometimes counted in units rather than single thousands, and others that the figures were copied in round form; Chronicles gives the same totals (2 Chronicles 7:5).

The bronze altar was too small, and they had to consecrate the middle of the courtyard as an overflow, because there was more coming than the equipment could handle.

Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt is the full extent of the land, north to south: every part of the country is represented.

The Hebrew text reads seven days and seven days, fourteen days; the ESV follows the Greek Old Testament here. Chronicles explains the two weeks: seven days dedicating the altar, then the seven days of the feast, and the people sent home after the closing assembly (2 Chronicles 7:8–10).

This is the last verse of the high-water mark, and little in the rest of the Old Testament is like it. The whole nation goes home, and they are joyful and glad of heart, and the writer says what about: not the building, the king, the empire or the wealth, but all the goodness that the LORD had shown to David his servant and to Israel his people.

The ark is in its place. The glory has filled the house. Not one word of God's promise has failed. The borders run from the Euphrates to Egypt, every man sits under his own vine and fig tree, and a hundred and forty-two thousand animals have been eaten at one feast by people who came from every corner of the country.

This is as good as it ever gets.

Three chapters from now the same writer will record that Solomon's heart was not whole, that God raised up adversaries against him, and that a prophet met a young official on a road outside Jerusalem and tore a new cloak into twelve pieces.

But not yet. On this day the people went home glad.

8.theology:
God is not tied to the building (vv. 1-11). The ark comes up in the week Israel remembered God travelling with them in tents, with its poles still in it, so that it could always be carried. At the heart of the costliest building in Israel's history are two stones, the covenant made when they came out of the land of Egypt. And when the glory comes, the trained priests can do nothing but walk out, as Moses could not enter the finished tabernacle (Ex. 40:34-35).

God chose a man, not a place (vv. 16-18). The building is downstream of a promise to David, and the son of David who finally builds God’s house is Christ, faithful over God's house as a son. And we are his house (Hebrews 3:6). David himself was refused the work and told that the wanting was good: a refused desire to serve God is not wasted. Solomon then prays the promise back, let your word be confirmed, as his father had done (2 Sam. 7:25-27): not informing God of anything, but taking him at his word in his hearing.

Will God indeed dwell on the earth? (v. 27). The builder says, on the day his work is finished, that it cannot hold God. Seven years of labour, the finest timber in the world, gold over every surface, the glory visibly inside and the nation watching, and he names it as his own work, this house that I have built, and says it is not adequate to its purpose. Nobody required it of him. That is what an understanding mind looks like after seven years of use: the more magnificent the work became, the clearer it was that it could not do the one thing it was for. Isaiah gives the thought back as God's own words and adds where God does look: to the humble and contrite (Isa. 66:1-2). Stephen and Paul repeat it to those who trusted in temples (Acts 7:48; 17:24). And the question was answered beyond anything Solomon could ask: God did dwell on the earth, in the flesh, and Jesus called his own body the temple (John 1:14; 2:19–21). The place to turn to God is now a person.

His name, and praying toward it (vv. 28-30). The building cannot contain God, yet God has chosen to make himself available at a particular place to people who cannot come to heaven. Both need holding. The house is where God has put his name, his self-disclosure, so that people far away know where to turn; almost nobody in Israel could get to Jerusalem often, and the exiles could not get there at all. Heaven remains his dwelling place, and the prayer asks him to hear from there.

A prayer about sin, with a way back (vv. 31-53). The petitions assume trouble, much of it deserved, and ask that there be a road home from it: hear in heaven, and forgive. They make room for the single man who knows the affliction of his own heart, for the foreigner who has heard of the exodus, and for exiles in a land not yet lost. Solomon says in passing that there is no one who does not sin, the conviction Paul will build a chapter of Romans on.

Each knowing the affliction of his own heart (v. 38). In the middle of a national occasion the prayer stops for the one man who knows something about himself that nobody else in the crowd knows. The reason it works is the parenthesis: God alone knows the hearts of all the children of mankind, so the prayer needs no words anyone else hears, and nobody is processed in a group.

The foreigner, with no conditions (vv. 41-43). Israel's petitions run through repentance; the foreigner's asks God to do all he asks, so that all the peoples of the earth may know his name. The temple was never meant to be a wall: Isaiah called it a house of prayer for all peoples (Isa. 56:7), and Jesus cleared the one court a foreigner could stand in with that verse on his lips (Mark 11:17).

Prayed for in advance (vv. 46-50). Kings was completed in the exile; its first readers had watched this temple burn, and they found in the record of its opening a prayer that had already asked God to hear them in the land of their captors. The first answer was the humbler request, that their captors would show them compassion: Daniel in a Babylonian court, Nehemiah at a Persian king's table, Esther.

Hear and forgive, but on what ground? (vv. 30-50). Seven times the prayer asks God to forgive, and never says how a holy God can. The answer was in the building: blood on the altar outside, blood carried once a year into the room behind the curtain. Those sacrifices could not take away sins (Hebrews 10:4); they pointed to the one who could. Christ offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:12), and now he is the one we turn toward when we pray. Every repentant Israelite who faced Jerusalem and asked for mercy was, without knowing his name, leaning on him.

Never merit, always the exodus (vv. 51-53). In the most beautiful building in the world, the king's last argument for why God should hear is that he brought his people out of the iron furnace. That is the ground of every appeal to God: not what we have built, but what he has done.

Not one word has failed (vv. 54-61). The writer holds back until now that the king prayed all this on his knees, hands open and empty, in front of the nation. He rises to say what Joshua said at the end of the conquest (Josh. 21:45; 23:14): the promises to Abraham, to Moses and to David have all come true. Then he asks God to incline their hearts, the prayer of Jeremiah's and Ezekiel's new covenant before its time (Jer. 31:33; Ezek. 36:26-27), and calls for hearts wholly true. Chapter 11 measures him by that word, and he falls short. The command rests on the prayer: God must give the heart he commands.

As good as it ever gets (vv. 62-66). The great peace offerings are a shared meal for the whole nation, a portion burned and the rest eaten, so many that the bronze altar could not take them and the middle of the court had to be consecrated as an overflow; and the people go home glad, not about the building or the king, but about all the goodness that the LORD had shown. Three chapters on, the decline begins; but not yet.
8.examples:
Then: The richest king on earth finished the most expensive building in his nation's history, watched the glory of God fill it so completely that the priests had to walk out of the room, and then knelt down in the courtyard in front of the whole country and said out loud that the thing he had just spent seven years building could not possibly hold the God it was built for.

Now: three things. Verse 27 is the one to take away, and its power is who said it and when. It is easy to be humble about somebody else's achievement; Solomon said his own finest work was inadequate on the day it was finished, with everyone watching and nobody requiring it of him. Second, verse 38: in the middle of a national occasion with a hundred and forty thousand animals being offered, the prayer stops for the one man who knows the affliction of his own heart and cannot say it to anybody. If you are that person, the temple was for you, and the reason it works is the parenthesis: God alone knows the hearts of all the children of mankind. And third, verse 58, which is the honest request. He did not ask for help obeying. He asked God to incline their hearts, because the heart does not lean the right way on its own, and the man who prayed it had his own heart turned away in the end, which is why it is the prayer to keep praying. God has answered it in his Son, whose heart was wholly true in our place, and in the Spirit he now gives to incline ours (Ezek. 36:27; Gal. 5:16).

9.title: The LORD Appears a Second Time
9.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as Solomon had finished building the house of the LORD and the king's house and all that Solomon desired to build,<sup>2</sup>the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon.<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and your plea, which you have made before me. I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time.<sup>4</sup>And as for you, if you will walk before me, as David your father walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing according to all that I have commanded you, and keeping my statutes and my rules,<sup>5</sup>then I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever, as I promised David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.'<sup>6</sup>But if you turn aside from following me, you or your children, and do not keep my commandments and my statutes that I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them,<sup>7</sup>then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and the house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight, and Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples.<sup>8</sup>And this house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone passing by it will be astonished and will hiss, and they will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?'<sup>9</sup>Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore the LORD has brought all this disaster on them.'"<sup>10</sup>At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the two houses, the house of the LORD and the king's house,<sup>11</sup>and Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress timber and gold, as much as he desired, King Solomon gave to Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee.<sup>12</sup>But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the cities that Solomon had given him, they did not please him.<sup>13</sup>Therefore he said, "What kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother?" So they are called the land of Cabul to this day.<sup>14</sup>Hiram had sent to the king 120 talents of gold.<sup>15</sup>And this is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon drafted to build the house of the LORD and his own house and the Millo and the wall of Jerusalem and Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer<sup>16</sup>(Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and captured Gezer and burned it with fire, and had killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and had given it as dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife;<sup>17</sup>so Solomon rebuilt Gezer) and Lower Beth-horon<sup>18</sup>and Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness, in the land of Judah,<sup>19</sup>and all the store cities that Solomon had, and the cities for his chariots, and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.<sup>20</sup>All the people who were left of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of the people of Israel—<sup>21</sup>their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction — these Solomon drafted to be slaves, and so they are to this day.<sup>22</sup>But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. They were the soldiers, they were his officials, his commanders, his captains, his chariot commanders and his horsemen.<sup>23</sup>These were the chief officers who were over Solomon's work: 550 who had charge of the people who carried on the work.<sup>24</sup>But Pharaoh's daughter went up from the city of David to her own house that Solomon had built for her. Then he built the Millo.<sup>25</sup>Three times a year Solomon used to offer up burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar that he built to the LORD, making offerings with it before the LORD. So he finished the house.<sup>26</sup>King Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom.<sup>27</sup>And Hiram sent with the fleet his servants, seamen who were familiar with the sea, together with the servants of Solomon.<sup>28</sup>And they went to Ophir and brought from there gold, 420 talents, and they brought it to King Solomon.
9.overview:
