God appears a second time, and the writer points back to Gibeon, because two chapters from now this fact aggravates the charge: Solomon's heart turned from the God who had appeared to him twice (11:9).

God grants the prayer of chapter 8 and adds his heart to the eyes Solomon asked for; and four verses later he says the consecrated house will be cast out of his sight if Israel turns to other gods. Verse 8 asks the question of the first readers, who had watched that house burn, and verse 9 answers it. The condition of verse 4, a son of David walking before God with integrity of heart and uprightness, is met at last by only one: Jesus, to whom the throne promised here is given for ever.

The rest of the chapter is the reign's accounts: a soured settlement with Hiram, a town given by Pharaoh as a dowry, the labour force, a scruple about Pharaoh's daughter, and gold from Ophir.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — My Eyes and My Heart Will Be There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD appears to Solomon a second time (vv. 1-2): he has heard the prayer and consecrated the house (v. 3); the throne is promised on the condition of walking as David did (vv. 4-5); and if they turn to other gods, Israel will be cut off and the house made a heap of ruins (vv. 6-9).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the answer to chapter 8: Solomon asked for God's eyes on the house (8:29), and God adds his heart, which nobody asked for.
verseByVerse.examples: In the same breath God says the building may become a heap of ruins. Verse 8 asks the question the first readers were asking in Babylon, and verse 9 is the answer that the whole of Kings works out.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Solomon had finished building the house of the LORD and the king's house and all that Solomon desired to build, the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, as he had appeared to him at Gibeon. And the LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and your plea, which you have made before me. I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time. And as for you, if you will walk before me, as David your father walked, with integrity of heart and uprightness, doing according to all that I have commanded you, and keeping my statutes and my rules, then I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever, as I promised David your father, saying, 'You shall not lack a man on the throne of Israel.' But if you turn aside from following me, you or your children, and do not keep my commandments and my statutes that I have set before you, but go and serve other gods and worship them, then I will cut off Israel from the land that I have given them, and the house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight, and Israel will become a proverb and a byword among all peoples. And this house will become a heap of ruins. Everyone passing by it will be astonished and will hiss, and they will say, 'Why has the LORD done thus to this land and to this house?' Then they will say, 'Because they abandoned the LORD their God who brought their fathers out of the land of Egypt and laid hold on other gods and worshiped them and served them. Therefore the LORD has brought all this disaster on them.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house of the LORD, the king's house, and all that Solomon desired to build. The writer has been keeping a running account and he keeps adding to it without comment.

God appears a second time, and the writer says so explicitly and points back to Gibeon, and it is not a stylistic detail. Two chapters from now, when the account of the reign comes due, this exact fact is what makes the charge so heavy: and the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice (11:9).

God does not appear twice to many people: Abraham, Moses, Jacob, and this man, once as a young king who asked for an understanding mind, and once here.

This is the answer to chapter 8, and it should be read with that prayer open beside it.

Solomon asked that your eyes may be open night and day toward this house, the place of which you have said, "My name shall be there" (8:29). God grants it in the words it was asked in, and then adds something nobody asked for: Solomon asked for the eyes, and God adds the heart.

That is a remarkable thing for God to say about a building, and the urge to soften it into a figure of speech should be resisted. The word is lev, the word Solomon used when he asked for a hearing heart, and the word that will be used against him in chapter 11. God is saying that his attention and his affection will both be fixed on that place, permanently.

Consider what that means for what follows. When the building is looted by Shishak within a generation, stripped by Ahaz and Hezekiah to pay tribute, defiled by Manasseh, and finally burned by Nebuchadnezzar's men, God's heart is in it the whole time.

He is not indifferent to the destruction of his own house. He says so before he threatens it.

The standard given is his father, and the terms are the conditional half of the covenant, the same half David quoted to him on his deathbed (2:4).

The phrase for what David had is integrity of heart and uprightness. Integrity is tom, wholeness, undividedness. It is very close to the wholly true heart Solomon asked for in his own benediction, and it is what 11:4 will say he did not have.

Verse 6 names the sin in advance, and it is exactly the one he commits: not injustice, cruelty or pride, but serving and worshipping other gods.

Chapter 11 opens with seven hundred wives, and within five verses says Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites (11:5).

He was told the precise thing to avoid, twice, by God in person.

Now God says what he will do to the building he has just put his heart in.

Read the two sayings together, because they are four verses apart and they are the whole theology of the temple: God's eyes and heart will be there for all time, and the house consecrated for his name may be cast out of his sight.

The building is not the guarantee. God said it in the middle of the scaffolding in chapter 6, Solomon said it himself on dedication day in chapter 8, and here God says it a third time in the harshest available form: a house with his name on it and his heart in it will go if Israel goes after other gods.

The first readers of this sentence, in the exile, had seen it happen. Nebuchadnezzar's men burned the house of the LORD and the king's house and every great house in Jerusalem, and broke up the bronze pillars and carried the metal away, and the men of Judah were marched off in chains (2 Kings 25:9-13).

And those people had a question, and it is not a theoretical one. Their whole national theology said that this God had chosen Zion and put his name there and would defend it. So when it burned, the question was not "is God angry". It was "is God finished, or is he defeated?"

Verse 8 puts that question into the mouth of a passer-by, nearly four centuries before it happened, in a word spoken to the man who laid the foundations.

The exiles found their own question in the middle of the account of the temple, and they found it already answered.

Verse 9 is the answer, and it is the thesis of both books of Kings. Everything from here to the end of 2 Kings is the working out of this one sentence. Chapter after chapter of kings who did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and prophets sent and ignored, and high places not taken away, and finally the armies from the north.

The point of the answer is what it rules out. It was not that God failed. It was not that Babylon's gods were stronger, which is what any other nation in the ancient world would have concluded from the same evidence, and which is why the writer puts the answer in the mouth of foreign passers-by.

The exodus again, at the end of the sentence, exactly where Solomon kept putting it in chapter 8. The charge is not that Israel broke rules. It is that they walked away from the God who had come and got them out of a furnace.

There is a mercy inside the shape of it that is easy to miss. A God who has been defeated cannot help you. A God who has judged you can. If the ruin is God's own doing and for a stated reason, then repentance is a live option and there is somebody to repent to, which is exactly what Solomon asked for in the seventh petition, and exactly what a man in Babylon needed to know.

Was the Davidic covenant conditional? The promise of a throne for ever was unconditional (2 Samuel 7:16); whether each son of David enjoyed it depended on his faithfulness (2 Samuel 7:14). The line was judged, but not ended, and the promise is kept in Christ. Every king after David failed the test of verse 4; Jesus alone walked before his Father with a whole heart, and God raised him to sit on David’s throne (Acts 2:30–36). And he wept over the next temple on this hill and foretold its fall (Luke 19:41–44), because the house that mattered was his own body, destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Twenty cities in Galilee for Hiram, who dislikes them, and the name Cabul (vv. 10-14); then the levy for Solomon's building works, with Gezer given as Pharaoh's dowry (vv. 15-19).
verseByVerse.theology: A sour note with Hiram, the best friend Israel had, is recorded and left there, and the name it gave a district stuck.
verseByVerse.examples: Gezer arrives as a wedding present from Pharaoh: the marriage of 3:1 delivering territory, and with it the dealings with Egypt the law warned about.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the two houses, the house of the LORD and the king's house, and Hiram king of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress timber and gold, as much as he desired, King Solomon gave to Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee. But when Hiram came from Tyre to see the cities that Solomon had given him, they did not please him. Therefore he said, "What kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother?" So they are called the land of Cabul to this day. Hiram had sent to the king 120 talents of gold. And this is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon drafted to build the house of the LORD and his own house and the Millo and the wall of Jerusalem and Hazor and Megiddo and Gezer (Pharaoh king of Egypt had gone up and captured Gezer and burned it with fire, and had killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and had given it as dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife; so Solomon rebuilt Gezer) and Lower Beth-horon and Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness, in the land of Judah, and all the store cities that Solomon had, and the cities for his chariots, and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his dominion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty years: seven on the temple and thirteen on the palace, and the writer adds them up for us. The settlement is paid in territory rather than money.

The land of Israel was not the crown's to sell. It was allotted by lot under Joshua, tribe by tribe and family by family, as each household's portion of what God had promised Abraham, and the law made permanent sale nearly impossible: the land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me (Lev. 25:23).

Solomon hands over twenty towns of it to pay a bill, and Hiram comes to look at them and does not like what he sees. It is a small sour scene set down in the middle of the glory, and the writer does nothing with it at all.

Hiram has been the best friend Israel had. He loved David and sent him cedar unasked. He blessed the LORD by name and credited him with Solomon's wisdom. He supplied every beam in the house of God, sent his own craftsmen, and shipped a hundred and twenty talents of gold on top.

And when the account is settled he is given twenty towns in Galilee, and he travels down to inspect them, and asks a question with an edge on it: what kind of cities are these that you have given me, my brother?

The word brother is treaty language between allied kings, and here it is doing the work that word does when a business relationship has just soured.

The district got its name from his displeasure: Cabul probably sounded to Hebrew ears like as good as nothing. And it stuck. The writer says to this day, which means people were still calling that stretch of Galilee by a Phoenician king's rude remark long afterwards.

Chronicles records the transaction the other way round, with Hiram giving cities to Solomon (2 Chron. 8:2); the likeliest reading is that they were returned and rebuilt after this exchange.

What it leaves behind is smaller than a doctrine and true to life. The most generous foreign friendship in Israel's history ends its recorded dealings with a disappointed man looking at what he has been paid and asking what kind of cities these are.

The list keeps growing. It began with the house of the LORD and it now includes fortifications and three major cities and the Millo, which was some kind of earthwork or terracing on the Jerusalem ridge.

Verse 16 is a parenthesis with a great deal in it.

An Egyptian army came up into the land, took a Canaanite town inside Israel's borders, burned it, and killed the population. Then Pharaoh gave the site to his daughter as a wedding present, and she brought it to Solomon.

Gezer was in the territory allotted to Ephraim (Josh. 16:3), and it had never been properly taken; Judges records that the Canaanites lived on in it (Judg. 1:29). So the town had been a standing failure of the conquest for four centuries, and it is now handed to Israel by a foreign power that solved the problem for them.

It sounds like a gift, and the writer states it flatly, and there are two things underneath it that he does not state.

The first is that Egypt has just conducted a military operation inside the land of promise and been thanked for it.

The second is the marriage. This is what the alliance of 3:1 actually produced: territory, a burned town, and an obligation. The law's warning about a king and Egypt was not superstition about a country; it was that the deal always costs more than the goods.

The forty thousand stalls of 4:26 have to be somewhere, and here are the towns built to hold them. Archaeologists have found what may be stabling at Megiddo, which is named four verses earlier, though many date those buildings a century or so later.

The phrase at the end of the verse is the one the writer keeps using and never comments on: whatever Solomon desired to build. It appeared in verse 1 as well. Twice now the account of a reign that began by asking God for an understanding mind has been summarised as a list of what the king wanted.
verseByVerse.note: Gezer, Hazor and Megiddo guarded the main routes through the land: Megiddo the pass on the coastal road, Hazor the road north to Damascus, Gezer the approach to Jerusalem from the coast.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Canaanite peoples put to permanent forced labour, while Israelites serve as soldiers and officials (vv. 20-23); Pharaoh's daughter moved to her own house (v. 24); the three yearly offerings (v. 25); and the fleet at Ezion-geber bringing gold from Ophir (vv. 26-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 22 sits beside 5:13, and the note on verses 20-28 sets out how the two fit.
verseByVerse.examples: Pharaoh's daughter is moved out of the city of David out of a genuine scruple about holiness, carefully applied; and it does not touch the marriage, which is where the danger lay.

verseByVerse.quote: All the people who were left of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of the people of Israel— their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction — these Solomon drafted to be slaves, and so they are to this day. But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves. They were the soldiers, they were his officials, his commanders, his captains, his chariot commanders and his horsemen. These were the chief officers who were over Solomon's work: 550 who had charge of the people who carried on the work. But Pharaoh's daughter went up from the city of David to her own house that Solomon had built for her. Then he built the Millo. Three times a year Solomon used to offer up burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar that he built to the LORD, making offerings with it before the LORD. So he finished the house. King Solomon built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, which is near Eloth on the shore of the Red Sea, in the land of Edom. And Hiram sent with the fleet his servants, seamen who were familiar with the sea, together with the servants of Solomon. And they went to Ophir and brought from there gold, 420 talents, and they brought it to King Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The permanent labour force is drawn from the peoples Israel never drove out.

The phrase whom the people of Israel were unable to devote to destruction (the Hebrew herem, handing a people over wholly to God in judgment) is the writer reaching back to Joshua and Judges. The conquest was never completed; the book of Judges opens with a long list of what each tribe failed to take, and God said at Bochim they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you (Judg. 2:3).

Two chapters from now, Solomon is worshipping their gods.

Verse 22 sits against 5:13, and both should be stated. This one says Solomon made no slaves of Israelites, and lists what they were instead: soldiers, officials, commanders, captains, chariot commanders, horsemen.

Chapter 5 said: King Solomon drafted forced labor out of all Israel, and the draft numbered 30,000 men, sent to Lebanon ten thousand a month in shifts.

The reconciliation is a real one. Two different arrangements are being described: a permanent Canaanite bondage and a rotational Israelite levy for a specific project. Legally the distinction holds.

But the men who came to Rehoboam three chapters from now did not experience it as a large distinction. Their word for it was yoke.

Moving Pharaoh's daughter out of the city of David is a genuine scruple, carefully applied, and it deserves to be taken seriously.

The reason is given in Chronicles, in Solomon's own words: my wife shall not live in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of the LORD has come are holy (2 Chron. 8:11).

He has thought about it. The ark came into the city of David; the ground it touched is holy; and a woman who worships the gods of Egypt should not be living on it. So he builds her a house elsewhere and moves her out.

That is not hypocrisy and it is not nothing. It is a man taking holiness seriously enough to rearrange his household over it.

But it does not touch the marriage. He has correctly identified that there is a problem with a foreign wife and the holiness of God, and he has solved it by moving her to a different postcode. The law's concern was never the address. You shall not intermarry with them... for they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut. 7:3-4). The danger was in the house, not in the neighbourhood.

It is a very recognisable kind of care: real, thought about, sincerely costly, and aimed slightly to one side of the actual problem. And chapter 11 says exactly what happened.

Three times a year is the requirement of the law (Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Booths, the three pilgrim feasts when all Israel's males were to appear before the LORD, Deut. 16:16), and he keeps them.

Israel builds ships and has to borrow sailors, the same pattern as the timber: the fleet is Solomon's, the port is on the Red Sea in territory his father conquered, and the men who can actually handle a ship come from Tyre. The Phoenicians were the great sailors of the ancient world, and Israel was not a seafaring people.

Hiram, having just complained about his twenty cities, sends his crews anyway. The alliance survives the argument.

Ophir is somewhere down the Red Sea, in Arabia or Africa or further; nobody knows, and it became a byword for the finest gold. Job speaks of it, and a psalm has the queen standing in gold of Ophir.

Four hundred and twenty talents is something in the order of fourteen tons.

The chapter that began with God saying my eyes and my heart will be there for all time ends with a shipment of gold, and the next chapter is about what came in yearly.

Was it right to make the Canaanites forced labourers? It was what Israel did instead of driving them out (Judges 1:28), and Scripture records it without approving it. The law did allow a city far off that surrendered to be put to forced labour (Deuteronomy 20:10–11), but the same law forbade oppressing the foreigner (Exodus 22:21), and in Christ, Paul says, there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28).

The officers number 550 here and 250 in 2 Chronicles 8:10; the two lists probably count different ranks. The gold from Ophir (v. 28), 420 talents here and 450 in Chronicles, may differ by the cost of the voyage, or by a copying slip.
verseByVerse.note: A talent weighed roughly 30 kilograms (about 75 pounds).

9.theology:
Eyes, heart, and a warning (vv. 1-7). God appears to Solomon a second time, and 11:9 will make that the aggravation of his fall. He grants the prayer of chapter 8 and adds his heart: he is not indifferent to the house he will later judge. Then he names in advance the one sin to avoid, other gods, and holds up David's integrity of heart, the undivided heart Solomon himself called for in his benediction. For the third time (chapters 6, 8 and here), the building is not the guarantee.

The exiles' question, answered (vv. 8-9). For the first readers, who had seen the house burned (2 Kings 25:9-13), the question was whether God was finished or defeated. The answer rules out both: the ruin is his judgment on a people who walked away from the God who brought them out of Egypt. And there is a mercy in the shape of it. A God who has been defeated cannot help you; a God who has judged you can, and there is somebody to repent to. The condition of verse 4 is finally met by one King only. Jesus kept it, and bore the judgment the faithless deserved, so that the throne promised here is his and the way back is open (Acts 2:30–36).

The accounts of a reign (vv. 10-28). The rest of the chapter reads like a ledger, and the writer lets each entry speak. Land that was God's gift, not the crown's to sell (Lev. 25:23), pays a bill and disappoints the friend who receives it: Hiram, who loved David, blessed the LORD and supplied every beam of the temple, ends his recorded dealings asking what kind of cities these are. The most generous friendship of the reign closes on a sour note, and the writer does nothing with it. A failure of the conquest four centuries old is solved by Pharaoh and received as a dowry: the deal with Egypt costs more than the goods. The peoples Israel never drove out become a labour force, as Judges warned they would become thorns and their gods a snare (Judg. 2:3). Israelites are spared that bondage, and the distinction from the levy of 5:13 is a legal one that holds; but the men who came to Rehoboam had one word for it, and the word was yoke. A real scruple about holiness moves Pharaoh's daughter to another house but leaves the marriage, where the danger lay (Deut. 7:3-4). The feasts are kept, the alliance with Tyre survives, and the gold arrives.

Whatever Solomon desired to build (vv. 1, 19). Twice in one chapter the list grows: the house of the LORD, the king's house, the Millo, the wall, Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer, store cities, and the cities for his chariots and horsemen. A reign that began by asking God for an understanding mind is now summarised as a list of what the king wanted.
9.examples:
Then: When the building was finished, twenty years in, God appeared to the man who had built it and said that his eyes and his heart would be in that house for all time, and four verses later that if Israel went after other gods he would cast it out of his sight and leave it a heap of ruins that passers-by would ask questions about. Nearly four centuries later, people standing in the ash of it read that paragraph and found their own question written down in it.

Now: three things. Verse 3 and verse 7 belong together and neither survives alone: God is not detached about the things he gives, and he will not be held hostage by them either. Second, verse 9 is the answer to the hardest question anybody asks in a national catastrophe, and notice the mercy hidden in it. (It is not a verdict on every private grief: Jesus refused to read every disaster as a judgment on the sufferer, Luke 13:1-5.) A God who has been defeated cannot help you. A God who has judged you can, and there is somebody to go back to. And third, verse 24, which is the uncomfortable one: Solomon took holiness seriously enough to move his wife out of a whole district over it, and the danger was never the district. Real scruple, real cost, aimed a few degrees off the actual problem, and chapter 11 records exactly what that was worth. The remedy is not sharper scruples but the undivided heart God himself gives by his Spirit, the very thing Solomon prayed for (8:58; Ezek. 36:26-27).

10.title: The Queen of Sheba and Solomon's Wealth
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to test him with hard questions.<sup>2</sup>She came to Jerusalem with a very great retinue, with camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind.<sup>3</sup>And Solomon answered all her questions; there was nothing hidden from the king that he could not explain to her.<sup>4</sup>And when the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built,<sup>5</sup>the food of his table, the seating of his officials, and the attendance of his servants, their clothing, his cupbearers, and his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her.<sup>6</sup>And she said to the king, "The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom,<sup>7</sup>but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, the half was not told me. Your wisdom and prosperity surpass the report that I heard.<sup>8</sup>Happy are your men! Happy are your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom!<sup>9</sup>Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel! Because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king, that you may execute justice and righteousness."<sup>10</sup>Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices and precious stones. Never again came such an abundance of spices as these that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.<sup>11</sup>Moreover, the fleet of Hiram, which brought gold from Ophir, brought from Ophir a very great amount of almug wood and precious stones.<sup>12</sup>And the king made of the almug wood supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, also lyres and harps for the singers. No such almug wood has come or been seen to this day.<sup>13</sup>And King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what was given her by the bounty of King Solomon. So she turned and went back to her own land with her servants.<sup>14</sup>Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold,<sup>15</sup>besides that which came from the explorers and from the business of the merchants, and from all the kings of the west and from the governors of the land.<sup>16</sup>King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold; 600 shekels of gold went into each shield.<sup>17</sup>And he made 300 shields of beaten gold; three minas of gold went into each shield. And the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.<sup>18</sup>The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with the finest gold.<sup>19</sup>The throne had six steps, and the throne had a round top, and on each side of the seat were armrests and two lions standing beside the armrests,<sup>20</sup>while twelve lions stood there, one on each end of a step on the six steps. The like of it was never made in any kingdom.<sup>21</sup>All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. None were of silver; silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon.<sup>22</sup>For the king had a fleet of ships of Tarshish at sea with the fleet of Hiram. Once every three years the fleet of ships of Tarshish used to come bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.<sup>23</sup>Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom.<sup>24</sup>And the whole earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind.<sup>25</sup>Every one of them brought his present, articles of silver and gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.<sup>26</sup>And Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.<sup>27</sup>And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah.<sup>28</sup>And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, and the king's traders received them from Kue at a price.<sup>29</sup>A chariot could be imported from Egypt for 600 shekels of silver and a horse for 150, and so through the king's traders they were exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
10.overview:
What the queen heard about was not the gold. It was the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, which is what Solomon had asked for at the dedication, that God would answer the foreigner in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name (8:43). She came a very long way to test him with hard questions, and what finished her, last in the list of what she saw, was the worship at the house of the LORD. Verse 9, spoken by a pagan queen, is the finest thing said in the chapter.

Then comes the inventory, staged in tones of wonder: gold by the ton, golden shields, an ivory throne, silver not counted as anything. The law about Israel's kings had three prohibitions, and this chapter describes two of them as achievements. The remaining one, whose reason is the king's heart, is answered by the first verse of chapter 11.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Half Was Not Told Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon's fame concerning the name of the LORD and comes to test him (vv. 1-3); she sees his wisdom, house and worship, confesses that the half was not told me, and blesses the LORD for loving Israel (vv. 4-9); gifts are exchanged and she goes home (vv. 10-13).
verseByVerse.theology: She came a very long way on a rumour, and the rumour was not about the gold. What reached the ends of the earth was something about God. When God's people live under his blessing and worship him openly, others notice, and some come asking hard questions. That was always the purpose of Israel's blessing: that the nations might know his name.
verseByVerse.examples: She did not take the reports on trust; she came to see for herself, and was honest about how much she had doubted. Faith is not afraid of that kind of testing, and Christ invites it: come and see was Philip's answer to a doubting Nathanael (John 1:46). Those who come to see him honestly find more than they were told.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD, she came to test him with hard questions. She came to Jerusalem with a very great retinue, with camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. And when she came to Solomon, she told him all that was on her mind. And Solomon answered all her questions; there was nothing hidden from the king that he could not explain to her. And when the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built, the food of his table, the seating of his officials, and the attendance of his servants, their clothing, his cupbearers, and his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of the LORD, there was no more breath in her. And she said to the king, "The report was true that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom, but I did not believe the reports until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, the half was not told me. Your wisdom and prosperity surpass the report that I heard. Happy are your men! Happy are your servants, who continually stand before you and hear your wisdom! Blessed be the LORD your God, who has delighted in you and set you on the throne of Israel! Because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king, that you may execute justice and righteousness." Then she gave the king 120 talents of gold, and a very great quantity of spices and precious stones. Never again came such an abundance of spices as these that the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon. Moreover, the fleet of Hiram, which brought gold from Ophir, brought from Ophir a very great amount of almug wood and precious stones. And the king made of the almug wood supports for the house of the LORD and for the king's house, also lyres and harps for the singers. No such almug wood has come or been seen to this day. And King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all that she desired, whatever she asked besides what was given her by the bounty of King Solomon. So she turned and went back to her own land with her servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What drew her was not his wealth in the first instance, and not even his wisdom on its own, but the fame of Solomon concerning the name of the LORD. What travelled to the ends of the earth was something about God. That is precisely what Solomon asked for at the dedication, that God would hear the foreigner in order that all the peoples of the earth may know your name (8:43), and here is a foreigner arriving because she has heard the name.

Sheba is most probably in south-west Arabia, in the region of modern Yemen (Ethiopian tradition places her across the Red Sea in Africa, but the kingdom of Saba in Arabia is the better fit). That is a journey of something like fifteen hundred miles across desert, each way, by camel: months of travelling, at enormous expense, on the strength of a report.

She comes to test him with hard questions, so she is not a tourist. The word is the one for riddles, used of Samson's riddle at his wedding feast (Judg. 14:12), and testing a foreign king's wisdom with hard questions seems to have been a recognised diplomatic contest. She has come to find out whether the reports are true.

All that was on her mind is, in Hebrew, all that was in her heart. She had brought hard questions, and she ended up telling him everything she was carrying. That is what happens when somebody turns out to be worth talking to.

Read the list of what she saw in its order: wisdom, house, table, officials, servants, cupbearers, and last his burnt offerings. The thing that finished her was the worship. The writer's phrase for the effect is physical: there was no more breath in her. It knocked the wind out of her.

She is honest about her own scepticism, which is why her testimony counts for something. She did not take it on trust; she came to check, and what she found exceeded what she had refused to believe. And she envies, not the king, but the servants: the men who get to stand in the room every day and listen. She has had one visit of it, and she can see what a lifetime of it would be worth.

Verse 9 gets three things right that Israel keeps forgetting. First, she does not congratulate Solomon on his achievements. She credits God, with a warm word: delighted in you. Everything she has just been shown, she attributes to God's pleasure in this man.

Second, because the LORD loved Israel forever, he has made you king. That is a remarkable piece of theology from a foreigner. She has worked out that the king is a gift to the nation and not the other way round: Solomon exists because God loves Israel. It is exactly what David knew at his best: the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel (2 Sam. 5:12).

Third, and this is the one that lands hardest: that you may execute justice and righteousness. She names the purpose of the throne. Not glory, not building, not wealth, not empire: the office exists so that right is done for people. Nobody in the story has said it so plainly since 2 Samuel 8:15, and she is not an Israelite, and she is only visiting.

There is something uncomfortable in that, and it is meant to be felt. The visitor has looked at all of it (the gold, the table, the servants in their clothing, the House of the Forest of Lebanon) and identified the actual point of the thing better than the people living in it. Hold verse 9 for two chapters: when the north comes to Rehoboam, what they ask for is relief from a yoke, and what they get is scorpions.

Then she goes home. The writer does not tell us what she did with any of it, and there is no record of her worshipping the LORD or of Sheba turning to him. She came, she saw, she blessed God, and she went back across the desert.

A thousand years later, when scribes and Pharisees demanded a sign, the Lord Jesus brought her up: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with the men of this generation and condemn them, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here (Luke 11:31; cf. Matt. 12:42). Her journey will be the case against them. She had no Scriptures, no covenant, no prophets and no invitation. What she had was a rumour about the name of a God she did not worship, and she crossed a desert on the strength of it because she wanted to know whether it was true. The men he was speaking to were standing in front of the wisdom of God in a body, in the street, asking him to do a trick first.

And everything the queen praised in Solomon is true of Christ without the shadow that falls across chapter 11. He is the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). His throne is the one that truly does justice and righteousness for ever (Isaiah 9:7). A psalm of Solomon pictured kings of Sheba bringing gifts to David’s son (Psalm 72:10, 15), and Isaiah saw those from Sheba bringing gold and frankincense to Zion (Isaiah 60:6); many Christians have heard an echo of that when wise men from the east laid gold and frankincense before the child Jesus (Matthew 2:11). Those who come to him find, as she did, that the half was not told them.
verseByVerse.note: Sheba was probably in south-west Arabia (modern Yemen).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–25 — Silver Was Not Considered as Anything
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon's yearly gold, the golden shields, the ivory throne and the gold vessels, the Tarshish fleet with its apes and peacocks, and a name for riches and wisdom that brings the whole earth with tribute (vv. 14-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything here is stated as glory and the writer stages it beautifully. Yet the law about Israel's kings had said nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold (Deut. 17:17), the last of its three prohibitions, and here it is described in a tone of wonder.
verseByVerse.examples: Abundance changes what we notice. When enough comes in, things that once cost something stop registering at all, and gratitude goes quiet. David once refused to offer God what cost him nothing; a generation later silver was not counted. The remedy is not to despise God's gifts but to keep counting them as gifts, and to give in a way that still costs something.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold, besides that which came from the explorers and from the business of the merchants, and from all the kings of the west and from the governors of the land. King Solomon made 200 large shields of beaten gold; 600 shekels of gold went into each shield. And he made 300 shields of beaten gold; three minas of gold went into each shield. And the king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. The king also made a great ivory throne and overlaid it with the finest gold. The throne had six steps, and the throne had a round top, and on each side of the seat were armrests and two lions standing beside the armrests, while twelve lions stood there, one on each end of a step on the six steps. The like of it was never made in any kingdom. All King Solomon's drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. None were of silver; silver was not considered as anything in the days of Solomon. For the king had a fleet of ships of Tarshish at sea with the fleet of Hiram. Once every three years the fleet of ships of Tarshish used to come bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom. And the whole earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put into his mind. Every one of them brought his present, articles of silver and gold, garments, myrrh, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The yearly gold was something over twenty tons, in twelve months.

The number six hundred and sixty-six turns up again at the end of the Bible: this calls for wisdom: let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and his number is 666 (Rev. 13:18). Some readers connect the two, and there is a certain grim aptness to it, since this chapter is the inventory of a man's accumulation.

Honesty requires saying this, though. The writer of Kings makes nothing of the number; he records it as an annual revenue figure and moves straight on to shields. And Revelation does not cite this verse or allude to Solomon anywhere in the passage. Whatever John meant by the number, he does not tell us he got it from here. A reader may notice the figure; it should not be built on.

And that is only the top line. The tribute, the trade, the tolls and the provincial revenue all came on top of it.

Five hundred shields of beaten gold hung in the great pillared hall. Gold is a soft metal, so these are not fighting equipment; they are ceremonial, carried in procession and displayed on the walls of a room built to be walked through.

Keep them in mind, because the writer comes back for them. Five years after Solomon dies, Shishak king of Egypt comes up against Jerusalem and takes away the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the king's house: he took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made (14:26). Rehoboam replaces them with bronze ones and gives them to the guard, who carry them in front of him when he goes into the house of the LORD and take them back to the guardroom afterwards (14:27-28). It is the same ceremony, with cheaper metal, and everybody pretending not to notice.

The throne has six steps, twelve lions, a rounded back, ivory and gold. The lion is the emblem of Judah: Judah is a lion's cub... he stooped down; he crouched as a lion and as a lioness; who dares rouse him? (Gen. 49:9). Twelve of them, probably for the tribes, line the way up to the seat. It is a magnificent object, and it is also, precisely, a chair for judging in. This is the seat in the Hall of Judgment, and the man on it asked for an understanding mind.

Silver was not considered as anything is more than an exchange rate. It says what happens to a scale of value when enough comes in: the second-best metal in the world stopped registering. Consider what silver was earlier in this history. It is what a threshing floor cost David, fifty shekels of it, and he insisted on paying rather than take the ground free, because I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing (2 Sam. 24:24). Fifty shekels of silver was a real price to a real man once. Now the metal is not counted.

The apes and peacocks are the tell (the second word is uncertain; some translate it baboons). Gold, silver and ivory are wealth; these are curiosities, fetched on three-year voyages because they are interesting to have. “Ships of Tarshish” were large ocean-going trading ships, named after Tarshish, a far western port, probably in Spain; Ophir was a source of gold, perhaps in Arabia or East Africa.

In verse 23 the writer puts two words in an order worth noticing. At Gibeon it was the other way round: Solomon asked for wisdom and did not ask for riches, and God said I give you also what you have not asked (3:13). Riches came second, as an addition. Here the summary sentence reads in riches and in wisdom. It may be nothing, but it is the sort of small thing this writer does.

The credit is still given correctly, and the writer refuses to let the wisdom become the man's own property: which God had put into his mind. And horses are now arriving as tribute, year by year; the next verse says where the rest came from.
verseByVerse.note: 666 talents of gold is roughly 20 to 25 tons.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–29 — And Horses Were Imported from Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chariots and horsemen, silver as common as stone, and horses imported from Egypt and Kue and sold on to the kings of the Hittites and Syria (vv. 26-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Four verses, and they complete the breach. The law said Israel's king must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, and nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold (Deut. 17:16-17). Horses, Egypt, and silver like stones, in the space of one paragraph.
verseByVerse.examples: Only one prohibition is left, and its reason is the king's heart: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away. The very next verse in the book shows what became of it. Outward success and inward drift can run side by side for years, which is why the heart needs guarding most when things go well.

verseByVerse.quote: And Solomon gathered together chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem. And the king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stone, and he made cedar as plentiful as the sycamore of the Shephelah. And Solomon's import of horses was from Egypt and Kue, and the king's traders received them from Kue at a price. A chariot could be imported from Egypt for 600 shekels of silver and a horse for 150, and so through the king's traders they were exported to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These last four verses are the indictment. Fourteen hundred chariots, twelve thousand horsemen, and cities built to house them, which chapter 9 listed. (Chapter 4:26 gives forty thousand stalls, where Chronicles has four thousand (2 Chronicles 9:25); the smaller figure fits fourteen hundred chariots, and most think a numeral was miscopied in Kings.)

The law about Israel's kings is a short paragraph with three prohibitions in it, and this is the first: only he must not acquire many horses for himself or cause the people to return to Egypt in order to acquire many horses, since the LORD has said to you, "You shall never return that way again." (Deut. 17:16). Silver as common as stone breaks the third, in the same law, two clauses later: nor shall he acquire for himself excessive silver and gold (Deut. 17:17).

Kue is Cilicia, in the south-east of modern Turkey. And the horses came from Egypt, in as many words. The law did not merely say a king should not have many horses. It said he should not cause the people to return to Egypt in order to get them, and it gave the reason as a quotation from God himself.

The law's concern was not economic. Israel came out of Egypt. That was the founding act, the thing the whole calendar is dated from, the thing Solomon's own prayer went back to again and again on one day. The danger was that a king with a taste for cavalry would open a road back to the country God had brought them out of, and that trade would run the wrong way down it. That is exactly what has happened: there is now a standing commercial relationship with Egypt for military horseflesh, run by the king's own traders.

The last verse turns him into the middleman. Israel is now the broker in the arms trade of the region, buying Egyptian chariots and horses and selling them on to the Hittites and the Syrians at a margin. Within a century the Syrians will besiege Samaria, and a king of Israel will hear of his people eating their own children (2 Kings 6). Their kings are being supplied with cavalry by the king of Israel, out of Egypt, for cash.

Every item in these twenty-nine verses is glorious. The queen is genuinely awestruck and her praise is genuinely good theology. The wisdom is real and God gave it. The throne is magnificent. The trade is skilful. The reputation reaches the ends of the earth and it reaches them, as verse 1 says, concerning the name of the LORD. Yet two of the law's three prohibitions are here, described as achievements: horses, and from Egypt, in verses 26 and 28; silver and gold beyond counting, in verses 14 to 27.

There is one left. It sits between the other two in the same law, and its reason is the king's heart: and he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). The next verse in the book is: now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh (11:1).

The writer has spent a chapter describing the summit of Israel's history in tones of wonder, and every rung he described was one the law told a king not to climb. He does not say so. He puts chapter 10 next to chapter 11 and lets the reader do it.

The law about kings ends with what a king should do instead: write out a copy of the law, read it all his life, and not lift his heart above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:18–20). Only one son of David has kept that paragraph whole. He had nowhere to lay his head; though he was rich, he became poor for our sakes (2 Corinthians 8:9), and he rode into Jerusalem on a donkey rather than a war horse (Matthew 21:5). The glory of chapter 10 is real, and it fades; his does not.

10.theology:
The name of the LORD reaching the nations (vv. 1-9). The chapter opens with the answer to Solomon's prayer for the foreigner (8:43). What crossed the desert was not the wealth but a report about God, and what the queen found most breathtaking was the worship at his house. Her blessing in verse 9 is a small summary of what kingship in Israel was for: God's delight, God's love for his people, and a throne that exists for justice and righteousness. It is good theology from an outsider, and it quietly judges the insiders, as Jesus' use of her judges his own generation (Matt. 12:42).

Glory that the law forbade (vv. 14-29). The law of the king in Deuteronomy 17 named three dangers: many horses (and the road back to Egypt), many wives, and excessive silver and gold. This chapter describes two of them with wonder, and the writer adds no criticism. He lets the arrangement speak, and the next verse names the third. Scripture often works like this: a thing can look like blessing at the time and be the beginning of a fall. Success is not proof of faithfulness, and the account is not always presented at the time.

Why the road to Egypt mattered (v. 28). The law's worry about horses was not mainly military or economic. Egypt was the house of slavery God had brought his people out of, and the exodus was the founding act of the nation, the event its calendar and its worship looked back to. A king who opened a standing trade route back there for cavalry was undoing, in commercial form, the story that made Israel Israel. The commandment had given the reason in God's own words: You shall never return that way again. Solomon did not go back to Egypt as a slave. He went back as a customer, which is harder to notice and in some ways more dangerous. Many of the drifts that take God's people back to what he rescued them from look like this: not a dramatic return, but a profitable arrangement.

Gold and bronze. The golden shields of verses 16-17 are the chapter's quiet prophecy. Within five years of Solomon's death they are gone to Egypt, and Rehoboam's bronze copies are carried in the same procession as if nothing had happened (14:26-28). Glory that rests on accumulation can be carried off; the form of religion can continue after the substance has gone. That is a warning for churches as well as kings.

Gifts that slip out of their place. Wisdom was God's gift, and the writer says so even at the height of the display (v. 24). But the order of verse 23, riches before wisdom, and the silver that no longer counted, hint at what abundance does to a heart. The gifts are not evil; the danger is that they stop being received as gifts.

The greater Solomon. Israel had to wait for a King who would keep that law whole and, though rich, become poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). He is the wisdom of God in person (1 Corinthians 1:24), the King whose throne truly does justice and righteousness (Isaiah 9:7), and the one Solomon’s glory could only point toward. The number in verse 14 sometimes gets linked to the number of the beast (Rev. 13:18), but the real contrast in this chapter is simpler: the glory of a man who accumulated, against the glory of the Son who gave himself away.
10.examples:
Then: A queen crossed fifteen hundred miles of desert on the strength of a rumour about the name of a God who was not hers, because she wanted to find out. What took her breath in the end was not the gold or the throne but the king's burnt offerings at the house of the LORD.

Now: Three things. Verse 9 stings: the outsider on a single visit named the purpose of the whole institution more plainly than anybody inside it, and people at a distance often see what a thing is for more clearly than those running it. Second, silver was not considered as anything is a warning about what abundance does to a scale of value. And third, the shape of the chapter: nothing in it is condemned and much of it is against the law. Remember that in seasons when everything is going extremely well. Our safety then is not our own record but the Son of David who kept the law whole for us, and whose Spirit keeps our hearts from turning.

11.title: Solomon's Heart Turned Away
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh: Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women,<sup>2</sup>from the nations concerning which the LORD had said to the people of Israel, "You shall not enter into marriage with them, neither shall they with you, for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods." Solomon clung to these in love.<sup>3</sup>He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines. And his wives turned away his heart.<sup>4</sup>For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father.<sup>5</sup>For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.<sup>6</sup>So Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and did not wholly follow the LORD, as David his father had done.<sup>7</sup>Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites, on the mountain east of Jerusalem.<sup>8</sup>And so he did for all his foreign wives, who made offerings and sacrificed to their gods.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice<sup>10</sup>and had commanded him concerning this thing, that he should not go after other gods. But he did not keep what the LORD commanded.<sup>11</sup>Therefore the LORD said to Solomon, "Since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you and will give it to your servant.<sup>12</sup>Yet for the sake of David your father I will not do it in your days, but I will tear it out of the hand of your son.<sup>13</sup>However, I will not tear away all the kingdom, but I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem that I have chosen."<sup>14</sup>And the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite. He was of the royal house in Edom.<sup>15</sup>For when David was in Edom, and Joab the commander of the army went up to bury the slain, he struck down every male in Edom<sup>16</sup>(for Joab and all Israel remained there six months, until he had cut off every male in Edom).<sup>17</sup>But Hadad fled to Egypt, together with certain Edomites of his father's servants, Hadad still being a little child.<sup>18</sup>They set out from Midian and came to Paran and took men with them from Paran and came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave him a house and assigned him an allowance of food and gave him land.<sup>19</sup>And Hadad found great favor in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him in marriage the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen.<sup>20</sup>And the sister of Tahpenes bore him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house. And Genubath was in Pharaoh's house among the sons of Pharaoh.<sup>21</sup>But when Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers and that Joab the commander of the army was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, "Let me depart, that I may go to my own country."<sup>22</sup>But Pharaoh said to him, "What have you lacked with me that you are now seeking to go to your own country?" And he said to him, "Only let me depart."<sup>23</sup>God also raised up as an adversary to him, Rezon the son of Eliada, who had fled from his master Hadadezer king of Zobah.<sup>24</sup>And he gathered men about him and became leader of a marauding band, after the killing by David. And they went to Damascus and lived there and made him king in Damascus.<sup>25</sup>He was an adversary of Israel all the days of Solomon, doing harm as Hadad did. And he loathed Israel and reigned over Syria.<sup>26</sup>Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zeredah, a servant of Solomon, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow, also lifted up his hand against the king.<sup>27</sup>And this was the reason why he lifted up his hand against the king. Solomon built the Millo, and closed up the breach of the city of David his father.<sup>28</sup>The man Jeroboam was very able, and when Solomon saw that the young man was industrious he gave him charge over all the forced labor of the house of Joseph.<sup>29</sup>And at that time, when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the road. Now Ahijah had dressed himself in a new garment, and the two of them were alone in the open country.<sup>30</sup>Then Ahijah laid hold of the new garment that was on him, and tore it into twelve pieces.<sup>31</sup>And he said to Jeroboam, "Take for yourself ten pieces, for thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes<sup>32</sup>(but he shall have one tribe, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel),<sup>33</sup>because they have forsaken me and worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites, and they have not walked in my ways, doing what is right in my sight and keeping my statutes and my rules, as David his father did.<sup>34</sup>Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand, but I will make him ruler all the days of his life, for the sake of David my servant whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my statutes.<sup>35</sup>But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand and will give it to you, ten tribes.<sup>36</sup>Yet to his son I will give one tribe, that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city where I have chosen to put my name.<sup>37</sup>And I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your soul desires, and you shall be king over Israel.<sup>38</sup>And if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you.<sup>39</sup>And I will afflict the offspring of David because of this, but not forever.'"<sup>40</sup>Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam arose and fled into Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon.<sup>41</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon?<sup>42</sup>And the time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years.<sup>43</sup>And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father. And Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
11.overview:
The previous chapter ended with silver as common as stone and horses arriving from Egypt. This one opens with the last of the three prohibitions in the law about Israel's kings, and its reason is the king's heart: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). The writer quotes the warning in verse 2 and reports its exact fulfilment in verse 3: and his wives turned away his heart.

It happens when Solomon was old, after every advantage a king could have, and it happens without any single decision: one shrine at a time, each a courtesy to a wife. God's judgment follows, all the heavier because God had appeared to him twice: the kingdom is to be torn, adversaries are raised up from David's old wars, a servant is promised ten tribes, and the chapter ends with the wisest king who ever lived trying to kill the man God had named.

Yet the chapter is not only a warning. The kingdom is torn, but a lamp is kept for David's sake (v. 36), and the promise that outlives Solomon is the one that reaches Christ. Jesus said of himself, something greater than Solomon is here (Matt. 12:42): the Son of David whose heart was wholly true to his Father to the end. Solomon's marriages to the nations drew him after their gods; Christ gave himself for a bride gathered from every nation (Eph. 5:25; Rev. 5:9), and his love draws strangers home to the one God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Now King Solomon Loved Many Foreign Women
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Solomon loves many foreign women from the nations the law had warned would turn away your heart after their gods (vv. 1-2); when he is old his wives turn his heart away, and his heart is not wholly true to the LORD his God (vv. 3-6); he builds high places for Chemosh and Molech, and for all his foreign wives (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the last of the three prohibitions in the law about Israel's kings, and its reason is the king's heart: lest his heart turn away (Deut. 17:17). Chapter 10 broke the other two.
verseByVerse.examples: Hearts are rarely lost in one decision. They are lost in accommodations, each reasonable on its own, made for people we love or need. It is worth asking, gently and with the gospel in view, what has quietly been given a place beside God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with the daughter of Pharaoh: Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women, from the nations concerning which the LORD had said to the people of Israel, "You shall not enter into marriage with them, neither shall they with you, for surely they will turn away your heart after their gods." Solomon clung to these in love. He had 700 wives, who were princesses, and 300 concubines. And his wives turned away his heart. For when Solomon was old his wives turned away his heart after other gods, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as was the heart of David his father. For Solomon went after Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, and after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites. So Solomon did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and did not wholly follow the LORD, as David his father had done. Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Molech the abomination of the Ammonites, on the mountain east of Jerusalem. And so he did for all his foreign wives, who made offerings and sacrificed to their gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The daughter of Pharaoh is named first, which is the writer collecting a debt. She has been in this account since 3:1, before Gibeon and before the temple, given a house of her own in chapter 7 and moved out of the city of David in chapter 9 for reasons of holiness: four flat mentions with no comment attached. Here is the comment.

The writer quotes the law, including its reason. The command is from Deuteronomy 7, and what should be noticed is that the reason given is never about blood or nationality: They will turn away your heart after their gods. It is a warning about worship, and the mechanism is the household.

This passage has been misused, so it should be said plainly. Rahab of Jericho married into Israel and is in the genealogy of Christ. Ruth was a Moabitess, from one of the nations named in verse 1, and she is David's great-grandmother. Uriah was a Hittite and one of the mighty men. What made the difference was not ancestry but which God they had come to.

Solomon clung to these women, and clinging is what Deuteronomy asks of Israel toward God: you shall fear the LORD your God. You shall serve him and hold fast to him (Deut. 10:20). The devotion that belonged to God went to seven hundred women.

With a thousand women in the household, the writer reports the outcome in the law's own words. Deuteronomy said lest his heart turn away. This verse says his wives turned away his heart. The law named the mechanism and the history records it working.

It should also be said what seven hundred princesses actually are. These are not romances. Each one is a treaty, a marriage alliance sealing a political relationship with a neighbouring house, which is exactly what the daughter of Pharaoh was. The harem is a foreign policy.

Does the Bible approve of Solomon's many wives? No. Scripture records polygamy without commending it. God's pattern from the beginning is one man and one woman (Gen. 2:24), and Jesus goes back to that beginning (Matt. 19:4-6); the law for kings forbade exactly this multiplying of wives (Deut. 17:17); and almost every household with several wives in the Old Testament, from Jacob's to David's, is shown full of rivalry and grief. The numbers are huge, but ancient royal harems could be very large, and the writer gives them to show how far the king had gone.

The treaty marriages make it worse rather than better. A man who marries a princess to secure an alliance has to let her worship her own gods, or the alliance is insulted. Every one of those marriages carried an obligation, and verse 8 is Solomon meeting them.

Verse 4 holds three things, and each one matters. The first is when Solomon was old. Not in the reckless years, but at the end: after Gibeon, after the building and the dedication prayer, after God appeared to him a second time, after forty years on the throne. He had every advantage a man could have, for four decades, and he went wrong at the end. That ought to be felt. There is no age at which a person is past this, and the drift can begin in the part of life that looks safest.

That is a warning, not a sentence hanging over every believer who fears growing cold. The same Scriptures promise that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Phil. 1:6), and that God is able to keep you from stumbling (Jude 24). The way to be kept is not to lean on past advantages but to keep coming back to him, and a heart troubled by its own coldness is already being drawn near.

The second is the phrase his heart was not wholly true. The word is shalem: whole, complete, undivided, and it shares its root with the man's own name. He used it himself on the greatest day of his life. Standing before the finished temple with the glory of God inside it, his last word to Israel was: let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God, walking in his statutes and keeping his commandments (8:61). The writer waits three chapters and then takes the word off him.

He does not call Solomon false or apostate. Solomon kept the feasts, the temple stood, and the sacrifices went up. What he lost was the undividedness. His heart had more than one thing in it, and he had told the nation that would not do.

The third is the comparison: as was the heart of David his father. A reader fresh from 2 Samuel may find that hard, and it should not be smoothed over. David committed adultery and arranged a murder, failed to act when his daughter was raped, and handed his son a deathbed list of men to kill. So what is being compared?

Not sinlessness. The measure in this book is single: whether a king served the LORD alone or went after other gods. On that measure the difference between the two men is total. David never once, in seventy years, worshipped another god or built a shrine to one. Everything he did wrong he did as a man belonging to the LORD, and when he was confronted he broke and said I have sinned against the LORD, and wrote Psalm 51. Solomon built high places for Chemosh and Molech on the hill facing the temple. That is the comparison, and it is not a whitewash of David. It is the distinction the whole book runs on: every king who follows is measured against an adulterer and a murderer, because whatever else he was, he had one God.

Ashtoreth (Astarte) is the Canaanite fertility goddess. Milcom was the national god of Ammon; verse 7 calls him Molech, the name the law links with the offering of children, though scholars debate whether the two names always mean the same god. The law is explicit about Molech: any one of the people of Israel... who gives any of his children to Molech shall surely be put to death (Lev. 20:2). The writer calls him the abomination of the Ammonites and does not soften it.

Did what was evil in the sight of the LORD appears here for the first time. From here to the end of 2 Kings it will be stamped on king after king until it becomes the drumbeat of the whole history, and the first man it is used of is the wisest king who ever lived, who built the temple.

A high place was a local open-air shrine, usually on raised ground, with an altar and often a standing stone or a sacred pole. On the mountain east of Jerusalem is the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron valley from the temple mount: a person in the courtyard of the house of the LORD could look up and see them. They were still there three hundred years later, when Josiah destroyed every shrine he could find: and the king defiled the high places that were east of Jerusalem, to the south of the mount of corruption, which Solomon the king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the abomination of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh the abomination of Moab, and for Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites (2 Kings 23:13). Still standing, and still called Solomon's.

The mechanism deserves precision, because it is not what most people imagine. There is no scene in which Solomon renounces the LORD. He does not abolish the priesthood or declare for Ashtoreth. He builds his wives their shrines.

Each one is a courtesy. A princess arrives from Moab as part of a treaty and needs somewhere to worship; refusing would insult her father. So a high place goes up. Then another, for the Ammonite. Verse 8 says he did it for all his foreign wives. One reasonable concession at a time, each defensible on its own, and at the end the hill facing the house of God is covered in altars and the king is going up to them. That is how a heart stops being wholly true: not by a decision, but by a series of arrangements nobody would have called a decision.

Does the ban on foreign wives apply to Christians? The danger named is that surely they will turn away your heart after their gods (v. 2). The principle carries over: a believer must marry only in the Lord (1 Cor 7:39).

Was Solomon saved? Scripture does not say whether he repented. Some take Ecclesiastes as the reflection of an old king who came back to God, and the Lord had loved him from birth (2 Sam 12:24–25); others see in his end a warning of how far a gifted man can fall. The text gives no verdict on his soul, and we should not claim more than it says; the plain lesson is that his heart was turned away (11:4), and that even wisdom does not keep a heart that will not stay near God.

Why does Chronicles say nothing about this? Its account of Solomon (2 Chron. 1-9) leaves out the foreign wives and the high places altogether. That is not a denial. Chronicles was written later, for readers who already had Kings, and it concentrates on the temple and David's line, which is what the returned exiles needed in order to rebuild. Nehemiah, from the same period, names Solomon's sin outright: foreign women made even him to sin (Neh. 13:26). The two books choose different things to tell; they do not disagree about what happened.
verseByVerse.note: Chemosh was the god of Moab; Molech (Milcom) the god of Ammon.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–25 — Because He Had Appeared to Him Twice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD is angry with Solomon, who had been warned twice in person (vv. 9-10), and will tear the kingdom from him and give it to his servant, yet not in his days and not all of it, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem (vv. 11-13). Then the adversaries: Hadad the Edomite, who had fled to Egypt as a boy (vv. 14-22), and Rezon, who reigned in Damascus (vv. 23-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Who had appeared to him twice. God did not send a prophet or a dream; he came in person, twice, and told him the exact thing to avoid. The more light we are given, the more seriously our turning from it is taken.
verseByVerse.examples: Judgment here does not come out of nowhere. Old wars, old grievances and men who had waited a lifetime become the instruments God uses. Sin's consequences often travel a long road before they arrive, and that is a reason to deal with it early, while the way back is open.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice and had commanded him concerning this thing, that he should not go after other gods. But he did not keep what the LORD commanded. Therefore the LORD said to Solomon, "Since this has been your practice and you have not kept my covenant and my statutes that I have commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom from you and will give it to your servant. Yet for the sake of David your father I will not do it in your days, but I will tear it out of the hand of your son. However, I will not tear away all the kingdom, but I will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of David my servant and for the sake of Jerusalem that I have chosen." And the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon, Hadad the Edomite. He was of the royal house in Edom. For when David was in Edom, and Joab the commander of the army went up to bury the slain, he struck down every male in Edom (for Joab and all Israel remained there six months, until he had cut off every male in Edom). But Hadad fled to Egypt, together with certain Edomites of his father's servants, Hadad still being a little child. They set out from Midian and came to Paran and took men with them from Paran and came to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt, who gave him a house and assigned him an allowance of food and gave him land. And Hadad found great favor in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him in marriage the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen. And the sister of Tahpenes bore him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house. And Genubath was in Pharaoh's house among the sons of Pharaoh. But when Hadad heard in Egypt that David slept with his fathers and that Joab the commander of the army was dead, Hadad said to Pharaoh, "Let me depart, that I may go to my own country." But Pharaoh said to him, "What have you lacked with me that you are now seeking to go to your own country?" And he said to him, "Only let me depart." God also raised up as an adversary to him, Rezon the son of Eliada, who had fled from his master Hadadezer king of Zobah. And he gathered men about him and became leader of a marauding band, after the killing by David. And they went to Damascus and lived there and made him king in Damascus. He was an adversary of Israel all the days of Solomon, doing harm as Hadad did. And he loathed Israel and reigned over Syria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now we see why chapter 9 bothered to say a second time: the writer laid that fact down two chapters ago so that it would aggravate the charge here. God did not leave this man to work it out. He came himself, twice, once at Gibeon to a young king who asked for an understanding mind, and once when the building was finished, and both times he said the same thing.

Concerning this thing means that this was not a general exhortation to godliness. God had named the specific sin in advance, and Solomon committed that one. Go back and read it: but if you turn aside from following me, you or your children... but go and serve other gods and worship them, then I will cut off Israel from the land (9:6-7).

Since this has been your practice describes a settled state of affairs rather than an incident: the high places had been there for years. And the kingdom goes to your servant: not to a rival dynasty or a foreign power, but to one of his own officials, named in verse 26, the superintendent of Solomon's forced labour.

Then the mercy, and it is inside the judgment rather than instead of it, three times over: not in your days, not all of it, and one tribe kept. Solomon is spared the sight of it, and the reason has nothing to do with Solomon. God is honouring a promise made in a night vision to a man, dead now forty years, who wanted to build him a temple and was told no. One tribe out of twelve is a kindness rather than a right. And God says he chose the city: the promise now hangs on a man and a place, both God's own selections. That is the shape of the gospel too: sinners kept on account of another, the Son of David whose obedience is counted for them (Romans 5:19).
