The LORD raised up an adversary. The word is satan, in the ordinary Hebrew sense of an opponent, and the writer uses it three times in this section (vv. 14, 23, 25). What follows is a piece of history with a long fuse in it, not recorded anywhere in 2 Samuel.

Joab spent six months in Edom systematically killing every male he could find. The campaign is mentioned in 2 Samuel 8 in a single verse about eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt; here is what the occupation was like. Joab’s slaughter (2 Sam 8:13–14) is recorded as fact, not commended; it explains why Hadad hated Israel.

A small boy is carried out of the massacre by his father's servants. He grows up in the Egyptian court and marries the queen's sister. He has a house, land, a royal marriage and a son raised among the sons of Pharaoh. He waits until David and Joab are dead, and then goes home. The writer gives him no speech about vengeance and no plan, only let me depart.

Rezon, the second adversary, comes out of David's Syrian campaign the way Hadad came out of the Edomite one. Damascus will be the great northern enemy for two centuries: Ben-hadad besieges Samaria in chapter 20, Naaman commands the army of Syria, and the Syrian wars run through the whole of 2 Kings. It starts here, with a man who escaped from David's victory.

Both adversaries are consequences of David's wars. They were boys and fugitives while Solomon was building his temple, and they have been waiting all his life. The writer says twice that God raised them up. The judgment arrives on legs, from a long way back, using things already in the world. God did not manufacture Solomon's adversaries; he raised up the ones that were already there.

Is it fair that the kingdom is torn from Solomon’s son? It was a judgment on Solomon’s house, softened for David’s sake; Rehoboam lost the north by his own folly (12:13–15).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite set over the forced labour of the house of Joseph, lifts up his hand against the king (vv. 26-28). Ahijah the Shilonite meets him alone in the open country, tears a new garment into twelve pieces and gives him ten (vv. 29-31); one tribe is kept for David's sake (vv. 32-36), and Jeroboam is offered David's covenant terms (vv. 37-39). Solomon seeks to kill him, and he flees to Egypt (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: A prophet tears a new cloak into twelve pieces on an empty road. A torn garment has stood for a torn kingdom before in this history, when Saul lost his throne (1 Sam. 15:27-28), and the sign is meant to be remembered.
verseByVerse.examples: Jeroboam is offered David's own covenant terms. The offer is genuine and it is conditional, and chapter 12 records what he did with it. God's gifts come with his word attached, and they are kept by keeping close to that word.

verseByVerse.quote: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zeredah, a servant of Solomon, whose mother's name was Zeruah, a widow, also lifted up his hand against the king. And this was the reason why he lifted up his hand against the king. Solomon built the Millo, and closed up the breach of the city of David his father. The man Jeroboam was very able, and when Solomon saw that the young man was industrious he gave him charge over all the forced labor of the house of Joseph. And at that time, when Jeroboam went out of Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite found him on the road. Now Ahijah had dressed himself in a new garment, and the two of them were alone in the open country. Then Ahijah laid hold of the new garment that was on him, and tore it into twelve pieces. And he said to Jeroboam, "Take for yourself ten pieces, for thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Behold, I am about to tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon and will give you ten tribes (but he shall have one tribe, for the sake of my servant David and for the sake of Jerusalem, the city that I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel), because they have forsaken me and worshiped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh the god of Moab, and Milcom the god of the Ammonites, and they have not walked in my ways, doing what is right in my sight and keeping my statutes and my rules, as David his father did. Nevertheless, I will not take the whole kingdom out of his hand, but I will make him ruler all the days of his life, for the sake of David my servant whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my statutes. But I will take the kingdom out of his son's hand and will give it to you, ten tribes. Yet to his son I will give one tribe, that David my servant may always have a lamp before me in Jerusalem, the city where I have chosen to put my name. And I will take you, and you shall reign over all that your soul desires, and you shall be king over Israel. And if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you. And I will afflict the offspring of David because of this, but not forever.'" Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam. But Jeroboam arose and fled into Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and was in Egypt until the death of Solomon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third adversary is an Israelite and a servant of the household. Jeroboam is an Ephraimite, from the leading tribe of the north, the tribe of Joshua, which had never been comfortable under a Judahite king. And his mother was Zeruah, a widow: a widow's son from the north, as the writer said of Hiram the craftsman.

The appointment is almost unbelievable in hindsight. Solomon noticed a capable young man and put him in charge of the forced labour of the house of Joseph, the conscripted work gangs of the northern tribes. So the man who will take ten tribes away from Solomon's son spent his formative years administering the exact grievance that the ten tribes will secede over. He knows every man in those gangs, the quotas, what the levy costs a farming family, and what is said about the king in the north when nobody from Jerusalem is listening. Solomon gave him that education himself, because he was good at his job.

Ahijah the Shilonite is from Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood for centuries, where Hannah prayed and Samuel was called, and which God destroyed and made a byword (Jer. 7:12). He has put on a new garment specifically for this, because he is about to destroy it. And they are alone in the open country: the most seditious conversation in the kingdom, with no witnesses.

He rips his own new coat into twelve. Prophets in Israel acted the message out, and this sign has a history in these books. When Samuel turned to leave Saul after the Amalekite affair, Saul caught at the hem of his robe and it tore, and Samuel said: the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you (1 Sam. 15:27-28). That tear was an accident and this one is deliberate, and the sentence that follows is nearly the same sentence.

The one tribe is kept again, for the same reason again: David, and the city God chose. Twelve pieces, ten given and one kept, leaves one unaccounted for. The likeliest answer is that the one tribe is Judah with little Benjamin bound to it (12:21), while Simeon's land had long lain inside Judah's (Josh. 19:1); the numbers describe the map, not a count of tribes.

Notice too that they have forsaken me. It is not only Solomon. The high places were public and had been there for years, and the nation had grown used to them.

A lamp is a word that goes back a long way. David's own men used it about him on a battlefield when he grew weary and a giant nearly killed him: you shall no longer go out with us to battle, lest you quench the lamp of Israel (2 Sam. 21:17). Here God takes the word up as his own. He uses it again when Abijam reigns badly (nevertheless, for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, 15:4), and again when Judah deserves destruction: the LORD was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever (2 Kings 8:19).

A lamp is a small thing, and it is not extinguished: not a blaze, not a guarantee of prosperity, just a light God undertakes not to let go out. And it does not go out. It burns down to almost nothing, a king in a Babylonian prison at the end of 2 Kings, and then to a carpenter's family in a village, where a child was born of whom the angel said, the Lord God will give to him the throne of his father David (Luke 1:32).

What is offered in verse 38 is astonishing and easy to miss. A sure house, as I built for David is the language of 2 Samuel 7: an enduring dynasty in the north on David's own footing. It is not a consolation prize but everything, on the one condition that governs everything in this book: listen, walk in my ways, keep my statutes, as David my servant did. Hold it for one chapter: the first substantial thing Jeroboam does with his kingdom is make two golden calves. And even the sentence on David's line has a limit written into it: but not forever.

Then comes the last recorded act of the wisest man who ever lived: he tries to have Jeroboam murdered. God has told him in person that the kingdom will be torn from his son. Solomon's response is not repentance, not the removal of the high places, not a word to God. It is an assassination order.

He is doing what Saul did. Told by a prophet that the kingdom was going to a neighbour, Saul spent the rest of his life trying to kill the neighbour. You cannot kill your way out of a word from God. Solomon of all people knew it, and he tried anyway.

Jeroboam goes to Egypt, to Shishak, where Hadad went as a boy and the daughter of Pharaoh came from. Egypt has now sheltered two of Solomon's three adversaries, and five years after his death Shishak comes up and takes everything in Jerusalem that is not nailed down.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–43 — So Solomon Slept with His Fathers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of Solomon's acts are in the Book of the Acts of Solomon (v. 41); he reigns forty years, sleeps with his fathers, and Rehoboam his son reigns in his place (vv. 42-43).
verseByVerse.theology: The formula arrives, and from here to the end of both books it will be repeated over king after king: the rest of his acts, the source, the years, the burial, the successor. Solomon is the first to receive it in full.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer, who has told us about the wisdom and the temple and the gold and the seven hundred wives, closes the account by pointing at a book we do not have and telling us there was more. Every life is larger than its record, and only God holds the full one.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, and all that he did, and his wisdom, are they not written in the Book of the Acts of Solomon? And the time that Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel was forty years. And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father. And Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here the formula appears for the first time: the rest of his acts, the source, the length of the reign, the burial, the successor. It will be applied to some forty kings, most in a few lines, and it gives Kings its relentless quality: a man's whole life summarised, filed, and closed, and then the next one.

The writer is also citing a source we do not have, as Kings does dozens of times. He knows he is not writing an exhaustive account. He is writing a theological one, and he selects: four chapters on the temple, one on the wives, none on the administration of a forty-year empire.

Solomon reigned forty years, like David, and like Saul (Saul's forty is given in Acts 13:21; the numbers in the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 13:1 are damaged). Three kings, forty years each, and then the kingdom breaks. Stand back from the whole account, because the shape of it matters.

He began by asking God for an understanding mind, and God was pleased with the request and gave him more than he asked. He judged two prostitutes rightly, built the house of God, and stood before it and confessed that heaven itself cannot contain God, let alone a house built by hands. He prayed for the foreigner and the exile and the man who knows the affliction of his own heart. A queen crossed a desert on a rumour about the name of his God.

He also acquired horses, traded with Egypt, made silver as common as stone, married seven hundred princesses, built shrines for them on the hill facing the temple, and tried to murder the man God had chosen to succeed him.

All of it is the same man, and the writer records all of it, and does not resolve it. What he does instead is put two words in Solomon's mouth in chapter 8 and take them away in chapter 11: wholly true. He told the nation their hearts must be that toward God. And at the end, with every advantage a man has ever had, his was not.

11.theology:
The heart is the issue. The law's ban on marrying into the nations of Canaan was never about blood or nationality (Rahab and Ruth are in the line of Christ); it was about worship: they will turn away your heart after their gods. Kings shows the warning coming true in the household of the wisest man alive. The undivided heart that Solomon urged on the nation (8:61) is the thing he lost, and it is the measure the whole book will use. David, for all his terrible sins, never went after another god; Solomon did. Faithfulness in Kings is not sinlessness but belonging to the LORD alone, with a heart that returns to him when it is confronted.

How drift happens. There is no scene in which Solomon renounces the LORD. Each shrine is a courtesy owed to a treaty wife, and each is defensible on its own. That is why the chapter is a mirror rather than a curiosity. Hearts are rarely turned by one dramatic choice; they are turned by arrangements nobody would call a decision. And it happens when Solomon was old, after Gibeon, the temple and two appearances of God, so no stage of life or spiritual history makes anyone safe in themselves. The safety the Bible offers is in God's keeping, not in our record.

Light makes the sin heavier. God had appeared to Solomon twice and named this very sin in advance (9:6-7). The anger of verse 9 is the anger of a Father who warned his son face to face. Judgment follows in the ordinary stuff of history: a servant promoted over the forced labour, and two adversaries left over from David's wars, whom God raised up. God governs even the long consequences of old violence, and he is not hurried.

Mercy inside judgment. Every restraint in the sentence (not in your days, not all the kingdom, one tribe kept) is for the sake of David my servant and of the city God chose. The lamp of verse 36 is small but God will not let it go out, and it burns on to the Son of David. That is the gospel shape of the chapter: unworthy people kept on account of another, whose obedience is counted for them (Romans 5:19).

Fighting a word from God. Jeroboam is offered David's own covenant terms, and Solomon answers the prophecy with an assassination order, as Saul once did. Neither the promise nor the threat of God can be managed by force. The only fitting response to a word from God is to bow to it, and Solomon, who knew more than anyone, is never recorded doing so.

Egypt again. The chapter keeps glancing south. The daughter of Pharaoh heads the list of wives; Hadad grows up in Pharaoh's court; Jeroboam takes refuge with Shishak; and within five years of Solomon's death Shishak will be in Jerusalem carrying off the gold. The road back to Egypt that the law of the king had closed, and that Solomon reopened for horses and marriages, becomes the road by which his enemies are sheltered and his treasures leave. The writer does not draw the line for us, but it is there to be seen.

A life filed and closed. The closing formula (vv. 41-43) will be stamped on king after king. Solomon's account contains real wisdom, true prayer and a temple God filled with his glory, and it also contains the high places and the assassination order. Scripture does not average the two. It records both and leaves the verdict on his soul with God, while making plain that gifts, learning and a great past do not keep a heart. Only the King who is greater than Solomon does that.
11.examples:
Then: A king who had asked God for an understanding mind, built him a temple, prayed one of the longest prayers in the Old Testament and been visited by God twice in person, spent his old age putting up shrines to other gods on the hill facing that temple, one at a time, for one wife at a time; and when God told him the kingdom would be torn away, he sought to kill the man the prophet had named.

Now: Three things, and they are all uncomfortable. First, the timing: when Solomon was old, after every spiritual advantage a human being has ever had. There is no stage of life at which a person becomes safe in their own strength. Second, the mechanism. There was never a moment when he decided to abandon God, only seven hundred reasonable accommodations, each owed to somebody, until the hill facing the house of God was covered in altars. And third, wholly true: he preached it to a nation and lost it. The question the chapter leaves is not whether your religion is functioning. It is whether there is anything else in the room. Where there is, the way back is the one Solomon is never recorded taking: confess it to the God who promised to forgive (1 John 1:9), and rest on the Son of David whose heart was wholly true to his Father in our place. His Spirit, now given to believers, is the one who makes a divided heart whole and keeps it near (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

12.title: The Kingdom Torn in Two
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.<sup>2</sup>And as soon as Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), then Jeroboam returned from Egypt.<sup>3</sup>And they sent and called him, and Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came and said to Rehoboam,<sup>4</sup>"Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you."<sup>5</sup>He said to them, "Go away for three days, then come again to me." So the people went away.<sup>6</sup>Then King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he was yet alive, saying, "How do you advise me to answer this people?"<sup>7</sup>And they said to him, "If you will be a servant to this people today and serve them, and speak good words to them when you answer them, then they will be your servants forever."<sup>8</sup>But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him.<sup>9</sup>And he said to them, "What do you advise that we answer this people who have said to me, 'Lighten the yoke that your father put on us'?"<sup>10</sup>And the young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Thus shall you speak to this people who said to you, 'Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us,' thus shall you say to them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs.<sup>11</sup>And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.'"<sup>12</sup>So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king said, "Come to me again the third day."<sup>13</sup>And the king answered the people harshly, and forsaking the counsel that the old men had given him,<sup>14</sup>he spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, "My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions."<sup>15</sup>So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD that he might fulfill his word, which the LORD spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.<sup>16</sup>And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So Israel went to their tents.<sup>17</sup>But Rehoboam reigned over the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah.<sup>18</sup>Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot to flee to Jerusalem.<sup>19</sup>So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day.<sup>20</sup>And when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. There was none that followed the house of David but the tribe of Judah only.<sup>21</sup>When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against the house of Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam the son of Solomon.<sup>22</sup>But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God:<sup>23</sup>"Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people,<sup>24</sup>'Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives the people of Israel. Every man return to his home, for this thing is from me.'" So they listened to the word of the LORD and went home again, according to the word of the LORD.<sup>25</sup>Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. And he went out from there and built Penuel.<sup>26</sup>And Jeroboam said in his heart, "Now the kingdom will turn back to the house of David.<sup>27</sup>If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the temple of the LORD at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me and return to Rehoboam king of Judah."<sup>28</sup>So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold. And he said to the people, "You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt."<sup>29</sup>And he set one in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan.<sup>30</sup>Then this thing became a sin, for the people went as far as Dan to be before one.<sup>31</sup>He also made temples on high places and appointed priests from among all the people, who were not of the Levites.<sup>32</sup>And Jeroboam appointed a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month like the feast that was in Judah, and he offered sacrifices on the altar. So he did in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves that he made. And he placed in Bethel the priests of the high places that he had made.<sup>33</sup>He went up to the altar that he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, in the month that he had devised from his own heart. And he instituted a feast for the people of Israel and went up to the altar to make offerings.
12.overview:
The coronation is at Shechem, not Jerusalem: a long way north, on the northern tribes' ground, where Abraham built an altar and Joshua said choose this day whom you will serve. That alone tells you the state of the union before a word is spoken.

The demand is not religious and not separatist. It is about the levy, the conscripted labour the writer has been recording since chapter 4 without a word of comment. Here is the comment, and it comes from the people who carried it, and their word for it is yoke. Rehoboam is offered wise counsel by the men who ran his father's government, prefers the advice of the friends he grew up with, and loses ten tribes with a single speech; the north answers with a slogan some forty years old. The old men's advice, be a servant to this people today, is the sentence to keep from the first half of the chapter, and the Son of David would one day show what it means in full.

Then Jeroboam, who had been promised a sure house by God, secures his new kingdom out of fear, with two golden calves and a festival of his own devising. Over the whole catastrophe the writer lifts the curtain twice, a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD and this thing is from me, though not one person is coerced and every one behaves exactly as you would expect.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — My Little Finger Is Thicker
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All Israel comes to Shechem to make Rehoboam king, with Jeroboam back from Egypt, and asks one thing: lighten his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you (vv. 1-5). The old men advise him to be a servant to this people today (vv. 6-7); he takes the young men's counsel instead and promises scorpions (vv. 8-14), for it was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The one thing ten tribes ask of a new king is relief from the conscripted labour that built the temple and the palace and the chariot cities. Godly rule listens to a just complaint, even one that wounds the ruler's pride.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has charge of others (a parent, an employer, an elder) will one day be asked for relief by people who have carried a load. How we answer in that moment says more about our leadership than any amount of success before it.

verseByVerse.quote: Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king. And as soon as Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), then Jeroboam returned from Egypt. And they sent and called him, and Jeroboam and all the assembly of Israel came and said to Rehoboam, "Your father made our yoke heavy. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke on us, and we will serve you." He said to them, "Go away for three days, then come again to me." So the people went away. Then King Rehoboam took counsel with the old men, who had stood before Solomon his father while he was yet alive, saying, "How do you advise me to answer this people?" And they said to him, "If you will be a servant to this people today and serve them, and speak good words to them when you answer them, then they will be your servants forever." But he abandoned the counsel that the old men gave him and took counsel with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him. And he said to them, "What do you advise that we answer this people who have said to me, 'Lighten the yoke that your father put on us'?" And the young men who had grown up with him said to him, "Thus shall you speak to this people who said to you, 'Your father made our yoke heavy, but you lighten it for us,' thus shall you say to them, 'My little finger is thicker than my father's thighs. And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.'" So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam the third day, as the king said, "Come to me again the third day." And the king answered the people harshly, and forsaking the counsel that the old men had given him, he spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, "My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions." So the king did not listen to the people, for it was a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD that he might fulfill his word, which the LORD spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coronation is not held in Jerusalem. Shechem is in the hill country of Ephraim, one of the oldest covenant sites in the country. Abraham built an altar there; Joshua gathered all Israel there and said choose this day whom you will serve (Josh. 24); Joseph's bones are buried there. The new king must travel a long way north to be made king on the northern tribes' ground.

What the demand is and is not deserves precision. It is not about religion. Nobody mentions the high places on the mountain east of Jerusalem, and Ahijah's word is not quoted at anybody. Nor is it separatism: we will serve you is the last clause of the sentence, and it is an offer. It is about the levy.

That meant thirty thousand men conscripted in monthly shifts to Lebanon, seventy thousand burden-bearers, eighty thousand quarrymen, and a minister of forced labour with a department. It meant twenty years of building the temple, the palace, the Millo, the wall, Hazor, Megiddo, Gezer and the store and chariot cities. And it meant twelve districts drawn across the tribal inheritances, each feeding the court for a month. The writer has been laying that down since chapter 4 without comment. Here is the comment, from the people who carried it, and their word for it is yoke: what you put on an animal to make it pull.

Rehoboam asks for three days, and he uses them properly at first: he asks two sets of advisers. The old men ran Solomon's government. They know exactly what the levy was, because they administered it, and they know what the country thinks of it.

Their advice is not what people assume when they hear that a king was told to be nice. It is one day against a lifetime. The old men are not asking him to be soft. They are telling him the arithmetic: serve them once, when they have asked for something and it costs you, and you will have them for the rest of your life. Both verbs, be a servant... and serve them, come from the ordinary word for a bondman, which is what the assembly offered in verse 4: and we will serve you. You take the servant's place today; they take it permanently. And speak good words to them is not about tone. In the language of treaties, good words are favourable terms.

A thousand years later, when two of the Twelve asked for the chief seats, the Son of David said: You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:42-45).

The correspondence should be stated carefully. The old men are giving prudential advice to a king, about outcomes. Jesus is not offering a technique for retaining power. He is describing what greatness is in his kingdom, grounded in what he came to do, and the cost is not a day of concessions but his life. So the verse is not the gospel. It is the shadow the gospel casts backwards over every position of authority, and even at the level of statecraft, at Shechem in the tenth century before Christ, the old men had noticed that serving is the only thing that works.

Rehoboam had that advice from the men who had run the country for forty years. Then he turned to the young men who had grown up with him, and those words are the whole explanation. These are his friends. They grew up in the palace during the richest reign in Israel's history, among the gold shields and the ivory throne, and never once carried a stone.

Rehoboam is about forty-one years old (14:21), so these are not boys. They are men of his own age who have never done anything except be near power. Then why are they called young men? The Hebrew word is the ordinary one for children or lads, and here it is probably a slighting term, something like the boys, for men who had never carried responsibility. (The Greek Old Testament, in a longer alternative account of these events, makes Rehoboam sixteen, and his son later calls him young and irresolute, 2 Chron. 13:7; but most follow the Hebrew's forty-one.)

He asked both, which makes this worse rather than better. He did not fail to seek advice. He sought two opinions and picked the one he wanted. Note how he frames the question to the second group: what shall we answer this people who have said to me, quoting their demand back as a complaint about his father. He has already decided how he feels. He is looking for support.

The young men's line about his little finger is crude and it is meant to be: a boast about virility and force that says, whatever you thought my father was, I am more of it. A scorpion here is generally taken to be a whip with barbs or metal worked into the lashes, designed to tear. The men asked for the yoke to be lightened. He promises to add to it and change the instrument. He does not deny that his father used whips; he takes Solomon's record as the baseline he intends to exceed.

The young advisers are not stupid about tactics; they are certain the north will do what it is told, because in their experience it always has. They grew up watching the gangs go north ten thousand a month and come back. People who have only ever seen power obeyed cannot imagine it refused. And Rehoboam says it out loud, to their faces, in the assembly.

Here the writer lifts the curtain for one sentence, as he did at 2 Samuel 17:14, and the verse insists on both halves without explaining how they fit. On the human side, everything is fully accounted for. A frightened, vain man of forty-one chose the flatterers, afraid of looking weak in his first week. The young men were arrogant because they had never carried anything. The north had a real grievance that nobody in Jerusalem had taken seriously. Not one person is coerced. And the writer says God did it.

This is the structure the books of Samuel and Kings keep using at the great hinges. Ahithophel gave sound advice and Absalom preferred a better speech, for the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel (2 Sam. 17:14). Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good, of the same act (Gen. 50:20). And the cross: delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God and crucified by the hands of lawless men in the same sentence (Acts 2:23). Scripture never resolves the mechanism and never drops either half. God is not a spectator to whom history happens, and no man in this chapter has an excuse.

Does that make God the author of Rehoboam's pride? No. The Westminster Confession puts it carefully: God's providence reaches even to the sins of men, yet the sinfulness comes only from the creature, and God neither causes nor approves it (Westminster 5.4). He did not put folly into Rehoboam; he let a proud man be himself and steered the outcome to keep his word. The cross is the plainest case, and there the rule ran toward mercy: the worst thing men ever did became the salvation of the world.

Note the purpose clause: that he might fulfill his word, which the LORD spoke by Ahijah. The tearing of the cloak was one chapter ago, on an empty road, with two men present.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — To Your Tents, O Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel answers with Sheba's old cry, What portion do we have in David?, and goes to its tents (v. 16). Rehoboam sends Adoram, the taskmaster over the forced labour, who is stoned, and the king flees to Jerusalem (vv. 17-19). Jeroboam is made king over Israel; only Judah follows David (vv. 20-21). Rehoboam musters to fight, but Shemaiah brings the word, this thing is from me, and they obey (vv. 22-24).
verseByVerse.theology: A careless word can outlive the one who says it. A slogan shouted by a rebel in David's day becomes, forty years later, the founding cry of a separate kingdom. And behind it lay a quarrel about precedence that nobody troubled to heal. Divisions among God's people seldom start large; they start with pride and are left to grow.
verseByVerse.examples: When trust has broken, sending the very person who embodies the grievance is the surest way to finish it off. Repairing a wrong usually begins by changing what caused it, not by sending its enforcer.

verseByVerse.quote: And when all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, "What portion do we have in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, O Israel! Look now to your own house, David." So Israel went to their tents. But Rehoboam reigned over the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah. Then King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was taskmaster over the forced labor, and all Israel stoned him to death with stones. And King Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot to flee to Jerusalem. So Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day. And when all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent and called him to the assembly and made him king over all Israel. There was none that followed the house of David but the tribe of Judah only. When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, 180,000 chosen warriors, to fight against the house of Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam the son of Solomon. But the word of God came to Shemaiah the man of God: "Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people, 'Thus says the LORD, You shall not go up or fight against your relatives the people of Israel. Every man return to his home, for this thing is from me.'" So they listened to the word of the LORD and went home again, according to the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The northerners' cry is some forty years old. In David's day there happened to be there a worthless man, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri, a Benjaminite. And he blew the trumpet and said, "We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel!" (2 Sam. 20:1).

It is almost the same sentence, in the same order. A man the writer of Samuel called worthless, with no army and no case, said it at a river crossing, and his rebellion was over inside a chapter with his head thrown over a wall. His sentence survived him by some forty years, and here it is the constitutional act of ten tribes.

The crack opened in the last verse of 2 Samuel 19, when Israel and Judah argued about who had the right to escort David home across the Jordan, a quarrel about precedence. The writer ends by recording only this: the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel (2 Sam. 19:43). The very next verse is Sheba's trumpet. So the line runs: a squabble about who walked beside the king; a slogan handed to humiliated men; a failed revolt; decades of the levy; and a king who would rather sound strong than be obeyed.

Look now to your own house, David is the coldest clause in the verse. It is a dismissal (go and manage your own family) addressed to a dynasty God had promised would last forever.

Few decisions in the book are more foolish than the next one. Ten tribes have just walked out over the forced labour, and Rehoboam sends them the minister of forced labour. Whether to negotiate or to start collecting, the text does not say. Adoram is the human face of the thing they have just seceded over. He has been in this history a long time: in David's last cabinet list as Adoram... in charge of the forced labor (2 Sam. 20:24), in Solomon's as Adoniram the son of Abda (4:6), and running the levy to Lebanon (5:14). He is named three times across three reigns without comment. Here is the comment: they stone him to death. And the man who three days ago compared his little finger to his father's thighs is getting into a chariot as fast as he can.

To this day. The division never healed. The north lasted two centuries and fell to Assyria; the south went to Babylon nearly a century and a half later. They were never one nation again.

Yet the prophets would not let the split be the last word. Ezekiel took two sticks, one for Judah and one for Joseph, and held them as one in his hand, promising one king over a reunited people and my servant David as their one shepherd (Ezek. 37:15-24). The New Testament sees that promise met in the Son of David, who lays down his life for the sheep and dies to gather the scattered children of God into one (John 10:11-16; 11:52). What Rehoboam's pride broke, Christ's death mends, on a scale Ezekiel could only begin to see.

Rehoboam then musters a hundred and eighty thousand men to take the north back by force. The word Shemaiah brings is the second half of the chapter's theological spine, and it is stronger than the first. Verse 15 called the refusal a turn of affairs brought about by the LORD. This says the whole breaking of the kingdom David spent his life uniting is God's own doing. Not permitted, not foreseen, but from me.

The prophet calls the northerners your relatives, literally your brothers: the argument Abner shouted across a valley at Joab eighty years earlier, How long will it be before you tell your people to turn from the pursuit of their brothers? (2 Sam. 2:26).

They obey, which is the one thing anybody in this chapter does right. A hundred and eighty thousand armed men go home on one sentence from a prophet. Rehoboam would not listen to the old men or to ten tribes standing in front of him, but he listens to Shemaiah. It is his one good decision, and also the shape of what is wrong with him: he can obey God when a prophet tells him plainly, and he cannot govern people.

Where is the twelfth tribe? Ahijah’s ten and one leave one piece unexplained. Benjamin joined Judah (v. 21), and Simeon had long been absorbed within Judah’s territory (Josh 19:1); the “one tribe” is Judah with Benjamin.

Was Jeroboam at the assembly or not? Verses 2-3 put him there, while verse 20 reads as if the tribes sent for him afterwards. Many think verses 2-3 tell his part in advance and verse 20 records the formal summons to make him king. The Greek Old Testament tells his rise in a different order, which shows the story was handed down in more than one form; the events themselves are not in doubt.
verseByVerse.note: From here the kingdom is divided: Israel (ten tribes) in the north, Judah in the south.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–33 — Behold Your Gods, O Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeroboam fortifies Shechem and Penuel (v. 25) and reasons that if the people go up to sacrifice at Jerusalem, they will kill me (vv. 26-27). He makes two calves of gold, Behold your gods, O Israel, and sets them in Bethel and Dan, and this thing became a sin (vv. 28-30). He appoints priests who were not Levites and a feast in the eighth month that he had devised from his own heart (vv. 31-33).
verseByVerse.theology: He had been offered David's own covenant on condition of obedience (11:38), and his first act as king is the thing that forfeits it. His stated reasoning is entirely about security: they will kill me. He does it because he is afraid, and fear that will not trust God's promise always finds another way to feel safe.
verseByVerse.examples: Fear is a poor architect of worship. When we arrange our approach to God around what keeps us safe or comfortable rather than around what he has asked, we may keep the forms of religion and lose the God they were meant to serve.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. And he went out from there and built Penuel. And Jeroboam said in his heart, "Now the kingdom will turn back to the house of David. If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the temple of the LORD at Jerusalem, then the heart of this people will turn again to their lord, to Rehoboam king of Judah, and they will kill me and return to Rehoboam king of Judah." So the king took counsel and made two calves of gold. And he said to the people, "You have gone up to Jerusalem long enough. Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." And he set one in Bethel, and the other he put in Dan. Then this thing became a sin, for the people went as far as Dan to be before one. He also made temples on high places and appointed priests from among all the people, who were not of the Levites. And Jeroboam appointed a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month like the feast that was in Judah, and he offered sacrifices on the altar. So he did in Bethel, sacrificing to the calves that he made. And he placed in Bethel the priests of the high places that he had made. He went up to the altar that he had made in Bethel on the fifteenth day in the eighth month, in the month that he had devised from his own heart. And he instituted a feast for the people of Israel and went up to the altar to make offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jeroboam fortifies a capital and a crossing point east of the Jordan; Penuel is where Jacob wrestled all night and was named Israel.

Said in his heart is a phrase the reader has met before, at a bad moment: Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines" (1 Sam. 27:1). No priest, no prophet: a man doing his own thinking in a crisis, and it cost him sixteen months in enemy country. Jeroboam has more reason not to do it than David had: a word from a prophet, in person, with an offer attached.

Every step of the reasoning is politically sound. Three times a year every male in Israel was required at Jerusalem: his entire adult population walking into his rival's capital to worship at a temple built by the dynasty he has just replaced. No new state could survive that.

Note where the reasoning ends: they will kill me. That is the engine. Not theology, not a vision for the north, not even ambition, but fear. Set that against what he had been given: if you will listen to all that I command you, and will walk in my ways, and do what is right in my eyes by keeping my statutes and my commandments, as David my servant did, I will be with you and will build you a sure house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you (11:38). David's own covenant, in David's own words.

The security he fears for has already been guaranteed by God before he was king. And within a few verses of getting the kingdom he protects it by means that forfeit the promise. That is the tragedy of the man, and a very ordinary one: he believed the prophecy enough to take the throne and not enough to trust the God who gave it.

Read his proclamation beside Exodus 32. Aaron, with Moses on the mountain, took the people's gold and made a calf, and they said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" (Ex. 32:4). Jeroboam says it almost exactly, and makes two. It is not an accidental echo. Everybody knew that story: the worst day in the nation's history, three thousand dead, the calf ground to powder and drunk. Jeroboam repeats it deliberately and at national scale.

And it is subtler than simple idolatry, which is what makes it work. He names no foreign god. The sentence is about the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, the right God, correctly identified by the right act. In the surrounding cultures a bull was usually the pedestal the god stood on rather than the god itself, and Jeroboam very likely presented these as thrones for the invisible LORD. That is what Aaron did: he made the calf and announced, Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD (Ex. 32:5).

So this is worship of the true God by means he has forbidden, a breach of the second commandment rather than the first, and that is why it is so dangerous. Nobody in the north had to decide to abandon the LORD. They had to accept a more convenient way of approaching him, sanctioned by the state, closer to home, requiring no journey.

The placement is expert. Dan is at the far north and Bethel at the southern border, about a dozen miles from Jerusalem; nobody has to travel far. Both sites already had religious history. Bethel, whose name means house of God, is where Jacob saw the ladder and said surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it... this is none other than the house of God (Gen. 28:16-17). Dan had housed an illegitimate shrine since the judges, with a stolen idol and a hired Levite (Judg. 18). He invents nothing; he uses ground people already felt religious about.

This thing became a sin becomes the writer's shorthand for the whole northern kingdom. To the fall of Samaria, king after king is condemned in one formula: he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. Two centuries of kings are measured against this day.

The second thing he does is as serious as the calves. The priesthood belonged to Aaron's line within Levi, and the tribe had no territory precisely so that they would be spread through the country to teach. Even a king of Judah, Uzziah, was struck with leprosy for burning incense in the temple (2 Chron. 26:16-21). Chronicles records what happened next: the northern Levites left their pasturelands and came south, because Jeroboam and his sons cast them out from serving as priests of the LORD (2 Chron. 11:14). He emptied the north of the men whose job was to teach the law.

Then a festival one month late. The Feast of Booths was the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the feast Solomon chose for the dedication; Jeroboam moves it to the eighth. Everything is almost right: almost the same festival, date and God, at sites with genuine history, with priests and altars, and all of it one month and one tribe and one commandment out.

Devised from his own heart is the writer's verdict on the whole enterprise: not the month God appointed, but the month he thought of. The charge is not that he was irreligious. He was extremely religious: sanctuaries, clergy, festival, and the king at the altar himself. Every element of it came out of a man's own head, for the reason he had stated: they will kill me.

The old men told Rehoboam what would keep his kingdom and he preferred what his friends said. Ahijah told Jeroboam what would build him a sure house and he preferred what he had worked out himself. Both had the answer in their hands, and between them they broke the kingdom of God's people in half.
verseByVerse.note: Bethel and Dan lay at the southern and northern ends of Jeroboam’s kingdom. The calves echoed Aaron’s golden calf.

12.theology:
Authority is for service. The old men's counsel to Rehoboam is plain statecraft, but it rests on something deeper: a ruler exists for the good of the ruled. Israel's kings were never meant to be masters over their brothers (Deut. 17:20), and the levy had turned the king into a taskmaster. Jesus takes the principle much further, grounding greatness in his own service and his ransoming death (Mark 10:42-45). Rehoboam is the opposite picture: a man who heard the truth from the experienced, preferred the flattery of the comfortable, and turned a just request into an insult. Pride did not merely spoil his reign; it broke the people of God.

Grievances that are heard too late. The writer recorded Solomon's levy for eight chapters without a word of criticism: the thirty thousand to Lebanon, the burden-bearers, the quarrymen, the districts drawn across the tribal lands. The comment comes only now, from the people who carried it, and their word is yoke. Glory built on other people's backs can look like blessing for a long time. Scripture does not let us admire the temple and the palaces without hearing, in the end, what they cost the ordinary families of the north. God hears the cry of the burdened even when the court does not, and the stoning of Adoram, the man who had run the levy through three reigns, shows how deep the anger had gone.

Counsel that confirms what we want. Rehoboam did seek advice. He sought two sets of it, framed the question differently to each, and chose the one that agreed with what he already felt. That is the ordinary way wise people make foolish decisions, and it is a warning to anyone who asks for counsel while hoping for permission.

God's rule over human choices. Twice the writer says the breach was God's doing (vv. 15, 24), yet no one is forced and no one is excused. Scripture holds both truths without explaining how they fit, at Ahithophel's counsel, in Joseph's story, and supremely at the cross (Acts 2:23). God's providence does not make him the author of sin; it means that even proud and frightened men cannot stop his word from coming true, and that he can turn the worst human acts toward his good purposes.

Old wounds and long fuses. The cry of verse 16 comes from Sheba's failed revolt, and behind that from a quarrel about precedence at the Jordan. Resentments left unhealed in one generation can become the policy of the next. The division itself never healed in Old Testament history, but the prophets promised one people under one Shepherd, and that promise is kept in Christ, who dies to gather God's scattered children into one (John 11:52).

Obedience in one place. When Shemaiah speaks, Rehoboam and his army go home. It is the one good decision in the chapter, and it shows that hearing God's plain word and doing it is possible even for a foolish man. The trouble is that he could obey a prophet and still not govern people with justice. Obedience to God at the moment of crisis is good, and it spared a civil war; but it is meant to flow into the whole of life, including the way we treat those under us. Rehoboam's religion and his rule never quite met.

Fear and the second commandment. Jeroboam had God's promise of a sure house, and he answered it with calculation. His calves did not replace the LORD with another god. They offered the LORD a more convenient worship: closer to home, approved by the state, at places with a religious past, with a priesthood and a festival that were all nearly right. That is why it worked and why it was so deadly. The second commandment guards not only whom we worship but how, because worship devised to suit us slowly reshapes our picture of God. Devised from his own heart is the verdict on all of it.

Teachers driven out. The most lasting damage may have been the least visible. By appointing priests from any tribe, Jeroboam pushed out the Levites, whose task was to teach the law in every part of the land, and Chronicles says they went south (2 Chron. 11:14). A people without faithful teachers soon forgets what true worship was, and two centuries of northern kings would be measured against the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which he made Israel to sin. The way back for any church that has drifted begins with recovering the word of God taught plainly by those he has called.

Almost right is not right. Jeroboam's festival was a month late, his priests from the wrong tribe, his calves a breach of one commandment rather than all ten. Each change could be defended, and together they made a religion that looked familiar and led away from God. The danger for churches is rarely the open denial of Christ; it is the slow redesign of worship to suit our fears and conveniences. The answer is not anxiety about every detail but a glad return to what God has given: his word, his appointed means, and the one Mediator through whom we come.

Two kings who had the answer. Rehoboam had wise counsel, and Jeroboam had a promise from God. Both preferred their own thinking, and between them they broke the kingdom in half. The chapter's hope lies outside both of them, in the Son of David who did not grasp at security but trusted his Father, served instead of being served, and through his obedience gathers a people who will never be divided again.
12.examples:
Then: Ten tribes asked a new king for one thing, that the conscripted labour be lightened, and offered to serve him if it was. The men who had run the government for forty years told him that one day of serving them would buy him their loyalty for life. He asked his friends instead, promised to beat them with something worse than his father had used, and then sent them the minister of forced labour, who was stoned to death in the road.

Now: Three things. The old men's sentence is the one to keep, and its force is that it is not sentiment but arithmetic: a day of genuine service, when somebody has asked for something and it costs you, buys what no authority can command. Anyone who has charge of anybody is standing in Rehoboam's three days. We do not serve that way by nature, and we do not do it perfectly; the one who did, the Son of Man who came to serve and gave his life as a ransom, gives his Spirit to those who follow him, and that is where the strength for it comes from. Second, Rehoboam did not fail to seek counsel: he sought two opinions, chose the one he already wanted, and framed the question differently to each. That is the ordinary way people get bad advice. And third, Jeroboam, whose golden calves were not apostasy but convenience: the right God, correctly named, approached by a method he had devised himself. Worship quietly redesigned to cost less is the danger this chapter is about, and the remedy is to come to God the way he has given, through the one Mediator he has provided.

13.title: The Man of God from Judah
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And behold, a man of God came out of Judah by the word of the LORD to Bethel. Jeroboam was standing by the altar to make offerings.<sup>2</sup>And the man cried against the altar by the word of the LORD and said, "O altar, altar, thus says the LORD: 'Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you, and human bones shall be burned on you.'"<sup>3</sup>And he gave a sign the same day, saying, "This is the sign that the LORD has spoken: 'Behold, the altar shall be torn down, and the ashes that are on it shall be poured out.'"<sup>4</sup>And when the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar at Bethel, Jeroboam stretched out his hand from the altar, saying, "Seize him." And his hand, which he stretched out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back to himself.<sup>5</sup>The altar also was torn down, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign that the man of God had given by the word of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And the king said to the man of God, "Entreat now the favor of the LORD your God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me." And the man of God entreated the LORD, and the king's hand was restored to him and became as it was before.<sup>7</sup>And the king said to the man of God, "Come home with me, and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward."<sup>8</sup>And the man of God said to the king, "If you give me half your house, I will not go in with you. And I will not eat bread or drink water in this place,<sup>9</sup>for so was it commanded me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water nor return by the way that you came.'"<sup>10</sup>So he went another way and did not return by the way that he came to Bethel.<sup>11</sup>Now an old prophet lived in Bethel. And his sons came and told him all that the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told to their father the words that he had spoken to the king.<sup>12</sup>And their father said to them, "Which way did he go?" And his sons showed him the way that the man of God who came from Judah had gone.<sup>13</sup>And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." So they saddled the donkey for him and he mounted it.<sup>14</sup>And he went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak. And he said to him, "Are you the man of God who came from Judah?" And he said, "I am."<sup>15</sup>Then he said to him, "Come home with me and eat bread."<sup>16</sup>And he said, "I may not return with you, or go in with you, neither will I eat bread nor drink water with you in this place,<sup>17</sup>for it was said to me by the word of the LORD, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water there, nor return by the way that you came.'"<sup>18</sup>And he said to him, "I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'Bring him back with you into your house that he may eat bread and drink water.'" But he lied to him.<sup>19</sup>So he went back with him and ate bread in his house and drank water.<sup>20</sup>And as they sat at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back.<sup>21</sup>And he cried to the man of God who came from Judah, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have disobeyed the word of the LORD and have not kept the command that the LORD your God commanded you,<sup>22</sup>but have come back and have eaten bread and drunk water in the place of which he said to you, "Eat no bread and drink no water," your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers.'"<sup>23</sup>And after he had eaten bread and drunk, he saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back.<sup>24</sup>And as he went away a lion met him on the road and killed him. And his body was thrown in the road, and the donkey stood beside it; the lion also stood beside the body.<sup>25</sup>And behold, men passed by and saw the body thrown in the road and the lion standing by the body. And they came and told it in the city where the old prophet lived.<sup>26</sup>And when the prophet who had brought him back from the way heard of it, he said, "It is the man of God who disobeyed the word of the LORD; therefore the LORD has given him to the lion, which has torn him and killed him, according to the word that the LORD spoke to him."<sup>27</sup>And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." And they saddled it.<sup>28</sup>And he went and found his body thrown in the road, and the donkey and the lion standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey.<sup>29</sup>And the prophet took up the body of the man of God and laid it on the donkey and brought it back to the city to mourn and to bury him.<sup>30</sup>And he laid the body in his own grave. And they mourned over him, saying, "Alas, my brother!"<sup>31</sup>And after he had buried him, he said to his sons, "When I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones.<sup>32</sup>For the saying that he called out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the houses of the high places that are in the cities of Samaria shall surely come to pass."<sup>33</sup>After this thing Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way, but made priests for the high places again from among all the people. Any who would, he ordained to be priests of the high places.<sup>34</sup>And this thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, so as to cut it off and to destroy it from the face of the earth.
13.overview:
He is never named. The writer calls him the man of God fifteen times in thirty-four verses, and he arrives at the exact moment Jeroboam is standing at the altar he devised, in the middle of the festival he moved. He names a king three hundred years before he is born, and the historian of 2 Kings stops his narrative to point back at this chapter.

Everything about him at first is admirable: he denounces the altar, faces down an arrest, prays for the king who ordered it, and refuses the king's hospitality because God has told him to eat and drink nothing in that place. Then, tired and sitting under a tree, he is met by an old prophet who claims an angel has revised the command. But he lied to him, says the writer, and the man of God goes back, eats, and dies on the road.

The chapter's point is sharp: he had the word himself, and he weighed the messenger instead of the message. Paul states the principle at its strongest and includes himself in it: even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed (Gal. 1:8). And the chapter ends with Jeroboam, who saw all of it in one day and changed nothing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man of God from Judah cries against Jeroboam's altar at Bethel, naming Josiah as the king who will burn the priests' bones on it, and gives a sign (vv. 1-3). Jeroboam's outstretched hand dries up and the altar splits; at the prophet's prayer the hand is restored (vv. 4-6). Offered hospitality, he refuses: he is to eat no bread, drink no water, and not return by the way he came (vv. 7-10).
verseByVerse.theology: He names a king three hundred years before the man is born, and it happens (2 Kings 23:15-16). The God who rules history can tell its end from its beginning, and his word against false worship does not lapse with time.
verseByVerse.examples: The instruction he has been given is threefold and strange, and it is not explained to him. He does not ask for reasons; he obeys. Some of God's commands we understand only later, and some we are simply asked to keep because he has spoken.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a man of God came out of Judah by the word of the LORD to Bethel. Jeroboam was standing by the altar to make offerings. And the man cried against the altar by the word of the LORD and said, "O altar, altar, thus says the LORD: 'Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, Josiah by name, and he shall sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who make offerings on you, and human bones shall be burned on you.'" And he gave a sign the same day, saying, "This is the sign that the LORD has spoken: 'Behold, the altar shall be torn down, and the ashes that are on it shall be poured out.'" And when the king heard the saying of the man of God, which he cried against the altar at Bethel, Jeroboam stretched out his hand from the altar, saying, "Seize him." And his hand, which he stretched out against him, dried up, so that he could not draw it back to himself. The altar also was torn down, and the ashes poured out from the altar, according to the sign that the man of God had given by the word of the LORD. And the king said to the man of God, "Entreat now the favor of the LORD your God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me." And the man of God entreated the LORD, and the king's hand was restored to him and became as it was before. And the king said to the man of God, "Come home with me, and refresh yourself, and I will give you a reward." And the man of God said to the king, "If you give me half your house, I will not go in with you. And I will not eat bread or drink water in this place, for so was it commanded me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water nor return by the way that you came.'" So he went another way and did not return by the way that he came to Bethel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man of God arrives at the exact moment: Jeroboam is standing at the altar he devised, at the festival he moved, in the middle of the ceremony. He addresses the altar rather than the king, which is its own comment, since that is where the offence actually is. And then he names a man three hundred years before he is born: Josiah by name.

There is almost nothing else like this in the Old Testament; Isaiah's naming of Cyrus is the other case (Isa. 44:28). Prophecies of a coming ruler are common; a personal name, given three centuries in advance, is not.

Some scholars think the name was added after Josiah's reform, since a name given so far ahead seems to them impossible. The question is fair to ask, and the answer turns largely on whether God can tell the future. The Bible openly claims that he can, declaring the end from the beginning (Isa. 46:10), and it offers this case as a test of that claim, with the fulfilment recorded in a later book.

It happened. When Josiah tore through the country destroying shrines, the historian records what he did at this altar and stops the narrative to point at this verse: Moreover, the altar at Bethel, the high place erected by Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin, that altar with the high place he pulled down and burned... And as Josiah turned, he saw the tombs there on the mount. And he sent and took the bones out of the tombs and burned them on the altar and defiled it, according to the word of the LORD that the man of God proclaimed, who had predicted these things (2 Kings 23:15-16). Human bones were burned on that altar, exactly as this man said, by a king with exactly this name.

The long prophecy needs three hundred years to be verified, so he gives a short one for today. The hand Jeroboam stretches out to have the prophet arrested seizes up where it is: not struck off, but frozen in the gesture, pointing at the man, where everybody at the festival can see it.

Two things stand out in the exchange that follows. The first is what the king asks for. Not forgiveness, not what must I do: he wants his hand back. And note how he refers to God: the LORD your God. Standing at an altar he built for the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, he calls him the prophet's God.

The second is that the man of God prays for him at once, without conditions, for the king who tried to arrest him, and the hand is restored on the spot. That is mercy, more than Jeroboam asked for and much more than he deserved.

Then comes the second attack, and it is more dangerous than the first. The soldiers failed; the hospitality is the real threat. A prophet who denounces an altar in the morning and dines at the king's table in the evening has unsaid everything he said. Jeroboam would not need to answer the prophecy; he would only need to be seen with the prophet.

The man of God quotes the command, and none of its three parts is explained to him: no bread, no water, and not home by the road he came on. Eating and drinking with somebody in that world was not merely a meal; it was fellowship, and a measure of peace between the parties. To take bread at Bethel would be to say that there was something here a man of God could sit down with.

The third part is stranger. Why should the route matter? He is not told. It looks like an arbitrary instruction attached to a reasonable one, and the arbitrariness is the point, because a command you can see the sense of is not much of a test. It is also the command he will break first, when he turns back.

He obeys all three, at the moment when obeying costs most. Everything about this man so far is admirable: he interrupted a state ceremony in a foreign kingdom, denounced the altar to its face, faced down an arrest, prayed for the man who ordered it, and refused half the king's house. He is within reach of being one of the great figures of the Old Testament, and he has very little time left.
verseByVerse.note: Josiah fulfilled this prophecy about 300 years later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — But He Lied to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An old prophet in Bethel hears from his sons what happened, rides after the man of God, and finds him under an oak (vv. 11-14). Refused, he claims an angel told him to bring the man home, but he lied to him, and the man of God goes back and eats (vv. 15-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The credentials offered are a fellow prophet, an angel, and the phrase by the word of the LORD: exactly what would make the lie convincing. Deception in God's name rarely looks like deception.
verseByVerse.examples: A newer word from a more impressive person does not overrule a clear word we already have. The question to ask is not who is speaking, but whether what they say agrees with what God has said.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an old prophet lived in Bethel. And his sons came and told him all that the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told to their father the words that he had spoken to the king. And their father said to them, "Which way did he go?" And his sons showed him the way that the man of God who came from Judah had gone. And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." So they saddled the donkey for him and he mounted it. And he went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak. And he said to him, "Are you the man of God who came from Judah?" And he said, "I am." Then he said to him, "Come home with me and eat bread." And he said, "I may not return with you, or go in with you, neither will I eat bread nor drink water with you in this place, for it was said to me by the word of the LORD, 'You shall neither eat bread nor drink water there, nor return by the way that you came.'" And he said to him, "I also am a prophet as you are, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD, saying, 'Bring him back with you into your house that he may eat bread and drink water.'" But he lied to him. So he went back with him and ate bread in his house and drank water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is a prophet living in Bethel, and that raises a question the text never answers. He is a prophet of the LORD (he receives a genuine word in verse 20), and he has been living in the capital of Jeroboam's counterfeit religion, apparently without saying anything. His sons had seen what happened at the calf-altar. Whatever their father is, he is not a man who has been crying out against that altar himself.

Why the old man goes after him is not stated, and the temptation to fill it in should be resisted. It may be admiration, or loneliness, or something worse. The text tells us what he did, not why.

He finds the man of God sitting under an oak: not walking, but stopped. He has been on his feet since morning, with nothing to eat or drink all day by command, and has sat down under a tree in the heat. Attacks often come when a man is tired and has stopped moving. Even so, he refuses a second time and quotes the command a second time, accurately. He knows exactly what he was told.

Then comes the sentence that kills him, and every element of it is chosen. I also am a prophet as you are offers peer credentials: not a king or a courtier, but somebody in the same office, who would know. And an angel spoke to me claims a higher authority than a mere prophetic impression. By the word of the LORD is the exact formula the man of God has just used twice, so he is being answered in his own vocabulary.

And the content is plausible. It does not ask him to praise the altar or bless Jeroboam. It only revises one small logistical detail, and it flatters: an angel was sent about you specifically. A better word from a better source, delivered to a tired man under a tree.

But he lied to him. The writer refuses to leave any ambiguity: not mistaken, not a false impression. He lied, deliberately, in the name of God, about an angel. Why, we are never told. The writer gives the lie and withholds the motive.

Here is the thing this chapter exists to say: he had the word himself. God spoke it to him directly. He had already refused a king with it and quoted it twice, word for word. Then a man with better credentials brought a newer word that contradicted it, and he did not test it against the one he already had. He weighed the messengers instead of the messages.

The New Testament states the principle in the strongest terms available, and Paul includes himself and angels in it: a new revelation that contradicts a clear one is to be refused no matter who brings it (Gal. 1:8). And the old prophet did not have to argue that God had not said it. He only had to say that God had said something else, more recently, to someone qualified. That is how it is nearly always done.

Set this beside another hungry man in another lonely place. At the end of forty days without food the Lord Jesus was offered bread by a tempter who would soon be quoting Scripture at him, and he answered with the word God had already given: man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matt. 4:4). The man of God from Judah had the word and let it go when he was tired; the true Prophet held it when he was starving, and later said, My food is to do the will of him who sent me (John 4:34). His obedience did not fail at the end of the day, and it is counted for those who, like this prophet, have failed at the end of theirs.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the table the word of the LORD comes to the old prophet, who pronounces that his guest's body will not reach his fathers' tomb (vv. 20-22). On the road a lion kills the man of God and stands beside the body with the donkey (vv. 23-25). The old prophet recognises the judgment, buries him in his own grave mourning alas, my brother!, and asks to be buried beside him, because the word against Bethel shall surely come to pass (vv. 26-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The word of God comes to the liar, at his own table. God's truth does not depend on the character of the one who carries it, and being used by God is no proof of being right with him.
verseByVerse.examples: The old prophet weeps over the man he deceived, calls him my brother, and gives him his own grave. Grief over the harm we have done is real and right, but it cannot undo the harm. That is why the gospel offers not only sorrow but forgiveness.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they sat at the table, the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back. And he cried to the man of God who came from Judah, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have disobeyed the word of the LORD and have not kept the command that the LORD your God commanded you, but have come back and have eaten bread and drunk water in the place of which he said to you, "Eat no bread and drink no water," your body shall not come to the tomb of your fathers.'" And after he had eaten bread and drunk, he saddled the donkey for the prophet whom he had brought back. And as he went away a lion met him on the road and killed him. And his body was thrown in the road, and the donkey stood beside it; the lion also stood beside the body. And behold, men passed by and saw the body thrown in the road and the lion standing by the body. And they came and told it in the city where the old prophet lived. And when the prophet who had brought him back from the way heard of it, he said, "It is the man of God who disobeyed the word of the LORD; therefore the LORD has given him to the lion, which has torn him and killed him, according to the word that the LORD spoke to him." And he said to his sons, "Saddle the donkey for me." And they saddled it. And he went and found his body thrown in the road, and the donkey and the lion standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey. And the prophet took up the body of the man of God and laid it on the donkey and brought it back to the city to mourn and to bury him. And he laid the body in his own grave. And they mourned over him, saying, "Alas, my brother!" And after he had buried him, he said to his sons, "When I die, bury me in the grave in which the man of God is buried; lay my bones beside his bones. For the saying that he called out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the houses of the high places that are in the cities of Samaria shall surely come to pass."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the strangest verse in the chapter: the word of the LORD comes to the liar. He is at his own table, eating a meal he obtained by inventing an angel, opposite the man he has deceived, and God speaks through him a genuine word, fulfilled that same day.

The writer does not pause over this and does not explain it, and it should not be smoothed away.
