It tells us something about how God works that is uncomfortable and true: the truth of a message is not guaranteed by the character of the man carrying it, and a man's usefulness is not evidence of his integrity. Balaam prophesied truly. Caiaphas prophesied truly and did not know he was doing it (John 11:51).

The charge is stated with care: you have disobeyed the word of the LORD and have not kept the command that the LORD your God commanded you. The offence is located in the man who had the command, and the deception is not mentioned. That is severe, and the severity should be faced rather than argued down.

He was lied to. He was tired, hungry, thirsty, and a long way from home, and a fellow prophet invoked an angel. Most people would have gone. And he was responsible, because the word had been given to him, and he was the one who knew what it said, and he had already proved he could refuse a king with it. Being deceived is a reason and it is not a defence, and Scripture is consistent about this from Eden onward: the woman said the serpent deceived me, and I ate, which was entirely true and changed nothing.

The writer is very deliberate with the details. A lion kills him, and then nothing else happens. The donkey does not bolt, which is the one thing a donkey certainly does near a lion. The lion does not eat the body or take the donkey, and it does not leave. People walk past it. This was not a hungry animal on a dangerous road. It is a judgment carried out under orders, and it stops the instant it is done.

The old prophet knows immediately what it means, and he says the theology correctly, and he is the reason for all of it. The writer repeats that the lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey; it is still there when the old man arrives, and lets him take the body.

Here this man becomes genuinely difficult to read. He puts the body in the grave he had prepared for himself and mourns, alas, my brother, and nothing suggests the grief is not real. So we have, in one person: a prophet living quietly in the capital of a false religion; a man who invented an angel; a man through whom God then spoke truly; a man who wept over the consequence of his own lie; and a man who gave away his own grave. The writer reconciles none of it and does not tell us whether he repented. People are like this, and Scripture declines to tidy them up.

His request to be buried beside the man of God is strange and rather moving, and it is not sentimental. He believes the prophecy. He has heard a man name a king three centuries early and watched the same man die within the day for disobedience, which has convinced him every word was from God. So he makes a practical arrangement about his own bones. If bones are going to be dug up and burned on that altar, the safest place in the country to be buried is beside the man who said so.

It worked. Three hundred years later Josiah is at Bethel, and the account continues: Then he said, "What is that monument that I see?" And the men of the city told him, "It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and predicted these things that you have done against the altar at Bethel." And he said, "Let him be; let no man move his bones." So they let his bones alone, with the bones of the prophet who came out of Samaria (2 Kings 23:17-18). The old prophet's bones were left alone because they were lying next to the right man's.

Why did the deceived prophet die while the liar lived? The man of God had God’s own word to him directly, and abandoned it for a man’s claim to a revelation. The test of any word is whether it agrees with what God has already said (Deut 13:1–3; Gal 1:8). The old prophet’s guilt was real, and God judged him in his own way; but the man of God was the one entrusted with the message, and his disobedience undermined it.

Does God deal this harshly with every believer who is misled? No. This man was a prophet whose obedience was itself part of his message to Bethel, and the lion was a public, earthly judgment on that message being broken. The text says nothing against his soul, and the old prophet buries him as my brother. Christians who have been led astray by a confident voice should hear the warning, test what they are told by Scripture, and come back; the Lord who came to Jonah a second time and restored Peter beside the lake (John 21:15-17) receives those who return.

“The cities of Samaria” uses the name the region later bore, after Omri built the city (16:24).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After this Jeroboam does not turn, but ordains anyone who would as priests of the high places, and it becomes the sin that cuts off his house (vv. 33-34).
verseByVerse.theology: After this thing means after an altar split in front of him, after his own hand withered and was healed by the prayer of the man he had tried to arrest, and after a prophet from Judah named his kingdom's end and died on the road for eating a meal. None of it moved him.
verseByVerse.examples: Jeroboam received judgment and mercy in the same hour: a withered hand, and then a healed one. Neither moved him. God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance (Romans 2:4), and the danger is growing used to it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this thing Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way, but made priests for the high places again from among all the people. Any who would, he ordained to be priests of the high places. And this thing became sin to the house of Jeroboam, so as to cut it off and to destroy it from the face of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Count what after this thing includes. A stranger walked out of Judah into his festival, denounced the altar, named a king three hundred years ahead, and the altar split in front of the assembly. Jeroboam's own hand seized up in the air, and he had to ask the man he was arresting to pray for him, and it was healed. Within the day that prophet was killed by a lion on the road for eating a forbidden meal, which proved to everybody that his words were God's.

All of it happened in one day, in front of the king. He went back to ordaining priests, and the phrase is contemptuous: any who would, he ordained.

The lesson of the last two verses runs against most people's instincts. Signs do not produce repentance. He saw an altar destroyed by a word and a hand restored by a prayer, and was not moved an inch. The evidence was never the problem.

The Lord Jesus said this in a story about a rich man who wanted somebody sent back from the dead to warn his brothers: if they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31). And he said it about his own generation, who had watched him heal and feed and raise the dead, and who asked him for a sign. What Jeroboam lacked was never information.

The rich man's request was in a sense granted: a man did rise from the dead. Some believed and many did not, which is the point. What changes a heart is not a bigger sign but God opening it to his word (Luke 24:45; Acts 16:14), and that is why the risen Christ is preached and not merely displayed.

The chapter ends on the epitaph of the whole northern kingdom. His dynasty lasts one more generation: Nadab reigns two years and is murdered, and Baasha kills every member of the house of Jeroboam, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite (15:29).

The formula outlives the family. Nineteen kings of Israel reign over two centuries, and the verdict on almost every one of them is the same: he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in the sins that he made Israel to sin. The man who was offered David's own covenant (I will build you a sure house, as I built for David) becomes the standing measure of what went wrong with a nation.

13.theology:
God's word stands across centuries. A prophet names Josiah three hundred years ahead, and the later history records the fulfilment with the writer pointing back. The God of Israel is not guessing about history; he rules it. His word against false worship may wait a long time, but it does not lapse.

Mercy to the man who struck first. When Jeroboam's hand froze, the prophet did not gloat or bargain. He prayed at once for the king who had tried to arrest him, and God healed him. Faithfulness to God's word and kindness to its enemies belong together; the prophet is a small picture of the One who prayed for those who crucified him. Jeroboam, for his part, asked only for his hand and called the LORD the prophet's God, which shows how far a man can receive mercy without receiving the Giver.

Obedience when the reason is hidden. The man of God's three commands were not explained, and one of them (the route home) seems arbitrary. That was part of the test. Faith does not obey only what it can see the sense of; it trusts the one who commands. And refusing the king's table mattered: in that world, a shared meal meant fellowship, and a prophet cannot denounce an altar in the morning and dine with its builder at night.

Testing every word by the word already given. The heart of the chapter is the old prophet's lie, dressed in every credential that could make it persuasive: a fellow prophet, an angel, and the very formula by the word of the LORD. The man of God had a clear word and let a newer, more flattering one overrule it. Scripture's rule is consistent: no messenger, however impressive, may contradict what God has plainly said (Deut. 13:1-3; Gal. 1:8). For Christians that clear word is now the written Scripture, and the Spirit who gave it keeps believers in it.

Deceived and still responsible. The judgment on the man of God is severe, and the commentary does not soften it. Being lied to explains his fall but does not excuse it, because the command was given to him. Yet the lion's work was a public judgment on a prophet whose obedience was itself his message; the text does not pass sentence on his soul, and the old prophet mourns him as a brother. Those who have been led astray are called not to despair but to return, and Christ, who held the word when he was starving, has kept it in their place.

God's freedom with flawed messengers. The true word comes through the liar at his own table. God's truth is not guaranteed by the messenger's character, and usefulness is no proof of integrity. The old prophet is a tangle of compromise, deceit, grief and real faith, and Scripture leaves him unresolved. That is honest about people, and it warns us not to judge a message by its bearer or a bearer by his gifts. Even his last act, asking to be buried beside the man of God, is an act of faith in the prophecy, and three centuries later Josiah left both sets of bones alone (2 Kings 23:17-18).

Signs do not change hearts. Jeroboam saw a split altar, a withered and restored hand and a dead prophet in a single day, and went straight back to ordaining any who would. The problem was never a lack of evidence. Only God opening a heart to his word brings repentance, and that is why the church preaches the risen Christ and prays.
13.examples:
Then: A prophet who had faced down a king, watched an altar split at his word, and refused half the king's house because God had told him not to eat or drink in that place, sat down under a tree at the end of a long day. An older prophet told him an angel had said it was all right now, and he went back and ate, and was dead the same day.

Now: Three things. The first is the whole chapter: a newer word from a better-credentialled person does not overrule a clear word you already have. The lie nearly always has this shape: nobody says God did not say it; they say God has said something else, more recently, to someone qualified. The test is never who is speaking. We are not left to hold the word alone; the Spirit who gave it is given to believers to keep them in it (John 14:26). Second, the severity, which should not be argued down. He was genuinely deceived and genuinely responsible, because the word had been given to him. Being lied to is a reason and it is not a defence. Yet failure is not the end of the story for those who belong to the Lord: the way back is to return to his word and confess, and he restores. And third, verse 33. Jeroboam saw an altar destroyed by a word and his own hand healed by a prayer, in one day, and changed nothing. If you are waiting for evidence dramatic enough to shift somebody, this chapter says the evidence was never what was missing; pray instead for the God who opens hearts to his word.

14.title: Ahijah's Word and Rehoboam's Shields

Behold, Ahijah the prophet is there, who said of me that I should be king over this people.<sup>3</sup>Take with you ten loaves, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what shall happen to the child."<sup>4</sup>Jeroboam's wife did so. She arose and went to Shiloh and came to the house of Ahijah. Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were dim because of his age.<sup>5</sup>And the LORD said to Ahijah, "Behold, the wife of Jeroboam is coming to inquire of you concerning her son, for he is sick. Thus and thus shall you say to her." When she came, she pretended to be another woman.<sup>6</sup>But when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, he said, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another? For I am charged with unbearable news for you.<sup>7</sup>Go, tell Jeroboam, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: "Because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel<sup>8</sup>and tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you, and yet you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, doing only that which was right in my eyes,<sup>9</sup>but you have done evil above all who were before you and have gone and made for yourself other gods and metal images, provoking me to anger, and have cast me behind your back,<sup>10</sup>therefore behold, I will bring harm upon the house of Jeroboam and will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both bond and free in Israel, and will burn up the house of Jeroboam, as a man burns up dung until it is all gone.<sup>11</sup>Anyone belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone who dies in the open country the birds of the heavens shall eat, for the LORD has spoken it."'<sup>12</sup>Arise therefore, go to your house. When your feet enter the city, the child shall die.<sup>13</sup>And all Israel shall mourn for him and bury him, for he only of Jeroboam shall come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the LORD, the God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam.<sup>14</sup>Moreover, the LORD will raise up for himself a king over Israel who shall cut off the house of Jeroboam today. And henceforth,<sup>15</sup>the LORD will strike Israel as a reed is shaken in the water, and root up Israel out of this good land that he gave to their fathers and scatter them beyond the Euphrates, because they have made their Asherim, provoking the LORD to anger.<sup>16</sup>And he will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and made Israel to sin."<sup>17</sup>Then Jeroboam's wife arose and departed and came to Tirzah. And as she came to the threshold of the house, the child died.<sup>18</sup>And all Israel buried him and mourned for him, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Ahijah the prophet.<sup>19</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he warred and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.<sup>20</sup>And the time that Jeroboam reigned was twenty-two years. And he slept with his fathers, and Nadab his son reigned in his place.<sup>21</sup>Now Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite.<sup>22</sup>And Judah did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins that they committed, more than all that their fathers had done.<sup>23</sup>For they also built for themselves high places and pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree,<sup>24</sup>and there were also male cult prostitutes in the land. They did according to all the abominations of the nations that the LORD drove out before the people of Israel.<sup>25</sup>In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem.<sup>26</sup>He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made,<sup>27</sup>and King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze, and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house.<sup>28</sup>And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.<sup>29</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>30</sup>And there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.<sup>31</sup>And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Abijam his son reigned in his place.
14.overview:
His son is dying, and Jeroboam sends to a prophet of the LORD. He has two golden calves, sanctuaries at Bethel and Dan, a priesthood he appointed himself and a festival he devised, and he consults none of it. He sends his wife in disguise to Ahijah, who is blind, and God tells the prophet who is at the door before she reaches it. Why do you pretend to be another? is the question that hangs over the first half of the chapter.

The word she carries home is judgment on Jeroboam's house, and in the middle of it one of the most tender verses in Kings: the dying boy is the one in whom God found something pleasing, the only one of that family to be mourned and buried.

Then Judah, five years after Solomon: worship as corrupt as anything in the north, an Egyptian army at the gates, he took away everything, including the gold shields. Rehoboam makes bronze replacements, and the guard still carries them in procession. The same ceremony, a cheaper metal, and nobody says anything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — Why Do You Pretend to Be Another?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeroboam's son Abijah falls sick, and Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise to the blind prophet Ahijah at Shiloh (vv. 1-4). Forewarned by the LORD, Ahijah greets her by name and gives the word: God exalted Jeroboam, but he has cast me behind your back, and his house will be cut off (vv. 5-11). The child will die as she enters the city, the only one of the house to come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the LORD (vv. 12-13), and Israel will be scattered beyond the Euphrates (vv. 14-16). The child dies as she crosses the threshold (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The disguise fails because the prophet is blind: he does not get his information by looking. Nothing is hidden from God, and that is a terror to the one who hides and a comfort to the one who comes openly.
verseByVerse.examples: Jeroboam knew where to go when his child was sick. In a crisis people often reach past the religion they have built for themselves to the God they have neglected. That turning is a doorway; the tragedy is to come in costume instead of coming home.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Abijah the son of Jeroboam fell sick. And Jeroboam said to his wife, "Arise, and disguise yourself, that it not be known that you are the wife of Jeroboam, and go to Shiloh. Behold, Ahijah the prophet is there, who said of me that I should be king over this people. Take with you ten loaves, some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him. He will tell you what shall happen to the child." Jeroboam's wife did so. She arose and went to Shiloh and came to the house of Ahijah. Now Ahijah could not see, for his eyes were dim because of his age. And the LORD said to Ahijah, "Behold, the wife of Jeroboam is coming to inquire of you concerning her son, for he is sick. Thus and thus shall you say to her." When she came, she pretended to be another woman. But when Ahijah heard the sound of her feet, as she came in at the door, he said, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you pretend to be another? For I am charged with unbearable news for you. Go, tell Jeroboam, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: "Because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel and tore the kingdom away from the house of David and gave it to you, and yet you have not been like my servant David, who kept my commandments and followed me with all his heart, doing only that which was right in my eyes, but you have done evil above all who were before you and have gone and made for yourself other gods and metal images, provoking me to anger, and have cast me behind your back, therefore behold, I will bring harm upon the house of Jeroboam and will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both bond and free in Israel, and will burn up the house of Jeroboam, as a man burns up dung until it is all gone. Anyone belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone who dies in the open country the birds of the heavens shall eat, for the LORD has spoken it."' Arise therefore, go to your house. When your feet enter the city, the child shall die. And all Israel shall mourn for him and bury him, for he only of Jeroboam shall come to the grave, because in him there is found something pleasing to the LORD, the God of Israel, in the house of Jeroboam. Moreover, the LORD will raise up for himself a king over Israel who shall cut off the house of Jeroboam today. And henceforth, the LORD will strike Israel as a reed is shaken in the water, and root up Israel out of this good land that he gave to their fathers and scatter them beyond the Euphrates, because they have made their Asherim, provoking the LORD to anger. And he will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam, which he sinned and made Israel to sin." Then Jeroboam's wife arose and departed and came to Tirzah. And as she came to the threshold of the house, the child died. And all Israel buried him and mourned for him, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by his servant Ahijah the prophet. Now the rest of the acts of Jeroboam, how he warred and how he reigned, behold, they are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. And the time that Jeroboam reigned was twenty-two years. And he slept with his fathers, and Nadab his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At that time means after the altar split and the hand withered and the man of God died on the road, and after Jeroboam went back to ordaining anybody who wanted to be a priest.

Every part of what he does is revealing. He has two golden calves, sanctuaries at Bethel and Dan, a priesthood he appointed himself and a festival he devised, and when his child is sick he consults none of it. He sends to Shiloh. He knows perfectly well that the calves cannot help him. That is the most damning thing in the chapter, and the writer never says a word about it.

The prophet he chooses is the one who said of me that I should be king, the man who gave him ten pieces of a torn cloak and the offer of David's own covenant. So his wife goes in disguise to the one man in Israel who knows exactly what Jeroboam was promised and what he did with it. The gift is chosen to match the costume: bread, cakes and a jar of honey are what a village woman would bring a holy man, and exactly what a queen would not.

Then the writer places the detail that makes the whole scene. She has walked some twenty miles in a disguise good enough that nobody on the road knew her, to consult a man who is blind. There is something almost comic about it, and it is the sort of comedy Scripture uses when it wants to expose a way of thinking. Jeroboam has calculated the deception carefully (the clothes, the gift, the anonymity), and he has forgotten that the man he is deceiving does not get his information by looking.

God tells Ahijah before she arrives, even announcing the pretence. He hears her feet and says her name. She has not spoken. She is standing in the doorway of a blind man's house in borrowed clothes, and before she can say anything at all he greets her by the identity she has spent a day concealing.

Why do you pretend to be another? is a real question. What did they think they were doing? The disguise could only ever have fooled a man; it was never going to touch the thing they actually wanted, which was a word from God. A great deal of religion is this shape: approaching God in a costume, presenting a version of ourselves, offering the right sort of gift, when the whole point of him is that he already knows who is at the door.

The gospel answers that question from the other side. No costume works with God, because nothing is hidden from his sight (Heb. 4:13), and that would be unbearable news if it were all there was. But the same letter goes straight on: we have a great high priest who sympathises with our weakness, so we may come to the throne of grace openly and receive mercy (Heb. 4:14-16). Jeroboam's wife came disguised and went home with hard things. Anyone who comes to Christ as he really is has this promise: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

The indictment starts where every indictment in Scripture starts: with what God did first. I exalted you from among the people. He was a labour foreman, and God gave him a kingdom. The standard is the one Solomon was measured by, my servant David: not sinlessness, since this book knows what David did, but that he never went after another god. That measure does not change from the first page of Kings to the last.

Cast me behind your back pictures throwing something over your shoulder: discarded, out of sight, not worth turning round for. And you have done evil above all who were before you is the phrase the writer will now use of king after king in the north. Jeroboam is the first.

The judgment is total and the image contemptuous: no burial, the final indignity in that world, said of an entire dynasty. Then the word turns to the child. She came to ask whether her son would live. He will die the moment she gets home, and her walking through the gate is what will do it. She has to carry that for twenty miles.

Verse 13 is one of the most tender verses in Kings, and it is easy to read past in the middle of a judgment oracle. In that house, the family of the man who made the calves and cast God behind his back, God looked, and in one child found something he was pleased with. The Hebrew is literally "a good thing toward the LORD was found in him". We are told nothing else about the boy: not his age, not what he did or said. Something in him pleased God, God noticed, and Scripture still records it three thousand years later.

Of that whole family, this boy is the one who gets a grave and a nation's mourning. And he dies first. The writer puts his death right after the sentence about dogs and birds, so that the reader cannot miss what he is being spared. Isaiah says the same thing in a sentence that people find difficult until they have needed it: the righteous man perishes, and no one lays it to heart; devout men are taken away, while no one understands. For the righteous man is taken away from calamity; he enters into peace (Isa. 57:1-2).

This should be said carefully, because it is not a general explanation of why children die, and it must not be turned into one. Scripture does not offer that, and anybody who has buried a child has been offered enough tidy explanations already. Nor does the verse make the boy's death anything other than a grief: his mother walked home to it, and all Israel mourned. Death remains an enemy, even where God is kind within it. What this verse does say is smaller and steadier: that God saw something good in a boy in a house that had turned its back on him, that he said so, and that in taking him before the calamity he was not careless of him.

For parents who have lost a child there is more to hold than this verse alone. The Lord Jesus took children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16), and wept at a friend's grave though he was about to raise him (John 11:35). Many Christians, with David at the death of his infant son (2 Sam. 12:23), have found hope that the little ones God takes are safe with him; and the Christian hope is not only that they are spared, but that they will be raised.

Here too, in the first generation of the northern kingdom, is its ending. Beyond the Euphrates is Assyria, two hundred years away. The northern tribes were deported in stages, the last when Samaria fell in about 722 BC, and 2 Kings 17 gives the same reasons Ahijah gives here. The image is exact: as a reed is shaken in the water. A reed has no root worth the name, and nothing holds it.

She walks twenty miles knowing what will happen, and it happens as she crosses the threshold. The writer gives her no words, here or anywhere. Jeroboam's reign closes with the formula after twenty-two years, and the son who succeeds him will be murdered within two.

Is it just for a whole house to be destroyed for a father’s sin? Human courts were forbidden to punish children for their fathers (Deut 24:16). This was God’s own judgment on a royal house that led the nation into idolatry, and its sons carried on the same sins. God as Judge may take any life, and he never punishes the innocent as guilty (Ezek 18:20).
verseByVerse.note: Tirzah became the capital of the northern kingdom for a time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — He Made Bronze Shields Instead
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rehoboam, son of Naamah the Ammonite, reigns seventeen years in the city the LORD chose (v. 21). Judah does evil more than their fathers, with high places, pillars, Asherim and cult prostitutes, according to all the abominations of the nations (vv. 22-24). In the fifth year Shishak of Egypt takes the treasures, everything, including Solomon's gold shields, and Rehoboam replaces them with bronze ones that the guard still carries into the house of the LORD (vv. 25-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Five years after Solomon's death an Egyptian army carries away the treasures of his reign, and the writer says he took away everything. Glory that rests on accumulation can be lost in a season.
verseByVerse.examples: The bronze shields are carried in the same procession as the gold ones were. It is possible to keep every form of worship and lose what it once carried. The remedy is not to abandon the forms but to come back to the Lord they exist to honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that the LORD had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, to put his name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Judah did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and they provoked him to jealousy with their sins that they committed, more than all that their fathers had done. For they also built for themselves high places and pillars and Asherim on every high hill and under every green tree, and there were also male cult prostitutes in the land. They did according to all the abominations of the nations that the LORD drove out before the people of Israel. In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house. He took away everything. He also took away all the shields of gold that Solomon had made, and King Rehoboam made in their place shields of bronze, and committed them to the hands of the officers of the guard, who kept the door of the king's house. And as often as the king went into the house of the LORD, the guard carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer sets two things side by side in verse 21 without comment. He takes a whole clause to say that Jerusalem is the city that the LORD had chosen, which he did not need to do. And the king ruling there is the son of an Ammonite woman, one of the seven hundred, from Milcom's country, the god Solomon built a high place for facing the temple. The writer repeats her name in the last verse of the chapter, which means he wants it noticed.

Now the south, and the verdict is as bad as anything said about the north. A reader coming out of chapter 12 might think the calves were the problem and Judah the faithful remnant. The writer will not allow it: more than all that their fathers had done.

They provoked him to jealousy: the language of a marriage, and the word God uses of himself in the commandment about images. It is not a landlord's indifference but a husband's offence. The full apparatus of Canaanite religion is here, and the phrase on every high hill and under every green tree becomes the standard description of it through the prophets.

Asherah was a Canaanite goddess of fertility, Baal’s consort; an “Asherah” was a wooden pole or carved image set up for her worship beside altars. Pillars were standing stones for Baal, and “high places” were hilltop shrines. The word translated male cult prostitutes means consecrated ones, men attached to the shrines; most take it as the ESV does, though some scholars doubt that ritual prostitution was as common as was once thought.

And here is the sentence that ought to stop a reader. God dispossessed the Canaanites because the land vomited out its inhabitants (Lev. 18:25), and Israel was warned in the same passage that the land would do the same to them. Judah is now doing what the previous occupants were expelled for, on the same ground, a generation after the temple was dedicated.

Solomon has been dead five years, the temple has stood about thirty-five, and an Egyptian army is at the gates of Jerusalem. Shishak is one of the few figures in this history independently documented: he is Sheshonq I, and he left a record of this campaign carved at Karnak, listing the towns he took. Most are in the north and the Negev, and Jerusalem does not appear in what survives, which fits a city that bought off the invader rather than being stormed. The campaign, usually dated about 925 BC, is a fixed point for the dates of the period. And he is the man who sheltered Jeroboam (11:40).

Four chapters ago the reader was standing in a room where silver was not considered as anything, where a fleet came every three years with gold and ivory and apes and peacocks, and where a foreign queen ran out of breath. It lasted five years past its owner. And the writer specifies the shields, because they are what he wants us watching: all the shields of gold that Solomon had made, two hundred large and three hundred small, hanging in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.

Rehoboam makes replacements, and here is an exact picture of religious decline, drawn in one sentence about a routine. Everything continues. The king still goes up to the house of the LORD. The guard still turns out. The shields are still carried in front of him in procession, and afterwards they are still taken back and put away in the guardroom, and presumably somebody still polishes them. The form is intact down to the last detail. The metal is not.

Nobody stopped the ceremony. Nobody stood up and said that gold shields carried before the king had meant something and bronze ones do not. They made the replacements the same size and carried on exactly as before, and within a generation nobody in that guardroom would have remembered that they were ever gold. That is how decline usually goes: not a repudiation and not a scandal, but a substitution, quietly made, with the liturgy unaltered.

And they are not even displayed. Solomon's shields hung in a hall built to be walked through; these are locked away between uses, because they are for the procession and nothing else. A reader ought to feel the question the verse asks without asking it. What in your own practice is bronze now, carried with the same ceremony, in the same order, by people who have never seen the gold?
verseByVerse.note: Shishak is Pharaoh Sheshonq I; he left an inscription listing towns he took in Israel and Judah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–31 — And There Was War Continually
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of Rehoboam's acts are in the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah; there is war between him and Jeroboam continually, and he is buried, Naamah the Ammonite named again, and Abijam reigns (vv. 29-31).
verseByVerse.theology: War between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually: two kings of one people, brothers by the prophet's own word, fighting for the rest of their lives. Division among God's people, once begun, is hard to stop.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer names Rehoboam's mother a second time, Naamah the Ammonite, and does not explain why. Sometimes Scripture teaches by placing two facts side by side and trusting us to think.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the rest of the acts of Rehoboam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually. And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. And Abijam his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The formula appears again, and from here it will alternate: the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel, back and forth, for the rest of both books.

Chronicles fills in a good deal that Kings leaves out about Rehoboam, including a moment this account does not mention: when Shishak came up, Shemaiah told the king and the princes you abandoned me, so I have abandoned you to the hand of Shishak, and they humbled themselves and said the LORD is righteous, and God said they have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them (2 Chron. 12:5-7). So Jerusalem was stripped rather than sacked, because of a moment of repentance the writer of Kings does not record. He is writing a theological account and he selects. What he wants us to see here is the bronze.

Continually. Two chapters ago a hundred and eighty thousand men went home at one sentence from a prophet (12:24). They obeyed, and then spent the rest of their lives at war anyway. Not the invasion they were forbidden, but something slower: border raids, skirmishes, garrison towns, two Israelite kings fighting over a frontier that ran through the middle of Benjamin, for seventeen years. A man can obey the letter of a prohibition and give his whole life to the thing it was meant to prevent.

And there she is again, in the last verse of the chapter: Naamah the Ammonite. There was no need to say it twice, and he offers no comment either time. What he is doing, quietly, is closing an account that was opened in 3:1 and left running for eight chapters. Solomon married foreign women. His wives turned away his heart. He built high places for all of them on the mountain east of Jerusalem. God tore the kingdom in two. And the king left sitting in the city God chose, ruling one tribe, doing more evil than his fathers, with an Egyptian army walking off with the gold, is the son of one of those women.

The writer does not draw the line. He writes her name at the top of the reign and at the bottom of it, and leaves it there.

14.theology:
Coming to God in costume. Jeroboam's own religion is useless to him in a crisis, and he knows it; he sends to the prophet of the LORD. Yet he sends his wife disguised, as if God could be consulted without being faced. The blind prophet who knows her by her footsteps is Scripture's quiet joke on every attempt to manage God. He sees who is at the door. That is fearful for the one who hides, and it is the ground of hope for the one who comes openly, because the God who sees all has given a High Priest through whom we may approach him as we are.

Grace despised is the heart of sin. Ahijah's indictment begins with what God had given: I exalted you from among the people. Jeroboam's sin is not only that he broke rules but that he threw behind his back the God who had raised him. Sin, at bottom, is ingratitude toward a generous God, and it carries consequences for a whole household and a whole nation.

God's eye for the hidden good. In the worst house in Israel God found something pleasing in one boy, said so, and gave him a grave and a nation's mourning. That is not an explanation of why children die. It is a glimpse of a God who notices what others overlook, who does not lose his own in the crowd of the wicked, and whose kindness can be present even in a death that is truly a grief.

The end seen from the beginning. In the first generation of the northern kingdom, Ahijah already sees its exile beyond the Euphrates, two centuries away, and 2 Kings 17 gives the same reasons when it comes. A nation built on worship of its own devising will be shaken as a reed is shaken in the water: it may stand for a long while, but it has no root, and nothing holds it. The only kingdom that cannot be shaken is the one God himself gives (Hebrews 12:28).

Judah no better. The south has the temple and David's line, and it still does more than all that their fathers had done. Privilege does not protect. God's jealousy is the jealousy of a husband, not a landlord, and Judah's practices are the very ones for which the land had expelled the Canaanites. The kingdom with the right temple can be as unfaithful as the kingdom with the wrong one.

Form without substance. The gold shields go to Egypt, and bronze ones take their place in the same procession. Nothing is renounced; something is quietly substituted. That is how religious decline usually works, and it is a question for churches and for individual believers: whether our routines still carry what they once carried. The cure is not polishing the bronze but returning to the Lord, and Chronicles shows that even in this reign, when the king and princes humbled themselves, God held back the worst (2 Chron. 12:5-7).

Obedience in the letter. Rehoboam obeyed the prophet and did not invade the north, and then fought Jeroboam for the rest of his life. It is possible to keep the letter of a command and pursue the very thing it forbade by other means. God looks for obedience of the heart, and that is what only his grace can give.
14.examples:
Then: A king sent his wife twenty miles in disguise, dressed as a villager and carrying a villager's gift, to get a word from God about their dying son; and the prophet she was deceiving was blind, and greeted her by name from the sound of her feet in the doorway before she had said anything at all.

Now: Three things. Why do you pretend to be another? is the question the chapter leaves standing: the costume could only ever have fooled a man. A great deal of religious practice is that shape, and the whole point of God is that he knows who is at the door; which is good news, because in Christ we may come as we really are and not be cast out. Second, verse 13, for anybody who has stood at a small grave: it does not explain why children die, and the loss is still a loss. What it does say is that God found something good in a boy whom no one else in that house would have thought to notice, said so, and was not careless of him in his death. And third, the bronze shields. The procession went on, and within a generation nobody remembered they had ever been gold. The question the verse asks without asking it is which parts of your own practice are bronze now. The answer is not to polish the bronze harder but to come back to the Lord himself, who has not changed, and to ask for the Spirit who makes worship living again.

15.title: Abijam, Asa, Nadab and Baasha

His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom.<sup>3</sup>And he walked in all the sins that his father did before him, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father.<sup>4</sup>Nevertheless, for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, setting up his son after him, and establishing Jerusalem,<sup>5</sup>because David did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.<sup>6</sup>Now there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of his life.<sup>7</sup>The rest of the acts of Abijam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam.<sup>8</sup>And Abijam slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa his son reigned in his place.<sup>9</sup>In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa began to reign over Judah,<sup>10</sup>and he reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom.<sup>11</sup>And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done.<sup>12</sup>He put away the male cult prostitutes out of the land and removed all the idols that his fathers had made.<sup>13</sup>He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother because she had made an abominable image for Asherah. And King Asa sent them to Ben-hadad the son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying,<sup>19</sup>"Let there be a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending to you a present of silver and gold. Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me."<sup>20</sup>And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel and conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all Chinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali.<sup>21</sup>And when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and he lived in Tirzah.<sup>22</sup>Then King Asa made a proclamation to all Judah, none was exempt, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them King Asa built Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah.<sup>23</sup>Now the rest of all the acts of Asa, all his might, and all that he did, and the cities that he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? But in his old age he was diseased in his feet.<sup>24</sup>And Asa slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.<sup>25</sup>Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel two years.<sup>26</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.<sup>27</sup>Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him. And Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, for Nadab and all Israel were laying siege to Gibbethon.<sup>28</sup>So Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and reigned in his place.<sup>29</sup>And as soon as he was king, he killed all the house of Jeroboam. He left to the house of Jeroboam not one that breathed, until he had destroyed it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite.<sup>30</sup>It was for the sins of Jeroboam that he sinned and that he made Israel to sin, and because of the anger to which he provoked the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>31</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Nadab and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>32</sup>And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days.<sup>33</sup>In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over all Israel at Tirzah, and he reigned twenty-four years.<sup>34</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.
15.overview:
Here the book changes shape. From this chapter to the end of 2 Kings the narrative runs on a fixed pattern, alternating between the two kingdoms and dating each reign by the other, and every king is weighed by one yardstick: whether his heart was wholly true to the LORD, the words Solomon preached at the dedication and lost in his old age.

Abijam fails that test, and the dynasty survives him only because God keeps a lamp in Jerusalem for David's sake. Verse 5 adds a carefully weighed sentence about David himself, naming his worst sin in the middle of a verse about God's faithfulness. It is neither a whitewash nor a dismissal: one matter, named once, with the rest of a seventy-year life on the other side, and God's promise kept for David's sake rather than because of his record.

Then Asa, who removes his own grandmother from the office of queen mother and burns her image at the Kidron, yet leaves the high places standing, and later strips the temple to hire a Syrian. The writer still gives him the phrase Solomon lost: the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days. In the north, meanwhile, Ahijah's word against Jeroboam's house is carried out by a conspirator who then walks in Jeroboam's sins himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abijam reigns three years, walking in his father's sins with a heart not wholly true (vv. 1-3); yet for David's sake the LORD gives him a lamp in Jerusalem, because David did right except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite (vv. 4-5). War with Jeroboam continues (vv. 6-8).
verseByVerse.theology: His heart was not wholly true: the words taken from Solomon are applied to his grandson in the same terms. The writer has found his yardstick, and it asks about the heart before it asks about achievements.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer names David's great sin plainly and does not let it define the whole man. That is how God's people should speak of the failures of those they love and honour: honestly, without hiding them and without reducing a life to them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now in the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam the son of Nebat, Abijam began to reign over Judah. He reigned for three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom. And he walked in all the sins that his father did before him, and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father. Nevertheless, for David's sake the LORD his God gave him a lamp in Jerusalem, setting up his son after him, and establishing Jerusalem, because David did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. Now there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of his life. The rest of the acts of Abijam and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam. And Abijam slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David. And Asa his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By dating Judah's kings from Israel's and Israel's from Judah's, the writer refuses to let either half be read alone. It can feel like a filing system, but it is doing something: they are one people who have broken in two, and he keeps making the reader look across the border.

The figures do not always add up at first sight, and it helps to know why. Abijam begins in Jeroboam's eighteenth year and reigns three years, yet Asa begins in Jeroboam's twentieth; Nadab reigns two years but begins in Asa's second year and is killed in his third. Ancient scribes usually counted any part of a year as a year, and the two kingdoms seem at times to have counted differently, so a reign of fourteen months could be written as two years. With these customs most of the numbers in Kings fit together; a few remain hard, and careful scholars still differ over the details. The division of the kingdom is usually dated about 930 BC.

Not wholly true again: the phrase of Solomon's benediction, taken off him at 11:4, is applied to his grandson in the same form and against the same standard, as the heart of David his father. The writer will use this yardstick for three centuries.

Then comes nevertheless. Here is a bad king whose heart was divided, and the dynasty survives him, not because of anything in him. The word is the one from Ahijah's oracle: a lamp in Jerusalem. David's own soldiers used it about him when he grew weary on a battlefield (lest you quench the lamp of Israel, 2 Sam. 21:17), and God took it up as his own at 11:36. He uses it here, and again when Judah deserves destruction: he was not willing to destroy Judah, for the sake of David his servant, since he promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever (2 Kings 8:19).

A lamp is a small light, and the promise is that it will not go out. Not that it will blaze, and not that the men holding it will be worth much. It burns through Abijam, and Ahaz, and Manasseh, down to almost nothing, and it does not go out. It was still burning when an old man in the temple took a baby in his arms and called him a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32). The lamp kept for David's sake was kept for the sake of David's greater Son. And the mercy shown to Abijam, given for another man's sake and not his own, is the shape of every mercy God shows sinners: we too are dealt with for the sake of Another.

Verse 5 is carefully weighed. That David did not turn aside from anything that he commanded him is an enormous claim, and a reader fresh from 2 Samuel may want to object. Then, in eight words, the writer objects for him: except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.

Two things about that exception. The first is that he makes it at all. The worst thing David ever did is named, by the man's name, in a verse about why God kept the promise, and the man named is not Bathsheba but Uriah, whose name closes the roll of the mighty men (2 Sam. 23:39). The second is how narrow it is: one matter, named once, with everything else in a seventy-year life on the other side. That is not a whitewash. It is the judgment Kings makes everywhere: whether a man belonged to the LORD alone. God kept the promise for David's sake, and the writer will not let anybody think that means David was better than he was.

Only one Son of David has no such exception in his record. He was tempted as we are, yet without sin (Heb. 4:15), and he is the one for whose sake God now keeps his promises to people with an Uriah in their past.

The war with Jeroboam is mentioned twice in three verses: the war that began when a hundred and eighty thousand men went home is still running in the second generation.

Chronicles calls him Abijah and records a speech and victory over Jeroboam (2 Chr 13). God gave him that victory, but his heart was not wholly true to the LORD; both books are true. Maacah (v. 2) was his mother, and the queen mother to Asa, his son (v. 10): “mother” can mean grandmother.

Chronicles also names Abijah's mother differently, Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah (2 Chron. 13:2), where Kings has Maacah the daughter of Abishalom. Abishalom is very likely Absalom (2 Chron. 11:20-21), and daughter can mean granddaughter just as mother can mean grandmother; a common suggestion is that Absalom's daughter married Uriel, so that Maacah was Absalom's granddaughter. The Greek and Syriac read Maacah in Chronicles as well, so the spelling there may be a copying slip.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–24 — The Heart of Asa Was Wholly True
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asa reigns forty-one years and does right, as David his father had done (vv. 9-11). He puts away the cult prostitutes and idols, removes Maacah from being queen mother and burns her Asherah image at the Kidron (vv. 12-13). The high places remain, nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days (v. 14). When Baasha fortifies Ramah, Asa sends the temple's silver and gold to Ben-hadad of Syria, who breaks with Baasha (vv. 16-22). In his old age he is diseased in his feet (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: The heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days. The phrase Solomon preached and lost is given, at last, to someone far less gifted. God weighs the heart's loyalty, not the size of a man's gifts.
verseByVerse.examples: Asa's verdict sits in the same verse as his failure, but the high places were not taken away. A believer can be wholly given to God and still leave something standing that should have come down. That is not a reason for complacency, but neither is it a reason to despair.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa began to reign over Judah, and he reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Maacah the daughter of Abishalom. And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done. He put away the male cult prostitutes out of the land and removed all the idols that his fathers had made. He also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother because she had made an abominable image for Asherah. And Asa cut down her image and burned it at the brook Kidron. But the high places were not taken away. Nevertheless, the heart of Asa was wholly true to the LORD all his days. And he brought into the house of the LORD the sacred gifts of his father and his own sacred gifts, silver, and gold, and vessels. And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days. Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah, that he might permit no one to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah. Then Asa took all the silver and the gold that were left in the treasures of the house of the LORD and the treasures of the king's house and gave them into the hands of his servants. And King Asa sent them to Ben-hadad the son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, saying, "Let there be a covenant between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending to you a present of silver and gold. Go, break your covenant with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me." And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel and conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and all Chinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali. And when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and he lived in Tirzah. Then King Asa made a proclamation to all Judah, none was exempt, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and its timber, with which Baasha had been building, and with them King Asa built Geba of Benjamin and Mizpah. Now the rest of all the acts of Asa, all his might, and all that he did, and the cities that he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? But in his old age he was diseased in his feet. And Asa slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asa reigns forty-one years, the longest reign in Judah so far. Since verse 2 said the same woman was Abijam's mother, Maacah is most likely Asa's grandmother, mother being used of a female ancestor, which also explains why she still holds the office of queen mother into a new reign.

This is the first good verdict in the book since Solomon's early years, and for the moment it comes without qualification. The idols were made by his father Abijam, and the high places built by his great-grandfather Solomon, and Asa takes the idols out. That is not a small thing. Every one had a constituency, and some had acquired the respectability anything acquires if it stands long enough. Removing them means telling people that what their fathers did was wrong.

Then he does the costliest thing of all. The queen mother in Judah held a real office, sitting at the king's right hand, and in a court of many wives she was often the most powerful woman in the kingdom. Asa removes her. The grounds are stated, an abominable image for Asherah, and he does not simply confiscate it. He burns it at the Kidron, below the city, where everybody could see the smoke. This is his grandmother, in an office she has held through two reigns. He is stripping his own family's matriarch of her position and destroying her religious property in front of the capital.

The principle underneath is one Scripture does not soften. The Lord Jesus said whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me (Matt. 10:37). Most obedience is not costly because a stranger opposes it. It is costly because somebody at the table does.

But the high places were not taken away is the qualification this writer will attach to almost every good king from here to the end. Hezekiah finally does it, and Josiah, and nobody else.

Chronicles says that Asa took away the foreign altars and the high places (2 Chron. 14:3), and later that the high places were not taken out of Israel (2 Chron. 15:17). The likeliest reading is that he removed the shrines to foreign gods and some of the high places, but not the local hilltop altars where the LORD himself was worshipped. Chronicles itself holds both statements side by side, and so does Kings.

What the high places were should be stated, because it is not simple idolatry. Many were places where the LORD himself was worshipped: local hilltop sanctuaries, convenient, ancient, exactly like Bethel. The trouble was that they were not the place God had chosen, and they were how Canaanite practice kept seeping in. So Asa's failure is that he tidied the country and left the alternative structures standing, because taking them down would have cost more than removing his grandmother's idol.

Now the verse the chapter exists for. Wholly true translates shalem, the root of Solomon's own name. They are the words Solomon used standing before the finished temple with the glory of God inside it: let your heart therefore be wholly true to the LORD our God (8:61). The writer took them off him when he was old (11:4), and off Abijam eleven verses ago. Here they are given to somebody.

Asa is not a better man than Solomon. He is nowhere near as gifted, he leaves the high places, he strips the temple to buy a foreign alliance, and Chronicles records that he ended badly. And the writer says his heart was whole toward God all his days.

A heart wholly true is not a measure of achievement or even of consistency. It is a question about whether there is anything else in the room. Solomon had seven hundred marriages and a hill full of altars; Asa had one God and a job half done. The writer records the failure and refuses to let it cancel the verdict, and a reader who can only hold one of them will misread every king in this book.

Asa puts treasure back into the temple, which had been stripped by Shishak in his grandfather's fifth year. Hold that for four verses. Ramah is about five miles north of Jerusalem, on the main road, so Baasha's fortifying it is a blockade.

Here is one of the hard numbers. Chronicles dates Baasha's move on Ramah to Asa's thirty-sixth year (2 Chron. 16:1), and says there was no war until his thirty-fifth (2 Chron. 15:19); but by Kings' figures Baasha died in Asa's twenty-sixth year (16:6, 8), and verse 16 here speaks of war all their days. Two answers are usually offered: that Chronicles is counting from the division of the kingdom, which would make it about Asa's sixteenth year, or that a numeral was miscopied at some stage. Neither can be proved, and it is better to say so than to force it. Nothing in the account of what happened depends on the exact year.

Then comes the other side of the man. He takes the silver and gold out of the house of the LORD, presumably including what he had just put in, and sends it to a foreign king to buy a military favour. (Damascus is the kingdom founded by Rezon, one of the adversaries God raised up against Solomon, 11:23-25.) He is paying a pagan king to be treacherous, and he says so in the letter: go, break your covenant. It works: Baasha pulls north, the blockade lifts, and Asa rebuilds his own frontier with the enemy's stones.

The strategy was a complete success, and Chronicles records what God thought of it. Hanani the seer came to Asa and said: because you relied on the king of Syria, and did not rely on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped you. Were not the Ethiopians and the Libyans a huge army with very many chariots and horsemen? Yet because you relied on the LORD, he gave them into your hand. For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him (2 Chron. 16:7-9).

Asa put the seer in the stocks. And the last clause of the rebuke, those whose heart is blameless toward him, uses shalem, the very word Kings uses of Asa's heart, quoted back at him as the thing he had just stopped acting on. So the record is genuinely mixed, and the two books make no attempt to harmonise it. His heart was whole toward God all his days, and he stripped the temple to hire a Syrian. Both are true.

The last clause of the account reads almost as an afterthought, and Chronicles supplies what is behind it: In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became severe. Yet even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but sought help from physicians (2 Chron. 16:12).

Be careful with that verse, because it has been badly used. It is not a rule against doctors. Isaiah prescribed a poultice of figs for Hezekiah's boil, Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach, and Luke is the beloved physician. The charge is he did not seek the LORD. A man whose heart had been whole toward God for forty years, at the end, in pain, went everywhere except to him. It is the pattern of the Syrian alliance: not apostasy but competence. He handled the problem himself, effectively, and did not ask.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–34 — According to the Word of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nadab son of Jeroboam reigns two years in his father's way (vv. 25-26). Baasha kills him at Gibbethon and destroys the whole house of Jeroboam, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah (vv. 27-30). Baasha reigns twenty-four years in Tirzah and walks in the way of Jeroboam (vv. 31-34).
verseByVerse.theology: The word Ahijah gave to a woman in disguise is carried out to the letter: not one that breathed. God's word, spoken quietly in a private house, governs the violent public events that follow.
verseByVerse.examples: The man God used to execute judgment on Jeroboam's calves walked in the way of Jeroboam. Seeing clearly what was wrong with someone else is no protection against doing the same; it may even blind us to ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Nadab the son of Jeroboam began to reign over Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah, and he reigned over Israel two years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father, and in his sin which he made Israel to sin. Baasha the son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, conspired against him. And Baasha struck him down at Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, for Nadab and all Israel were laying siege to Gibbethon. So Baasha killed him in the third year of Asa king of Judah and reigned in his place. And as soon as he was king, he killed all the house of Jeroboam. He left to the house of Jeroboam not one that breathed, until he had destroyed it, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite. It was for the sins of Jeroboam that he sinned and that he made Israel to sin, and because of the anger to which he provoked the LORD, the God of Israel. Now the rest of the acts of Nadab and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all their days. In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha the son of Ahijah began to reign over all Israel at Tirzah, and he reigned twenty-four years. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nadab reigns two years, and then the house of Jeroboam is finished. Here the formula about Jeroboam's sin arrives for the first of many times. From here to the fall of Samaria it is stamped on king after king, each measured against a day at Bethel when Jeroboam set up a calf because he was afraid. Which he made Israel to sin is the part that will not go away: he built the sin into the machinery of a nation, so that ordinary people went on doing it without ever choosing it.

Nadab is murdered by one of his own officers in the middle of a siege. Then the writer stops and tells us what has happened. A blind man in Shiloh said: I will cut off from Jeroboam every male, both bond and free in Israel, and will burn up the house of Jeroboam, as a man burns up dung until it is all gone (14:10).

The word was given in a private house to a woman in disguise, and it is executed by a soldier of Issachar acting, so far as the text shows, for reasons entirely his own. He is a conspirator eliminating a rival dynasty, which is standard practice. And the writer says the word of the LORD was fulfilled: the structure of 12:15 and 2 Samuel 17:14, a man acting freely, from his own motives, completing something God said. The reason is given plainly: the family is not being punished for Baasha's ambition, but cut off for what their father built.

The last verse of the chapter is the one to take away. Baasha was the instrument by which God's word against the calves was carried out, and the first thing recorded of his own reign is that he walked in the way of Jeroboam and in his sin which he made Israel to sin. He wiped out a family for a sin and then committed it. The calves, the priesthood and the festival go on untouched. Baasha changes the dynasty and leaves the religion as he found it, because it made the northern kingdom possible and he needs it as much as Jeroboam did.

That is why the judgment does not fix anything. Chapter 16 opens with a prophet coming to Baasha with almost word for word the same oracle Ahijah gave Jeroboam, and Baasha's house is destroyed the same way. Being the instrument of a judgment teaches a man nothing. He can carry out God's sentence on somebody else's sin in the morning and take it up himself in the afternoon, and it will not occur to him that there is any connection.

15.theology:
One people, one measure. From here Kings alternates between Judah and Israel and weighs every king by a single question: was his heart wholly true to the LORD, as David's was? It is not a question about talent, success or even consistency. It asks whether God had a rival. That measure explains why a gifted king like Solomon can lose the verdict and a limited king like Asa can receive it.

Mercy for another's sake. Abijam deserved to lose the throne, and God kept a lamp burning in Jerusalem for David's sake. The lamp is small, and it burns through many unworthy kings, but it does not go out, and it leads at last to the Light of the world. That is the shape of the gospel: God deals with sinners for the sake of Another, the Son of David whose record has no exception, and whose obedience is counted as theirs.

Honesty about the saints. Verse 5 praises David without pretending. His worst sin is named, Uriah by name, in a verse about God's faithfulness to him. Scripture never needs to hide the sins of its heroes, because its hope never rested on them. And it does not let one terrible failure erase a life that belonged to God; it holds both together, as it does for every believer who has fallen and been restored.

Costly obedience. Asa's removal of his grandmother shows that faithfulness often costs most at home. The demand Jesus makes, that he be loved above father and mother (Matt. 10:37), is not a call to cruelty but to first loyalty, and Asa shows it can be done with public clarity.

A whole heart and a half-done task. Asa left the high places, bought a Syrian alliance with temple silver, jailed a prophet, and in his last illness did not seek the LORD. Yet Kings says his heart was wholly true all his days. The commentary takes both statements as true together. The verdict is not a grade for performance; it is God's gracious judgment on where the heart belonged. That is encouragement for believers who know how much they leave undone, and also a warning: Asa's later reliance on Syria and on his own competence is the kind of drift that can coexist with real faith and still do real harm. Seeking help from physicians was not his sin; not seeking the LORD was.

The old shrines. The high places Asa left were mostly not shrines to other gods. They were local places where the LORD himself was worshipped, ancient and convenient and loved, like Bethel. Their fault was that they were not where God had chosen to put his name, and they were the channel through which Canaanite practice kept seeping back. Removing a grandmother's obscene image was hard; removing the popular, long-established, half-right places of worship would have been harder still, and Asa did not attempt it. The most stubborn obstacles to faithfulness are often not the open evils but the familiar compromises everybody is used to.

Sin built into a system. The phrase which he made Israel to sin begins here its long run through the book. Jeroboam did not only sin; he built his sin into the institutions of a nation, so that ordinary people went on doing it without ever choosing it. Leaders bear a heavier responsibility for this reason (James 3:1), and believers living inside such systems need the word of God to see what everyone around them has stopped noticing.

Sovereignty through free agents. Ahijah's word against Jeroboam is fulfilled by Baasha's coup, done for Baasha's own reasons. As at Rehoboam's assembly, God's purpose is accomplished through people acting freely, without making them less responsible or him the author of their sin.

The judge who learns nothing. Baasha destroyed Jeroboam's house for its sin and then walked in that sin himself. Executing judgment does not make anyone righteous, and being right about another's failure does not free us from our own. The only remedy for the sins of Jeroboam is a changed heart, which no new dynasty could give and which God promises in Christ.
15.examples:
Then: A king of Judah stripped his own grandmother of the highest office a woman could hold in the kingdom, cut down the idol she had made, and burned it in the valley below the city where everybody could watch the smoke; and he left the hilltop shrines standing all over the country, because they were popular and old and everybody used them.

Now: Three things. Verse 14 is the one to keep, and it is the most encouraging sentence in the chapter: a heart wholly true is not a score for achievement or even consistency; it asks whether there is anything else in the room. Asa left a job half done, hired a pagan army with temple silver, and put a prophet in the stocks, and God's verdict on his heart stands in the same verse as the failure. That is grace, not grading, and for us it rests on the one Son of David whose record has no exception in it. Second, Maacah. Obedience is rarely expensive because strangers object; it is expensive because somebody at your own table does. The Lord who asks for that first loyalty is the one who loved us first, and his Spirit gives the courage it takes. And third, Baasha, the warning nobody expects: he executed God's judgment on another man's sin and then walked straight into it. Being right about somebody else's failure is not the same as being free of it.

16.title: From Baasha to Ahab
16.text: <sup>1</sup>And the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins,<sup>3</sup>behold, I will utterly sweep away Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat.<sup>4</sup>Anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the field the birds of the heavens shall eat."<sup>5</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Baasha and what he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>6</sup>And Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried at Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned in his place.<sup>7</sup>Moreover, the word of the LORD came by the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, both because of all the evil that he did in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he destroyed it.<sup>8</sup>In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah the son of Baasha began to reign over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years.<sup>9</sup>But his servant Zimri, commander of half his chariots, conspired against him. When he was at Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was over the household in Tirzah,<sup>10</sup>Zimri came in and struck him down and killed him, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place.<sup>11</sup>When he began to reign, as soon as he had seated himself on his throne, he struck down all the house of Baasha. He did not leave him a single male of his relatives or his friends.<sup>12</sup>Thus Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet,<sup>13</sup>for all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, which they sinned and which they made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their idols.<sup>14</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Elah and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>15</sup>In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. Now the troops were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines,<sup>16</sup>and the troops who were encamped heard it said, "Zimri has conspired, and he has killed the king." Therefore all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp.<sup>17</sup>So Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah.<sup>18</sup>And when Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house over him with fire and died,<sup>19</sup>because of his sins that he committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD, walking in the way of Jeroboam, and for his sin which he committed, making Israel to sin.<sup>20</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and the conspiracy that he made, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>21</sup>Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts.
