Half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri.<sup>22</sup>But the people who followed Omri overcame the people who followed Tibni the son of Ginath. So Tibni died, and Omri became king.<sup>23</sup>In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for twelve years; six years he reigned in Tirzah.<sup>24</sup>He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, and he fortified the hill and called the name of the city that he built Samaria, after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill.<sup>25</sup>Omri did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and did more evil than all who were before him.<sup>26</sup>For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in the sins that he made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger by their idols.<sup>27</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Omri that he did, and the might that he showed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>28</sup>And Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and Ahab his son reigned in his place.<sup>29</sup>In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel, and Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years.<sup>30</sup>And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him.<sup>31</sup>And as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took for his wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him.<sup>32</sup>He erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he built in Samaria.<sup>33</sup>And Ahab made an Asherah. Ahab did more to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him.<sup>34</sup>In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun.
16.overview:
The chapter is built as an accelerating collapse. Baasha receives Ahijah's oracle with the name changed. Elah is stabbed while drunk in his palace manager's house, with his whole army in the field. Zimri holds the throne for seven days and burns the palace down on top of himself. Then come four years of civil war and a fourth dynasty. Fifty years earlier there was one kingdom and a house on the temple mount that a foreign queen had run out of breath looking at.

Verse 7 adds a clause that repays attention: Baasha is condemned for destroying Jeroboam's house, though chapter 15 said that destruction fulfilled the word of the LORD. God's purpose stood, and the man who carried it out for his own ends still answered for them. Being used by God is not the same as being commissioned by him.

Omri is the point of the middle of the chapter, though not in the way a historian of the ancient world would tell it. He founded Samaria, began a dynasty of four kings, and gave his name to Israel in foreign records for a century. He gets six verses, four of them about how he took the throne, because this writer's scale of measurement is not the world's.

Then Ahab, and something genuinely new: not the wrong worship of the right God, but another god installed in the capital with a temple and an altar, and a Sidonian queen whose father carries Baal in his own name. The chapter's last verse is a curse centuries old collected in full, placed immediately before Elijah walks in.

Five kings and a rival in one chapter, most of them reaching the throne by the sword, is the north's long answer to the question of what a people becomes without the king God chose. Meanwhile the lamp in Jerusalem still burns (15:4). Chapters like this taught the prophets to long for a King who would come not by conspiracy but by God's appointment, a shepherd who lays down his own life instead of taking other men's (Ezek. 34:23; John 10:11).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehu the son of Hanani brings Baasha almost word for word the oracle Ahijah brought Jeroboam, down to the dogs and the birds (vv. 1-4), and verse 7 adds a second charge. Baasha's son Elah is murdered while drunk by Zimri, who wipes out Baasha's house as the word said (vv. 8-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The oracle against Baasha is Ahijah's oracle against Jeroboam with the name changed: the same opening, the same charge, the same sentence. He wiped out one house for its sin and is destroyed for the same sin himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Baasha was the instrument of a judgment, and he is still answerable for how he carried it out (v. 7). It is a warning to anyone tempted to think that serving a good end excuses the means: a manager who removes a dishonest colleague by lying about him, or a campaigner who wins a just cause by cruelty, has not been vindicated by the result.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha, saying, "Since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam and have made my people Israel to sin, provoking me to anger with their sins, behold, I will utterly sweep away Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat. Anyone belonging to Baasha who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the field the birds of the heavens shall eat." Now the rest of the acts of Baasha and what he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Baasha slept with his fathers and was buried at Tirzah, and Elah his son reigned in his place. Moreover, the word of the LORD came by the prophet Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, both because of all the evil that he did in the sight of the LORD, provoking him to anger with the work of his hands, in being like the house of Jeroboam, and also because he destroyed it. In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah the son of Baasha began to reign over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years. But his servant Zimri, commander of half his chariots, conspired against him. When he was at Tirzah, drinking himself drunk in the house of Arza, who was over the household in Tirzah, Zimri came in and struck him down and killed him, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, and reigned in his place. When he began to reign, as soon as he had seated himself on his throne, he struck down all the house of Baasha. He did not leave him a single male of his relatives or his friends. Thus Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke against Baasha by Jehu the prophet, for all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, which they sinned and which they made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their idols. Now the rest of the acts of Elah and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
verseByVerse.commentary:
This prophet Jehu is not to be confused with the later king of the same name. His father Hanani is the seer who rebuked Asa about the Syrian alliance and was put in the stocks for it (2 Chron. 16:7-10).

Read verse 2 against 14:7; the writer is repeating himself on purpose. Jeroboam heard through Ahijah that God had exalted him and made him leader, and that he had done evil above all before him. Baasha hears the same opening and the same charge, and the same sentence is coming.

Out of the dust is if anything more pointed. Jeroboam was a labour foreman; Baasha was an officer of Issachar with a knife and an opportunity. God took him off the ground.

Verse 4 is almost word for word what Ahijah said about Jeroboam's house, down to the dogs and the birds (14:11). Baasha stood over the corpses of Jeroboam's family. He heard how they died and why. And the oracle that comes to him is the same oracle, in almost the same words, and he will have recognised it.

Verse 7 condemns Baasha on two counts: he was like the house of Jeroboam, and he destroyed it. Yet chapter 15 said that destruction happened according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite (15:29). So the same act is both the fulfilment of God's word and a crime the man is answerable for.

That is not a contradiction, and the Bible states it in several places. Assyria is the rod of God's anger against Israel, and God then punishes Assyria for the arrogance with which it swung (Isa. 10:5-12). Men did what God's hand and plan had predestined at the cross, and they were lawless men (Acts 4:28; 2:23).

Being used by God is not the same as being commissioned by him. Baasha was not obeying an order; he was a conspirator murdering a rival dynasty for his own advancement, and God's word was fulfilled through what he freely chose to do for his own reasons. The purpose was God's. The motive was his, and he answers for it.

The cross is the great instance. There the worst act in history, done by men who answered for it, was the very means God had planned to save sinners, including some of the men who had called for it (Acts 2:36-41). Baasha's story shows the rule; Calvary shows it turned to mercy.

Anybody inclined to think that a good outcome vindicates how they got there is looking at the verse that says otherwise.

The detail is contemptuous, and it is meant to be: the king of Israel is killed while drinking himself drunk in the house of his palace manager.

Notice where he is not. His whole army is besieging Gibbethon (v. 15), the siege line where his father murdered Nadab. Elah is at home, in a subordinate's house, incapable.

The same thing happens again one generation later: Baasha did it to Jeroboam's house, and Zimri does it to Baasha's. The phrase or his friends is new; Zimri goes wider than the family. The word is fulfilled exactly, by a man who is about to last a week.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zimri lasts seven days: the army at Gibbethon makes Omri king, and Zimri burns the palace over himself (vv. 15-20). After a civil war with Tibni, Omri reigns twelve years, founds Samaria, and does more evil than all before him (vv. 21-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Zimri held the throne for a week, and the writer still applies the full formula to him, because a week was long enough to show what he would have done with it.
verseByVerse.examples: Omri was one of the most consequential kings the north ever had, and he gets six verses. A life is not measured here by its reputation, its buildings or its place in other people's records, but by what it did with the God who gave it. That is sobering for the ambitious and a comfort for the obscure.

verseByVerse.quote: In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. Now the troops were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines, and the troops who were encamped heard it said, "Zimri has conspired, and he has killed the king." Therefore all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp. So Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah. And when Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house over him with fire and died, because of his sins that he committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD, walking in the way of Jeroboam, and for his sin which he committed, making Israel to sin. Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and the conspiracy that he made, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts. Half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri. But the people who followed Omri overcame the people who followed Tibni the son of Ginath. So Tibni died, and Omri became king. In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel, and he reigned for twelve years; six years he reigned in Tirzah. He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver, and he fortified the hill and called the name of the city that he built Samaria, after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill. Omri did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and did more evil than all who were before him. For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in the sins that he made Israel to sin, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger by their idols. Now the rest of the acts of Omri that he did, and the might that he showed, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? And Omri slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria, and Ahab his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is the shortest reign in either book and the writer still gives him the full treatment: an accession formula, a verdict, a cause of death, and a summary. Seven days was long enough to be judged.

Gibbethon appears again: the same Philistine town the army was besieging when Baasha murdered Nadab twenty-four years earlier, and they are still besieging it.

Two kings have been assassinated on the strength of that one siege line, and the town is still not taken.

And the army makes its own commander king that day in the camp. No prophet, no anointing, no elders, no assembly. The soldiers vote and the general is king.

He burns the palace down with himself inside it. Whatever drove him (despair, defiance, refusal to be taken alive) is not recorded; the only explanation the writer gives is his sins (v. 19).

A week. He cannot have instituted anything or changed any policy. What the verdict means is that in seven days he did nothing about the calves either, and that he was going to be exactly what all of them were.

The writer disposes of a civil war inside the northern kingdom in two verses. So Tibni died. He does not say how, and the placement leaves little doubt.

The dates look tangled and are not. Zimri died in Asa's twenty-seventh year; Omri began to reign as sole king in the thirty-first, after four years of rivalry with Tibni; and his twelve years are most naturally counted from the day the army proclaimed him, which brings his death and Ahab's accession to Asa's thirty-eighth (v. 29), counting part-years as years as the scribes usually did.

The one solid achievement is real. Samaria is a superb site, isolated, defensible and commanding the trade roads, and it remained the northern capital until the Assyrians took it after a three-year siege in 722, a considerable testimony to the man's judgment.

And note that he bought it, and the writer records the price and the seller's name. That is a proper transaction, not a seizure.

By external measures he is one of the most significant kings the northern kingdom ever had, and one of the few figures in this book who left a mark on the wider records of the ancient world. Assyrian royal inscriptions call Israel "the house of Omri" long after his descendants were dead, and the Moabite Stone, set up by King Mesha, names him and describes his conquest of Moab. The writer of Kings gives his reign six verses (vv. 23-28) and never mentions the international reputation at all. That is not ignorance. It is a scale of measurement.

This historian is not writing about power, and he is not impressed by it. He gives four chapters to a building and one line to an empire's foreign policy; he spends thirty-four verses on a man of God who ate a meal he should not have eaten, and six on the king whose name a superpower used for Israel for a century.

Verse 25 is the entry in the ledger that matters to him: more evil than all who were before him. The formula is escalating, and it will escalate again in three verses. As for the might that he showed (v. 27), the writer knows about it; he simply refers the interested reader to another book.
verseByVerse.note: Omri founded Samaria as the new capital; Assyrian records long after called Israel “the house of Omri.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab marries Jezebel of Sidon, serves Baal, and builds him a temple in Samaria, doing more to provoke the LORD than any king before him (vv. 29-33). In his days Hiel rebuilds Jericho at the cost of two sons, as Joshua had said (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Something new has happened, and the writer marks it. Jeroboam's calves were the wrong worship of the right God; Ahab builds a temple to a different god in the capital, and the Tyrian alliance Solomon began comes home a century later as a marriage.
verseByVerse.examples: A man rebuilds Jericho in defiance of Joshua's curse and buries two sons (Josh. 6:26), and the writer puts it in the last verse before Elijah walks in. A land that has turned to the god of rain is about to learn that the LORD's word, not Baal's, governs the sky.

verseByVerse.quote: In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab the son of Omri began to reign over Israel, and Ahab the son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years. And Ahab the son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him. And as if it had been a light thing for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, he took for his wife Jezebel the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and went and served Baal and worshiped him. He erected an altar for Baal in the house of Baal, which he built in Samaria. And Ahab made an Asherah. Ahab did more to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him. In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-two years, and the next six chapters belong to his reign.

The writer has covered five kings in twenty-eight verses, and from here to chapter 22 he slows almost to a stop, because Elijah is about to arrive.

The formula has been climbing all through the book. Jeroboam had done evil above all who were before him; Omri did more than all before him; Ahab does more than all of them.

As if it had been a light thing (v. 31): the calves were not enough for him. Sixty years of Jeroboam's religion was, in Ahab's estimation, a small matter.

Jeroboam's calves were an offence against the second commandment. He never named another god; he used the covenant name, quoted the exodus, and called his images thrones for the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. It was the wrong worship of the right God.

Ahab went and served Baal. That is a different commandment and a different sin: not a corrupted approach to the LORD but another god, brought in and installed.

Jezebel is from Sidon, which is Phoenicia: the same coast, the same people, the same gods as Tyre. Hiram of Tyre loved David, sent him cedar unasked, blessed the LORD by name and supplied every beam in the temple.

A century later the alliance comes home as a marriage. Her father carries Baal in his own name, and Josephus records that he was a priest of Astarte before he took the throne.

She is not a princess who happens to have brought her own religion. She is the daughter of a priest of a fertility cult, married to the king of Israel, and chapter 18 will say she keeps four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and four hundred of Asherah at her own table, and has been killing the prophets of the LORD.

Ahab builds a temple for a Canaanite storm god in the city his father founded, and puts an altar in it. For the second time in four verses the writer says he exceeded everybody (v. 33).

Go back some five centuries (on the traditional dating of the conquest; rather less on the later dating many scholars prefer). Jericho has fallen; the walls came down; and Joshua puts the city under a curse:

Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates (Josh. 6:26).

Jericho was the firstfruits of the land: the first city taken, devoted entirely to God, with everything in it destroyed. (The Hebrew word is herem: something given over wholly to God, here by destruction, as his judgment on peoples whose wickedness had run its full course, Gen. 15:16.) It was never to be rebuilt as a fortified city. People did live on the site after Joshua (Judg. 3:13), but now a man from Bethel rebuilds it with foundations and gates, the very act Joshua had cursed.

The writer records the price with terrible precision: at the cost of Abiram his firstborn when the foundation went in, and at the cost of his youngest son Segub when the gates went up. That most naturally means it took years: he buried his eldest son at the beginning and his youngest at the end, and he kept building.

That is the detail that makes the verse unbearable. It was not a single catastrophe he could not have foreseen. The first son died at the foundation, and there was the curse, five centuries old and public, and he went on and finished the gates.

The writer's only comment is according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun. Centuries later, it was still live.

The verse has nothing to do with Ahab, who appears only as a date: in his days. Its position is the point. The writer puts it last, and chapter 17 begins with a man walking in from nowhere and saying as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word.

The country is worshipping Baal, who is the god of storm and rain and fertility. His temple is in the capital and his prophets eat at the queen's table. And into that, on the far side of a verse about a curse that took five hundred years and did not fail, walks a man who says it will not rain again until he says so.

Some think Hiel sacrificed his sons himself as foundation offerings; the text does not say so. What it says is that God judged the man who defied his word, and the sons died as the curse had said. That is a hard thing to read, and the writer does not soften it: defiance of God's word does not stay private, and those nearest to us can bear its cost.
verseByVerse.note: Jezebel was a Phoenician princess from Sidon who promoted the worship of Baal.

16.theology:
Two generations of one family (v. 1). Jehu the son of Hanani brings this word; his father is the seer who rebuked Asa over the Syrian alliance and was put in the stocks for it (2 Chron. 16:7-10). Father and son told kings on both sides of the border what they did not want to hear, and God kept raising up such voices in a kingdom that would not listen.

The same oracle with the name changed (vv. 2-4). To Jeroboam: because I exalted you from among the people and made you leader over my people Israel... but you have done evil (14:7). To Baasha: since I exalted you out of the dust and made you leader over my people Israel, and you have walked in the way of Jeroboam. The opening, the charge and the dogs and birds are the same. Baasha had seen the first oracle fulfilled, and he had learned nothing from it.

Used, and answerable (v. 7). Baasha is condemned on two counts: for being like the house of Jeroboam, and for destroying it, though 15:29 called that destruction the fulfilment of God's word through Ahijah. This is not a contradiction. Baasha was not obeying an order but murdering a rival dynasty for his own advancement, and God's word was fulfilled through what he freely chose for his own reasons. The purpose was God's; the motive was his. Anyone inclined to think a good outcome vindicates how they reached it is looking at the verse that says otherwise.

Seven days, and a full verdict (vv. 15, 19). The shortest reign in either book still gets an accession formula, a verdict, a death and a summary. A week was long enough to show what Zimri was. And Gibbethon is still not taken: two kings assassinated on the strength of one siege line, twenty-four years apart, and the town holds.

The historian's measure is not the world's (vv. 23-28). By external standards Omri is one of the most significant kings the north ever had: a dynasty of four kings where the previous three managed fifty years between them, a capital at Samaria, which he bought honestly and which outlived his line by more than a century, and enough weight that Assyrian royal inscriptions called Israel "the house of Omri" for over a hundred years after his family was destroyed. The Moabite Stone names him. He gets six verses, four about how he took the throne. The writer knows about the might that he showed and files it in another book. He gives four chapters to a building and one line to an empire's foreign policy; thirty-four verses to a man of God who ate a meal he should not have eaten, and six to this.

As if it had been a light thing (v. 31). Be precise about what is new. Jeroboam never named another god: he used the covenant name, quoted the exodus, and called his images thrones for the God who brought Israel out of Egypt. That was the wrong worship of the right God, a breach of the second commandment. Ahab went and served Baal and worshiped him, and built him a house in the capital. That is a different commandment and a different sin: not a corrupted approach to the LORD but another god installed. The slide took sixty years, and it began with treating the first sin as small.

The Tyrian alliance comes home (v. 31). Sidon is Phoenicia, the same coast, people and gods as Tyre. Hiram loved David, blessed the LORD by name and supplied every beam in the temple; a century later the friendship returns as a marriage that brings Baal to Samaria. What looked like a harmless alliance in one generation carried the seed of idolatry into the next.

Why verse 34 is placed here. Hiel's story has nothing to do with Ahab, who appears only as a date, in his days. The writer puts it last, immediately before a man walks in from nowhere and says there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word. The country is worshipping Baal, the god of storm and rain and fertility, with his temple in the capital and his prophets at the queen's table, and the last thing we are told before Elijah arrives is that a word God spoke centuries ago has just come true, exactly. The reader is meant to know whose word holds.
16.examples:
Then: A man from Bethel rebuilt Jericho against a curse five hundred years old, buried his eldest son when the foundations went in, and went on building for years until the gates were finished, and buried his youngest son when they were hung.

Now: Three things. Verse 7 will not let anybody off: Baasha carried out God's own judgment and is condemned for how he did it. A right outcome does not sanctify the motive that produced it, and being useful to God's purposes is not the same as being sent. Second, Omri is the quiet rebuke to every way of keeping score. He was the most consequential man in that kingdom's history by every measure the world uses, and this historian gives him six verses and one sentence of verdict. And third, Hiel. The first death was the warning, and he finished the gates anyway. Most people who go on with something ruinous are not ignorant of the cost; they have already paid an instalment of it. The way out is not fresh resolve but the mercy Hiel never asked for: the God whose word against Jericho stood for five centuries has a word of pardon that stands as firmly for anyone who stops and confesses (Psalm 32:5; 1 John 1:9), and a Son whose perfect obedience is counted to those who could not finish well.

17.title: Elijah, the Ravens and the Widow
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Elijah the Tishbite, of Tishbe in Gilead, said to Ahab, "As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word."<sup>2</sup>And the word of the LORD came to him:<sup>3</sup>"Depart from here and turn eastward and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan.<sup>4</sup>You shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there."<sup>5</sup>So he went and did according to the word of the LORD. He went and lived by the brook Cherith that is east of the Jordan.<sup>6</sup>And the ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook.<sup>7</sup>And after a while the brook dried up, because there was no rain in the land.<sup>8</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to him,<sup>9</sup>"Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and dwell there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to feed you."<sup>10</sup>So he arose and went to Zarephath. And when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks. And he called to her and said, "Bring me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink."<sup>11</sup>And as she was going to bring it, he called to her and said, "Bring me a morsel of bread in your hand."<sup>12</sup>And she said, "As the LORD your God lives, I have nothing baked, only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. And now I am gathering a couple of sticks that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, that we may eat it and die."<sup>13</sup>And Elijah said to her, "Do not fear; go and do as you have said. But first make me a little cake of it and bring it to me, and afterward make something for yourself and your son.<sup>14</sup>For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'The jar of flour shall not be spent, and the jug of oil shall not be empty, until the day that the LORD sends rain upon the earth.'"<sup>15</sup>And she went and did as Elijah said. And she and he and her household ate for many days.<sup>16</sup>The jar of flour was not spent, neither did the jug of oil become empty, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by Elijah.<sup>17</sup>After this the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became ill. And his illness was so severe that there was no breath left in him.<sup>18</sup>And she said to Elijah, "What have you against me, O man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to remembrance and to cause the death of my son!"<sup>19</sup>And he said to her, "Give me your son." And he took him from her arms and carried him up into the upper chamber where he lodged, and laid him on his own bed.<sup>20</sup>And he cried to the LORD, "O LORD my God, have you brought calamity even upon the widow with whom I sojourn, by killing her son?"<sup>21</sup>Then he stretched himself upon the child three times and cried to the LORD, "O LORD my God, let this child's life come into him again."<sup>22</sup>And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah. And the life of the child came into him again, and he revived.<sup>23</sup>And Elijah took the child and brought him down from the upper chamber into the house and delivered him to his mother. And Elijah said, "See, your son lives."<sup>24</sup>And the woman said to Elijah, "Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth."
17.overview:
Elijah enters with no introduction whatever. He has no genealogy, no call narrative and no commissioning, only a place name from the wrong side of the Jordan and a sentence spoken to the king's face. That sentence lands immediately after 16:34, where a curse centuries old has just been fulfilled: God's old words are still live, and here is a new one.

The chapter runs on the word of the LORD and says so six times (vv. 1, 2, 5, 8, 16, 24). Its three scenes descend in scale and rise in weight. A nation loses its rain, a household loses its last meal, a mother loses her only child, and the same word meets each. It ends in the mouth of a Sidonian woman who says what nobody in Israel has said: the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth (v. 24).

He is not the last man to step out of the wilderness like this. Malachi closed the prophets with the promise that Elijah would come again before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5), and when John the Baptist appeared by the Jordan, dressed as Elijah had been and calling a divided nation to turn, Jesus said of him: he is Elijah who is to come (Matthew 11:14). The voice that shut the sky over Ahab was the forerunner of a greater forerunner, and both pointed to the King who would come after them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — No Rain Except By My Word
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man nobody has heard of is suddenly standing in front of the king, swearing by the living God that there will be no dew or rain except by his word (v. 1). Then he is told to vanish east of the Jordan, where ravens feed him by the brook Cherith, until the brook itself dries up (vv. 2-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The drought is not a stunt. Deuteronomy 11 says in as many words that if Israel turns to other gods the LORD will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain (Deut. 11:16-17). Ahab has installed the storm god in the capital, and God answers at the one point where Baal's reputation lies.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 7 carries the weight: the brook fails. The prophet who called the drought down is not exempt from it. God's provision was real and it had an end date, and the end date was not a sign of God's displeasure but the next instruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Elijah the Tishbite, of Tishbe in Gilead, said to Ahab, "As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain these years, except by my word." And the word of the LORD came to him: "Depart from here and turn eastward and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, which is east of the Jordan. You shall drink from the brook, and I have commanded the ravens to feed you there." So he went and did according to the word of the LORD. He went and lived by the brook Cherith that is east of the Jordan. And the ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook. And after a while the brook dried up, because there was no rain in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verse before this one is placed beside it on purpose. A builder from Bethel has just buried two sons rebuilding Jericho, a curse spoken by Joshua centuries before and collected in Ahab's reign. Then, with no transition of any kind, a man is standing in the throne room.

He has no introduction. Consider how unusual that is. Moses gets a bush and a whole chapter of argument; Isaiah gets the temple and the coal; Jeremiah is told he was known before he was formed; Ezekiel gets the wheels; Amos stops to explain that he was a herdsman and no prophet's son. Elijah gets a few words of address, the Tishbite, of Tishbe in Gilead, and no father, no tribe, no call, no commission. He is simply there, mid-sentence, in front of the most powerful man in the northern kingdom.

(The Hebrew of of Tishbe is uncertain; it may mean of the settlers of Gilead, while the Greek translation reads Tishbe as a town. Either way the point is the same: he comes from the edge.) Gilead is east of the Jordan: high, rough grazing country, the frontier. He is not a Samaria man. He has walked in from the wrong side of the river with the accent of the hills, and the court would have known it the moment he opened his mouth.

He speaks in a capital where the queen is the daughter of the king of the Sidonians (16:31), where a temple to Baal has just gone up, where eight hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and Asherah eat at the palace expense (18:19), and where the prophets of the LORD are being hunted and hidden in caves (18:4). The question in the air is whose god this country belongs to, and a man walks in to answer it.

As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives. It is a standard oath formula, and here it is loaded. In the Canaanite stories about Baal, Baal dies. He goes down into the throat of Mot, who is death, and while he is down there the rains stop and the crops fail and the world goes brown; then he comes back up and the sky opens. That is the whole shape of the religion Ahab has installed: a god who is seasonally dead.

Elijah opens his mouth in the temple-builder's palace and swears by a God who is alive, and then shuts the sky.

Before whom I stand. This is court language: to stand before a king is to be his servant, on duty. Elijah is standing in front of Ahab and tells him this is not the court he serves in. The physical facts of the room are that a man from Gilead is at the mercy of a king with an army. The claim of the sentence is that a servant of the real throne has come to deliver a message to a provincial one.

Neither dew nor rain. Both, and the second matters more than a modern reader might guess. In that climate the rain stops every year around May and nothing falls until October, and everybody survives the dry months because the heavy Mediterranean dew comes down at night. Elijah does not merely delay the rain. He takes away the fallback.

Nor is this an arbitrary display of power, and it should not be preached as one. It is the contract. Moses had put it in writing: take care lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and worship them; then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and he will shut up the heavens, so that there will be no rain, and the land will yield no fruit (Deut. 11:16-17). Ahab has done the first half. God is doing the second, exactly as printed.

What makes it more than bookkeeping is where it lands. Baal is the storm. He is drawn with a lightning bolt for a spear; he is called the rider on the clouds; he is worshipped precisely for rain and grain and calves and children. God does not attack Baal at his weak point. He shuts off the one thing Baal exists to supply, and leaves him three years to produce it.

Then the clause that should stop any reader: except by my word. Not except by the word of the LORD, but by mine. God has put the weather of a nation at the disposal of a man's mouth, and the man says so out loud to the king.

Keep hold of that, because the New Testament does. James picks up this exact scene to teach ordinary Christians how to pray: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth (Jas. 5:17). James's point is not that Elijah was a giant. It is that he was not. The astonishing thing is not the drought; it is that God takes a man into his confidence far enough to hand him the timing of it, and he gives the same Spirit who helps us in our weakness when we pray (Rom. 8:26).

The man has just made the most public statement in the kingdom, and the first instruction he receives is to hide.

He goes east, back over the Jordan, into his own home country and out of Ahab's reach. Chapter 18 will tell us what he was being hidden from: Ahab searched every kingdom and nation for him and made them swear they did not have him (18:10).

Then the ravens. A raven is on the list of birds Israel may not eat (Lev. 11:15); it is a scavenger, a carrion bird. God keeps his prophet alive by a twice-daily delivery from unclean birds, and the food is bread and meat morning and evening: meat twice a day, in a famine, which is better than most Israelites ate in a good year.

He went and did according to the word of the LORD (v. 5). The writer will say this about him again and again. It is the difference between Elijah and every king in the book.

He prayed the drought down, and the drought came for him. The word did its work on the land, and the land included his ravine; he was not woken one morning to find the brook gone, but watched it narrow to a trickle and the pools go green and then dry, with no word from God about what came after.

Say the obvious thing plainly, because it is the pastoral weight of the whole section. He was exactly where God told him to be, doing exactly what God told him to do, and his supply ran out. That was not a rebuke, and not a sign that he had misheard. God also brings his own provisions to an end. The job that carried you for nine years, the church that fed you, the health that let you serve: these were commanded of God as truly as the ravens were, and they can dry up while you stand in the middle of his will.

It is natural to read a drying brook as evidence that God has gone off you. Elijah did not. He watched it go down and waited, and the next verse begins then the word of the LORD came to him. The water ran out and the word did not.

Luke and James give three and a half years of drought (Luke 4:25; Jas 5:17); “in the third year” (18:1) counts from Elijah’s stay with the widow, after a dry season had already begun.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah means “my God is the LORD.” Baal was worshipped as the god of rain, so a drought struck at his heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — The Jar That Did Not Empty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends Elijah to Zarephath in Sidon, Jezebel's home country, to be fed by a widow who is gathering sticks for her son's last meal (vv. 8-12). He asks her to feed him first, with a promise that the flour and oil will not run out until the rain comes; she does, and they hold out (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is exactly worded: not filled, not multiplied, but never empty. She is never given more than one day's flour, which is manna again, and the petition Jesus put in the middle of the prayer he taught: give us this day our daily bread.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the passage Jesus preached in Nazareth (Luke 4:25-26), and his hearers tried to throw him off a cliff. The offence was that God had gone past Israel to a Sidonian before, and might do it again.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to him, "Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and dwell there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to feed you." So he arose and went to Zarephath. And when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks. And he called to her and said, "Bring me a little water in a vessel, that I may drink." And as she was going to bring it, he called to her and said, "Bring me a morsel of bread in your hand." And she said, "As the LORD your God lives, I have nothing baked, only a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. And now I am gathering a couple of sticks that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, that we may eat it and die." And Elijah said to her, "Do not fear; go and do as you have said. But first make me a little cake of it and bring it to me, and afterward make something for yourself and your son. For thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'The jar of flour shall not be spent, and the jug of oil shall not be empty, until the day that the LORD sends rain upon the earth.'" And she went and did as Elijah said. And she and he and her household ate for many days. The jar of flour was not spent, neither did the jug of oil become empty, according to the word of the LORD that he spoke by Elijah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zarephath belongs to Sidon, which is Phoenicia, where Jezebel comes from (16:31). God's hiding place for the most wanted man in Israel is in the home territory of the woman who is killing his prophets, a short walk from her father's cities.

The second half of the sentence has a quiet joke in it, and the joke carries the theology. I have commanded a widow there to feed you. It is the same verb used of the ravens. And when Elijah arrives, the widow has plainly not been told anything at all. She is gathering firewood for the last meal of her life. God says I have commanded of a woman who has received no orders and knows nothing about it, and the arrangement holds anyway.

Consider the supply line. A widow in that world has no income, no land in her own right and no man to represent her, which is why the law keeps naming her with the orphan and the sojourner. A widow with a child, in a foreign country, in year two of a famine, is the bottom of the economy. That is where the LORD banks his prophet.

He asks first for water, in a drought, from a stranger, and she goes; then, as she walks away, he adds the bread (vv. 10-11).

As the LORD your God lives. She swears by the covenant name, and she says your. She knows who this is and whose he is, and she does not claim him. A Sidonian woman at a city gate can identify the God of Israel and does not pretend to belong to him.

Then she itemises what is left, and the inventory is unbearable in its smallness. She has a handful of flour and a little oil in the bottom of a jug. Two sticks are all the fire one small cake needs, and all the wood she intends to gather, because there will not be another meal to cook.

She is not performing. She has done the arithmetic and reached the end of it. That we may eat it and die. She is out at the gate collecting the fuel for her son's last supper, and she tells a stranger so in a level voice.

Do not soften this. Read cold, it is one of the most shocking demands in Scripture: a prophet tells a starving woman to bake her last handful of flour for him and feed her child with whatever is left.

Two things in the text make it something other than that. The first is the order of the words. Do not fear comes before the demand, and the promise comes immediately after it, in the same breath. He is not proposing a transaction in which she loses and he eats. He is telling her what is about to be true and asking her to act on it one meal early.

The second is what he is actually asking her to risk. She is going to die tomorrow either way; that is her own settled conclusion. The choice in front of her is not between food and no food, but between eating the last of it alone and staking it on a word from the God she has just named correctly and does not serve.

The jar is not filled, and the flour is not multiplied into sacks. She is promised only that a nearly empty jar will not become an empty one.

So she never has more than one day's flour in the house. Every morning, for something like two years, she walks over to a jar that by every law of arithmetic ought to be scraped bare, and puts her hand in, and there is a handful. And the next morning she does it again. She is not delivered out of dependence; she is put inside it and held there.

That is manna, and God did it that way on purpose the first time too: gather each day what you need, and what you hoard overnight breeds worms (Ex. 16:19-20). And it is the petition the Lord Jesus put in the middle of the prayer he taught us: not give us this year our annual bread, but give us this day our daily bread (Matt. 6:11).

Suppose you were offered two arrangements: a full barn, provision secured for years, or the widow's jar, never empty and never more than a day ahead.

Almost everybody wants the barn. And what we want when we want the barn is not really food; it is to be done with needing him. The jar is the better gift and it does not feel like it, because the jar keeps you at the jar.

She went and did it. A Sidonian widow, on the strength of one sentence from a foreign prophet, handed over her son's last meal. Nobody in Israel does anything like this in the whole book.

See who eats: she and he and her household. She fed him and was fed. What she poured out came back to her every morning for two years, which is the arithmetic the whole Bible keeps insisting on and which nobody quite believes until they have tried it.

According to the word of the LORD that he spoke by Elijah. The drought and the flour are the same word doing opposite work: closing the heavens over a king with a temple and eight hundred and fifty prophets, and holding open a clay jar for a foreign woman who has nothing.

And keep this passage in view, because it is the one Jesus chose for his first sermon. In the synagogue at Nazareth he told his neighbours that there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the heavens were shut up three years and six months, and a great famine came over all the land, and Elijah was sent to none of them but only to Zarephath, in the land of Sidon, to a woman who was a widow (Luke 4:25-26).

There were Israelite widows, covenant widows, starving in the same famine, and God walked his prophet past all of them to a Gentile. Luke says that when the congregation heard it they were filled with wrath and drove him out of the town and tried to throw him off a cliff.

They were not confused. They understood him exactly, and that is why they wanted him dead. This chapter is the Gentile mission in seed, nine centuries before Paul, and it was already offensive enough to kill for.

Is “first make me a little cake” a pattern for giving to a minister to receive provision? No. God commanded a particular widow to trust his particular promise through his prophet. It is not a formula of seed-faith; Christians give out of thanks, not to get (2 Cor 9:7).
verseByVerse.note: Zarephath lay on the coast between Tyre and Sidon, in Jezebel’s home territory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the miracle the widow's son dies, and she turns on Elijah as if his presence had brought her sin to God's notice (vv. 17-18). Elijah carries the boy upstairs, puts the complaint to God, stretches himself on the child three times, and the LORD listens; the boy lives, and the woman confesses that the word of the LORD in his mouth is truth (vv. 19-24).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the first raising of the dead in the Bible. Until now every death Scripture records, from Abel to David's infant son, has been final. Here a dead child breathes, and the hope is planted that death need not have the last word: a hope that the empty tomb of Jesus turns into a promise.
verseByVerse.examples: And her confession is the measure of what it took. The jar had fed her for months and she still met the crisis by assuming God had come to collect an old debt. Provision, however sustained, had not made her sure of him. A resurrection did.

verseByVerse.quote: After this the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became ill. And his illness was so severe that there was no breath left in him. And she said to Elijah, "What have you against me, O man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to remembrance and to cause the death of my son!" And he said to her, "Give me your son." And he took him from her arms and carried him up into the upper chamber where he lodged, and laid him on his own bed. And he cried to the LORD, "O LORD my God, have you brought calamity even upon the widow with whom I sojourn, by killing her son?" Then he stretched himself upon the child three times and cried to the LORD, "O LORD my God, let this child's life come into him again." And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah. And the life of the child came into him again, and he revived. And Elijah took the child and brought him down from the upper chamber into the house and delivered him to his mother. And Elijah said, "See, your son lives." And the woman said to Elijah, "Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this means after the jar, after two years of a miracle every single morning. That order should not be tidied away. The boy does not die during the famine, before help arrives, in the part of the story where we expect death. He dies after God has visibly and repeatedly intervened to keep this household alive. She has bread in her hands and a dead son in the next room.

Her theology comes out under pressure, as everybody's does, and a great many people hold it.

She believes that having a holy man in the house has drawn God's attention to her. That while she was an obscure widow in a Phoenician town, whatever she had done was overlooked; and that once God started coming close, something old got noticed, and this is the bill.

She is not attacking the prophet's competence. She is saying that God has now looked at her properly, and that when he looks at you properly the news is bad.

Anyone who has been near a church for long has met this: a man begins to take God seriously, the diagnosis comes, and the first sentence out of him is that he was fine while he kept his distance.

The chapter gives the answer in an event rather than an argument (v. 22). But its direction is already visible in what Elijah does next: not defending himself, not correcting her doctrine, but holding out his hands for the boy.

He took him from her arms; she had been holding him. Elijah does not explain to the widow that God's ways are higher than ours, or defend God to her at all. He goes upstairs and puts the accusation to God directly, and the verb he chooses is killing: have you done this, to her, of all people?

The argument he presses is relational, not abstract: the widow with whom I sojourn. She took me in. She fed me out of an empty jar. This is the household that housed your prophet, and this is what has happened in it.

The writer records this without a word of rebuke, and the LORD answers it. Which tells you what kind of speech God is prepared to receive from people who are actually his. Elijah is not being irreverent. He is doing what the psalms do a hundred times over: taking the complaint to the only address where it can do any good.

Grief that argues with God is still praying. And grief that has run out of words is not shut out either; the Spirit intercedes with groanings too deep for words.

He lies down on the body three times, full length, a living man over a dead one. There is no technique here, whatever later readers have found in the number. It is a man putting his own warmth and breath and weight over a child who has none, and asking. Elisha will do the same over another dead boy (2 Kgs. 4:34).

The request itself is the plainest sentence in the chapter: let this child's life come into him again. The word is nephesh, the breath, the life, the self.

Everything Scripture has said about death up to this verse runs one direction. Abel does not come back. The generation of the flood does not come back. Nor do the firstborn of Egypt, Nadab and Abihu, Eli's sons, or David's infant: I shall go to him, but he will not return to me (2 Sam. 12:23). Ten books, and the road has no other lane.

In an upstairs room in a Phoenician town, over the body of a boy whose name we are never told, the door that had only ever opened one way is shown to open both. This is the first raising of the dead anywhere in Scripture, and God gives it to a Gentile child in the house of a widow, in the middle of the worst reign in the book.

And the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah. The chapter opened with a man saying there would be no rain except by my word, and it turns here on the LORD listening to that same voice. Nobody should build a doctrine of prayer that makes God the servant of a man's mouth. But neither should anybody read this chapter and go on assuming that what he says to God is received politely and filed.

Now put this beside a road outside a town called Nain, nearly nine hundred years later. A widow is following the body of her only son out through the gate, and a man stops the procession, and touches the bier, and says young man, I say to you, arise. Luke, who knew this chapter and expected his readers to know it, ends the scene on the same note: Jesus gave him to his mother (Luke 7:14-15). The crowd's verdict was a great prophet has arisen among us. They had Elijah in mind. They were right, and they were aiming too low.

Measure the two scenes against each other and the difference is the whole gospel. Elijah goes upstairs, lies on the body three times, argues, pleads, and waits for God to listen. Jesus stops walking, touches a plank, and speaks to the corpse. No prayer. No stretching out. No asking. Elijah borrowed the authority and had to knock for it; the Son of God carries it in his own person, and death hears him the way a servant hears a master.

And the boy Elijah raised died again, eventually, as the boy at Nain did, and Lazarus did. They were all handed back to their mothers for a while. Only one man has come out of a grave and not gone back in, and he is the reason the rest is not merely a reprieve.

The great confession of faith in this chapter comes from a Sidonian widow: not from Ahab, with the whole apparatus of a state religion, nor from anyone in Samaria, but from a foreign woman in the country Jezebel came from.

Weigh what finally produced it. Two years of daily bread out of nothing did not: she had eaten that miracle for something like seven hundred mornings, and when the crisis came her first instinct was still that God had turned up to collect an old debt. It took a resurrection, and that is a fair description of what it takes with any of us. Providence, however kind and however long sustained, does not by itself convince anybody; the same mercies that ought to have settled us are the ones we forget by Thursday. What settles it is a dead thing living. She got her answer in an upstairs room; we get ours at an empty tomb.

Her last phrase deserves the final word, because the chapter has been laying track for it since verse 1: the word of the LORD in your mouth is truth. That word shut the heavens, sent him east, fed him by carrion birds, moved him to Sidon, held a jar from emptying, and now has called a child back. The book of Kings is about to spend five chapters on a contest between a king with an army and a man with a word, and a widow in a foreign town has already announced the result.

17.theology:
The drought is the contract, not a stunt (v. 1). Turn aside to other gods, Moses had written, and the LORD will shut up the heavens (Deut. 11:16-17). What makes it more than bookkeeping is the aim: God shuts off the single commodity Baal, the rider on the clouds, exists to supply, and leaves him three years to produce it.

Except by my word (v. 1), and the LORD listened to the voice of Elijah (v. 22). The chapter opens and closes with God binding his action to a man's speech. James takes exactly this scene to teach ordinary Christians to pray, and his emphasis falls on the smallness of the man: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours (Jas. 5:17). The wonder is not the drought. It is that God took a man from Gilead far enough into his confidence to hand him the timing of it.

The brook dries up (v. 7). God ends his own provisions: the ravens were commanded, and the ravens still stopped. The water ran out and the word did not.

The jar, not the barn (v. 14). Not filled, not multiplied, but never empty: one day's flour for two years, which is manna again (Ex. 16:19-20). God gives the kind of provision that keeps a person at his hand rather than the kind that lets them leave it.

Sent past Israel to Sidon (v. 9). Jesus chose this for his sermon at Nazareth (Luke 4:25-26). The Gentile mission is here in seed, and it was offensive the first time.

The first raising of the dead (v. 22). Nothing in the ten books before this goes that direction (2 Sam. 12:23). And when it finally happens, compare the prophet and the Lord. Elijah stretches himself out three times, argues and pleads and waits to be heard; Jesus touches the bier at Nain and speaks to the dead man (Luke 7:14), and Luke closes on this chapter's own note: Jesus gave him to his mother (Luke 7:15; cf. 1 Kings 17:23). The prophet had to knock for the authority. The Son has it.
17.examples:
Then: A Sidonian widow gathering two sticks at a city gate, planning her son's last supper out loud to a stranger, handed him the flour instead, and put her hand into a jar that should have been empty every morning for two years.

Now: Three things this chapter presses. First, the brook. Christians are quick to read a failing provision as a verdict on themselves; when something dries up, the better question is not what did I do wrong but what am I now being told. Second, the widow's fear in verse 18: that God's nearness has drawn his attention to her sin and this is the bill. That is a real belief and many hold it: I was safer at a distance. The chapter does not argue her out of it; it hands her back a living son, and the answer to the fear that God has come to collect is a God who has come to raise. Third, what actually convinced her: not two years of daily bread but a resurrection. Our certainty rests where hers did, on a grave that did not hold.

18.title: Fire on Mount Carmel
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After many days the word of the LORD came to Elijah, in the third year, saying, "Go, show yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain upon the earth."<sup>2</sup>So Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. Now the famine was severe in Samaria.<sup>3</sup>And Ahab called Obadiah, who was over the household. (Now Obadiah feared the LORD greatly,<sup>4</sup>and when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the LORD, Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water.)<sup>5</sup>And Ahab said to Obadiah, "Go through the land to all the springs of water and to all the valleys. Perhaps we may find grass and save the horses and mules alive, and not lose some of the animals."<sup>6</sup>So they divided the land between them to pass through it. Ahab went in one direction by himself, and Obadiah went in another direction by himself.<sup>7</sup>And as Obadiah was on the way, behold, Elijah met him. And Obadiah recognized him and fell on his face and said, "Is it you, my lord Elijah?"<sup>8</sup>And he answered him, "It is I. Go, tell your lord, 'Behold, Elijah is here.'"<sup>9</sup>And he said, "How have I sinned, that you would give your servant into the hand of Ahab, to kill me?<sup>10</sup>As the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent to seek you. And when they would say, 'He is not here,' he would take an oath of the kingdom or nation, that they had not found you.<sup>11</sup>And now you say, 'Go, tell your lord, "Behold, Elijah is here."'<sup>12</sup>And as soon as I have gone from you, the Spirit of the LORD will carry you I know not where. And so, when I come and tell Ahab and he cannot find you, he will kill me, although I your servant have feared the LORD from my youth.<sup>13</sup>Has it not been told my lord what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of the LORD, how I hid a hundred men of the LORD's prophets by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water?<sup>14</sup>And now you say, 'Go, tell your lord, "Behold, Elijah is here"'; and he will kill me."<sup>15</sup>And Elijah said, "As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will surely show myself to him today."<sup>16</sup>So Obadiah went to meet Ahab, and told him. And Ahab went to meet Elijah.<sup>17</sup>When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, "Is it you, you troubler of Israel?"<sup>18</sup>And he answered, "I have not troubled Israel, but you have, and your father's house, because you have abandoned the commandments of the LORD and followed the Baals.<sup>19</sup>Now therefore send and gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel, and the 450 prophets of Baal and the 400 prophets of Asherah, who eat at Jezebel's table."<sup>20</sup>So Ahab sent to all the people of Israel and gathered the prophets together at Mount Carmel.<sup>21</sup>And Elijah came near to all the people and said, "How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him." And the people did not answer him a word.<sup>22</sup>Then Elijah said to the people, "I, even I only, am left a prophet of the LORD, but Baal's prophets are 450 men.<sup>23</sup>Let two bulls be given to us, and let them choose one bull for themselves and cut it in pieces and lay it on the wood, but put no fire to it. And I will prepare the other bull and lay it on the wood and put no fire to it.<sup>24</sup>And you call upon the name of your god, and I will call upon the name of the LORD, and the God who answers by fire, he is God." And all the people answered, "It is well spoken."<sup>25</sup>Then Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, "Choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first, for you are many, and call upon the name of your god, but put no fire to it."<sup>26</sup>And they took the bull that was given them, and they prepared it and called upon the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, "O Baal, answer us!" But there was no voice, and no one answered. And they limped around the altar that they had made.<sup>27</sup>And at noon Elijah mocked them, saying, "Cry aloud, for he is a god. Either he is musing, or he is relieving himself, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened."<sup>28</sup>And they cried aloud and cut themselves after their custom with swords and lances, until the blood gushed out upon them.<sup>29</sup>And as midday passed, they raved on until the time of the offering of the oblation, but there was no voice. No one answered; no one paid attention.<sup>30</sup>Then Elijah said to all the people, "Come near to me." And all the people came near to him. And he repaired the altar of the LORD that had been thrown down.<sup>31</sup>Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the LORD came, saying, "Israel shall be your name,"<sup>32</sup>and with the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD. And he made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two seahs of seed.<sup>33</sup>And he put the wood in order and cut the bull in pieces and laid it on the wood. And he said, "Fill four jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and on the wood."<sup>34</sup>And he said, "Do it a second time." And they did it a second time. And he said, "Do it a third time." And they did it a third time.<sup>35</sup>And the water ran around the altar and filled the trench also with water.<sup>36</sup>And at the time of the offering of the oblation, Elijah the prophet came near and said, "O LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that you are God in Israel, and that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things at your word.<sup>37</sup>Answer me, O LORD, answer me, that this people may know that you, O LORD, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back."<sup>38</sup>Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the burnt offering and the wood and the stones and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench.<sup>39</sup>And when all the people saw it, they fell on their faces and said, "The LORD, he is God; the LORD, he is God."<sup>40</sup>And Elijah said to them, "Seize the prophets of Baal; let not one of them escape." And they seized them. And Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon and slaughtered them there.<sup>41</sup>And Elijah said to Ahab, "Go up, eat and drink, for there is a sound of the rushing of rain."<sup>42</sup>So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. And Elijah went up to the top of Mount Carmel. And he bowed himself down on the earth and put his face between his knees.<sup>43</sup>And he said to his servant, "Go up now, look toward the sea." And he went up and looked and said, "There is nothing." And he said, "Go again," seven times.<sup>44</sup>And at the seventh time he said, "Behold, a little cloud like a man's hand is rising from the sea." And he said, "Go up, say to Ahab, 'Prepare your chariot and go down, lest the rain stop you.'"<sup>45</sup>And in a little while the heavens grew black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. And Ahab rode and went to Jezreel.<sup>46</sup>And the hand of the LORD was on Elijah, and he gathered up his garment and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
18.overview:
Everything on Carmel happens inside a promise made before Elijah set out. Go, show yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain upon the earth (v. 1). The fire does not buy the rain; the rain was settled in the first sentence. What the mountain is for is the people standing on it: a nation that had not swapped the LORD for Baal but had quietly kept both.

The chapter moves in four scenes. On the road Elijah meets Obadiah, the highest official in Ahab's government and a secret believer. On the mountain he asks the question nobody answers (v. 21). Then a day of shouting and self-wounding is set against a short prayer and a fire from heaven. Then rain comes, as a cloud the size of a man's hand on the seventh look.

It ends with the prophet at the summit of his whole life, running through a storm ahead of the king's chariot, and the writer has arranged it so that the next thing on the page is a message from Jezebel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Obadiah in the Cave Country
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God promises rain before anything happens on Carmel (v. 1). On the way Elijah meets Obadiah, Ahab's chief minister, who fears the LORD and has hidden a hundred prophets from Jezebel, and who is out hunting grass for the king's horses (vv. 2-6). Told to announce Elijah, he is terrified until Elijah swears he will show himself, and he goes (vv. 7-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Two men serve the same God under the same regime and do it in opposite ways. One stands in the open and calls the king a liar; the other keeps his post, keeps his nerve, and keeps a hundred men alive on the palace budget for years. The writer sets them on one road and commends both.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 shows where a ruler's heart lies: three years into a famine, the king's emergency programme is fodder for the chariot horses. What we protect first in a crisis tells us what we really trust.

verseByVerse.quote: After many days the word of the LORD came to Elijah, in the third year, saying, "Go, show yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain upon the earth." So Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. Now the famine was severe in Samaria. And Ahab called Obadiah, who was over the household. (Now Obadiah feared the LORD greatly, and when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the LORD, Obadiah took a hundred prophets and hid them by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water.) And Ahab said to Obadiah, "Go through the land to all the springs of water and to all the valleys. Perhaps we may find grass and save the horses and mules alive, and not lose some of the animals." So they divided the land between them to pass through it. Ahab went in one direction by himself, and Obadiah went in another direction by himself. And as Obadiah was on the way, behold, Elijah met him. And Obadiah recognized him and fell on his face and said, "Is it you, my lord Elijah?" And he answered him, "It is I. Go, tell your lord, 'Behold, Elijah is here.'" And he said, "How have I sinned, that you would give your servant into the hand of Ahab, to kill me? As the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent to seek you. And when they would say, 'He is not here,' he would take an oath of the kingdom or nation, that they had not found you. And now you say, 'Go, tell your lord, "Behold, Elijah is here."' And as soon as I have gone from you, the Spirit of the LORD will carry you I know not where. And so, when I come and tell Ahab and he cannot find you, he will kill me, although I your servant have feared the LORD from my youth. Has it not been told my lord what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of the LORD, how I hid a hundred men of the LORD's prophets by fifties in a cave and fed them with bread and water? And now you say, 'Go, tell your lord, "Behold, Elijah is here"'; and he will kill me." And Elijah said, "As the LORD of hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will surely show myself to him today." So Obadiah went to meet Ahab, and told him. And Ahab went to meet Elijah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God settles the rain in verse 1, in a sentence spoken to one man, before the altars are built or a single prophet of Baal opens his mouth. Whatever the fire on the mountain is for, it is not for persuading God to end the drought.

Which reorders the whole chapter. Carmel is not a bargain struck with heaven. It is a public examination held for the benefit of the people standing on the mountain, and God has already written the last line of it.

Put some substance behind the words third year. The winter rains have failed twice running; the cisterns cut into the rock are down to silt; the seed grain has been eaten, which means that even when rain comes there is nothing to sow; the flocks have been culled and then the breeding stock culled after them. In an economy where nine people in ten farm, a third year without rain is not hardship. It is the end of the country.

Take the office first, because it changes how the man reads. (He is not the prophet Obadiah of the short book that bears the name, who lived later.) Over the household is not a butler. It is the highest appointment in the kingdom, the chief of the royal administration; it is the post Arza held when Elah was murdered in his house (16:9), and the post Shebna held in Judah before God took it off him and gave it to Eliakim with the key of David on his shoulder (Isa. 22:15-22).

So the second man in the northern kingdom fears the LORD greatly. Ahab's chief of staff, the man who runs the palace where Jezebel keeps eight hundred and fifty prophets, is a believer.

Then the writer tells us what he did with the position. When Jezebel began killing the LORD's prophets (the first the reader hears of it, dropped in as background as though everyone knew), Obadiah took a hundred of them and hid them fifty to a cave and fed them.

Think what it meant to feed a hundred men through a famine. In a country with no rain, where the king is out looking for grass, somebody has been drawing bread and water for a hundred hidden men, month after month, for years, out of the household he administers. If one guard talks, or one supplier counts the sacks, he is dead, and so are they.

Preachers have been hard on Obadiah for centuries, as though a man in a palace must be a compromiser. The writer is not hard on him. Before we are told one thing he did, we are told he feared the LORD greatly, and the deeds follow as evidence.

Verse 5 is an indictment in one sentence. His people are starving, and the king splits the kingdom with his chief minister and goes out himself to look for grass for the horses. Ahab is not lazy and he is not stupid; he is out in the field doing the work himself, which is more than most kings in this book manage. He simply has the wrong list. Chariot horses are the army, and the army is the throne, and the throne is what he is preserving. The prophets are in a cave, the farmers are burying their children, and the crown's emergency programme is fodder.

Each of them goes alone, which tells you how far things have gone: a king does not travel unattended unless there is nothing left to feed the attendants on. It is also why the meeting can happen. God empties the road first, and then he puts the two of them on it.

He falls on his face in the road. That is not the wariness of an official meeting a fugitive; it is homage, and the second man in the kingdom is paying it to a peasant in a field.

Then hear the two possessives, one in each verse. Obadiah says my lord Elijah. Elijah answers, go, tell your lord. Obadiah has said whose man he is, and Elijah in a few words reminds him whose payroll he is on. There is a needle in it, and there is also a plain fact that the chapter refuses to resolve tidily: a man can fear the LORD greatly and still have a lord in Samaria who signs his warrants.

That is the second time in two chapters that somebody who fears God meets Elijah and immediately begins hunting for the sin that must be behind this. The widow said you have come to me to bring my sin to remembrance (17:18), with a dead child in her arms. Obadiah says it on an open road with nothing whatever having happened yet, at the bare prospect of trouble.

It is the reflex of people who take God seriously and have never quite believed he is on their side. Bad news arrives, or merely threatens, and before any other thought there is an audit: what have I done. Elijah does not answer the question in either chapter, and not because it deserves contempt. It is simply the wrong question, and no argument has ever cured anybody of it. What cured the widow was a living son put back into her arms; what settles Obadiah is a promise he can hold, and Elijah gives him one under oath six verses later.

The manhunt has been international, and Ahab put neighbouring states on oath. He has sent embassies to swear before their own gods that they were not sheltering one man from Gilead. That is the scale of the search a peasant prophet has provoked, and it tells us what these three years have been like in Samaria.

Obadiah assumes as a matter of course that the Spirit of the LORD moves this man about without notice, and that if he fetches the king and the spot is empty, his own life is the forfeit.

He produces his credentials, not boasting, to a man he fears does not know him: years of secret and expensive courage, explained to the one colleague who ought to be glad to see him.

He repeats behold, Elijah is here three times (vv. 8, 11, 14). Frightened men do not argue in straight lines; they circle.

The oath from chapter 17 again, with an addition: the LORD of hosts, of armies. Obadiah is frightened of one king with one army, and Elijah swears by the commander of all of them, and the frightened man takes his word.

One sentence and Obadiah leaves the story for good. He walked back across a famished country to tell a king who had spent three years hunting a man that the man was standing in a field a half day away, and he did it on nothing but a promise.

Most Christians reading this chapter are not Elijah. They are somewhere in an institution that has gone wrong, doing what good can still be done inside it, unable to fix any of it, and quite sure that a braver person would have walked out years ago. The Bible's word about that person is in verse 3, before he does anything at all: he feared the LORD greatly. The caves came after.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — How Long Will You Go Limping
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab calls Elijah the troubler of Israel and gets the word handed back (vv. 17-18). Elijah summons the nation and Jezebel's prophets to Carmel and asks the people how long they will limp between two opinions; they say nothing (vv. 19-21). Then he sets the terms of a fair test: the God who answers by fire is God (vv. 22-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel was not choosing Baal instead of the LORD but keeping both, and Elijah asks them to stop being two things at once.
verseByVerse.examples: Their silence is the loudest sound in the chapter. It is neither defiance nor repentance; they have no answer because the question is exactly right.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ahab saw Elijah, Ahab said to him, "Is it you, you troubler of Israel?" And he answered, "I have not troubled Israel, but you have, and your father's house, because you have abandoned the commandments of the LORD and followed the Baals. Now therefore send and gather all Israel to me at Mount Carmel, and the 450 prophets of Baal and the 400 prophets of Asherah, who eat at Jezebel's table." So Ahab sent to all the people of Israel and gathered the prophets together at Mount Carmel. And Elijah came near to all the people and said, "How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him."
