And the people did not answer him a word. Then Elijah said to the people, "I, even I only, am left a prophet of the LORD, but Baal's prophets are 450 men. Let two bulls be given to us, and let them choose one bull for themselves and cut it in pieces and lay it on the wood, but put no fire to it. And I will prepare the other bull and lay it on the wood and put no fire to it. And you call upon the name of your god, and I will call upon the name of the LORD, and the God who answers by fire, he is God." And all the people answered, "It is well spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After three years of hunting, this is Ahab's first sentence, and it is not a general insult. The Hebrew word behind troubler is the word attached to Achan, the man who took the devoted things at Jericho and brought defeat on the army: why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today (Josh. 7:25), which is why the place is called the Valley of Achor. Ahab is calling Elijah an Achan: the one man inside the camp whose private sin is costing everybody else.

That is exactly what a man says when he cannot afford to look at the actual cause. The prophet announced the drought, so the prophet is the drought. Blame lands on whoever said the word out loud, because the alternative is a mirror.

He hands the word straight back, and then he says why, and the why is not a personality clash. It is covenant. You have abandoned the commandments of the LORD. Deuteronomy 11 said what happens to a nation that turns aside to other gods, and Ahab built the temple, and here is the sky.

A hunted man gives the king an order and the king obeys it (vv. 19-20). The detail at the end of verse 19 deserves more.

Who eat at Jezebel's table. Eight hundred and fifty men on the queen's household budget, fed daily, in year three of a famine, in the country whose chief minister has just been sent out to look for grass. The clergy of the state religion are the last people in Israel eating well.

Count them again on the mountain, though, because the writer quietly drops four hundred of them. Elijah summons the prophets of Baal and the prophets of Asherah, and from verse 22 onward only the four hundred and fifty are ever mentioned. Whether Jezebel kept her own household prophets at home or the writer simply loses interest in them, the text does not say and we should not invent an answer. What it does say is that Asherah's four hundred never take the field, and that the contest is fought against the storm god alone.

Carmel itself is chosen with care. It is the ridge running down to the sea on the north-west edge of the kingdom, close to Phoenicia, Jezebel's homeland and Baal's own territory, with a ruined altar of the LORD on it (v. 30).

Ask why, because the answer is not repentance. Ahab has just been told by the only man alive who can end the drought that he is to gather everybody at Carmel, and Ahab wants rain. He will do whatever the prophet says for as long as the prophet is the route to water, and the moment the water arrives he will go home to his dinner and his wife and change nothing. That is the whole of Ahab in one verse, and it is a common enough shape: perfect compliance, entirely self-interested, with the heart untouched throughout.

The verb is posechim, to limp, to hobble. Hold on to the verb limping, because in five verses the prophets of Baal will do their ritual dance around their altar and the writer will use the same word: they limped around the altar that they had made (v. 26). Elijah's name for what the nation is doing with its soul is the word for what the false prophets do with their feet.

Be precise about what he is accusing them of, because it is not what we usually assume. These people had not renounced the LORD. They had added to him. That was the entire religious settlement of the northern kingdom: keep the God who brought us out of Egypt for the national story and the oaths and the festivals, and keep Baal for the rain and the barley and the calving, because he is the one who handles that department. It is not apostasy as a decision. It is apostasy as a hedge.

So the demand is not stop being a pagan. It is stop being two things at once. And the choice is put with a fairness that is almost shocking: if Baal, then follow him. He offers them a clean break either way.

The people answer nothing: not an argument, not a jeer, not a confession. They have no answer because there is no answer. You cannot defend the two-opinion life, and almost nobody who lives it has ever decided to; it is not a position, it is an avoidance. Ask an ordinary divided man to justify himself and he will not fight you. He will go quiet, because the case against him is one he has been carefully not making to himself for years.

Here is the test in its modern dress. Not: do you believe in God. Rather: is there anything in your life that would have to change if the LORD is God, which has not changed? That, and not intellectual doubt, is the limp. And the cure Elijah looks for is not a firmer resolution but the LORD who turns hearts back (v. 37).

Mark verse 22, I, even I only, am left, because it is not true, and Elijah has particular reason to know it is not true.

He met Obadiah on the road only days before, and Obadiah told him to his face that a hundred prophets of the LORD were alive in two caves and had been for years. Elijah stands on the mountain soon afterwards and says he is the only one left.

He is not lying. He is a man who has been alone for three years and has begun to believe his own solitude. That belief will follow him off this mountain and into the next chapter, where he says the same words twice at Horeb, in the cave and at its mouth (19:10, 14), and where God will answer it with a number: seven thousand.

It is the great hazard of the faithful minority, and it is not humility. It is arithmetic done in the dark.

Elijah has given away every advantage there is. They pick the bull and go first; they have four hundred and fifty men and he has one. And the test is fire, the lightning Baal is drawn holding: his opponent's home ground and his opponent's equipment. Confidence looks like that. A man who thinks his God might not turn up hedges the rules.

It is well spoken. That is all the people say between his question in verse 21 and their cry in verse 39. They will not answer whether they believe, but they will agree that the test is fair. It is a very human place to stand, and it is about to be taken away from them.

Asherah was a Canaanite goddess of fertility, Baal’s consort; an “Asherah” was a wooden pole or carved image set up for her worship beside altars.
verseByVerse.note: Mount Carmel juts into the Mediterranean near modern Haifa.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–40 — The God Who Answers By Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophets of Baal call and cut themselves from morning past noon, and no one answers (vv. 26-29). Elijah repairs the LORD's altar with twelve stones, drenches it three times, and at the evening sacrifice prays briefly that the people may know the LORD is God and has turned their hearts back (vv. 30-37). The fire falls and consumes everything; the people fall on their faces, and the prophets of Baal are killed at the Kishon (vv. 38-40).
verseByVerse.theology: Fire is Baal's own advertised trade, for he is the lightning, the rider on the clouds. Elijah lets the challenge be decided on the one ground where Baal is supposed to be strongest, gives his opponents the whole day and the first turn, and then floods his own altar so that nothing natural could account for what happens.
verseByVerse.examples: What the crowd shouts in verse 39 is the answer to the question of verse 21, said twice by a nation on its face. Their silence is broken at last, and broken by God's act, not by Elijah's argument.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, "Choose for yourselves one bull and prepare it first, for you are many, and call upon the name of your god, but put no fire to it." And they took the bull that was given them, and they prepared it and called upon the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, "O Baal, answer us!" But there was no voice, and no one answered. And they limped around the altar that they had made. And at noon Elijah mocked them, saying, "Cry aloud, for he is a god. Either he is musing, or he is relieving himself, or he is on a journey, or perhaps he is asleep and must be awakened." And they cried aloud and cut themselves after their custom with swords and lances, until the blood gushed out upon them. And as midday passed, they raved on until the time of the offering of the oblation, but there was no voice. No one answered; no one paid attention. Then Elijah said to all the people, "Come near to me." And all the people came near to him. And he repaired the altar of the LORD that had been thrown down. Elijah took twelve stones, according to the number of the tribes of the sons of Jacob, to whom the word of the LORD came, saying, "Israel shall be your name," and with the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD. And he made a trench about the altar, as great as would contain two seahs of seed. And he put the wood in order and cut the bull in pieces and laid it on the wood. And he said, "Fill four jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and on the wood." And he said, "Do it a second time." And they did it a second time. And he said, "Do it a third time." And they did it a third time. And the water ran around the altar and filled the trench also with water. And at the time of the offering of the oblation, Elijah the prophet came near and said, "O LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known this day that you are God in Israel, and that I am your servant, and that I have done all these things at your word. Answer me, O LORD, answer me, that this people may know that you, O LORD, are God, and that you have turned their hearts back." Then the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the burnt offering and the wood and the stones and the dust, and licked up the water that was in the trench. And when all the people saw it, they fell on their faces and said, "The LORD, he is God; the LORD, he is God." And Elijah said to them, "Seize the prophets of Baal; let not one of them escape." And they seized them. And Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon and slaughtered them there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first stage alone lasts some six hours: four hundred and fifty voices on a ridge above the sea, from first light until the sun was overhead, four words repeated until the words stopped meaning anything: O Baal, answer us.

These men are not frauds putting on a show. They believe it. They have staked their lives on it, and their credibility, and the queen's favour, and they are working as hard as men can work.

The writer's finding is there was no voice, and no one answered, and he will repeat it in verse 29. Then the verb from verse 21 comes back: they limped around the altar. The nation has been limping between two opinions; here are the men they have been limping towards, hobbling round a cold fireplace in the noon sun. Elijah's insult was a diagnosis, and the writer makes it visible.

The mockery is deliberate, sustained, and rude, and it is not a lapse of taste on the prophet's part. The suggestions echo the way Baal's own worshippers pictured him.

Perhaps he is preoccupied, or relieving himself (the ESV says it as plainly as it deserves), or away travelling, or asleep and in need of waking. In the Canaanite stories Baal travels, feasts and fights, and he dies and goes down into the throat of Death and has to be brought back up. Elijah is not simply caricaturing their religion. He is echoing it.

That is what makes the taunt lethal rather than merely cruel. A god with a body has a schedule, and a god with a schedule can be unavailable, and if he can be unavailable he can be unavailable today. Set beside it the line Israel sang on the road up to Jerusalem: he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep (Ps. 121:4).

Is such mockery ever right? Isaiah does it at length: a man cuts down a tree, burns half of it to roast his dinner and bows down to the other half (Isa. 44:14-17). The distinction to keep is that this is contempt poured on an idol in a public contest which the idol's own priests have entered and agreed the rules of. It is not contempt poured on people in their grief, and it never licenses that.

Now the day turns, and verse 28 is the darkest thing on the mountain.

The logic is inescapable once you are inside it. He has not answered. Therefore we have not given enough. Therefore give more. And what is there to give when the shouting has failed for six hours? Your own body. So the swords come out and the blood runs down four hundred and fifty men in front of a watching nation.

There is no floor underneath that logic. It cannot stop at blood, and in this religion it did not: in time the same worship in the same land was putting children in the fire (2 Kgs. 17:17; Jer. 19:5). A god who never answers can always be told he was not paid enough, and the price only ever goes one way.

Hold that against the other altar, on the same hilltop, where in a few hours a bull will burn and not one drop of any worshipper's blood will be spilled. That is the difference between all religion and the gospel, and it is visible on this hillside before it is ever stated in a doctrine. False religion asks for your blood and keeps asking. The true God provides the sacrifice himself: a ram in a thicket, a lamb at Passover, and at last his own Son, so that there is nothing left for you to bleed.

Verse 29 stacks three negatives: no voice, nobody answering, nobody paying attention, from morning until the evening offering, some nine hours in all.

Elijah's first word is come near to me. He brings them off the ridge and around him where they can see his hands. Nothing on this altar is going to happen out of sight.

Then, quietly devastating: the altar of the LORD that had been thrown down. There had been one there. Somebody had built it, and worshipped at it, and somebody else had pulled it apart. Elijah's first act is not to invent anything. He picks up stones that were already lying on that hilltop and puts them back where they belong. Reformation is nearly always repair before it is innovation.

Twelve stones, in the northern kingdom, some sixty or seventy years after the split, with Judah a foreign country across a border.

It is a political act as much as a religious one, and the writer spells out the reason: the name Israel was given by God to a man, on a night when he had nothing to recommend him and had just been wrestled to the ground and crippled (Gen. 32:28; 35:10). Ten tribes have walked out and two are left and Elijah builds an altar that does not recognise the arrangement. In God's counting there is one people, and it is named after a limping man, which on a day when the accusation is limping is a mercy.

The trench is measured in the only unit that mattered to the people watching. Not so many cubits across, but as great as would contain two seahs of seed: the size of ground you would sow with roughly half a bushel of grain. In the third year of a famine, on a hillside full of farmers who have eaten their own seed corn, the prophet marks out his altar in the language of a field, and then fills the field with water.

There were springs on the ridge that outlasted the valleys, so the water could be got. The point is what it cost and what he did with it: in a country where men have been dying over wells, he has twelve jars carried up and pours every one on the ground.

He is removing explanations. When the fire comes, nobody on that hillside will be able to say the wood was dry and the sun was hot and these things happen. And he does it three times over, with the people carrying the jars, so that the extravagance is theirs as well as his.

The hour matters. The time of the offering of the oblation is the evening sacrifice, around the middle of the afternoon, and it is being offered at that moment in the temple in Jerusalem, in the other kingdom, which Ahab does not rule.

Elijah sets his watch by Jerusalem. Standing on a northern mountain in front of a northern king, he times the most important prayer of his life to the lamb on the altar in the city God chose. He is not starting a new religion for the north. He is bringing the north back.

Then the prayer, and how short it is: they shouted all day, and he speaks a few dozen words.

And he asks for three things, in order: that you are God in Israel; that I am your servant; that I have done all these things at your word. Not one of them is about winning. He wants his commission vindicated because the commission is God's, and he is careful to say that nothing on this mountain was his idea.

The last clause is easily read past and should not be. He does not pray that the people will turn their hearts back. He prays that they may know that God has turned them.

Even the repentance he is asking for is asked as God's own work. Elijah has laid on as persuasive a religious event as the Old Testament records, and he does not for a moment think that fire falling from heaven will change anybody's heart unless God changes it. Fire persuades a crowd for an afternoon. Only God turns a heart, and Elijah asks him to.

Count what the fire eats: the offering, which is what fire is for; the wood, which is what fire burns; then the stones, the dust, and the water in the trench. This is not a lightning strike that got lucky. It consumes the altar itself, the ground under it, and the very thing that puts fires out. A day of screaming and blood produced nothing at all; a short prayer produces a fire that eats the mountain.

A man walked in from Gilead with no father named and no call recorded, and a nation on its face gives him the answer he came for, twice.

Do not hurry past verse 40 or explain it away, and do not pretend it is comfortable. Three things have to be said, and all three are needed.

First, this is a judicial execution under a standing law, not a lynching. Deuteronomy is explicit that the prophet who calls Israel after other gods is to be put to death, and that the community carries it out after examination (Deut. 13:1-5; 17:2-7). The people seize them, which is exactly the procedure the law lays down. These are not private enemies; they are the leadership of a movement that has been executing the LORD's prophets (v. 4), and whose worship would go on to burn children.

Second, it is a covenant sanction inside one nation which God had constituted as his own, at a moment when its national existence as the people carrying the promise was genuinely at stake. It is described, and it is not commended as a template.

Third, and this is the one that settles it for a Christian: the New Testament takes the sword out of religion's hands and does it by name in this chapter's own terms. When a Samaritan village refused to receive Jesus, When his disciples James and John saw it, they said, 'Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?' But he turned and rebuked them (Luke 9:54-55). They were recalling Elijah's fire on the soldiers (2 Kgs. 1:10-12). They had the precedent exactly right and the era exactly wrong, and the Lord did not congratulate their zeal. My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36). Nobody may read 1 Kings 18:40 as a warrant for anything. (Readers of the King James or New King James will find Luke 9:54-55 longer, with the words even as Elias did and the rebuke ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of; the oldest manuscripts lack these phrases, but they only say aloud what the scene already means.)

And the fire itself points somewhere. On Carmel the fire of judgment fell on the sacrifice on the altar, and the people on their faces were spared. That is the shape of the gospel: at the cross the judgment the people deserved fell on the Lamb God provided, and those who trust him are not consumed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–46 — A Little Cloud Like a Man's Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Under a clear sky Elijah tells Ahab he hears rain, then climbs the summit, bows to the ground, and sends his servant to look at the sea seven times (vv. 41-43). The seventh time there is a cloud like a man's hand, then a great rain, and the hand of the LORD on Elijah as he outruns the king's chariot to Jezreel (vv. 44-46).
verseByVerse.theology: God had already said he would send rain, back in verse 1, before a word was spoken on Carmel. Elijah knows that, and still bows to the ground and sends a man to look seven times. A promise is not the end of praying; it is the only thing that makes praying anything other than shouting at the weather.
verseByVerse.examples: And the first instalment of a three-year answer was a smudge on the horizon you could hide behind your palm. That is the usual size of answered prayer when it first appears, and it is why the man who was told to go again six times matters more to most readers than the fire did.

verseByVerse.quote: And Elijah said to Ahab, "Go up, eat and drink, for there is a sound of the rushing of rain." So Ahab went up to eat and to drink. And Elijah went up to the top of Mount Carmel. And he bowed himself down on the earth and put his face between his knees. And he said to his servant, "Go up now, look toward the sea." And he went up and looked and said, "There is nothing." And he said, "Go again," seven times. And at the seventh time he said, "Behold, a little cloud like a man's hand is rising from the sea." And he said, "Go up, say to Ahab, 'Prepare your chariot and go down, lest the rain stop you.'" And in a little while the heavens grew black with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain. And Ahab rode and went to Jezreel. And the hand of the LORD was on Elijah, and he gathered up his garment and ran before Ahab to the entrance of Jezreel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No rain has fallen, there is not a cloud in the sky, and the sea to the west is flat and bright to the horizon, yet a man says he can hear it coming. He is not guessing and he is not claiming a private premonition. He was told in verse 1, before he left Zarephath: I will send rain upon the earth. What he hears is a promise. Faith is very often just this: a man reporting on a sound nobody else can hear yet, because he was told.

Two men come off the same mountain after the same afternoon. One goes to his dinner. The other climbs higher and folds himself onto the ground with his head between his knees, which is not a posture of dignity; it is the posture of a man in labour or in grief, doubled over.

Ahab has watched fire fall from heaven, and his response is lunch.

Hold the two halves together, because it matters for ordinary praying more than anything else on the mountain. God had already promised the rain, and Elijah has just quoted it to the king. And he goes up the mountain and prays himself double.

The promise did not make the praying unnecessary. The promise made the praying possible. Without it he would only be shouting at the weather; with it, he is asking God for what God has undertaken to do, which is the only kind of asking that has any purchase at all. James, teaching plain Christians to pray, sends them to this very scene and to this man: he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit (Jas. 5:18).

The servant's report is there is nothing, and we should not rush to the seventh trip. He has just been publicly, spectacularly answered with fire. Now he asks for rain, and six times a servant walks up to the lookout and comes back down with the same word for a man lying face down in the dirt.

If it happened to Elijah on the afternoon of Carmel it can happen to you, and it is not a verdict on your standing. The fire fell in one instant; the rain took seven journeys. Both were promised in the same sentence.

Hold your hand up at arm's length against the sky: that is the size of the answer to a three-year drought when it first appears, a smudge over the water that a less interested man would not have mentioned. Elijah does not wait for a second cloud; he sends the king to his chariot and tells him to run for Jezreel before the roads wash out.

Faith acts on a hand-sized cloud. Most answers arrive that size, and most people miss them because they are watching for the storm and not for the smudge: the one conversation that goes better than expected, the first week of sleep, the small unmistakable loosening of something that has held for years.

After three years the sky goes black in an afternoon, and Elijah runs some seventeen miles across the plain of Jezreel, in a downpour, on foot, in front of a chariot, at the end of a day that ran through a long contest and an execution at the Kishon.

The detail everybody misses is who he is running for. To run before a king's chariot is the office of a herald; it is what a royal escort does to honour the man riding behind. Elijah has just called Ahab a troubler of Israel to his face, and he now runs through a storm in front of him like a servant of the crown, bringing the king home. He has never once wanted Ahab's throne. He wanted Ahab's allegiance.

And so the chapter closes with the prophet at the highest point of his life. The fire has fallen, the nation has confessed, the rain has come, the prophets of Baal are dead, and the hand of the LORD is on him so that he outruns horses.

The next verse in the book is a message from Jezebel, and within days this man will be sitting alone under a bush a hundred miles to the south, asking God to kill him. The writer puts the summit and the collapse back to back on purpose, and anyone who has come down off a great day knows exactly why.
verseByVerse.note: Jezreel lay about 17 miles from Carmel.

18.theology:
The verdict precedes the contest (v. 1). God announces the rain before a single altar is built. Carmel is not leverage applied to heaven; it is an examination held for Israel's benefit, whose result was written before the candidates arrived. Prayer and public contending are how God's settled purpose comes to pass, not how it gets decided.

Two ways of serving God under a bad king (vv. 3-16). Elijah stands in the open; Obadiah keeps his post and keeps a hundred men alive. The Bible is kinder to the man inside the compromised institution than many of its preachers have been.

Limping between two opinions (v. 21). The sin is not apostasy chosen but apostasy hedged, and a divided life is not a position but an avoidance.

I, even I only, am left (v. 22). Untrue, and God will answer it at Horeb with a number (19:18). Isolation is the occupational danger of the faithful minority.

Blood, and whose (v. 28). One religion asks for your blood and keeps asking; the true God provides the sacrifice himself.

The hour and the twelve stones (vv. 31, 36). Twelve stones in a kingdom of ten, and a prayer timed to the evening lamb in Jerusalem. He is not founding a northern religion; he is bringing the north home.

That you have turned their hearts back (v. 37). He does not ask that the people turn. He asks that they may know God turned them. The great public event of his life is prayed over by a man who does not believe spectacle can convert anybody. Malachi took up the same longing when he promised that Elijah would come again to turn the hearts of fathers to their children (Malachi 4:6), and the angel told Zechariah that John the Baptist would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah to do it (Luke 1:17). The turning Elijah prayed for on Carmel is what the gospel of Christ does.

The Kishon, and Luke 9 (v. 40). A judicial execution under a standing covenant law (Deut. 13:1-5; 17:2-7), against the leadership of a movement that had been killing the LORD's prophets. Described, not commended as a template, and closed off for the church when Jesus rebuked James and John for wanting Elijah's fire (Luke 9:54-55).
18.examples:
Then: Four hundred and fifty men shouting four words at a clear sky for nine hours, cutting themselves with swords until they were slick with their own blood, hobbling round a cold fireplace in front of a watching nation, and no voice, and no one answering, and no one paying attention.

Now: Three things. First, verse 21 in its modern dress: is there anything in your life that would have to change if the LORD is God, which has not changed? That is the limp, and nobody can defend it. But Elijah did not expect the crowd to cure itself; he asked God to turn their hearts back (v. 37), and God now does that by his Spirit, giving a new heart and causing his people to walk in his ways (Ezek. 36:26-27). Every divided day of ours is covered by the one whose obedience never limped and is counted as ours (Rom. 5:19). Second, Obadiah. A great many Christians are inside an institution that has gone wrong, doing what good can still be done there. Scripture's word over that person is written before any of his deeds: he feared the LORD greatly. Third, the seventh look. The fire fell in an instant and the rain took seven journeys, and both had been promised in the same sentence. When the answer comes it is usually the size of a hand held up against the sky.

19.title: Elijah at Horeb
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.<sup>2</sup>Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, "So may the gods do to me and more also, if I do not make your life as the life of one of them by this time tomorrow."<sup>3</sup>Then he was afraid, and he arose and ran for his life and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there.<sup>4</sup>But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die, saying, "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers."<sup>5</sup>And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, "Arise and eat."<sup>6</sup>And he looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and drank and lay down again.<sup>7</sup>And the angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him and said, "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you."<sup>8</sup>And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mount of God.<sup>9</sup>There he came to a cave and lodged in it. And behold, the word of the LORD came to him, and he said to him, "What are you doing here, Elijah?"<sup>10</sup>He said, "I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of hosts. For the people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away."<sup>11</sup>And he said, "Go out and stand on the mount before the LORD." And behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind. And after the wind an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake.<sup>12</sup>And after the earthquake a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire the sound of a low whisper.<sup>13</sup>And when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave. And behold, there came a voice to him and said, "What are you doing here, Elijah?"<sup>14</sup>He said, "I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of hosts. For the people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away."<sup>15</sup>And the LORD said to him, "Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus. And when you arrive, you shall anoint Hazael to be king over Syria.<sup>16</sup>And Jehu the son of Nimshi you shall anoint to be king over Israel, and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah you shall anoint to be prophet in your place.<sup>17</sup>And the one who escapes from the sword of Hazael shall Jehu put to death, and the one who escapes from the sword of Jehu shall Elisha put to death.<sup>18</sup>Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him."<sup>19</sup>So he departed from there and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen in front of him, and he was with the twelfth. Elijah passed by him and cast his cloak upon him.<sup>20</sup>And he left the oxen and ran after Elijah and said, "Let me kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you." And he said to him, "Go back again, for what have I done to you?"<sup>21</sup>And he returned from following him and took the yoke of oxen and sacrificed them and boiled their flesh with the yokes of the oxen and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he arose and went after Elijah and assisted him.
19.overview:
The fire fell, a nation went on its face, the rain came, and one letter undoes it all. Ahab's account of Carmel to his wife leaves out the fire entirely (v. 1); Jezebel sends not soldiers but a threat with a day's notice; and the man who faced four hundred and fifty prophets runs a hundred miles, sheds his servant, and sits down under a desert bush asking to die.

His reason is not Jezebel. It is I am no better than my fathers (v. 4). He had hoped to be the one who turned the country back, and the greatest day of his life changed nothing. What God does about it, in order, is sleep, food, more sleep, more food, and one gentle sentence. There is no rebuke anywhere in the chapter.

Then comes Horeb, with a question asked twice and answered twice in identical words, and wind, earthquake and fire that God is not in. Out of the whisper that follows come three commissions, a successor, and a number Elijah had no way of knowing. The chapter ends in a field, with a cloak thrown over a young farmer who burns his plough to cook his own oxen and goes off to carry an old man's bags.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab reports Carmel to Jezebel without the fire, and she sends Elijah a threat with a day's notice (vv. 1-2). He runs to Beersheba, leaves his servant, and sits under a bush in the wilderness asking to die (vv. 3-4). God answers with sleep, a touch, food and water, twice, and one sentence about the journey, and he walks forty days on it (vv. 5-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Read verse 4 carefully and the despair turns out not to be about Jezebel. His reason is I am no better than my fathers: he has measured himself against what he hoped he was and come up ordinary.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what God does not do. There is no rebuke, no reminder of yesterday's fire, no summons to pull himself together. Care for the body comes first, and the word, when it comes, is kind.

verseByVerse.quote: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword. Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, "So may the gods do to me and more also, if I do not make your life as the life of one of them by this time tomorrow." Then he was afraid, and he arose and ran for his life and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there. But he himself went a day's journey into the wilderness and came and sat down under a broom tree. And he asked that he might die, saying, "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life, for I am no better than my fathers." And he lay down and slept under a broom tree. And behold, an angel touched him and said to him, "Arise and eat." And he looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and drank and lay down again. And the angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him and said, "Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you." And he arose and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mount of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the only eyewitness account of Carmel that survives from inside the palace, and it has no fire in it.

Ahab watched four hundred and fifty men shout at the sky all day and get nothing, and then fire fall out of heaven and a whole nation go down on its face. He goes home to his wife and reports a body count: all that Elijah had done, not what God did. It is possible to see everything and register none of it, and Ahab is the standing proof.

Look at what she does not do. She had every instrument of the state at her disposal and Elijah at the gate of her own city, and she sends one man with a sentence, and gives him twenty-four hours.

A woman who intends to kill a man at dawn does not write and tell him so the night before. What she wants is his absence, and she knows a threat will do what an arrest would not: it will make him run, and a prophet in flight unravels everything the mountain did.

She swears by the gods, incidentally, whose entire clergy died yesterday for failing to produce a spark. Evidence has never yet stopped anyone who did not wish to be stopped.

Many Christians have seen in Herodias, who wanted John the Baptist dead (Mark 6:19), a second Jezebel hunting the second Elijah, and Jesus seems to point that way: Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him (Mark 9:13).

He was afraid. Yesterday he stood alone in front of the assembled nation and dictated the terms; today a letter arrives and he runs.

Say plainly what that means. The fire fell, the people confessed, the rain came, the prophets of Baal are dead, and none of it changed the court. Ahab reports it as an atrocity. Jezebel is not even shaken. The nation that shouted the LORD, he is God has no voice in Jezreel the next morning. Elijah had prayed on Carmel that they might know God turned their hearts back (18:37), and now he finds out for himself what he already believed: fire does not turn hearts. It only lights altars.

He runs to Beersheba, which is the southern edge of the country, a hundred miles away, in another kingdom and out of Ahab's reach, and then leaves his servant behind and keeps going. Notice the deliberateness. He does not merely flee; he sheds the last human being with him. Grief of this kind always wants the room emptied.

The broom tree is a desert shrub, a tangle of thin green switches that throws a shade you could read a page through. It is not shelter. It is simply the only thing standing in that landscape, and a man sat down under it because he could not go any further.

Then the prayer, and it is not the one we expect. He does not say "they are trying to kill me." He says I am no better than my fathers.

The despair is not about Jezebel at all. It is about himself. He had hoped, as every servant of God hopes and few admit, that he might be the one. The one who broke the thing his predecessors could not break, who turned the nation back, who was not just another prophet in a long line of prophets who preached to a country that did not listen. Carmel was his best day, and it changed nothing, and the arithmetic he does under that bush is: I am ordinary, and it made no difference, and I would rather be dead than go on being ordinary.

People do not usually collapse when they fail. They collapse afterwards, when they succeed and discover that the success did not deliver what they were really asking of it.

There is a mercy hidden in the request that he could not have known about. He asks the LORD to take away his life, and he becomes one of only two men in Scripture, with Enoch, who are taken without dying. God's refusal of the prayer was better than the prayer, and it is not the last time that will be true of somebody.

Watch the order of what God does, because it is practical. He lets him sleep. Then an angel touches him, a hand on a man who has put a hundred miles between himself and every other human being. Then a cake baked on hot stones and a jug of water at his head, ready when he woke. Then more sleep.

There is no rebuke: not one word about Carmel, or the servant left at Beersheba, or the self-pity in verse 4. God does not yet tell him that his theology is faulty or his count wrong. That comes later, on a mountain, after two meals and a great deal of sleep.

If you are where Elijah was, hear this plainly. Wanting to die does not put you out of God's reach; a great prophet prayed for it, and God answered with bread, not anger, and James still calls him a man with a nature like ours (James 5:17). God used ordinary means first, and still does: a doctor, medicine, rest and a friend who sits with you are not a failure of faith. Tell someone today, a friend, a pastor, a doctor. If you are in danger of acting on the thought, call your local emergency number or a crisis line now. Elijah did not have to carry the journey alone, and neither do you.

The first sentence God addresses to his despair is a diagnosis, and it is astonishingly gentle. The journey is too great for you.

God does not say that Elijah is a coward, or that he has let him down. He says this is more than you can carry, and I know it. God is the first person in the story to say that Elijah's burden exceeded Elijah's strength, and he says it as a reason for breakfast.

Forty days and forty nights. The number belongs to Moses on this same mountain (Ex. 24:18; 34:28) and to Israel's forty years in this same desert, and later to a greater Man in a wilderness of his own, who was tempted forty days and did not fall, so that the failures of Israel and of her prophets could be answered (Matthew 4:1-11).

Horeb is Sinai. Elijah is walking back to the beginning, to the place where the covenant the nation has just broken was originally cut, where God came down in fire and the mountain shook. A prophet who has decided that his ministry has failed goes looking for the address where it all started.
verseByVerse.note: Beersheba was the southern edge of Judah; Horeb (Sinai), whose exact site is debated, lay perhaps 200 miles beyond; the journey took forty days.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — A Sound of Thin Silence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Horeb God asks Elijah what he is doing there, and he answers with three complaints ending in his being the only one left (vv. 9-10). Wind, earthquake and fire pass, and God is in none of them; then comes a low whisper (vv. 11-12). Asked again, Elijah gives the identical answer (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Wind, earthquake and fire are exactly what happened on this mountain when the covenant was cut (Ex. 19:16-18), and they are exactly what happened on Carmel a few weeks ago. God stages the whole repertoire and says he is not in it. What turns a nation is not the thing that fills the sky.
verseByVerse.examples: The second telling is the tenderest part. He says the same words again, unchanged, and God does not argue or withdraw the commission. He answers a repeated complaint with work to do and a fact Elijah did not have.

verseByVerse.quote: There he came to a cave and lodged in it. And behold, the word of the LORD came to him, and he said to him, "What are you doing here, Elijah?" He said, "I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of hosts. For the people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away." And he said, "Go out and stand on the mount before the LORD." And behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind. And after the wind an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire the sound of a low whisper. And when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the entrance of the cave. And behold, there came a voice to him and said, "What are you doing here, Elijah?" He said, "I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of hosts. For the people of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword, and I, even I only, am left, and they seek my life, to take it away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Hebrew says the cave, with the article, which has made readers wonder for centuries whether this is the cleft of the rock where God put Moses and covered him with his hand while the glory went past (Ex. 33:22). The text does not say so and we should not insist. It does say that the prophet has ended up in a hole in the side of the mountain where God once showed a broken man his back.

The two men who met God on this mountain, Moses and Elijah, meet again in the Gospels on another mountain, with Jesus. Luke says they appeared in glory and spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). What neither of them could see at Horeb, the glory of God in a face, they saw there; and what they talked about was the cross.

What are you doing here, Elijah? The question is about geography: not why did you run, but what are you doing here, hundreds of miles from the country you were sent to, in a cave.

There is no heat in it. This is the same voice that has just fed him twice and let him sleep. It is the question a friend asks when he finds you somewhere you had no business getting to, and it is designed to be answered.

Two parts of the answer are true and one is not. He begins with his own record, I have been very jealous for the LORD, and God never disputes it. Then the state of the nation: covenant forsaken, altars pulled down (he rebuilt one himself a few weeks ago), prophets killed. All true.

Then I, even I only, am left, already said on Carmel (18:22) days after meeting Obadiah, and to be said again in four verses. It has never once been true. Isolation is not a fact he has established; it is a feeling he has lived inside so long that it has hardened into a doctrine.

Three things come, and they are not random. Wind, earthquake and fire on this mountain are what happened the first time. When the covenant was given here, there was thunder and lightning and thick cloud and a mountain that trembled greatly and the whole of it wrapped in smoke and fire (Ex. 19:16-18). Elijah is being shown Sinai again.

They are also, and this is the sharper point, exactly what he has just been through. God answered by fire in front of a nation, and it was magnificent, and it fixed nothing. And after wind, earthquake and fire alike the writer says the same flat sentence: the LORD was not in it.

Then: the sound of a low whisper. The Hebrew is peculiar and translators have long struggled with it: qol demamah daqqah, "a sound, a thin silence," as the ESV margin puts it, a sound of fine stillness. The old rendering, a still small voice, has stayed in the language because nothing better has been found.

Now be careful, because there is a sentimental reading of this passage that is not quite the point. It is true that God often speaks quietly, and true that we are poor at listening. But what is being answered here is a specific despair by a specific man. Elijah staked everything on the spectacular and it left the country exactly where it was. God gives him the whole repertoire, the entire Carmel arsenal, and says: I am not in that. And then he speaks in a voice that would not carry across a room, and what the voice contains is a set of instructions and a number.

The kingdom does not come by the thing that fills the sky. It comes by a word, and by men and women who hear it and go where they are sent.

He covers his face, as Moses did at the bush (Ex. 3:6). He knows what is happening and he knows what happens to men who look.

Then the identical question, and the identical answer, word for word: the same three complaints in the same order, ending in the same untrue sentence, from a man who has just watched God tear a mountain to pieces and then whisper.

Most of us would not respond to a second hearing of the same speech as God does. There is no exasperation, no "were you not listening?" Instead God gives him three things to do and one fact he did not have. He is not, apparently, offended by having to say it twice.

Does the low whisper mean God speaks to believers in an inner voice? God was teaching Elijah that his work does not always come in fire and storm. The whisper was his spoken word to a prophet. Believers today hear God speak in the Scriptures, completed and sufficient (Heb 1:1–2; 2 Tim 3:16–17), applied by the Spirit; quiet impressions must be tested by that word. This commentary holds the cessationist view, that new revelation ended with the apostles because Scripture is now complete; many faithful Christians believe God still gives impressions or prophetic words today, and both agree that nothing may be set beside the Bible or obeyed against it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends Elijah back with three commissions: Hazael over Syria, Jehu over Israel, and Elisha as prophet in his place, a chain of judgment on Ahab's house (vv. 15-17). Then the correction he has needed since Carmel: seven thousand in Israel have not bowed to Baal (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not tell him his sorrow is wrong. He tells him his arithmetic is wrong, and by a factor of seven thousand. And these are not celebrated men; not one of them appears anywhere in the story, which is precisely why Elijah could not count them. God keeps a register the prophet has no access to.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul builds on this verse: I have kept for myself, and so too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace (Rom. 11:4-5). The seven thousand did not hold out. They were held.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to him, "Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus. And when you arrive, you shall anoint Hazael to be king over Syria. And Jehu the son of Nimshi you shall anoint to be king over Israel, and Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah you shall anoint to be prophet in your place. And the one who escapes from the sword of Hazael shall Jehu put to death, and the one who escapes from the sword of Jehu shall Elisha put to death. Yet I will leave seven thousand in Israel, all the knees that have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Go, return on your way. The first word to a man who has asked to die is to go back, though not to what he was doing. There are three new commissions, and they are enormous: the reordering of two kingdoms and the appointment of his own successor. God's answer to it is enough is a list of errands.

None of that is callousness, and it should not be preached as a rebuke. It comes after the sleep, after the food, after the whisper, in that order, and it is what a man in Elijah's condition most needs once he has been fed: something to do tomorrow that matters, and somebody expecting him to do it.

In your place. Read that as the mercy it is. Elijah has twice told God he is the only one left, and God's reply includes a young man in a field who will take the office off his hands. He is not indispensable, and being told so is the kindest thing that happens to him on that mountain. The work will go on and he will not have to be the one carrying it.

Here is a detail the reader should be told, because it looks like a loose end and is not. Elijah personally anoints none of these three. Elisha he calls, with a cloak and no words at all (v. 19). Hazael he never meets; it is Elisha who speaks to him, years later, in Damascus (2 Kgs. 8:13). Jehu is anointed by one of Elisha's servants after Elijah has gone (2 Kgs. 9:1-6). The commission was given to one man and carried out across two men and a generation, and every item on the list was done.

You are not obliged to complete the work. You are obliged to start walking back down the mountain.

A chain of judgment with no gaps in it. Hazael will devastate Israel from outside; Jehu will exterminate Ahab's house from inside; and Elisha, whose only weapon is a word, finishes what the two swords leave. It is grim, and it is meant to be: the house that installed Baal is going to be taken down, and there is no exit from the sentence.

Everything before the word yet has been swords; everything after it is a number. Seven thousand is not a token but a substantial body of people, in a country Elijah had written off as entirely lost, who have not bowed and have not kissed. Kissing the image was the ordinary gesture of homage before an idol, the thing you did in passing at a shrine as easily as touching a doorpost (Hos. 13:2). Seven thousand people had declined to do it, quietly, for years, with the queen's prophets eating at the palace and their neighbours watching.

None of the seven thousand is named or confronted a king; they are invisible, and that is precisely why Elijah could not count them. He was measuring the kingdom of God by the number of people doing what he was doing, which is the standard error of the brave and the exhausted. So God corrects not his feeling but his arithmetic.

Paul makes this verse carry more than it appears to. Arguing in Romans that God has not rejected his people, he quotes it with a change of subject that does all the work: I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal (Rom. 11:4). Kings says I will leave; Paul says I have kept for myself, and draws the line to his own day: so too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace (Rom. 11:5).

The seven thousand did not hold out by strength of character. They were held. Their loyalty is presented as God's achievement and God's property, which is why it is a comfort and not merely a statistic: a remnant that keeps itself can stop keeping itself at any time, and one that God has kept for himself cannot be lost.

If you have ever been the only believer in a family, an office, a village or a regiment, this verse is addressed to you, and it says two things. Your count is wrong. And the ones you cannot see are not managing on their own strength any more than you are.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elijah finds Elisha ploughing with the twelfth yoke of oxen and throws his cloak over him without a word (v. 19). Elisha asks to say goodbye to his parents, then slaughters the oxen, cooks them on the yokes, feeds the people, and follows Elijah as his servant (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The cloak does all the talking. With no speech, no persuasion and no terms, a garment lands on a young man's shoulders in a field, and the man is called.
verseByVerse.examples: Twelve yoke of oxen is a prosperous farm, and he cooks the team on the ploughing gear: there is no returning to that life because the means of it is dinner. Jesus stood on this scene and made it harder (Luke 9:62).

verseByVerse.quote: So he departed from there and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen in front of him, and he was with the twelfth. Elijah passed by him and cast his cloak upon him. And he left the oxen and ran after Elijah and said, "Let me kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you." And he said to him, "Go back again, for what have I done to you?" And he returned from following him and took the yoke of oxen and sacrificed them and boiled their flesh with the yokes of the oxen and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he arose and went after Elijah and assisted him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve yoke of oxen means twenty-four animals working one field, with eleven other ploughmen ahead of him and Elisha bringing up the rear on the last pair.

That is not a smallholding. Oxen are expensive; a family with twelve teams is a substantial farming concern, and the young man on the twelfth is evidently from a well-off farming family. He is not being rescued from poverty. He is being called out of a good life.

Elijah says nothing whatever. He walks past and throws his cloak over the man's shoulders and keeps going.

It is the same cloak he wrapped his face in a few weeks ago at the mouth of the cave. It is the cloak that will roll up and strike the Jordan so that the water divides, and that will fall out of a whirlwind for this same young man to pick up (2 Kgs. 2:8, 13-14). To put your cloak on a man is to put yourself on him: your office, your name, your obligations.

There is no sermon, no interview, no explanation. A weight lands across his shoulders in a field and he knows what it means, and he leaves the oxen in the furrow and runs after a stranger going up the road.

Elijah's reply is short and has been read two ways for a long time, and both readings end in the same place. Go back again, for what have I done to you? Either: go on, I have not stopped you, say your goodbyes. Or: go back and think about what has just happened to you before you take another step. What it plainly is not is recruitment. Elijah does not press him, does not warm to him, does not sell him the ministry. He puts the decision back into the young man's hands and walks on.

Set this beside a conversation on a road nine centuries later. A man says to Jesus, I will follow you, Lord, but let me first say farewell to those at my home. And Jesus says, no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:61-62).

He is standing on this scene, and everyone listening knew it. Elijah let his man go home to his parents. Jesus does not. The claim is harder because the one making it is greater; a prophet may hand you back your decision, and the Lord of the harvest does not. But the one who calls like that is the one who set his face to go to Jerusalem and did not look back, for us (Luke 9:51), and he does not send his followers down the furrow alone.

He kills the oxen and burns the ploughing gear to cook them. The yokes are the most valuable wooden objects on the farm, cut to fit those animals; the team that was breaking the ground an hour ago is the meat; and the whole village eats it, so that nothing is left over.

He has made it impossible to go back, and he has done it as a feast rather than a funeral. There is no bridge to burn afterwards, because the bridge is dinner.

Then the last clause, and it is the humblest sentence in the chapter: and assisted him. The word means ministered, served, waited on: the word used of Joshua as Moses' assistant. He did not become a prophet that day; he became a prophet's servant, and for years afterwards the way people identify him is as Elisha the son of Shaphat is here, who poured water on the hands of Elijah (2 Kgs. 3:11). The man who burned his farm signed on to carry the bags.

Now stand back and look at what this chapter has done. A man sat under a bush and asked God to end his life because he was no better than his fathers and it had all been for nothing. God gave him sleep, a hot meal, a second hot meal, a mountain, a whisper, three commissions, seven thousand names he could not see, and a young man in a field with a cloak on his shoulders.

Not one of those was what he asked for. He asked to die, and God gave him a companion, a successor, a country full of hidden brothers, and in the end a whirlwind instead of a grave.
verseByVerse.note: Throwing a cloak over someone signified calling him to succeed.

19.theology:
Fire does not turn hearts (vv. 1-3). The most spectacular answer to prayer in the Old Testament produced a confession that did not reach the palace, an eyewitness who reports it as a massacre, and a queen who is not shaken at all. Signs can silence an argument; only God changes a will.

The shape of the despair (v. 4). The wound is Elijah's own ordinariness, uncovered by his best day, which is why collapse so often follows success rather than failure. Not every despair has this cause; much is illness of body and mind with no reason anyone can find, and God's care in this chapter fits that too.

How God treats a servant who has broken (vv. 5-7). Sleep and food come before any word, and the word is a diagnosis offered as kindness. No rebuke is ever issued in this chapter.

Not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire (vv. 11-12). The point is not merely that God speaks softly; it is that the thing which fills the sky is not the thing that builds his kingdom.

Seven thousand, and whose achievement they are (v. 18). God answers a twice-repeated I only am left by correcting the count. Paul reads it as a remnant, chosen by grace (Rom. 11:4-5): they did not hold out; they were held.

The cloak and the plough (vv. 19-21). Elijah calls his successor without a word, with the garment that will one day divide the Jordan. Elisha answers by making return impossible and turning it into a feast. And Jesus, standing on this scene, raises the terms: no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62).
19.examples:
Then: A prophet a hundred miles from anywhere, under a shrub that casts almost no shade, having deliberately sent away the last human being with him, asking God to kill him because he had turned out to be no better than the men who went before him.

Now: Three things. First, the order of God's care. Think of the last person you knew in that condition and recall what you reached for; most of us reach for an argument, a verse, a correction. God reached for sleep and a hot meal, twice, and the first thing he did say was that the journey was too great for the man, not that the man was too small for the journey. Second, the miscount. Anybody who has been the only believer in a family or a workplace holds a private census that is wrong, and wrong in the same direction as Elijah's, because we count the kingdom by the number of people visibly doing what we are doing. Seven thousand people who never once appear in the narrative had not bowed. Third, the repeated complaint. He said the same aggrieved paragraph twice, word for word, after God had given him a private Sinai to answer it, and was met with work, a successor and a fact, and never once with impatience.

20.title: Ahab and Ben-hadad
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Ben-hadad the king of Syria gathered all his army together. Thirty-two kings were with him, and horses and chariots. And he went up and closed in on Samaria and fought against it.<sup>2</sup>And he sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel and said to him, "Thus says Ben-hadad:<sup>3</sup>'Your silver and your gold are mine; your best wives and children also are mine.'"<sup>4</sup>And the king of Israel answered, "As you say, my lord, O king, I am yours, and all that I have."<sup>5</sup>The messengers came again and said, "Thus says Ben-hadad: 'I sent to you, saying, "Deliver to me your silver and your gold, your wives and your children."<sup>6</sup>Nevertheless I will send my servants to you tomorrow about this time, and they shall search your house and the houses of your servants and lay hands on whatever pleases you and take it away.'"<sup>7</sup>Then the king of Israel called all the elders of the land and said, "Mark, now, and see how this man is seeking trouble, for he sent to me for my wives and my children, and for my silver and my gold, and I did not refuse him."<sup>8</sup>And all the elders and all the people said to him, "Do not listen or consent."<sup>9</sup>So he said to the messengers of Ben-hadad, "Tell my lord the king, 'All that you first demanded of your servant I will do, but this thing I cannot do.'" And the messengers departed and brought him word again.<sup>10</sup>Ben-hadad sent to him and said, "The gods do so to me and more also, if the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls for all the people who follow me."<sup>11</sup>And the king of Israel answered, "Tell him, 'Let not him who straps on his armor boast himself as he who takes it off.'"<sup>12</sup>When Ben-hadad heard this message as he was drinking with the kings in the booths, he said to his men, "Take your positions." And they took their positions against the city.<sup>13</sup>And behold, a prophet came near to Ahab king of Israel and said, "Thus says the LORD, Have you seen all this great multitude? Behold, I will give it into your hand this day, and you shall know that I am the LORD."<sup>14</sup>And Ahab said, "By whom?" He said, "Thus says the LORD, By the servants of the governors of the districts." Then he said, "Who shall begin the battle?" He answered, "You."<sup>15</sup>Then he mustered the servants of the governors of the districts, and they were 232. And after them he mustered all the people of Israel, seven thousand.<sup>16</sup>And they went out at noon, while Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk in the booths, he and the thirty-two kings who helped him.<sup>17</sup>The servants of the governors of the districts went out first. And Ben-hadad sent out scouts, and they reported to him, "Men are coming out from Samaria."<sup>18</sup>He said, "If they have come out for peace, take them alive. Or if they have come out for war, take them alive."<sup>19</sup>So these went out of the city, the servants of the governors of the districts and the army that followed them.<sup>20</sup>And each struck down his man. The Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them, but Ben-hadad king of Syria escaped on a horse with horsemen.<sup>21</sup>And the king of Israel went out and struck the horses and chariots, and struck the Syrians with a great blow.<sup>22</sup>Then the prophet came near to the king of Israel and said to him, "Come, strengthen yourself, and consider well what you have to do, for in the spring the king of Syria will come up against you."<sup>23</sup>And the servants of the king of Syria said to him, "Their gods are gods of the hills, and so they were stronger than we. But let us fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they.<sup>24</sup>And do this: remove the kings, each from his post, and put commanders in their places,<sup>25</sup>and muster an army like the army that you have lost, horse for horse, and chariot for chariot. Then we will fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they." And he listened to their voice and did so.<sup>26</sup>In the spring, Ben-hadad mustered the Syrians and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel.<sup>27</sup>And the people of Israel were mustered and were provisioned and went against them. The people of Israel encamped before them like two little flocks of goats, but the Syrians filled the country.<sup>28</sup>And a man of God came near and said to the king of Israel, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because the Syrians have said, "The LORD is a god of the hills but he is not a god of the valleys," therefore I will give all this great multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the LORD.'"<sup>29</sup>And they encamped opposite one another seven days. Then on the seventh day the battle was joined. And the people of Israel struck down of the Syrians 100,000 foot soldiers in one day.<sup>30</sup>And the rest fled into the city of Aphek, and the wall fell upon 27,000 men who were left. Ben-hadad also fled and entered an inner chamber in the city.<sup>31</sup>And his servants said to him, "Behold now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings. Let us put sackcloth around our waists and ropes on our heads and go out to the king of Israel. Perhaps he will spare your life."<sup>32</sup>So they tied sackcloth around their waists and put ropes on their heads and went to the king of Israel and said, "Your servant Ben-hadad says, 'Please, let me live.'" And he said, "Does he still live? He is my brother."<sup>33</sup>Now the men were watching for a sign, and they quickly took it up from him and said, "Yes, your brother Ben-hadad." Then he said, "Go and bring him." Then Ben-hadad came out to him, and he caused him to come up into the chariot.<sup>34</sup>And Ben-hadad said to him, "The cities that my father took from your father I will restore, and you may establish bazaars for yourself in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria." And Ahab said, "I will let you go on these terms." So he made a covenant with him and let him go.<sup>35</sup>And a certain man of the sons of the prophets said to his fellow at the command of the LORD, "Strike me, please." But the man refused to strike him.<sup>36</sup>Then he said to him, "Because you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD, behold, as soon as you have gone from me, a lion shall strike you down." And as soon as he had departed from him, a lion met him and struck him down.<sup>37</sup>Then he found another man and said, "Strike me, please." And the man struck him—struck him and wounded him.<sup>38</sup>So the prophet departed and waited for the king by the way, disguising himself with a bandage over his eyes.<sup>39</sup>And as the king passed, he cried to the king and said, "Your servant went out into the midst of the battle, and behold, a soldier turned and brought a man to me and said, 'Guard this man; if by any means he is missing, your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver.'<sup>40</sup>And as your servant was busy here and there, he was gone." The king of Israel said to him, "So shall your judgment be; you yourself have decided it."<sup>41</sup>Then he hurried to take the bandage away from his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets.<sup>42</sup>And he said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have let go out of your hand the man whom I had devoted to destruction, therefore your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people.'"<sup>43</sup>And the king of Israel went to his house vexed and sullen and came to Samaria.
20.overview:
Syria besieges Samaria, and Ahab surrenders his treasury, his wives and his children by return of messenger. He only stiffens when the demand becomes a search of his own house, and even then the backbone belongs to the elders and the people (v. 8).

Then God intervenes twice for a king he has already condemned, and both times states the reason: you shall know that I am the LORD (vv. 13, 28). A handful of junior retainers rout a great coalition at noon, and in the spring, because Syrian officers have decided the LORD is a god of the hills and not the valleys, an army that filled the country is destroyed on the plain.

Then Ahab gets Ben-hadad in his hands, calls him my brother, and lets him go for trade concessions. A wounded prophet with a story about a lost prisoner gets the king to pass sentence on himself. Ahab goes home vexed and sullen, the exact phrase that opens the Naboth story four verses later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Your Silver and Your Gold Are Mine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ben-hadad of Syria besieges Samaria with thirty-two allied kings and demands Ahab's silver, gold, wives and children, and Ahab agrees at once (vv. 1-4). When the demand becomes a search of the palace, the elders and the people tell him to refuse (vv. 5-9). Ben-hadad boasts, and Ahab answers with a proverb that reaches the Syrian king in his drinking booth (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Ahab surrenders his wives, his children and his treasury without a fight and only digs in when the demand becomes a search of his own house. He will give away anything he does not have to watch being taken.
verseByVerse.examples: The backbone in this chapter is not the king's. Ordinary people who refuse to be bullied can stiffen a weak leader, and God often keeps a nation from the worst through them.

verseByVerse.quote: Ben-hadad the king of Syria gathered all his army together. Thirty-two kings were with him, and horses and chariots. And he went up and closed in on Samaria and fought against it. And he sent messengers into the city to Ahab king of Israel and said to him, "Thus says Ben-hadad: 'Your silver and your gold are mine; your best wives and children also are mine.'" And the king of Israel answered, "As you say, my lord, O king, I am yours, and all that I have." The messengers came again and said, "Thus says Ben-hadad: 'I sent to you, saying, "Deliver to me your silver and your gold, your wives and your children." Nevertheless I will send my servants to you tomorrow about this time, and they shall search your house and the houses of your servants and lay hands on whatever pleases you and take it away.'" Then the king of Israel called all the elders of the land and said, "Mark, now, and see how this man is seeking trouble, for he sent to me for my wives and my children, and for my silver and my gold, and I did not refuse him." And all the elders and all the people said to him, "Do not listen or consent." So he said to the messengers of Ben-hadad, "Tell my lord the king, 'All that you first demanded of your servant I will do, but this thing I cannot do.'" And the messengers departed and brought him word again. Ben-hadad sent to him and said, "The gods do so to me and more also, if the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls for all the people who follow me." And the king of Israel answered, "Tell him, 'Let not him who straps on his armor boast himself as he who takes it off.'" When Ben-hadad heard this message as he was drinking with the kings in the booths, he said to his men, "Take your positions." And they took their positions against the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Syria here is Aram, with its capital at Damascus, and it will be Israel's chief enemy for the next century. The thirty-two kings are not equals; they are the rulers of small dependent city-states in the coalition, brought along to make the muster look like the world coming to the gate.

Ahab says yes (v. 4), and the answer is as striking as the demand. The treasury, the queens and the royal children are handed over by return of messenger, with my lord attached: no counter-offer, no delay. The king of the people God brought out of Egypt addresses a foreign besieger as his lord and makes over his own children.

This is not a bigger demand for goods; it is a different kind of demand altogether. The first was tribute, paid over at the gate. The second is a search: Syrian soldiers walking through the palace and through the houses of the court, opening chests, and taking whatever pleases you, which is to say whatever the owner values most.

Ben-hadad has raised the price precisely because the first price was met so quickly. A man who surrenders everything at the first letter has told you that he will surrender more at the second.

Hear what he admits in the middle of his complaint. I did not refuse him. He is asking the elders to be outraged on his behalf while telling them, in the same sentence, that he had already given away the wives and the children and the gold without a murmur.

The elders and the people of a starved and idolatrous kingdom are the ones who say no.

Even the refusal keeps my lord and your servant in it. He draws his line where the people told him to draw it, and apologises for the line while drawing it.

The boast is that his army is so large that when Samaria has been pulled down there will not be enough rubble to give every man a fistful as a souvenir. It is the swagger of a man drinking in a tent with thirty-two client kings watching him.

Verse 11 is the best sentence Ahab ever speaks, and it is a proverb: do not celebrate at the buckling-on, celebrate at the unbuckling. Count the battle when it is over and you are alive to take the harness off.

It is true and well said, and it should be remembered, because two chapters from now this same man will strap something on before a battle. He will go into Ramoth-gilead in disguise with the armour of a common soldier, and an arrow shot at nobody in particular will find the join in it, and he will be dead by sundown, propped up in his chariot. He never does take it off.

Notice where the reply reaches him, because the writer will say it again in four verses: he is drinking. Elah was drinking when Zimri killed him (16:9), and Ben-hadad is drinking now and will be drunk when the attack comes. In this book the cup is where kings are when the decisive thing happens to them.
verseByVerse.note: Ben-hadad was a name, perhaps a dynastic title, borne by several kings of Damascus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–22 — You Shall Know That I Am the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An unnamed prophet promises Ahab victory so that he may know that the LORD is God, through two hundred and thirty-two retainers of the district governors, with the king leading (vv. 13-15). They march out at noon while Ben-hadad is drinking, and the Syrians run (vv. 16-21). The prophet warns that the king of Syria will be back in the spring (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: God gives a victory to a king he has already condemned, not because Ahab deserves it but so that Ahab may know who the LORD is. Paul asks the question this chapter raises: do you presume on the riches of his kindness, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? (Rom. 2:4).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 22 keeps the reader honest about what a deliverance is: the enemy will be back in the spring. A rescue from one temptation or trouble is grace, and it is also a call to watchfulness for the next.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a prophet came near to Ahab king of Israel and said, "Thus says the LORD, Have you seen all this great multitude? Behold, I will give it into your hand this day, and you shall know that I am the LORD." And Ahab said, "By whom?" He said, "Thus says the LORD, By the servants of the governors of the districts." Then he said, "Who shall begin the battle?" He answered, "You." Then he mustered the servants of the governors of the districts, and they were 232. And after them he mustered all the people of Israel, seven thousand. And they went out at noon, while Ben-hadad was drinking himself drunk in the booths, he and the thirty-two kings who helped him. The servants of the governors of the districts went out first. And Ben-hadad sent out scouts, and they reported to him, "Men are coming out from Samaria." He said, "If they have come out for peace, take them alive. Or if they have come out for war, take them alive." So these went out of the city, the servants of the governors of the districts and the army that followed them. And each struck down his man. The Syrians fled, and Israel pursued them, but Ben-hadad king of Syria escaped on a horse with horsemen. And the king of Israel went out and struck the horses and chariots, and struck the Syrians with a great blow. Then the prophet came near to the king of Israel and said to him, "Come, strengthen yourself, and consider well what you have to do, for in the spring the king of Syria will come up against you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 13 raises the question the whole chapter exists to answer. God sends a prophet to Ahab, the man who married Jezebel and built the temple of Baal, and promises him not a warning but a gift: victory.

The reason is given in the same breath: you shall know that I am the LORD. He will say it again at Aphek (v. 28). The victories are not wages and they are not approval. They are one more attempt on a man who has now watched fire fall from heaven and learned nothing from it.

Verse 14 asks two questions, and both answers are designed to leave nobody any room to claim the credit. The instrument is not the army.
