It is the personal retainers of provincial administrators, junior men attached to the civil service of the districts, which is roughly as if a nation were defended by the office staff of its county councils. And to who shall begin the battle? the prophet answers that the king himself goes first: two hundred and thirty-two men against a coalition of thirty-three kingdoms.

Behind them stands the entire fighting strength Ahab can raise: seven thousand. Set that beside the number God gave Elijah on Horeb one chapter ago (19:18). The book does not draw the line between them and we should not press it, but the reader who has just come from that cave can hardly help hearing the echo: the number that looked pitiably small to a prophet who thought he was alone is the number of an army.

They walk out at noon: not dawn, not dusk, no attempt at surprise, but in the full glare of the middle of the day, in plain sight of a besieging army. And thirty-three kings are drunk.

Ben-hadad gives one order for both possibilities (v. 18). It does not occur to him that it could matter which. That is contempt in its purest form, and it is the reason he loses.

Each struck down his man is the whole account of the battle. The writer has no interest in the tactics; two hundred and thirty-two clerks' servants walked into the greatest army in the region at noon and every one of them killed the man in front of him.

Mark the last clause: Ben-hadad king of Syria escaped. He gets away here, and he will be caught in the next section, and what Ahab does with him then is what the chapter is really about.

The prophet comes back the same day, and what he brings is not congratulation but a warning to prepare. God's help today is not a discharge from the war. It is provision for one engagement in a campaign that is still running, and the man who treats a deliverance as the end of the matter has stopped paying attention halfway through the sentence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Syrians decide the LORD is a god of the hills and come back in the spring onto the plain at Aphek, filling the country while Israel looks like two little flocks of goats (vv. 23-27). God answers their theology for his own name's sake, and the army is destroyed (vv. 28-30). Ben-hadad's officers come out in sackcloth, and Ahab calls him my brother and lets him go on a trade agreement (vv. 31-34).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 28 states the motive with unusual bluntness. God does not act because Israel is deserving or even because Israel is desperate. He acts because foreign officers have said in council that the LORD's writ does not run in the valleys.
verseByVerse.examples: What Ahab took for the man God had devoted to destruction was market stalls in Damascus. A soft heart towards what God has condemned, especially when it pays, is not mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servants of the king of Syria said to him, "Their gods are gods of the hills, and so they were stronger than we. But let us fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they. And do this: remove the kings, each from his post, and put commanders in their places, and muster an army like the army that you have lost, horse for horse, and chariot for chariot. Then we will fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they." And he listened to their voice and did so. In the spring, Ben-hadad mustered the Syrians and went up to Aphek to fight against Israel. And the people of Israel were mustered and were provisioned and went against them. The people of Israel encamped before them like two little flocks of goats, but the Syrians filled the country. And a man of God came near and said to the king of Israel, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because the Syrians have said, "The LORD is a god of the hills but he is not a god of the valleys," therefore I will give all this great multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the LORD.'" And they encamped opposite one another seven days. Then on the seventh day the battle was joined. And the people of Israel struck down of the Syrians 100,000 foot soldiers in one day. And the rest fled into the city of Aphek, and the wall fell upon 27,000 men who were left. Ben-hadad also fled and entered an inner chamber in the city. And his servants said to him, "Behold now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel are merciful kings. Let us put sackcloth around our waists and ropes on our heads and go out to the king of Israel. Perhaps he will spare your life." So they tied sackcloth around their waists and put ropes on their heads and went to the king of Israel and said, "Your servant Ben-hadad says, 'Please, let me live.'" And he said, "Does he still live? He is my brother." Now the men were watching for a sign, and they quickly took it up from him and said, "Yes, your brother Ben-hadad." Then he said, "Go and bring him." Then Ben-hadad came out to him, and he caused him to come up into the chariot. And Ben-hadad said to him, "The cities that my father took from your father I will restore, and you may establish bazaars for yourself in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria." And Ahab said, "I will let you go on these terms." So he made a covenant with him and let him go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the ancient world's religion put plainly by men who believed it. Gods have territories. Israel's god is a highland god, effective in the ridges around Samaria; take the fight down onto the flat and his writ runs out.

It is not a stupid theory. It was the ordinary assumption of every nation around them, and it is why treaties were sworn before the gods of both parties, and why armies fought on ground where their own gods were thought to be strong. What the Syrians cannot conceive of is a god with no borders.

The military advice is sound. Replace thirty-two amateur allied kings with professional officers, rebuild the army to the same establishment, and choose your ground. Everything in the plan is competent except the premise underneath it.

The writer's picture of Israel's army, two little flocks of goats, is exact: two small huddles of animals on a hillside, while the opposing army covers the ground from one horizon to the other.

Read the reason God gives, because it is not the one we would have supplied. Not because Israel is outnumbered, or Ahab has improved, but because the Syrians have said: a sentence spoken in a staff meeting in Damascus about the limits of his jurisdiction.

God fights this battle for his name, and the writer states it as the whole of the motive. That ought to reorganise how a Christian prays. The first thing the Lord taught us to ask for is not our bread and not our forgiveness; it is hallowed be your name (Matt. 6:9). God's concern for his own name is not vanity: it is the only thing in the universe worth that much, and every other good thing we want depends on it being true.

The figures are very large, and the Hebrew word behind thousand can also mean a military unit or contingent, so the true count may be smaller than it reads in English. Either way the writer's point stands and does not depend on the arithmetic: the army that filled the country was annihilated, and its king ended up hiding in a back room.

The reputation of Israel's kings abroad is that they are soft. The sackcloth is mourning and the ropes around the head are the posture of a man offering his own neck, and they walk out dressed as condemned men to see whether the rumour is true.

He is my brother, says Ahab of the man who a year ago was demanding his wives and children and promising to leave nothing of Samaria but dust.

The detail about the envoys is superb reporting. They were watching his face for anything they could work with, and the moment the word brother was out of his mouth they had it and repeated it back to him before he could reconsider. Ahab has been read by professionals, and they were right about him.

Look at what he took in exchange. Some border towns returned, and trading rights: the privilege of running Israelite market stalls in the streets of Damascus. God had given him the man, and he sold him for a commercial concession, and thought he had done well.

This has happened before in exactly this shape, and the reader of these books is meant to feel it. Saul was sent to devote Amalek to destruction and came back with Agag alive and the best of the sheep, pleased with himself, and Samuel met him with because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has also rejected you from being king (1 Sam. 15:23). Same command, same exception made for a fellow king, same profitable spoil, and in eight verses the same sentence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 35–43 — While Your Servant Was Busy Here and There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A son of the prophets, refused by one colleague whom a lion then kills, gets himself wounded by another and waits for the king disguised under a bandage (vv. 35-38). He tells of a prisoner he lost while busy here and there, Ahab passes sentence, and the prophet turns it on the king for releasing the man God had devoted to destruction (vv. 39-42). Ahab goes home vexed and sullen (v. 43).
verseByVerse.theology: The method is Nathan's: get the king to judge a case he cannot see himself in, and then tell him whose case it is (2 Sam. 12:1-7).
verseByVerse.examples: The excuse in the parable is the one that indicts everybody: not defeat, but errands.

verseByVerse.quote: And a certain man of the sons of the prophets said to his fellow at the command of the LORD, "Strike me, please." But the man refused to strike him. Then he said to him, "Because you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD, behold, as soon as you have gone from me, a lion shall strike you down." And as soon as he had departed from him, a lion met him and struck him down. Then he found another man and said, "Strike me, please." And the man struck him—struck him and wounded him. So the prophet departed and waited for the king by the way, disguising himself with a bandage over his eyes. And as the king passed, he cried to the king and said, "Your servant went out into the midst of the battle, and behold, a soldier turned and brought a man to me and said, 'Guard this man; if by any means he is missing, your life shall be for his life, or else you shall pay a talent of silver.' And as your servant was busy here and there, he was gone." The king of Israel said to him, "So shall your judgment be; you yourself have decided it." Then he hurried to take the bandage away from his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets. And he said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Because you have let go out of your hand the man whom I had devoted to destruction, therefore your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people.'" And the king of Israel went to his house vexed and sullen and came to Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of the prophets are a company or guild of prophets, mentioned here for the first time and appearing all through Elisha's ministry afterwards. They live together, train together, and are sent on errands like this one.

This is hard, and it should be read as hard. A man is asked by a colleague to injure him, declines, as any decent person would, and is killed by a lion on the road home.

Two things have to be held together. The first is that the request was at the command of the LORD, and the writer says so before the refusal, so the reader knows what the man was refusing. It was not a strange favour asked by a friend; it was a word from God, delivered by a member of his own prophetic company, and the man decided that his own judgment about what was reasonable outranked it. Decency is not the standard by which a word from God is measured.

The second is why the incident is here at all, because the writer has not put it in as an isolated horror. Read what follows. The whole chapter turns on a king who was given a hard command about a captured enemy and did the humane, agreeable, profitable thing instead. Immediately before that parable is told, a man does the humane, agreeable thing instead of what God said, and dies for it. The narrative teaches by rhyme, and Ahab is about to hear the rhyme without recognising his own name in it.

Now the reason for the wound. He needs to look like a soldier who has been in the battle, and the bandage across his face is what keeps the king from recognising a man he would otherwise know.

Remember the disguise, because in two chapters Ahab will put one on himself and it will not save him. The method is Nathan's, and it works the same way it worked on David. Tell the king a case in which he has no personal stake, let his sense of justice do its work, get the sentence out of his own mouth, and then say you are the man (2 Sam. 12:7).

People will pass a clear and severe judgment on their own conduct all day long, provided somebody else's name is on the file. Ahab hears a story about a man entrusted with a prisoner who let him go, and does not hesitate for a second: so shall your judgment be; you yourself have decided it.

There is no claim that the prisoner overpowered him, or that he was outnumbered, ambushed or betrayed. He was busy here and there: occupied with a hundred small legitimate things, none of them wrong, none of them chosen instead of the duty, and at the end of the day the one thing he had actually been given to keep was not there any more.

That is how nearly everything of value is lost. Not in a battle and not by a decision: no man sits down and resolves to lose his children's affection, or his prayer life, or his marriage, or fifteen years. He is busy here and there, and the thing is gone, and he could not tell you the week it went.

The man whom I had devoted to destruction. That is the word herem, the ban: a thing placed under God's sentence and removed from all human use, not to be sold, spared, or turned to profit. Jericho was under it, which is why Achan's silver was fatal, and why Hiel's two sons paid for the gates. Ben-hadad was under it, and Ahab put him in his chariot and traded him for market stalls.

The sentence has two halves and both are collected. Your life shall be for his life is paid at Ramoth-gilead within three years, when an arrow drawn at random finds the seam in his armour (22:34). Your people for his people is paid over the following century, as Hazael of Damascus grinds the northern kingdom down (2 Kgs. 10:32-33; 13:7) until Assyria finishes it.

Hold the words vexed and sullen, because the writer is going to use them again in four verses, when Naboth declines to sell a vineyard: and Ahab went into his house vexed and sullen (21:4), and lay on his bed and turned away his face and would eat no food.

This is the man's settled response to being refused anything, whether it comes from a prophet carrying a death sentence or a farmer protecting his family's land. He does not repent and he does not argue. He goes home in a mood and lies down.

The first time it produces nothing. The second time his wife notices, and asks what is wrong, and a man is stoned to death for a piece of ground.

When was Ben-hadad devoted to destruction? God had given him into Ahab’s hand (v. 28), and Ahab let him go with a treaty. This was a judgment for Israel’s king in that moment, under God’s direct command, not a licence for killing enemies today.
verseByVerse.note: “Devoted to destruction” means set apart to the LORD for destruction (ESV note).

20.theology:
Kindness with an aim (vv. 13, 28). God hands victories to the worst king in the book and says why twice: so that he may know who the LORD is. Prosperity in a wicked man's hands is not a verdict of approval on him; it may be the last hand held out before the reckoning. God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance (Rom. 2:4).

God fights for his name (v. 28). The stated reason for Aphek is not Israel's danger and not Israel's deserving. It is that Syrian officers said in council that his authority stopped at the foothills. He is not a local deity with a jurisdiction, and the second battle is fought to establish it. This is the first petition of the Lord's Prayer given a battlefield: hallowed be your name.

Devoted to destruction, and sold (vv. 34, 42). Ahab exchanged the man under God's ban for border towns and market stalls. Saul had done precisely this with Agag and lost his kingdom for it (1 Sam. 15:23), and Ahab's sentence is paid in two instalments: his life at Ramoth-gilead (22:34), his people under Hazael in the decades that followed (2 Kgs. 10:32-33).

The lion (vv. 35-36). The refusal looks like decency and is disobedience. It is severe and is meant to be, and it is placed as a rhyme with Ahab's own failure to carry out a hard command.

Self-sentencing (vv. 39-40). Put the case at one remove and a man's sense of justice will convict him without hesitation; he only defends the conduct when he knows it is his. Jesus used the same method on the chief priests with the parable of the tenants: asked what the owner should do to men who killed his son, they passed the sentence themselves, and only then saw that he was speaking about them (Matthew 21:40-45). The Son they rejected is the one the parable was about, and his death, which they sentenced, is the death that saves.
20.examples:
Then: Two hundred and thirty-two men from the offices of provincial governors walked out of a besieged city at noon, in full view, against thirty-three kingdoms whose commander was too drunk to tell an embassy from an attack, and each one killed the man in front of him.

Now: Two things this chapter will not let go. The first is verse 40, your servant was busy here and there. Name what you were given to keep, and then account for yesterday, not as the price of getting back into God's favour but because there is a way back: the Son kept perfectly what the Father gave him (I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost, John 17:12), his keeping is counted to those who confess what they let slip (1 John 1:9), and the Holy Spirit who dwells in us is given to guard what we were entrusted with (2 Tim. 1:14). The second is Ahab's he is my brother. Mercy that costs nothing and pays a dividend is not mercy; it is a trade, and this one was struck with a man God had put under sentence, for the right to run market stalls in a foreign city.

21.title: Naboth's Vineyard
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.<sup>2</sup>And after this Ahab said to Naboth, "Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a vegetable garden, because it is near my house, and I will give you a better vineyard for it; or, if it seems good to you, I will give you its value in money."<sup>3</sup>But Naboth said to Ahab, "The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers."<sup>4</sup>And Ahab went into his house vexed and sullen because of what Naboth the Jezreelite had said to him, for he had said, "I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers." And he lay down on his bed and turned away his face and would eat no food.<sup>5</sup>But Jezebel his wife came to him and said to him, "Why is your spirit so vexed that you eat no food?"<sup>6</sup>And he said to her, "Because I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and said to him, 'Give me your vineyard for money, or else, if it please you, I will give you another vineyard for it.' And he answered, 'I will not give you my vineyard.'"<sup>7</sup>And Jezebel his wife said to him, "Do you now govern Israel? Arise and eat bread and let your heart be cheerful; I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite."<sup>8</sup>So she wrote letters in Ahab's name and sealed them with his seal, and she sent the letters to the elders and the leaders who lived with Naboth in his city.<sup>9</sup>And she wrote in the letters, "Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth at the head of the people.<sup>10</sup>And set two worthless men opposite him, and let them bring a charge against him, saying, 'You have cursed God and the king.' Then take him out and stone him to death."<sup>11</sup>And the men of his city, the elders and the leaders who lived in his city, did as Jezebel had sent word to them. As it was written in the letters that she had sent to them,<sup>12</sup>they proclaimed a fast and set Naboth at the head of the people.<sup>13</sup>And the two worthless men came in and sat opposite him. And the worthless men brought a charge against Naboth in the presence of the people, saying, "Naboth cursed God and the king." So they took him outside the city and stoned him to death with stones.<sup>14</sup>Then they sent to Jezebel, saying, "Naboth has been stoned; he is dead."<sup>15</sup>As soon as Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, Jezebel said to Ahab, "Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he refused to give you for money, for Naboth is not alive, but dead."<sup>16</sup>And as soon as Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, Ahab arose to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, to take possession of it.<sup>17</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,<sup>18</sup>"Arise, go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria; behold, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, where he has gone to take possession.<sup>19</sup>And you shall say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Have you killed and also taken possession?"' And you shall say to him, 'Thus says the LORD: "In the place where dogs licked up the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick your own blood."'"<sup>20</sup>Ahab said to Elijah, "Have you found me, O my enemy?" He answered, "I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do what is evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>21</sup>Behold, I will bring disaster upon you. I will utterly burn you up, and will cut off from Ahab every male, bond or free, in Israel.<sup>22</sup>And I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah, for the anger to which you have provoked me, and because you have made Israel to sin.<sup>23</sup>And of Jezebel the LORD also said, 'The dogs shall eat Jezebel within the walls of Jezreel.'<sup>24</sup>Anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the open country the birds of the heavens shall eat."<sup>25</sup>(There was none who sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife incited.<sup>26</sup>He acted very abominably in going after idols, as the Amorites had done, whom the LORD cast out before the people of Israel.)<sup>27</sup>And when Ahab heard those words, he tore his clothes and put sackcloth on his flesh and fasted and lay in sackcloth and went about dejectedly.<sup>28</sup>And the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying,<sup>29</sup>"Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself before me, I will not bring the disaster in his days; but in his son's days I will bring the disaster upon his house."
21.overview:
A king wants the field next to his summer palace for a kitchen garden and makes a perfectly fair offer: a better vineyard, or its full value in silver. The owner cannot accept, because the land is held in trust from God. Naboth is not haggling; he is telling the chief magistrate of the covenant that what is being asked of him is not lawful.

So the king goes to bed and turns away his face, and when his wife asks what is wrong he leaves the covenant out of his answer. She writes letters in his name and has Naboth killed by his own neighbours in a procedure that keeps every rule while breaking the law's whole purpose.

Elijah meets Ahab walking the dead man's vines, with a charge in which both verbs are in the second person. Then comes the writer's own verdict, the harshest in the book, and then the thing nobody expects: sackcloth next to the skin, and God stopping Elijah to say have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? (v. 29).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Inheritance of My Fathers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab offers Naboth a fair price for the vineyard beside his palace, and Naboth refuses because it is the inheritance of his fathers, which the law did not let him sell (vv. 1-3). The king goes home vexed and sullen and will not eat, and gives Jezebel an edited account of the refusal; she answers with a political theory in a question (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Jezebel's question is the collision the whole book has been building towards. In Sidon a king is the law; in Israel the king is under it, and Ahab is the officer charged with enforcing the very statute he is asking Naboth to break.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what he does with Naboth's answer: he drops the inheritance of my fathers when he reports it. How we tell our grievances shapes what others will do about them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria. And after this Ahab said to Naboth, "Give me your vineyard, that I may have it for a vegetable garden, because it is near my house, and I will give you a better vineyard for it; or, if it seems good to you, I will give you its value in money." But Naboth said to Ahab, "The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers." And Ahab went into his house vexed and sullen because of what Naboth the Jezreelite had said to him, for he had said, "I will not give you the inheritance of my fathers." And he lay down on his bed and turned away his face and would eat no food. But Jezebel his wife came to him and said to him, "Why is your spirit so vexed that you eat no food?" And he said to her, "Because I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and said to him, 'Give me your vineyard for money, or else, if it please you, I will give you another vineyard for it.' And he answered, 'I will not give you my vineyard.'" And Jezebel his wife said to him, "Do you now govern Israel? Arise and eat bread and let your heart be cheerful; I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jezreel is Ahab's second residence, in the wide fertile valley to the north, where he drove his chariot at the end of chapter 18 with Elijah running ahead of him through the rain. Next to the palace wall is a working vineyard belonging to a man named Naboth.

Take the offer seriously before condemning it. He does not seize the land. He asks, and offers a choice of terms: a better vineyard in exchange, or full market value in silver. That is more decent than most kings in that part of the world would have troubled to be. Ahab is not being a tyrant here; he is being a neighbour with money.

Only notice what he wants it for: a vegetable garden, a kitchen plot of herbs and greens close to the house. He intends to pull out a vineyard for salad.

A vineyard is not a crop; it is a lifetime. The terraces have to be cut and the stones cleared and the vines planted and staked, and the law would not even let the owner eat the fruit for the first three years and gave the fourth harvest to God (Lev. 19:23-25). What is growing on that slope was planted by a man's father or grandfather and tended through droughts by people whose graves are in sight of it.

Everything in the chapter depends on Naboth's answer in verse 3, and it is easy to hear it as stubbornness or as a man holding out for a better price. It is neither.

When Israel came into the land it was divided by lot under Joshua, tribe by tribe, clan by clan, family by family, and the allocation was not a gift of property so much as a tenancy from God. The law states it in as many words: the land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me (Lev. 25:23). Ground could be leased when a family fell on hard times, but it came back at the Jubilee, and an inheritance was not to pass out of the tribe at all (Num. 36:7).

So Naboth is not refusing to sell. He is explaining that the thing being asked of him is not in his power. The boundary stones on that slope were set when his family drew their lot centuries ago; the deed-holder is God; and his sons are the next tenants. The LORD forbid is not an exclamation of annoyance. It is the legal ground stated in one phrase.

Consider who he is saying it to. The king of Israel is the one man in the country charged with knowing this law, because Deuteronomy requires the king to write out his own copy of it in a book and read in it all the days of his life so that his heart is not lifted up above his brothers (Deut. 17:18-20). The chief magistrate of the covenant has just asked a farmer to break the covenant, and the farmer has had to tell him so.

Vexed and sullen are the words the writer used four verses ago, when a prophet with a bandage over his eyes told him that his life was forfeit (20:43). A man told he is under sentence of death and a man told he cannot buy a field react identically.

Then the picture, set out with something close to contempt. The most powerful man between Damascus and Egypt, who has just broken Ben-hadad twice, lies on his bed with his face turned away and will not eat, because a farmer said no to him.

She asks him what is wrong. It is a wife's question, put kindly enough, and she is the only person in the palace who asks it.

Everything that follows runs through his answer. A man lying in the dark with a grievance is at his most dangerous when somebody finally asks about it, because the version he gives is the version that will be acted on, and he will give it to whoever asks, in the shape most likely to get him what he wants. Choose carefully who hears your grievance in that condition. Some people will tell you to get up and eat; this one offers to fetch the vineyard.

Compare the two accounts. What Naboth actually said was the inheritance of my fathers. What Ahab reports to his wife is I will not give you my vineyard. He has taken out the covenant, God and the law of the land, and left a man refusing to sell a field.

He has done this before. When he came home from Carmel he left out the fire falling from heaven (19:1). Twice now he has handed his wife a version of events with God removed from it, and both times she acts on it and a knife comes out.

Whether he did it consciously is beside the point. A man who cannot bear to repeat the religious reason for his defeat, to the one person in the house who will do something about it, has already decided how he wants the story to end.

There is the whole quarrel of the book in one sneering question: do you now govern Israel? She is not being merely cruel; she is stating the political theory she was raised in. In Sidon, where her father was king, sovereignty means exactly this: what the king wants is what happens, and a monarch who is told no by a subject with a title deed is not a monarch. She genuinely cannot see what the difficulty is.

Israel was founded on the opposite principle, one of the most far-reaching political ideas in the Old Testament: the king is under the law, not over it. He answers to a covenant he did not write, and a farmer with a vineyard can stand in front of him and say the LORD forbid, and be right.

Jezebel is about to demonstrate what the other theory costs, and she will do it without breaking a single rule.
verseByVerse.note: Selling ancestral land was against Israel’s law.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jezebel writes in the king's name and under his seal to Naboth's own town, telling the elders to proclaim a fast, produce two false witnesses to a charge of cursing God and the king, and stone him (vv. 8-10). They do it, report his death, and Ahab goes down to take the vineyard (vv. 11-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Every step is legally correct: two witnesses (Deut. 17:6), a genuine capital charge (Lev. 24:16), execution outside the city (Lev. 24:14). Jezebel does not break the law's procedures; she operates them. Christians have long seen in Naboth a dark preview of a later trial: a righteous man condemned by false witnesses on a charge of blasphemy and put to death outside the city (Mark 14:56-64; Hebrews 13:12), as Stephen was after him (Acts 6:11-13; 7:58). The difference is that Jesus went knowingly, and the verdict men passed on him in wickedness God had appointed for our pardon.
verseByVerse.examples: It took the neighbours. Not one of the elders of his own town is recorded as objecting. Great wrongs usually need many small consents, and the courage to refuse one is rarely wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: So she wrote letters in Ahab's name and sealed them with his seal, and she sent the letters to the elders and the leaders who lived with Naboth in his city. And she wrote in the letters, "Proclaim a fast, and set Naboth at the head of the people. And set two worthless men opposite him, and let them bring a charge against him, saying, 'You have cursed God and the king.' Then take him out and stone him to death." And the men of his city, the elders and the leaders who lived in his city, did as Jezebel had sent word to them. As it was written in the letters that she had sent to them, they proclaimed a fast and set Naboth at the head of the people. And the two worthless men came in and sat opposite him. And the worthless men brought a charge against Naboth in the presence of the people, saying, "Naboth cursed God and the king." So they took him outside the city and stoned him to death with stones. Then they sent to Jezebel, saying, "Naboth has been stoned; he is dead." As soon as Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, Jezebel said to Ahab, "Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he refused to give you for money, for Naboth is not alive, but dead." And as soon as Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, Ahab arose to go down to the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, to take possession of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer does not tell us whether he handed it over or she took it, and there is no point guessing. What the detail establishes is that a royal seal is not a thing that goes missing without the king knowing. Whatever Ahab did or did not say, he stayed in bed while his seal went out on letters, and he never afterwards asks a single question about how the field came free.

Read the instructions with the law open beside them, because the most chilling thing about this plan is that it keeps the forms of the law at every point.

A fast is proclaimed, which in a town meant that some trouble was believed to lie on the community and was to be searched out. Naboth is seated at the head of the people, in the place of honour, both because he is a man of standing and because a fall is further from a height. Two men are produced, because the law will not convict on one: only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established (Deut. 17:6; 19:15). The charge is a genuine capital offence: blasphemy carried death by stoning (Lev. 24:16), and cursing the king made it treason as well, so that both God and the crown are named as injured parties. And the sentence is carried out outside the city, exactly as the law directs (Lev. 24:14).

That is the form wickedness takes wherever a society is orderly enough to have procedures. The crude tyrant sends soldiers; the sophisticated one sends paperwork. The fast was properly proclaimed, the witnesses duly sworn, the charge capital, the venue correct, the verdict unanimous, and a man was murdered for a vegetable patch.

The writer says twice that the elders lived in his city, and that repetition is the accusation. These are not strangers or professional enforcers sent up from Samaria. They are his neighbours, who knew his father, watched his sons grow and bought his wine. A letter arrived from the capital, and without delay they convened a solemn assembly, listened to two men they knew to be lying, and stoned him on the edge of their own town.

An evil like this cannot be done by a queen a day's journey away. It requires a town.

Not one word of Naboth's is recorded. He said his sentence in verse 3 and after that the chapter never lets him speak again. He sits in the seat of honour and listens to two men he probably knows by name explain that he has blasphemed, and the last thing he sees is the faces of the men he grew up among.

Scripture supplies one further detail elsewhere, and it should not be withheld from a reader here. Years later, when Jehu throws a body onto this same ground, he remembers the oracle as concerning the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons (2 Kgs. 9:26). The children were killed too.

Of course they were, because otherwise the whole exercise was pointless. Kill the father and the land passes to the heir; the family keeps the vineyard and the crown gains nothing. For the ground to fall to the king, the line has to end. That is why a man who would not sell an inheritance to a neighbour lost his sons the same day, and it is the coldest arithmetic in the book of Kings.

The council's report back to the palace is a brief notice of completion.

Which he refused to give you for money. She cannot resist it. Even in the moment of delivering the prize she has to remind him of the humiliation, which tells you a good deal about the marriage.

He gets up and goes, and asks nothing: not how Naboth died, not who gave evidence, not why a healthy landowner is suddenly dead and his field suddenly available. He had been lying on a bed refusing food, and now he is walking through the vines working out where the beds will go.

People often read this chapter as though Jezebel were the murderer and Ahab merely a weak man who let her. The next section is God's own assessment, and it does not agree. There is a kind of ignorance that is a moral achievement: carefully maintained, expensively defended, and chosen. Ahab knew that Naboth would sooner die than sell. And then Naboth died, and he did not ask.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “cursed” is literally “blessed”, probably a scribal way of avoiding writing “curse God.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–29 — Have You Killed and Also Taken Possession?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elijah meets Ahab in the dead man's vineyard with the charge and the sentence, and Ahab calls him his enemy (vv. 17-20). The whole house is condemned, and the writer adds the harshest verdict in the book (vv. 21-26). Then Ahab puts on sackcloth and fasts, and God points it out to Elijah and defers the disaster to his son's days (vv. 27-29).
verseByVerse.theology: The charge names both verbs and assigns both to him. He did not write the letters or throw a stone, and the word of the LORD says you have killed.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 29 is the surprise of the chapter. If God answers a repentance that shallow, no reader need wonder what he will give to the real thing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying, "Arise, go down to meet Ahab king of Israel, who is in Samaria; behold, he is in the vineyard of Naboth, where he has gone to take possession. And you shall say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Have you killed and also taken possession?"' And you shall say to him, 'Thus says the LORD: "In the place where dogs licked up the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick your own blood."'" Ahab said to Elijah, "Have you found me, O my enemy?" He answered, "I have found you, because you have sold yourself to do what is evil in the sight of the LORD. Behold, I will bring disaster upon you. I will utterly burn you up, and will cut off from Ahab every male, bond or free, in Israel. And I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and like the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah, for the anger to which you have provoked me, and because you have made Israel to sin. And of Jezebel the LORD also said, 'The dogs shall eat Jezebel within the walls of Jezreel.' Anyone belonging to Ahab who dies in the city the dogs shall eat, and anyone of his who dies in the open country the birds of the heavens shall eat." (There was none who sold himself to do what was evil in the sight of the LORD like Ahab, whom Jezebel his wife incited. He acted very abominably in going after idols, as the Amorites had done, whom the LORD cast out before the people of Israel.) And when Ahab heard those words, he tore his clothes and put sackcloth on his flesh and fasted and lay in sackcloth and went about dejectedly. And the word of the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite, saying, "Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Because he has humbled himself before me, I will not bring the disaster in his days; but in his son's days I will bring the disaster upon his house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The meeting is arranged with care. Not in the throne room or at the city gate: Ahab is walking between the rows of a dead man's vines, on ground owned that morning by a family that no longer exists, measuring out where the herbs will go. He looks up, and there is Elijah.

The last time these two men stood together was in the rain on the road to Jezreel, with the prophet running ahead of the chariot like a herald. Elijah has been at Horeb since, and out of the story entirely, and the word that brings him back is a murder in a garden.

The charge is short, and both verbs are in the second person. Ahab did not write the letters, swear false testimony, throw a stone or, so far as we are told, give a single order, and the word of the LORD says that he killed him. The man who arranged not to know is charged as the man who did it, and the taking of the field is named in the same breath as the taking of the life, because they were one act.

Have you found me, O my enemy? That is what Ahab calls the man who brings him the word of God, and it is the most revealing sentence he ever speaks. He has not once in four chapters said that Elijah was wrong. When a man has stopped disputing whether the word is true and started resenting the person who carries it, the argument he is having is not with a prophet.

The reply, you have sold yourself, is the language of a slave sale: a man putting himself on the block and taking the price. Ahab bought a vegetable garden, and the currency he paid in was himself.

Every male, bond or free means every last one, from the head of the house down to the slave who sweeps the yard, with nobody standing outside the category. And utterly burn you up is the language already used of Jeroboam's house (14:10): a house not merely punished but taken out of the record.

The formula has been used twice already in this book: Jeroboam's house and Baasha's house were both destroyed, and each time the writer recorded the oracle first and the slaughter afterwards. Ahab is now told that he is third in a series, in the same words, with the same outcome.

To be left unburied was, in that world, the last indignity a body could suffer, and dogs in an ancient city were not pets but half-wild scavengers around the middens. Jezebel will be thrown from a window in Jezreel some fourteen years later, and when men go out to bury her there is almost nothing to bury (2 Kgs. 9:30-37).

A word about verse 19, because a careful reader will check it and find that it does not appear to land where it was aimed. Elijah says the dogs will lick Ahab's blood in the place where they licked Naboth's, which is Jezreel; and 22:38 reports that they licked it at the pool of Samaria. The chapter itself supplies the explanation ten verses further on, where the sentence is expressly deferred out of Ahab's own days into his son's. And the Jezreel half of it is collected exactly: Jehu has Joram's body thrown on the plot of ground belonging to Naboth the Jezreelite, and quotes this oracle as he does it (2 Kgs. 9:25-26). The word did not miss. It was paid in two instalments, and the reason for the delay is written into the text that records it.

The writer steps out from behind the narrative to deliver his own verdict (v. 25), the severest he passes on anybody in these two books.

Notice how the clause about Jezebel functions. Whom Jezebel his wife incited is not an excuse offered on Ahab's behalf; it is part of the indictment of Ahab. The verse says that nobody ever sold himself as he did, and then explains that he let himself be driven to it by his wife, which is one more thing against him and not a mitigation.

The comparison at the end is the sharpest cut of all. He behaved as the Amorites had done, whom the LORD cast out, that is, like the people whose wickedness was so complete that God emptied the land of them and gave it to Israel. The king of Israel has become the reason the previous tenants were evicted.

Nobody expects verse 27, and it is put immediately after the harshest paragraph in the book so that nobody can miss the collision.

The detail is exact: sackcloth on his flesh, which is to say next to the skin, not worn over his clothes as a public display, and he sleeps in it. He tears his robes, he stops eating, and he walks about the palace like a man at a funeral.

Have you seen? God calls Elijah's attention to it, as if to make sure he did not look away. The prophet who has just delivered an extermination order is asked to notice that the condemned man is in sackcloth, and to notice it approvingly.

Be honest about what this repentance is and is not. It is not saving faith. Nothing is restored: the vineyard is not given back, the perjurers are not prosecuted, the elders of Jezreel are not called to account, Jezebel keeps her prophets and her table, and Naboth's family is still dead. Before long Ahab will imprison a prophet for telling him the truth and ride to a battle God warned him not to fight. This is a frightened man reacting to a death sentence, not a converted one.

Yet God answers it, with a real mercy and a real deferral of a real judgment.

He does the same at Nineveh, where a pagan city fasts on the strength of one sentence and God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them (Jon. 3:10), and he states the principle plainly through Jeremiah: if a nation under sentence turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it (Jer. 18:7-8).

This holds two things. The first is enormous encouragement, and it runs from lesser to greater. If God pays that much attention to the shabby, self-interested, unfinished humbling of the worst man in the book, enough to stop Elijah and point at it, then there is no serious question about what he will do with a repentance that is genuine. The verse exists to stop anybody concluding that he is too far gone to bother turning round. And the mercy that deferred Ahab's sentence for a few years is small beside the mercy offered in Christ, where the sentence is not postponed but borne, and the one who turns is not given time but forgiven (Romans 8:1).

The second is a warning, and it is in the last clause. But in his son's days. The judgment was postponed, not cancelled; and because it was postponed, it fell on people who had not yet been born when the letters went out. Joram will die on Naboth's plot of ground with Jehu quoting this oracle over the body, and seventy of Ahab's sons will have their heads sent to Jezreel in baskets (2 Kgs. 10:7-8).

Ahab got what he asked for on both counts. He asked for the vineyard and he got it, for about three years. He asked, in sackcloth, for time, and he got that too.

Is it just for a whole house to be destroyed for a father’s sin? Human courts were forbidden to punish children for their fathers (Deut 24:16). This was God’s own judgment on a royal house that led the nation into idolatry, and its sons carried on the same sins. God as Judge may take any life, and he never punishes the innocent as guilty (Ezek 18:20).

21.theology:
Why Naboth cannot sell (v. 3). The allotment under Joshua was a tenancy, not a freehold: the land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine. For you are strangers and sojourners with me (Lev. 25:23), and an inheritance was not to pass out of the family or the tribe (Num. 36:7). The refusal is a legal answer, not a stubborn one, and it is given to the one man in the kingdom required to write out the law in his own hand and read it all his days (Deut. 17:18-20).

Do you now govern Israel? (v. 7). Jezebel's sneer is a whole political philosophy. In Sidon the king is the law; in Israel the king is under it, and a farmer with a title deed can stand in front of him and be right. That single idea, that sovereign power answers to a covenant it did not write, is among the most consequential things the Old Testament gave the world, and this chapter is what happens when a throne rejects it.

Lawful murder (vv. 9-13). Nothing in the file would fail an audit. Crude tyranny sends soldiers; developed wickedness sends paperwork, and it needs a town to carry it out. Twice the writer says the men who did it lived in his city.

The version with God taken out (v. 6, cf. 19:1). A man who edits God out of his account of events has already decided how he would like them to end.

Arranged ignorance is not innocence (v. 19). He wrote nothing, swore nothing, threw nothing, and is charged in the second person with the murder.

Deferred, not cancelled (v. 29). God points out the sackcloth to Elijah and postpones the sentence, and the repentance is plainly shallow: nothing restored, nobody prosecuted, and a prophet in prison soon after. He answers it anyway, as he answered Nineveh (Jon. 3:10) on the principle he states in Jer. 18:7-8. The encouragement runs from lesser to greater: if he honours that, the question of what he does with real repentance is settled. The warning is in the last clause: the disaster fell in his son's days, on people not yet born when the letters went out.
21.examples:
Then: The elders and leaders of a small town opened a letter from the capital, proclaimed a solemn fast, seated a neighbour they had known all his life in the place of honour, listened to two men they knew were lying, and stoned him, and the paperwork was in perfect order.

Now: Three things. First, arranged ignorance. Ahab asked no questions because he already knew the answers, and heaven charges him with the murder in the second person. Not knowing is a defence only when the not-knowing was not chosen, and most of us can tell the difference in our own case if we are honest. Second, the edited report. Twice he tells his wife what happened with God removed from it. Notice what you leave out when you describe a difficulty to the person most likely to solve it for you. Neither of these is cured by hiding better; the cure is to bring it into the light, where the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7), and to ask the Spirit of truth to show us what we would rather not see (John 16:13). Third, verse 29, which is aimed at anybody who believes he has gone too far to turn round. God stopped a prophet in the street to point out the sackcloth on the worst man in the book, and shortened the sentence of a man who never gave the vineyard back. Whatever else that verse means, it disposes of the idea that he is reluctant.

22.title: Micaiah and the Death of Ahab
22.text: <sup>1</sup>For three years Syria and Israel continued without war.<sup>2</sup>But in the third year Jehoshaphat the king of Judah came down to the king of Israel.<sup>3</sup>And the king of Israel said to his servants, "Do you know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us, and we keep quiet and do not take it out of the hand of the king of Syria?"<sup>4</sup>And he said to Jehoshaphat, "Will you go with me to battle at Ramoth-gilead?" And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses."<sup>5</sup>And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Inquire first for the word of the LORD."<sup>6</sup>Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, about four hundred men, and said to them, "Shall I go to battle against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I refrain?" And they said, "Go up, for the Lord will give it into the hand of the king."<sup>7</sup>But Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?"<sup>8</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD, Micaiah the son of Imlah, but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but evil." And Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so."<sup>9</sup>Then the king of Israel summoned an officer and said, "Bring quickly Micaiah the son of Imlah."<sup>10</sup>Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, arrayed in their robes, at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them.<sup>11</sup>And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says the LORD, 'With these you shall push the Syrians until they are destroyed.'"<sup>12</sup>And all the prophets prophesied so and said, "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph; the LORD will give it into the hand of the king."<sup>13</sup>And the messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, "Behold, the words of the prophets with one accord are favorable to the king. Let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak favorably."<sup>14</sup>But Micaiah said, "As the LORD lives, what the LORD says to me, that I will speak."<sup>15</sup>And when he had come to the king, the king said to him, "Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall we refrain?" And he answered him, "Go up and triumph; the LORD will give it into the hand of the king."<sup>16</sup>But the king said to him, "How many times shall I make you swear that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of the LORD?"<sup>17</sup>And he said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. And the LORD said, 'These have no master; let each return to his home in peace.'"<sup>18</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?"<sup>19</sup>And Micaiah said, "Therefore hear the word of the LORD: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him on his right hand and on his left;<sup>20</sup>and the LORD said, 'Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?' And one said one thing, and another said another.<sup>21</sup>Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD, saying, 'I will entice him.'<sup>22</sup>And the LORD said to him, 'By what means?' And he said, 'I will go out, and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And he said, 'You are to entice him, and you shall succeed; go out and do so.'<sup>23</sup>Now therefore behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; the LORD has declared disaster for you."<sup>24</sup>Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "How did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?"<sup>25</sup>And Micaiah said, "Behold, you shall see on that day when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself."<sup>26</sup>And the king of Israel said, "Seize Micaiah, and take him back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king's son,<sup>27</sup>and say, 'Thus says the king, "Put this fellow in prison and feed him meager rations of bread and water, until I come in peace."'"<sup>28</sup>And Micaiah said, "If you return in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me." And he said, "Hear, all you peoples!"<sup>29</sup>So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.<sup>30</sup>And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your robes." And the king of Israel disguised himself and went into battle.<sup>31</sup>Now the king of Syria had commanded the thirty-two captains of his chariots, "Fight with neither small nor great, but only with the king of Israel."<sup>32</sup>And when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "It is surely the king of Israel." So they turned to fight against him. And Jehoshaphat cried out.<sup>33</sup>And when the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.<sup>34</sup>But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and carry me out of the battle, for I am wounded."<sup>35</sup>And the battle continued that day, and the king was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, until at evening he died. And the blood of the wound flowed into the bottom of the chariot.<sup>36</sup>And about sunset a cry went through the army, "Every man to his city, and every man to his country!"<sup>37</sup>So the king died, and was brought to Samaria. And they buried the king in Samaria.<sup>38</sup>And they washed the chariot by the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked up his blood, and the prostitutes washed themselves in it, according to the word of the LORD that he had spoken.<sup>39</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Ahab and all that he did, and the ivory house that he built and all the cities that he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?<sup>40</sup>So Ahab slept with his fathers, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.<sup>41</sup>Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.<sup>42</sup>Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.<sup>43</sup>He walked in all the way of Asa his father. He did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD. Yet the high places were not taken away, and the people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places.<sup>44</sup>Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel.<sup>45</sup>Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, and his might that he showed, and how he warred, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?<sup>46</sup>And from the land he exterminated the remnant of the male cult prostitutes who remained in the days of his father Asa.<sup>47</sup>There was no king in Edom; a deputy was king.<sup>48</sup>Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they did not go, for the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber.<sup>49</sup>Then Ahaziah the son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, "Let my servants go with your servants in the ships," but Jehoshaphat was not willing.<sup>50</sup>And Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place.<sup>51</sup>Ahaziah the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned two years over Israel.<sup>52</sup>He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father and in the way of his mother and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin.<sup>53</sup>He served Baal and worshiped him and provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger in every way that his father had done.
22.overview:
Three years of peace end (the peace Ahab bought by releasing a man God had devoted to destruction), and Judah's king comes north on a state visit that Chronicles tells us was sealed by a marriage. Ahab wants Ramoth-gilead back, and his case is good. Jehoshaphat commits his kingdom and only then asks for the word of the LORD.

Four hundred prophets give the answer the king wants. Micaiah, the one prophet Ahab hates for never being favourable, is fetched from a cell, hands back the party line until Ahab demands the truth, and then gives it: a leaderless flock, and a throne room where a spirit volunteers to be a lie in four hundred mouths.

Ahab believes it enough to take precautions and not enough to obey. His disguise works, and an arrow drawn by a man aiming at nobody finds the one gap in his harness. Then Judah's reign is summed up, Ahab's son takes the northern throne, and the book stops in the middle of the story.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab proposes a joint campaign for Ramoth-gilead, and Jehoshaphat pledges everything before he asks for the word of the LORD (vv. 1-5). Four hundred prophets give the answer the king wants, Ahab admits there is one prophet of the LORD and that he hates him (vv. 6-8), and Zedekiah acts out a victory with iron horns (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody in this section asks whether God is sending them into battle. They ask only whether the answer is favourable, and the order of verses 4 and 5 shows why: the commitment came first and the question afterwards.
verseByVerse.examples: Unanimity is presented here as a warning rather than a credential. Four hundred men say the same thing with a piece of theatre to back it, and one man in a cell turns out to be right.

verseByVerse.quote: For three years Syria and Israel continued without war. But in the third year Jehoshaphat the king of Judah came down to the king of Israel. And the king of Israel said to his servants, "Do you know that Ramoth-gilead belongs to us, and we keep quiet and do not take it out of the hand of the king of Syria?" And he said to Jehoshaphat, "Will you go with me to battle at Ramoth-gilead?" And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses." And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "Inquire first for the word of the LORD." Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, about four hundred men, and said to them, "Shall I go to battle against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I refrain?" And they said, "Go up, for the Lord will give it into the hand of the king." But Jehoshaphat said, "Is there not here another prophet of the LORD of whom we may inquire?" And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD, Micaiah the son of Imlah, but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but evil." And Jehoshaphat said, "Let not the king say so." Then the king of Israel summoned an officer and said, "Bring quickly Micaiah the son of Imlah." Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting on their thrones, arrayed in their robes, at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them. And Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made for himself horns of iron and said, "Thus says the LORD, 'With these you shall push the Syrians until they are destroyed.'" And all the prophets prophesied so and said, "Go up to Ramoth-gilead and triumph; the LORD will give it into the hand of the king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three years of quiet, and the reader knows what they cost.

Ahab bought this peace when he had Ben-hadad in his hands and let him go, and took border towns and market stalls in Damascus for a man God had placed under sentence. A prophet with a bandage over his eyes told him what the receipt would say: your life shall be for his life (20:42). The three years are the interval between the purchase and the bill.

Since the kingdom tore in two there has been no friendship between Jerusalem and Samaria at all: verse after verse in this book records war between them, and the rest record silence. Now the king of Judah comes north on a state visit to the house of Ahab.

The book of Chronicles supplies what Kings leaves out, and it changes the colour of everything that follows: Jehoshaphat had great riches and honor, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab (2 Chron. 18:1). His son Jehoram married Ahab's daughter Athaliah. That woman will one day hear that her son is dead and rise up and destroy all the royal family of the house of David, and for six years the whole line of promise will hang on one baby hidden in a bedroom in the temple (2 Kgs. 11:1-3).

Everything God had sworn to David comes within one infant of extinction, and the connection that made it possible is formed here, by a good king, over dinner.

Ramoth-gilead is east of the Jordan, in the high country Elijah came from, and it is Israelite territory. More than that, Ben-hadad had specifically undertaken to hand back the cities his father had taken, as the price of his life (20:34), and three years later he has not done it. Ahab has been cheated by a man he spared, and he says so with some feeling: we keep quiet, and do nothing, and it is ours.

The grievance is legitimate. The war is still the wrong war: a just cause is not a commission, and nobody in this chapter ever asks whether God is sending them.

Read those two verses in the order the writer put them, because the order is the whole point.

First: I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses. That is not agreement in principle; it is the total commitment of a kingdom, its army and its cavalry, given without qualification to a man he is newly allied with.

Only after everything has been promised does he say inquire first.

Jehoshaphat is a genuinely good man (the writer will say so plainly in a few verses), and this is exactly how genuinely good men come to grief. The decision was made in the warmth of a state visit and a family connection, and the seeking of God's mind is added afterwards as a covering, in a room where four hundred employees are waiting to be asked.

Ask yourself honestly how many of the prayers you have offered over a major decision were offered before the decision was made. Once you have said my horses as your horses, you are no longer inquiring; you are looking for permission. Asking first is not a hurdle set by a reluctant God. It is the trust of children who already belong to him, whose Father has promised to lead them by his Spirit and his word (Romans 8:14; Psalm 32:8).

The four hundred are on the payroll and produced on demand, and they give a unanimous answer to a question whose preferred outcome everybody in the room already knew.

Now look at one word, because your English Bible has preserved something the Hebrew does and it is easy to walk straight past it. Where the ESV prints LORD in small capitals it is translating the covenant name, the name God gave at the bush. Where it prints Lord in ordinary letters it is translating adonai, which simply means master, and which any nation could say of any god.

Do not make more of it than it will carry: the same four hundred men use the covenant name six verses later (v. 12), and one of them claims the Spirit of the LORD to Micaiah's face (v. 24). These are not prophets of Baal; they are professional prophets of Israel's God, or of a version of him domesticated for court use. But at the decisive moment, asked the decisive question, the answer they gave used the word that could have meant anybody's god.

Jehoshaphat has just heard four hundred men answer, and he asks whether there is a prophet of the LORD in the building. He does not say they were wrong. He does not accuse anybody. He sits through the whole performance and then asks, with as much politeness as the question allows, whether there is anyone here who actually speaks for God. Whatever it was that he heard, he heard it.

Ahab knows there is a real one. He can name him, and he knows where he lives, and he can distinguish him instantly from the four hundred he has just consulted, which means he also knows exactly what the four hundred are. There is no confusion in Ahab about who tells the truth.

His objection is not that Micaiah is wrong. In four chapters Ahab has never once said that a word brought to him was false. His objection is that it is unfavourable. I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me. It is the same note as have you found me, O my enemy? (21:20): a man who has stopped arguing with the message and now simply dislikes the messenger.

Jehoshaphat's reply is the measure of him. Let not the king say so. Six words of mild embarrassment, and then he says nothing more, and goes to the war.

Bring quickly. He has just finished explaining that he hates the man, and he sends for him at once, because his guest asked. Ahab is managing the room. He will not act on Micaiah's word and he will not be seen refusing to hear it in front of the king of Judah.

Stand in the square and look at it. A threshing floor is a wide circle of packed earth outside the gate, the one flat public space a walled town has, and everybody's business is done there. Two thrones have been carried out and set up on it. Two kings are sitting in their state robes in the open air, and in front of them four hundred men are prophesying at once, in public, with the whole city watching.

It is not a consultation but a rally.

Here is the uncomfortable part: Zedekiah is quoting Scripture. Moses blessed Joseph with exactly this image: his horns are the horns of a wild ox; with them he shall gore the peoples, all of them, to the ends of the earth (Deut. 33:17). Zedekiah has taken a genuine word of God about the northern tribes and staged it as a promise about tomorrow's battle.

That is how false assurance is normally built: not out of nothing, but out of real verses, correctly quoted, aimed at a situation they were never about.

Unanimity is a comfort and it is not evidence. Everyone in that square agreed, and every one of them was wrong, and the only man who was right was still walking up the road under escort.
verseByVerse.note: Ramoth-gilead was a fortress east of the Jordan.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–28 — What the LORD Says to Me, That I Will Speak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Coached to agree, Micaiah gives the four hundred's line until Ahab demands the truth (vv. 13-16). Then he gives it: a leaderless flock (v. 17), and the LORD's throne room, where a spirit volunteers to deceive the prophets (vv. 19-22). Struck and imprisoned, he stakes his life on the outcome (vv. 24-28).
verseByVerse.theology: The vision says something the Bible does not soften: God governs even the deceiving of a man who has refused the truth. But the spirit volunteers, the prophets were already selling favourable answers, and Ahab is told the whole of it: the verse notes below show why this is a sentence passed, not a trick played.
verseByVerse.examples: The deception is described to the man being deceived, in open court, before a horse is saddled. That is a last mercy in the shape of a warning, and Ahab imprisons the man who brought it and rides out anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: And the messenger who went to summon Micaiah said to him, "Behold, the words of the prophets with one accord are favorable to the king.
