verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the whole system in one sentence, spoken by a junior official who thinks he is doing the man a kindness.

There is no claim here that the four hundred are right. He says they are favorable, and that the wise course is to match them. Nobody in this chapter, from the king down to the messenger, evaluates a prophecy by whether it is true. The only category in use is whether it will please.

Twice in one short sentence, the covenant name. It is Elijah's oath, the formula that opened this whole section of the book (17:1), and after four hundred men and one small Lord, it lands like a door shutting.

He does not promise to bring bad news, or to be brave. He says he will say what he is given to say, which is the only vow a prophet is entitled to make.

He gives him the party line, word for word, and the sarcasm must have been audible from the back of the square. It is a mirror held up: Ahab had a favourable answer four hundred times over, and Micaiah hands him a four hundred and first so that he can hear what it sounds like from a man he cannot bully.

The moment he is given the answer he asked for by someone he knows is honest, he demands the truth. All the while four hundred men told him the same thing, he knew he was not being told the truth, and was content.

The first oracle, and it is a death notice delivered with extraordinary tenderness, not towards the king, but past him, towards the people.

The king of Israel is the shepherd; that is the standing image, and it is what God said to David: you shall be shepherd of my people Israel (2 Sam. 5:2). Sheep on a hillside with nobody gathering them means the shepherd is not there any more. These have no master is God saying, of the man sitting in front of him in his robes, that he is already as good as dead.

Then the strangest, kindest clause: let each return to his home in peace. God's instruction concerns the flock, and it is that they should go home safely. The army is not to be destroyed. The nation is not under sentence today. One man is, and the rest are to be let go.

Hold the picture, because the Lord Jesus picked it up and it is one of the tenderest things said about him. When he came out and saw the crowds, he had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:34): the same words, and the same diagnosis of a country whose leaders had failed it. And on the night he was betrayed he quoted Zechariah over his own disciples: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered (Matt. 26:31).

The difference is everything. At Ramoth-gilead the shepherd is struck because he is worthless and the sheep are sent home out of the way. At Calvary the Shepherd is struck for the sheep, and the scattering lasts three days.

Ahab has just been told he will die in this battle, and his answer is to turn to his guest and say I told you so. He treats his own death sentence as a point won in a domestic argument, with no thought at all about whether it might be true.

Now the second vision, and nothing in these chapters is harder to take straight. God is seated, and the host of heaven stands on both sides of him. Two kings sit on two thrones at the gate of Samaria; Micaiah has been shown the throne that matters.

Do not soften it: Scripture says in several places that God governs even the deceiving of a man, and uses it as judgment.

Four things have to be held together, and all four are in the text.

First, the spirit volunteers. God asks; a spirit steps forward and proposes the method himself. God does not put a lie into an unwilling mouth, and the Bible never says that he lies: God is not man, that he should lie (Num. 23:19); he cannot deny himself (2 Tim. 2:13).

Second, look at whose mouths receive it. The lying spirit goes into the mouth of all his prophets, men who had been selling favourable answers for a living for years before this morning. Nothing new is introduced into them. They are handed over to what they already were, and given the full run of it.

Third, Paul describes the identical arrangement and supplies the reason. Of those who perish because they refused to love the truth and so be saved, he writes, therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false (2 Thess. 2:10-11). The delusion is not the cause of the ruin. It is the sentence passed on people who had already made their choice about the truth, and Ezekiel says the same of a man who comes to a prophet with idols in his heart (Ezek. 14:9). It is the judgment Paul describes three times in one paragraph of Romans as God "giving them up" to what they wanted (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28).

Fourth, and this is the point that settles the fairness of it: Ahab is told. The entire proceeding is described to the man it concerns, in public, in the open air, before a horse has been saddled. He is informed that the four hundred are lying and why they are lying and who arranged it. Nobody has ever been deceived with more warning than this.

So it is not a trap. It is a last mercy in the form of a disclosure, and there is a way out of it standing open at every moment: believe the man telling you the truth. Ahab hears the whole thing, has him locked up, and rides out.

Does this mean God lies, or makes people sin? The plain reader is right to ask, and the honest answer has two halves. The text does say the LORD put the lying spirit there (v. 23), and Scripture never pretends that God is a bystander to evil: he rules it, sets its limits and turns it to his ends (Job 1:12; Genesis 50:20). It also says he cannot lie (Titus 1:2) and tempts no one (James 1:13), and that the guilt of a lie belongs to the liar. Many read the throne-room scene as a vision given to Micaiah, a picture of what was really happening, not a transcript of heaven's minutes; on either reading the meaning is the same. Christians have confessed it this way: God's rule reaches even to sin, yet he is neither its author nor its approver (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 5.4). The plainest proof is the cross, where wicked men did what God's hand had planned beforehand, and the false charge that Jesus was a blasphemer became the means of our salvation (Acts 2:23; 4:27-28). The God who ruled that lie without lying rules this one too.

There is a test in this for anyone honest enough to take it. If the friends who would tell you the truth have gradually been replaced by friends who will not, and the preaching you seek out never leaves a mark, and the one person who questions you is the one you have decided is difficult, then you do not need a lying spirit to be sent. The work is already largely done. The remedy is not a stronger will but the mercy that still speaks: God sends his word to people who have stopped listening, as he sent Micaiah, and the Spirit who opens ears is given to all who ask (Luke 11:13).

The man with the iron horns hits him in the face and claims the Spirit of the LORD as he does it. He does not think of himself as a liar. He has told kings what they wanted to hear for so long that he can no longer conceive of God saying anything else.

Many Christians have seen here a shadow of a later trial, where the one true Prophet stood alone before the religious establishment, and an officer struck him in the face for his answer (John 18:22).

The reply is quiet and exact. There will be a day, and you will spend it in a back room with the door shut.

The reader has met that room before. Ben-hadad, after Aphek, fled and entered an inner chamber in the city (20:30). The man on the platform with the iron horns will end up where the defeated king ended up, hiding, waiting to hear whether anyone is coming for him.

Note who he is handed to. Amon is the city governor, the civil administrator of Samaria, and Joash is called the king's son, which in these books is often a court title rather than a statement about parentage. Micaiah does not go to a military prison or a dungeon under the palace. He is signed over to the ordinary municipal authorities, on a routine committal, like a man being processed. The whole apparatus of a functioning state is used to file away the one voice in it that was telling the truth.

Bread and water, and until I come in peace: Ahab answers the prophecy with an insult rather than an argument. Take him back, he says: Micaiah may well have been in custody before. That would explain why he could be produced so quickly, and it explains a great deal about the tone of a man who was brought from a cell to a rally and told to agree with four hundred well-fed colleagues.

He puts his own neck on the block, publicly, and he knows exactly what he is doing. The law of Moses gives one test for a prophet: if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken — and it prescribes death for the man who fails it (Deut. 18:20-22).

So Micaiah is staking his life on a battle he will watch from a cell, against the unanimous opinion of every professional prophet in the kingdom. If Ahab walks home, Micaiah is executed.

Then he calls in the witnesses: hear, all you peoples, which is almost the opening line of the prophecy of Micah (Mic. 1:2). (The Greek translation lacks this clause, and many think a scribe added it from Micah; nothing in the story depends on it.) He wants the crowd on the record. When the news comes back from the battle nobody is to be able to say that this was not said, or that it was said quietly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–40 — A Certain Man Drew His Bow at Random
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahab puts his ally in the royal robes and himself in a common soldier's armour (v. 30). The Syrian captains go for Jehoshaphat and turn away (vv. 31-33), an arrow shot at random finds Ahab (v. 34), and he dies propped up in his chariot (v. 35). The army disperses in almost the words of Micaiah's oracle, and the dogs lick the chariot at the pool of Samaria (vv. 36-38).
verseByVerse.theology: Every precaution worked: the robes drew the enemy, the disguise held, the captains turned back. Yet an arrow loosed by a man aiming at nobody found the one man in the field who could not be identified.
verseByVerse.examples: A man who disguises himself against a prophecy has conceded that it is true; he has simply decided to out-manoeuvre it rather than repent.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead. And the king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle, but you wear your robes." And the king of Israel disguised himself and went into battle. Now the king of Syria had commanded the thirty-two captains of his chariots, "Fight with neither small nor great, but only with the king of Israel." And when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "It is surely the king of Israel." So they turned to fight against him. And Jehoshaphat cried out. And when the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him. But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the scale armor and the breastplate. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, "Turn around and carry me out of the battle, for I am wounded." And the battle continued that day, and the king was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, until at evening he died. And the blood of the wound flowed into the bottom of the chariot. And about sunset a cry went through the army, "Every man to his city, and every man to his country!" So the king died, and was brought to Samaria. And they buried the king in Samaria. And they washed the chariot by the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked up his blood, and the prostitutes washed themselves in it, according to the word of the LORD that he had spoken. Now the rest of the acts of Ahab and all that he did, and the ivory house that he built and all the cities that he built, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel? So Ahab slept with his fathers, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse contains the harder question, because it has two men in it.

Ahab's decision is no surprise by now. He has spent four chapters hearing the word of God and doing as he pleased, and a man who has already imprisoned the prophet is not going to be stopped by him.

But Jehoshaphat was there for all of it. He heard the four hundred and thought there was something wrong with them. He asked for a prophet of the LORD and got one. He heard the scattered flock and the throne room and the lying spirit; he watched an honest man take a blow to the face and be led away on bread and water; he heard him stake his life on the outcome in front of the whole city. And he had said let not the king say so, and that was the last word he spoke.

Then he went. He put on his robes, exactly as asked, and rode north into another man's war against a word he had personally sent for.

This is what the alliance had already cost him before a single arrow was fired. He was a good king and he did not disbelieve Micaiah; he simply had nothing left with which to refuse, because he had given it all away in verse 4 before he asked God anything. That is how commitments work. They do not usually take your convictions away from you. They take away your freedom to act on them.

He has just been told in public that he will not come back. His response is not to cancel the battle or to repent, but to dress as an ordinary soldier, and to ask the ally who said I am as you are to ride into the same battle dressed as a king.

No innocent reading of this is available. The enemy's whole effort goes at the man in the robes; that is what the robes are for. Ahab is using his son-in-law's father as a decoy.

The disguise shows that he believed Micaiah: not enough to obey him or stay home, but enough to take precautions.

Remember also what he said about armour three years ago, in the best sentence of his life: let not him who straps on his armor boast himself as he who takes it off (20:11). He straps this on at dawn. He does not take it off.

Thirty-two captains, where three years ago there were thirty-two allied kings: the very reorganisation Ben-hadad's advisers recommended after the first defeat (20:24). The Syrians learn.

The order is a single objective: one man. Ben-hadad wants the king of Israel, the man who once took him up into his chariot and called him brother.

And Jehoshaphat cried out. Chronicles tells us what the cry was for and what came of it: Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him; God drew them away from him (2 Chron. 18:31). He is rescued.

That needs saying carefully. God pulls him out of a danger he had no business being anywhere near, in an alliance he should never have made, in a war he was never asked to fight. The rescue is real mercy and it is not an endorsement. When he gets home a prophet meets him at the gate (Jehu the son of Hanani, who had rebuked Baasha a generation and more earlier, 16:1) and asks him: should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD? (2 Chron. 19:2). Being delivered out of a foolish decision is not the same as being told it was wise.

The Hebrew of at random is "in his innocence": an unnamed soldier, one of thousands, pulls back a bowstring at nobody and lets go.

The arrow had to find, among many thousands, the one man who had removed every mark that identified him, reach him behind his own chariotry, and strike the single seam between the scale armor and the breastplate.

The captains hunting him rode within yards and turned back. He did everything right, and it was all irrelevant.

Scripture states the principle in a proverb: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov. 16:33). And another, which reads as though it were written with this battlefield in view: no wisdom, no understanding, no counsel can avail against the LORD. The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but the victory belongs to the LORD (Prov. 21:30-31).

There is no such thing as a random arrow. Now turn that over, because the doctrine has a second side and most readers need that side far more than they need the first. The same providence that made Ahab's disguise useless means that no arrow has ever reached a child of God without having come through his hand first. Nothing in your life arrives at random either. The diagnosis, the redundancy, the phone call at two in the morning: the arrow was not loosed by chance, and the God who aimed one at a king in a disguise is your Father. Read from the other side of the cross, the same fact is not a terror but the ground of sleep. That does not make the arrow painless or the loss small; it means the hand that allowed it is the hand that holds you, and will not let go.

He asked to be carried out and he was not carried out. If the king's chariot leaves the field the army breaks, so they wedge him upright, facing the enemy, and leave him there.

He stands until evening in his disguise, held in position, watching a battle he cannot fight, bleeding steadily into the floor of the chariot. It takes him until sunset to die. It is the most undignified death in the book, and it is exactly the death of a man who spent his reign propped up by other people telling him he was winning.

Set that beside the oracle: let each return to his home in peace (v. 17).

At sunset the cry goes down the line, the army disperses, and not one of them is lost. The flock went home in peace, exactly as God had said, and the man in the cell was right.

After Carmel and Naboth and the four hundred and the disguise, Ahab gets a state funeral, and the writer records it without comment because the comment is in the next verse.

They bring the chariot back and wash it out at the public pool, and the dogs come.

The writer says according to the word of the LORD that he had spoken, and he is right to, though the reader who remembers chapter 21 will note that Elijah named Jezreel and this is Samaria. The reason is in that chapter: the sentence was expressly postponed out of Ahab's own days because he went into sackcloth (21:29). The Jezreel half is collected on his son, whose body Jehu has thrown onto Naboth's ground while quoting the oracle aloud (2 Kgs. 9:25-26). The word did not miss. It was paid in two instalments, and the delay was announced in advance.

The ivory house is a real building and it has been dug up. Excavations at Samaria have produced hundreds of pieces of carved ivory panelling, and a century later Amos is still denouncing the houses of ivory in that city (Amos 3:15). Ahab was one of the great builders and soldiers of the region; Assyrian records credit him with a large chariot force at the battle of Qarqar (about 853 BC).

The writer of Kings files all of it in another book, in one sentence, exactly as he did with Omri. He gave four chapters to a temple and a whole chapter to a widow's flour jar, and he gives the ivory house half a line. The historian's measure is not the world's, and by now the reader ought to have learned to expect it.

The formula is the gentle one, used of kings who die in their beds, applied to a man who bled to death in a chariot in a disguise. It is also the last quiet thing anyone will say about the house of Ahab.
verseByVerse.note: “At random” is literally “in his innocence” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–53 — Every Way That His Father Had Done
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jehoshaphat did right in the sight of the LORD, with two qualifications: the high places and his peace with the king of Israel (vv. 43-44). He clears out the cult prostitutes, loses his fleet, and declines Ahaziah's next offer (vv. 46-49). Then Ahab's son takes the northern throne (vv. 51-53).
verseByVerse.theology: Ahaziah is the only king in these books whose mother's way is named as a category of its own. Jezebel outlives her husband, and the writer marks it by making her a road that a king can walk in.
verseByVerse.examples: The book stops in the middle of the story. In the Hebrew Bible 1 and 2 Kings are one book, and the break here came in with the Greek translation, probably because the scroll was long.

verseByVerse.quote: Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel. Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi. He walked in all the way of Asa his father. He did not turn aside from it, doing what was right in the sight of the LORD. Yet the high places were not taken away, and the people still sacrificed and made offerings on the high places. Jehoshaphat also made peace with the king of Israel. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, and his might that he showed, and how he warred, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah? And from the land he exterminated the remnant of the male cult prostitutes who remained in the days of his father Asa. There was no king in Edom; a deputy was king. Jehoshaphat made ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold, but they did not go, for the ships were wrecked at Ezion-geber. Then Ahaziah the son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, "Let my servants go with your servants in the ships," but Jehoshaphat was not willing. And Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place. Ahaziah the son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and he reigned two years over Israel. He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father and in the way of his mother and in the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin. He served Baal and worshiped him and provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger in every way that his father had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer turns south and gives the other kingdom its accounting. The mother is always named in Judah: the queen mother held a real position at court.

Twenty-five years, a long and stable reign. While Samaria went through Carmel, a drought, two Syrian wars, a judicial murder and a king bleeding to death in a chariot, Jerusalem had one king throughout.

This is a good verdict, and one of only a handful in these books. He walked in his father's way and did not turn aside, and the writer says it without qualification before he says anything else.

Then the standing exception. The high places remained: local hilltop shrines where people went on offering sacrifices to the LORD in the old Canaanite manner, at the wrong altars, outside the temple God had appointed. Almost every good king in Judah gets this same footnote, and it is not pedantry. It is the difference between reforming a court and reforming a country. The king could tear down what was in Jerusalem; what he could not do was change what a village did on its own hill on an ordinary evening.

A reader who checks Chronicles will find it says both that Jehoshaphat took the high places out of Judah (2 Chronicles 17:6) and that the high places were not taken away (2 Chronicles 20:33). The likeliest answer is that he removed the shrines to other gods, and tried early in his reign, but the people's local altars to the LORD came back and stayed; Chronicles itself gives the reason: the people had not yet set their hearts on God.

The writer offers no opinion, and he is right not to. On its face this is the healing of a two-generation feud between brothers. What it produced was a battle that nearly killed him, a marriage that put Ahab's daughter into the house of David, and a generation in which that woman murdered the royal family and reigned six years over Jerusalem.

Some decisions cannot be evaluated in the year they are made. A peace, an alliance, an accommodation for the sake of good relations, and the account is presented two generations later to people who had no vote in the matter.

Once more a reign is filed in another book, and the file contains the most famous hour of Jehoshaphat's life.

Chronicles tells it. A coalition of Moabites and Ammonites came up against Judah, and the king proclaimed a fast and stood in the temple court and prayed a prayer that ends with a sentence anybody can use: we are powerless against this great horde that is coming against us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you (2 Chron. 20:12). The answer came back through a Levite: the battle is not yours but God's... you will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the LORD on your behalf (20:15, 17). And in the morning he put the singers out in front of the army.

It is the same man. At Ramoth-gilead he promised his horses before he asked, and had to cry for his life in a chariot. In the valley of Beracah he had nothing to promise and asked first, and stood still.

Real reform, and costly. Cult prostitution had come in with the Canaanite shrines and had survived his father's purge; Jehoshaphat finished it. Chronicles adds that he sent officials and Levites circuit by circuit through the towns of Judah with the book of the law, teaching (2 Chron. 17:7-9), which is the sort of thing that never gets into a chronicle of might and wars and is worth more than either.

Edom is under Judean control, which is why the next verse can speak of a fleet: the port at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba lies in Edomite territory.

He tried to revive Solomon's gold route, and the fleet was wrecked in harbour. Chronicles gives the reason, which belongs with verse 44: he had gone into partnership with Ahaziah of Israel, and a prophet told him because you have joined with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made (2 Chron. 20:35-37).

Asked again, he says no. He allied, lost the ships, and declined the next invitation, which is the honest shape of most people's obedience. It may be the most encouraging thing in the chapter: a good man, slow, expensive to teach, and taught by a God who did not give him up.

He is buried in the city of David, where his son's wife will one day make her attempt on David's whole line.

Ahaziah reigns two years. The son of the man who reigned twenty-two years and built an ivory house gets two, and the writer will spend most of them on a fall through a lattice and a question sent to the wrong god.

He walks in the way of his mother, and no other king in these books is given that. The writer opens a third column beside the father's way and Jeroboam's way and puts Jezebel's name in it: she has become a road, and her son is walking down it.

She outlives Ahab by some twelve years and sees two of her sons on the throne, and the sentence Elijah pronounced over her at Naboth's vineyard is still outstanding.

The last words of the book are that his father had done, and nothing whatever is resolved.

Elijah has not been heard from since Naboth's vineyard. Jezebel is queen mother and untouched. Micaiah, so far as we are told, is still in the cell. The sentence on the house of Ahab is pending; Hazael has not been anointed; Jehu is an officer in somebody's army; and Elisha is carrying an old man's bags somewhere in the north.

What does stand finished, at the end of these twenty-two chapters, is the thing the book has been about all along. Kings come and go in it at a bewildering rate; three dynasties fall in two chapters, a temple is built and looted, a kingdom splits, and the great men of the age get half a verse each. And running through it, never once failing, is the word of the LORD, spoken by Ahijah over a torn cloak, by Joshua over Jericho centuries before Hiel picked up a trowel, by Elijah over a rainless sky, by an unnamed man of God over an altar at Bethel, and by a prisoner in Samaria over an arrow that had not yet been shot.

Every one of them landed. Kings are what the book counts; the word is what it trusts. And the word was not finished with David's house: it would keep its promise through a hidden baby in the temple, through exile and silence, to the Son of David, the true Shepherd whom Ahab never was, and the Word made flesh.

Why do the reign lengths and synchronisms not seem to add up? Israel and Judah counted reigns differently at different times: one counted the year a king came to the throne as his first year, the other did not; sons often reigned alongside their fathers as co-regents, and the overlapping years were counted to both. When these practices are allowed for, the dates largely fit together, as Edwin Thiele showed, and match Assyrian records at key points.

The “ships of Tarshish” were large ocean-going trading ships, named after Tarshish, a far western port, probably in Spain; Ophir was a source of gold, perhaps in Arabia or East Africa.

22.theology:
The order of verses 4 and 5. A genuinely good man commits everything and afterwards asks God about it. Once the promise is made, the inquiry is no longer an inquiry but a search for permission.

One small word at verse 6. Where the ESV prints LORD in small capitals it renders the covenant name; where it prints Lord it renders adonai, master, which any nation could say of any god. The four hundred answer the decisive question with the ordinary word. It should not be pressed far, since the same men use the covenant name at v. 12, but Jehoshaphat at once asked for a prophet of the LORD, and Micaiah opens with as the LORD lives (v. 14). The reader is meant to hear the difference.

A just cause is not a commission (v. 3). Ahab is in the right and in the wrong war. The only test anyone applies to a prophecy here is whether it is favorable (v. 13).

The lying spirit (vv. 19-23). The spirit volunteers, and God never lies. The mouths that receive it had been selling favourable answers for years, and they are handed over to what they already were, as Paul says of those who refused to love the truth (2 Thess. 2:10-11). And Ahab is told, in public, before he saddles a horse. It is not a trap but a last warning, with the way out standing open.

Sheep without a shepherd (v. 17). The oracle is a death notice for the king delivered as tenderness towards the flock, and at sunset the flock goes home. Jesus took up the same words over the crowds (Mark 6:34), and at Calvary the Shepherd was struck for the sheep (Matt. 26:31).

No random arrow (v. 34). Every precaution Ahab took worked perfectly and was irrelevant, because the victory belongs to the LORD (Prov. 21:31). The same providence means no arrow has ever reached a child of God except through his Father's hand.
22.examples:
Then: A king told in open court that he would not come home dressed as a private soldier, put the visiting king in the robes, hid in his own army, and was held upright in his chariot until the sun went down.

Now: Three things. First, verse 5: after my horses as your horses, what looks like seeking guidance is shopping for approval. Second, the lying spirit is less exotic than it looks: surround yourself with agreeable voices and its work is largely done already. Third, the disguise: believing the word enough to take precautions and not enough to obey it, conceding that God is right and managing the consequences. That is the posture a respectable reader is most likely to be standing in. The way out is not more resolve but the mercy Ahab refused: God still speaks to those who have stopped listening, the Son of David obeyed his Father where every king of Israel failed, and those who come to him in confession are forgiven and given his Spirit to walk in the truth (1 John 1:9; Galatians 5:16).
